At each internal LLM call, MEMMARK samples among admissible candidates using keyed, distribution-preserving selection, and records cryptographic commitments with signed session anchors and reveal evidence. This makes attribution depend on reproducible backend behavior rather than mutable provenance fields. Across A-Mem and Graphiti on LOCOMO, with three LLM backbones, MEMMARK preserves memory utility: Overall F1 retains 99.6 percent of the unwatermarked baseline, while BLEU-1 changes by +0.2 percent. It also provides usable carrier capacity, with 1.16, 1.14, and 1.26 bits of mean entropy for update-target, link-target, and semantic-realization decisions. In the snapshot-only R3 setting, MEMMARK recovers the full 40-bit payload from final snapshots, while wrong-key verification remains near chance. Under nine memory-lifecycle attacks, verification distinguishes tampering, evidence deletion, and partial payload recovery. These results show that robust snapshot-only attribution is feasible for long-term agent memory without surviving traces, trusted metadata, or utility degradation.

t: SurveyGraph: Generating Academic Surveys via Methods-Entity Knowledge Graphs
ab: Automated survey generation systems increasingly rely on flat retrieval over document collections, limiting their ability to capture the evolutionary structure of research fields. We present SurveyGraph, a framework centered on a Methods-Entity Knowledge Graph (MEKG) that encodes method-level follow-on, competition, and shared-resource relations across papers. The MEKG serves as a unified backbone for core-paper discovery, graph-aware retrieval, hybrid outline generation, and evolutionary narrative synthesis.We evaluate SurveyGraph through a multi-level protocol spanning retrieval benchmarks, semantic-edge validation, citation grounding audits, benchmark-facing collection probes, and same-backend generation-stage diagnostics. In a controlled seven-method equal-budget benchmark, MEKG-anchored fusion achieves the best balance of recall and structural density among all tested methods, demonstrating that typed graph structure provides a complementary signal to simpler retrieval approaches. On the archived graph-native core diagnostic, graph-aware retrieval nearly doubles recall over flat lexical baselines across all eight runs (p = 0.004). A semantic evidence gate with AUC = 0.75 filters noisy edges, and citation-grounding audits over 160 generated sentences confirm 80.6% anchored-or-partial support with evidence-level contrasts validating genuine alignment. Human validation over 108 stratified semantic edges (Cohen’s κ = 0.64 for the binary support decision) confirms 68.5% supported-or-partial after adjudication, with improves relations strongest at 80.6% and extends weakest at 52.8%. A SurveyBench-facing collection probe reaches 0.521 mean reference coverage on four topics under an eight-paper budget; same-backend Qwen diagnostics over a 30-paper/74-relation MEKG further show that removing hybrid outlining lowers artifact organization signals. We report concurrent-system comparisons only as bounded diagnostics rather than same-backend end-to-end claims. Code and artifacts are available at: https://github.com/xzzvsxd/SurveyGraph.

t: A Survey of LLM Prompt Datasets: Taxonomy, Linguistic Patterns, and Practical Uses
a: Bowling Green State University and Aalborg University
ab: We compile 129 public LLM prompt datasets with more than 1.22TB and more than 673M instances and organise them into a unified taxonomy. We use seven datasets for detailed analysis and identify lexical, syntactic, and semantic patterns that distinguish prompts from general text. We evaluate these features in prompt filtering, source domain routing, and elicited response quality analysis. A 63 dimensional linguistic feature set that can be extracted on a CPU achieves over 91% of the F1 of GPU sentence embeddings and reduces latency per request by nearly half. In cross dataset routing, sentence embeddings reach 0.74 Macro-F1 and a structural feature subset reaches 0.61, compared with the chance level of 0.20. Structural routing features remain negatively associated with elicited response quality after prompt length is controlled on UltraFeedback. The apparent positive association of type to token ratio becomes much smaller under the same control. These findings support prompt processing pipelines that combine efficient structural features with robust semantic routing. Our catalogue, annotations, and code are given at https://github.com/ymzhang-cs/prompt-dataset-analysis.

t: TimelyRAG: Semantic-Temporal Hybrid Retrieval for Time-Critical Question Answering in Overlapping-Evolving Documents
a: Korea Advanced Institute of Science and Technology
Korea Advanced Institute of Science and Technology
ab: Although large language models (LLMs) and retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) have advanced open-domain question answering (QA), they remain unreliable when documents evolve through amendments. Existing time-sensitive retrieval methods address only the *disjoint*-evolving environment, where each update is an independent snapshot. However, laws, policies, and regulations often operate in *overlapping*-evolving environments, where amendments override earlier clauses while preserving most content, creating strong semantic overlap across versions. We propose ***TimelyRAG***, a retriever-agnostic framework that incorporates temporal distance into ranking to align queries with version-appropriate documents. We also introduce ***TimelyQABench***, the first benchmark for regulation-heavy domains with overlapping-evolving challenges. Experiments show consistent gains, up to +28.6% in nDCG@10, highlighting the importance of temporal reasoning for reliable QA over evolving documents. All resources are available at https://github.com/kaist-dmlab/TimelyRAG.

t: MedRAGChecker: Claim-Level Verification for Biomedical Retrieval-Augmented Generation
ab: Biomedical retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) produces long-form answers that mix supported, under-evidenced, and contradicted claims, demanding fine-grained verification. We propose MedRAGChecker, a claim-level diagnostic framework that combines textual natural language inference (NLI) with a biomedical knowledge-graph (KG) compatibility signal. Its asymmetric selective-gating rule preserves the textual prediction for most claims and applies KG adjustment only to confident textual entailments assigned low plausibility by the KG back-end. We distill GPT-4.1 claim decompositions and NLI pseudo-labels into compact student models and evaluate three biomedical generators on PubMedQA, MedQuAD, LiveQA, and MedRedQA. The student-ensemble results show that selective BioPortal gating increases macro-averaged faithfulness from 60.8% to 64.4% and reduces the contradiction rate from 19.9% to 15.0%. On 172 annotations of 86 claims whose decisions change after fusion, agreement with human evidence judgments increases from 63.4% to 69.8%. A comparison with DRKG shows that fusion behavior varies substantially with KG coverage, entity linking, score construction, and calibration; the comparison therefore characterizes back-end effects rather than isolating a causal effect of coverage.

t: Learned Sparse Lexical Representations for Large-scale Authorship Attribution
ab: Authorship attribution aims to determine whether a query text and a candidate document are written by the same author. %While dense embeddings are effective, recent work suggests that low-dimensional representations limit encoding capacity. We investigate high-dimensional learned sparse representations (LSR) and multi-vector retrieval for authorship attribution. We further propose Sparse ColBERT (SparCol), a late-interaction sparse lexical reranking model. To address the memory cost of vocabulary-size embeddings, we develop fused Triton kernels that can reduce peak memory usage by 5 11 times over the baseline torch implementation. Extensive experiments show that LSR can outperform dense embeddings in both single-genre and cross-genre settings, whereas improves reranking performance over single-vector models only in single-genre settings due to lexical matching bias. In addition to token-based embeddings, we also explore Lexicon-based embeddings that score clusters of tokens, which is competitive with the vocabulary-based LSR with reduced dimensions. We conduct interpretability analysis of LSRs, showing that they allow for a more transparent scoring process.

t: Latent Dreaming: Let Language Think Yet Latent See in Driving VLA
ab: Vision-language-action (VLA) models for autonomous driving typically express intermediate reasoning entirely in text, which may discard decision-relevant visual information. We propose Latent Dreaming (LatDM), a latent–text reasoning framework that complements textual chain-of-thought with continuous latent states. LatDM uses latent blocks to preserve visually grounded spatial and temporal information, while text handles semantic abstraction and decision communication. A pretrained visual encoder provides latent supervision during training, and the model autonomously interleaves latent and textual reasoning at inference. Experiments on VLADBench, CODA-LM, and NuInstruct show consistent improvements over the underlying VLA backbone, while ablations confirm that the latent channel contributes beyond standard textual fine-tuning.

t: Continual Graph Memory for Adaptive Recommendation under Intent Drift
a: Hanoi University of Science and Technology
ab: This paper studies adaptive recommendation under intent drift, where feedback from each recommendation outcome can reveal whether the relational evidence used for ranking is useful, missing, or misleading. While Knowledge Graphs (KGs) provide essential semantic structure to handle these shifts, traditional KG-enhanced systems treat the graph as a static retrieval substrate, making it brittle to evolving intents, noisy metadata, and recurring failure patterns. This paper proposes CGM-Rec, a continual graph memory framework for adaptive recommendation. CGM-Rec treats the graph state as a writable memory and maintains two complementary components. Therein, a Semantic Graph Memory is updated conservatively through quality-gated typed operations for storing stable and high-confidence relational knowledge. Meanwhile, an Episodic Lesson Memory acts as a fast reactive memory that learns recent outcomes, failure cases, and corrective hints. During testing, model parameters remain frozen and adaptation occurs only through memory writes. We evaluate CGM-Rec under a frozen-parameter, one-pass reranking protocol, where encoders and prompts remain fixed during testing and adaptation occurs only through memory writes. Experiments across multiple recommendation settings show that CGM-Rec improves over evaluated neural and LLM-based baselines on most metrics. Particularly, under sampled-candidate reranking, CGM-Rec improves HR@1 by up to 29.58% over the strongest LLM baseline on Bundle, and outperforms K-RagRec on metadata-rich ML-100K with HR@5 of 0.5941 versus 0.4746.

t: Rubric-as-Experts: Case-Specific MQM Rubrics for Translation Error Span Detection
ab: Large language models (LLMs) have shown potential for reference-free span-level translation quality estimation (QE), yet existing approaches based on Multidimensional Quality Metrics (MQM) typically rely on fixed rubric configurations shared across translation instances. However, translation instances often differ substantially in error complexity, ambiguity, and required evaluation granularity, making static rubric allocation suboptimal for span-level error detection. We find that larger MQM subtype spaces improve error coverage but also introduce more false positives, while different translation instances prefer different rubric granularities, suggesting that evaluation spaces should be allocated dynamically for each case. Therefore, we propose a case-specific dynamic rubric framework that adaptively constructs MQM evaluation spaces for individual translation instances. Unlike methods that generate fully free-form rubrics, our framework remains grounded in the predefined MQM taxonomy while dynamically selecting suitable subtype spaces and evaluation granularity for different cases. Experiments on span-level QE benchmarks from the Conference on Machine Translation (WMT) across multiple model scales demonstrate that the proposed framework consistently improves F1 and Matthews Correlation Coefficient (MCC).

t: SCAMBENCH: A Multi-Dimensional Scam Benchmark through Human-AI Collaborative Data Construction
ab: Online scams are a growing form of digital harm, yet scam research remains constrained by fragmented datasets and limited annotation depth. We introduce SCAMBENCH, a benchmark of 1,836 authentic scam messages curated from victim-reported incidents across six scam types: employment, investment, imposter, sweepstakes/lottery/prizes, tech support, and advance fee loan scams, along with 1,834 real-world non-scam examples from legitimate sources. SCAMBENCH provides multi-dimensional annotations that capture persuasion strategies from the scammer perspective, red flags from the user perspective, and severity levels reflecting potential harm and urgency. These annotations are produced through a human-AI collaborative pipeline that uses expert-labeled examples to calibrate and validate LLM-assisted annotation at scale. Our analysis shows that these signals vary significantly across scam types, highlighting substantial scam-type heterogeneity. We further use annotated evidence spans to generate cue-removed hard scam examples by rephrasing explicit persuasion and red-flag cues. Evaluating five LLM-based detectors on original and rewritten scams shows that all five detectors perform worse on cue-removed examples, and the performance drop persists on a human-validated subset, suggesting sensitivity to surface-level cues. A qualitative case study identifies five recurring failure patterns. SCAMBENCH provides a resource for scam detection, robustness evaluation, and scam education, publicly available at https://huggingface.co/datasets/Shouninger/ScamBench.

t: The Language of Looking: Motion Tokens Reveal Domain-Dependent Local Structure in Gaze Sequences
ab: Human gaze is the primary high-bandwidth interface through which we parse the semantics of our environment. While often modeled as a sequence, the degree to which gaze exhibits transferable local structure across domains remains underexplored. Using motion tokenization as a diagnostic lens across four diverse datasets, we investigate the transferability of local sequence structure. We demonstrate that while gaze can share a reusable motion-token vocabulary, identical motion tokens are organized into different local transition patterns depending on the dataset and task context. Our results show the limitations of naive data-pooling under low-semantic motion-token representations and provide a framework for evaluating behavioral sequences through information-theoretic diagnostics.

t: HGP: An on-device personalized agent memory via hybrid graph storage
a: China Mobile Communications Company Limited Research Institute
ab: LLM-based agents face challenges in personalized interactive tasks due to heterogeneous, multi-typed, and implicitly constrained long-term traces. Existing memory mechanisms struggle with accurate routing and retrieval, especially on-device where personalization is critical. Most methods use single-vector representations, blurring type distinctions and relational structure. We propose HGP, a hybrid graph memory framework. HGP employs a lightweight self-enhancement classifier for personalized memory routing and constructs episodic, semantic, and procedural memories as graphs. It also extracts working memory as a state trajectory to capture current state and implicit constraints, ensuring reliable decision- making. The classifier reduces large-model calls, enabling on-device deployment, while graph storage enables accurate retrieval and incremental user profile refinement. Experiments on two benchmarks show that on PAL-Set solution selection, HGP achieves an S-score of 35.58, nearly 7 points above the strongest baseline.

t: Reverse Probing: Supervised Token-level Uncertainty Quantification for Large Language Models in Clinical Text
ab: As large language models are increasingly deployed for clinical text, ensuring they can reliably signal their own uncertainty becomes critical. Most existing uncertainty quantification (UQ) methods are designed for open-domain generation and cannot localize uncertainty at the token or span level in long clinical text. We propose Reverse Probing, the first uncertainty quantification framework specialized for clinical summarization, which estimates token-level uncertainty directly from pre-existing clinical summaries. Rather than sampling new outputs, Reverse Probing treats the text as a probe into the model’s internal state, extracting uncertainty features from four categories of signals. We evaluate Reverse Probing on two expert-annotated clinical datasets and outperform eight adapted baselines, achieving up to 4\times higher AUPRC while running over 15\times faster than sampling-based methods. Feature analysis reveals that the log-logit difference induced by the source record and the neighborhood context are the most consistent predictors across all models. This study offers interpretable insights into how models internally respond to unsupported clinical content.

t: Super Paths, Better Reasoning: Multi-Hop Knowledge Graphs Reasoning with LLM via Super-Path Ranking and Constraint Verification
ab: Knowledge graph reasoning (KGR) composes multi-hop facts over KGs to support complex knowledge-intensive tasks, providing reliable external factual support for large language models (LLMs) and helping mitigate hallucinations. However, building compact, faithful, and high-quality contexts from large-scale KGs remains challenging. We observe a non-monotonic relationship between retrieval scale and reasoning quality: insufficient retrieval misses critical paths, while excessive retrieval introduces redundant and noisy paths that burden LLMs reasoning. Motivated by this observation, we propose super-path ranking and constraint verification (SPaRC), an efficient framework that constructs, ranks, and verifies super-paths before LLMs reasoning. SPaRC compresses redundant paths into super-paths, ranks them with contrastive learning, verifies top-ranked paths under query semantic constraints, and provides the verified context to the LLMs for answer reasoning. Experiments on WebQSP and CWQ show that SPaRC achieves state-of-the-art performance, improving Hit@1 by up to 12.0 points and F1 by up to 5.9 points on CWQ. On challenging settings covering deeper hop reasoning, multiple topic entities, and multi-answer questions, SPaRC further improves F1 on two benchmarks by up to 17.6% and 42.1%, 26.7% and 5.9%, and 10.4% and 79.4%, respectively, while reducing reasoning tokens by 29.7% and retrieval time by 25%.

t: Not All Acoustic Frames Contribute Equally: Frame-Selective Acoustic Conditioning for Dysarthric ASR Correction
ab: Not all acoustic frames are equally useful for correcting dysarthric ASR errors. In dysarthric speech, acoustic deviations are unevenly distributed across frames, but LLM-based generative error correction systems often inject acoustic features uniformly, under-emphasizing deviant frames and over-correcting reliable ones. We propose a frame-selective acoustic conditioning method driven by a Frame Deviation Score (FDS) and VGate. FDS is a control-referenced per-frame deviation score computed over Whisper encoder frames, and VGate uses standardized per-frame FDS to reweight acoustic value vectors. Across ten personalized TORGO settings, we compare VGate with Plain, an acoustic-adapter baseline without the VGate gating module, and show that VGate is conditional rather than universally beneficial. Three findings support conditional use. (1) Plain residual headroom (the gap between Plain and Oracle@5 WER) and utterance-mean FDS-DIV characterize high-benefit cases, with gains concentrated in ref-preserved and overgeneration cases and the largest improvements driven by insertion control. (2) A development-calibrated FDS-DIV router lowers pooled WER from 19.55% to 18.29% while routing only 20.72% of utterances. (3) Cross-corpus COPAS results and blinded listening further support this conditional-use strategy. Our code is publicly available at https://github.com/doraemon500/FSAC.

t: Explication of Refusal: Jailbreaking LLMs by Exploiting Refusal Explanations
ab: Safety-aligned large language models (LLMs) face a dilemma between helpfulness and harmlessness, where LLMs are expected to refuse harmful requests while remaining helpful by explaining their decisions. In this work, we observe a phenomenon caused by this dilemma. When asked to explain a refusal triggered by a harmful query, LLMs disclose exploitable elements in their refusal explanations. These elements allow attackers to induce the generation of harmful content. We formalize this vulnerability as Induced Refusal Explication (IRE). To identify and exploit IRE, we propose Explication of Refusal (EoR), a black-box and multi-turn jailbreak method with a dual-agent framework. EoR induces and analyzes refusal explanations from victim models and then generates follow-up queries to jailbreak them. We evaluate EoR across nine victim models. EoR achieves an average attack success rate (ASR) of **37.05** within five turns. When we apply EoR to the queries that PAIR fails to jailbreak, EoR reaches an average ASR of **66.0** across the nine victim models, which demonstrates that exploiting refusal explanations is complementary to existing automated jailbreak methods. We release our data and code at https://anonymous.4open.science/r/EoR-6234.

t: When Attention Escapes: Diagnosing and Mitigating Hallucination in Retrieval-Augmented Generation
a: Hangzhou High-Tech Zone (Binjiang) Institute of Blockchain and Data Security and Zhejiang University
Shanghai Institute for Advanced Study, Zhejiang University, The State Key Laboratory of Blockchain and Data Security, Zhejiang University and Zhejiang University
ab: Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) mitigates hallucinations by grounding generation in retrieved evidence, yet failures persist when models underutilize the retrieved context. While prior work attributes this to conflicts between external context and internal parametric knowledge encoded in Feed-Forward Networks (FFNs), our empirical analyses reveal that FFN-derived signals are unstable and insufficient for reliable diagnosis across diverse contexts. We therefore propose the Attention Escape Score (AES), a training-free diagnostic framework that provides a mechanistic lens on RAG hallucinations via dynamic attention routing failures. We models the failures as weakened Semantic Anchoring, increased Contextual Distraction, and heightened Generation Inertia, moving beyond static component-level analyses. Extensive experiments show that AES significantly outperforms state-of-the-art baselines with robust cross-model generalization. Furthermore, we introduce Pruning Escape Routes (PER), a lightweight inference-time intervention that suppresses hallucinations by attenuating identified escape pathways, achieving improved faithfulness with negligible degradation to complex reasoning and general capabilities.

t: SMRC: Aligning Large Language Models with Student Reasoning for Mathematical Error Correction
a: Northeastern University, Emory University, University of Pennsylvania, University of Pennsylvania, Harbin Institute of Technology, Beijing Normal-Hong Kong Baptist University, Zhejiang University, Westlake University, Alibaba Group, Peking University, Beijing University of Aeronautics and Astronautics, Beijing Zhongguancun Academy, Tsinghua University, Chinese Academy of Sciences and University of the Chinese Academy of Sciences
ab: Large language models (LLMs) often make reasoning errors when solving mathematical problems, and how to automatically detect and correct these errors has become an important research direction. However, existing approaches mainly focus on self-correction within the model, which falls short of the “teacher-style” correction required in educational settings, i.e., systematically guiding and revising a student’s problem-solving process. To address this gap, we propose SMRC (Student Mathematical Reasoning Correction), a novel method that aligns LLMs with student reasoning. Specifically, SMRC formulates student reasoning as a multi-step sequential decision problem and introduces Monte Carlo Tree Search (MCTS) to explore optimal correction paths. To reduce the cost of the annotating process-level rewards, we leverage breadth-first search (BFS) guided by LLMs and final-answer evaluation to generate reward signals, which are then distributed across intermediate reasoning steps via a back-propagation mechanism, enabling fine-grained process supervision. Additionally, we construct a benchmark for high school mathematics, MSEB (Multi-Solution Error Benchmark), consisting of 158 instances that include problem statements, student solutions, and correct reasoning steps. We further propose a dual evaluation protocol centered on solution accuracy and correct-step retention, offering a comprehensive measure of educational applicability. Experiments demonstrate that SMRC significantly outperforms existing methods on two public datasets (ProcessBench and MR-GSM8K) and our MSEB in terms of effectiveness and overall performance.

t: When Knowledge Is Not Free: Cost-Aware Evidence Selection in Retrieval-Augmented Generation
a: Technion - Israel Institute of Technology, Technion
ab: Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) typically assumes that external knowledge is free, but many high-quality sources are paywalled, licensed, restricted, or otherwise costly to access. We introduce cost-aware RAG, a setting where retrieved evidence is assigned access-cost tiers and systems must answer under an explicit evidence-access budget. We instantiate this setting by augmenting MS MARCO v2.1 with access-friction tiers and evaluate budgeted evidence selection across general-domain and domain-specific QA benchmarks. Our results show that static selection is brittle: no fixed selector uniformly dominates, and larger budgets do not reliably improve answer quality, even when costly evidence is domain-matched. We then study agentic cost-aware RAG, where an LLM decides when to retrieve, which tier to access, and when to stop. Agents show strong promise as adaptive evidence-acquisition controllers, but their behavior remains highly model- and task-dependent. These findings suggest that cost-aware evidence acquisition is a central challenge for the next generation of RAG systems. All code and data are available at https://github.com/Mignonmy/Cost-Aware.

t: Routing Is Not Enough: Diagnosing Intra-Adapter Subspace Contention in MoE+LoRA Fine-Tuning
ab: Multi-domain fine-tuning often combines MoE routing with LoRA, assuming that token-level routing separates domain-specific updates. We test this assumption in MoE+LoRA using Python code paired with biomedical text and mathematical reasoning. Although these domains show near-disjoint expert routing, adding biomedical data substantially increases code perplexity, indicating that routing separation alone may not prevent negative transfer. To localize the failure, we introduce Jaccard routing overlap and adapter-gradient cosine similarity, which measure expert sharing and update compatibility, respectively. These diagnostics indicate that interference arises mostly from nearly orthogonal domain gradients competing within the same low-rank adapter subspace. We address this issue with SpawnLoRA, which dynamically adds gated sub-adapters inside MoE experts when adapter-level contention is detected, while keeping the router fixed. We evaluate SpawnLoRA on Phi-tiny-MoE-instruct and OLMoE-1B-7B across multiple mixture settings and find that it effectively reduces negative transfer compared with standard and rank-adaptive LoRA. These results demonstrate that structural separation inside experts provides benefits beyond routing or rank expansion alone.

t: 0xClaw: Autonomous Open-ended Agents with Phase-aware Budget Allocation and Temporal Pressure
ab: Large language model agents handle structured coding tasks well, but open-ended projects are harder. A hackathon gives an agent an open goal, a hard deadline and several artifacts to deliver. The agent has to decide how to split its budget across phases and when to stop widening scope. Most agents do neither. 0xClaw is a multi-agent framework that splits a hackathon run into seven phases. Each phase hands a typed artifact to the next. The Budget Router is a small fine-tuned Qwen3.5-2B model. It reads the workspace state and predicts a per-phase control token for token budget, time, reasoning effort and repair rounds. The Deadline Framer turns each token, together with the cumulative execution log, into a plain deadline instruction given to the agent at the start of each phase. Our study covers 20 hackathon tasks, 10 baselines and more than 200 agent runs. 0xClaw matches Claude Code at the best pass@1 (1.00) and exceeds ARIS (0.95), the two strongest baselines. Against Claude Code, it achieves comparable quality and pass@1 while using 59% fewer tokens. The trade-off is wall-clock time, about 2.5 times that of ARIS.

t: On the Representation Bias of Disabilities in Generative Text-to-Image Models
ab: Emerging text-to-image (T2I) models perpetuate biases, creating stereotypical portrayals of disability. This study investigates whether an agent-based, human-in-loop, AI workflow, that iteratively refines user-provided queries, can produce fairer representations of disability compared to standard models like Stable Diffusion, DALL·E-3, and MidJourney. Sixteen raters (eight with disabilities and eight without) evaluated images generated from models, prompted with textual inputs that targeted professional, medical, or social contexts. In an initial survey, raters were asked if an image depicted a disability, the type of disability if present, and if the setting aligned with the given text prompt to the model. Qualitative comments were collected. A post-survey asked raters to choose which image of a pair (standard vs. agent-based workflow) more accurately represented disability. Results revealed that standard models disproportionately produced images featuring physical disabilities or wheelchairs (p < 0.001), consistent with broader dataset biases. In contrast, the agent-based model’s images were deemed more representative in approximately two-thirds of comparisons (p < 0.0001), especially among raters with disabilities. Qualitative analyses underscored the need for nuanced, contextually rich portrayals.These findings suggest disability bias and that targeted debiasing can help mitigate stereotypes in generative AI, fostering more equitable outputs.

t: Time Travel Engine: Ordered Temporal Geometry Enables Era-Level Historical Steering in Large Language Models
ab: Large language models compress centuries of discourse into fixed parameters, yet how they organize historical variation and whether this organization shapes generation remain unclear. We introduce the Time Travel Engine (TTE), a framework that compares geometric accounts of era-conditioned residual states and tests their behavioral accessibility under fixed prompts. Across six decoder language models in Chinese and English, broad eras repeatedly form ordered trajectories, although their exact spacing varies across model–language settings. Steering along these trajectories shifts both historical register and access to period-compatible knowledge, while adjacent anchors support local interpolation. Epistemic effects partly survive style removal, linking temporal steering to knowledge access beyond surface register. Across Chinese and English, partially alignable trajectories reveal corresponding chronological relations whose geometric realization remains language-specific. Together, ordered temporal geometry offers a testable account of how static language models organize diachronic variation, linking internal structure to historical register and access to period-compatible knowledge. Code and datasets: https://github.com/LilTiger/Time-Travel-Engine.

t: CycleIE: Robust Document Information Extraction through Iterative Verification and Refinement
a: The Hong Kong University of Science and Technology
The Hong Kong University of Science and Technology and South China University of Technology
The Hong Kong University of Science and Technology (Guangzhou) and Hong Kong University of Science and Technology
ab: In document AI, reliable analytics require converting long, noisy (often multi-document) corpora into heterogeneous structured data—e.g., tables for numerical fields, graphs for relations, and trees for hierarchies. Yet, one-pass LLM extraction often yields incomplete or inconsistent structures because it lacks explicit verification and opportunities to revise earlier choices. We present CycleIE, an iterative information extraction (IE) framework that closes the loop between reasoning and acting by coupling ReAct with Monte Carlo Tree Search (MCTS). CycleIE employs a multi-agent workflow to iteratively retrieve, structure, extract, and refine content under verification guidance. By treating extraction as a feedback-driven search process, CycleIE systematically corrects omissions and inconsistencies that defeat one-pass methods, while remaining orthogonal to retrieval-augmented generation (RAG). Experiments on challenging document-based QA benchmarks demonstrate that CycleIE delivers >10% relative improvements over strong baselines, particularly in lengthy or multi-document contexts.

t: Coordinate Structure Alignment of Patent Claims by LLMs
ab: This paper proposes an LLM-based method for cross-lingual alignment of coordinate structures in Japanese–English and Chinese–English patent claims. The approach has two components. First, we construct task-specific alignment datasets by translating Penn Treebank-3 English sentences into Japanese and Chinese and projecting coordinate-structure annotations using syntactic parse trees, word alignments, and the GHKM algorithm. Second, we formulate alignment as a TANL-based text generation task in which LLMs generate the target sentence with the corresponding span tagged. Although the training data are derived from a general-domain corpus, evaluation is conducted on manually annotated real patent claims. Across four translation directions, the proposed approach consistently outperforms SpanAlign, an encoder-based alignment baseline built on SQuAD-style cross-lingual span prediction and ILP-based alignment. Controlled analyses show that the TANL formulation improves performance independently of supervised fine-tuning and that automatically generated demonstrations achieve performance close to manually constructed examples in the tested 3-shot setting. Supervised fine-tuning with the automatically constructed datasets further improves open-weight LLMs, with the best fine-tuned model in each direction achieving an F1 score above 0.8.

t: Embedding-space Posterior Calibration for Zero-shot Vision-Language Models
a: Institute of High Performance Computing, Singapore, A*STAR
Institute of Advanced Intelligence and Computing, A*STAR
ab: Zero-shot vision-language models (VLMs) such as CLIP demonstrate strong open-vocabulary recognition capabilities, yet their prediction confidences are often poorly calibrated. Existing calibration methods often estimate prediction stability by applying multiple augmentations in input space, introducing substantial computational overhead and limiting practical deployment. To this end, this paper proposes an embedding-space posterior calibration approach for zero-shot VLMs, which shifts the sampling process from the input space to the embedding space. Our approach defines and computes a confidence stability score that measures how stable the sample remains under posterior embedding perturbations. This score is further converted into a sample-wise temperature, so that unstable samples receive stronger confidence smoothing while stable samples remain close to their original predictions. Compared with the original CLIP model, our method reduces the mean Expected Calibration Error from 5.83 to 2.05, achieving a 64.8% relative reduction. Meanwhile, our method achieves this improvement with only a minor increase in GFLOPs, from 8.83 to 8.84.

t: Some Emotions Run Deeper: Layer-wise Probing and Causal Intervention in Large Language Models
a: University Paris 13, Université Paris Nord (Paris XIII)
ab: Emotion is expressed in text along a wide spectrum, from surface lexical cues to inferences entangled with content. Most layer-wise analyses of emotion in LLMs use a single corpus, leaving open whether the depth at which emotion becomes accessible is a property of the model or also of the text source. We investigate this across three datasets spanning different degrees of explicitness and contextualization in emotion expression (Twitter posts, Reddit comments, and autobiographical narratives) and eight 1B–9B open-weight LLMs from the Llama, Qwen, and Granite families. We combine layer-wise probing with offline feature scaling and online forward interventions, transfer analyses, and an early-exit classifier. We find that (i) the best probing layer shifts systematically across corpora, from input-adjacent layers to over half model depth, and this ordering persists after matching label-by-length-bin distributions; (ii)across the evaluated settings, forward-pass interventions on probe-selected bands reduce test accuracy by 5–6 points more than same-width random bands (q < 0.01); (iii) selected bands transfer across datasets and emotion categories, suggesting partially shared affective information rather than strictly per-emotion substrates; and (iv) probe-selected early-exit representations outperform full-depth exits by 6.9 percentage points on average.

t: Facts Without Rules: Boundary Metadata Collapse in Multi-Agent LLM Handoffs
ab: Multi-agent LLM systems often coordinate by compressing an upstream interaction into a handoff artifact that downstream agents treat as shared state. We show that this handoff step is a structural source of privacy leakage: summaries preferentially preserve operational facts while weakening the boundary metadata that governs how those facts may be used—a failure mode we call summary collapse. On a controlled multi-agent coordination testbed we measure marker survival with a human-validated judge (\kappa = 0.74), where \sigma_b = 1 means every boundary marker survives verbatim and \sigma_b = 0 means all are lost. Boundary-marker and operational-fact survival are nearly uncorrelated at the handoff level on both GPT-5-mini and DeepSeek-R1-32B (Pearson r near zero): uncompressed free-text handoffs preserve boundaries at \sigma_b \approx 0.80, whereas a 25-word budget drops \sigma_b to {\approx}0.57 while operational-fact survival stays near ceiling. Controlled downstream tests reveal that protection depends on boundary explicitness: vague languages leak in 73% of GPT and 50% of DeepSeek cases, while explicit constraints reduce leakage to under 15% across all three tested models. A no-handoff single-agent control further shows the failure is not reducible to multi-agent topology as direct full-marker access still leaks more often than the operationalized handoff. Prompt-only mitigation and exact-string redaction only partially address the problem, while a gold-derived audience allowlist nearly eliminates leakage across models, showing that correctly identifying audience boundaries is the key factor.

t: Video-MME-Logical: A Controlled Diagnostic Benchmark for Video Temporal-Logical Reasoning
a: Hong Kong University of Science and Technology
The Chinese University of Hong Kong
The Hong Kong University of Science and Technology
Hong Kong University of Science and Technology
ab: Recent interest in multimodal large language models (MLLMs) raises a central question: can they reason over dynamic visual evidence rather than merely recognize objects or events in individual frames? This ability, which we refer to as *video temporal-logical reasoning*, requires models to maintain, update, and compose evidence as visual states evolve across frames. Existing video benchmarks often conflate this capability with scene complexity, static recognition, or uncontrolled temporal variation. To isolate this capability, we introduce Video-MME-Logical, a controlled benchmark organized around five temporal-logical operations: state tracking, sequential counting, temporal ordering, dynamic spatiality, and structural composition. The benchmark contains 25 fine-grained task categories generated with controlled object states, transitions, temporal dependencies, and logical compositions. It enables difficulty-controlled final-answer evaluation by varying temporal horizon and reasoning complexity, and supports intermediate-state diagnostics by verifying whether models recover the required logical reasoning trace before producing the final answer. Experiments with state-of-the-art MLLMs reveal a substantial human-model gap, especially as temporal-logical complexity increases. Supervised fine-tuning on up to 500K generated samples improves performance but remains insufficient to close the reasoning gap, positioning Video-MME-Logical as a scalable testbed for analyzing and improving temporal-logical reasoning in MLLMs.

t: SagE-QG: Skill-Aligned and Evidence-Grounded Educational Question Generation via Counterfactual Evidence Reinforcement Learning
a: Squirrel Ai Learning and Nanyang Technological University
ab: Automatic Question Generation (QG) can make reading-comprehension practice and assessment scalable. For educational use, generated questions should diagnose a target comprehension skill and rely on the passage evidence an expert would use to write the question. Existing answer-aware and skill-conditioned QG methods improve controllability, but often leave these skill-to-question and evidence-to-question dependencies implicit. We present SagE-QG, a Skill-aligned and Evidence-Grounding Framework for Question Generation. SagE-QG exposes evidence-grounded trajectories, optimizes multi-aspect rewards for answerability, skill alignment, and human similarity, and applies Counterfactual Evidence Intervention in reinforcement learning. The intervention removes selected evidence and rewards the Interventional Grounding Gap between full-passage and masked-evidence generations. Experiments on three reading-comprehension QG datasets show that SagE-QG delivers stronger educational quality, especially in skill alignment and answerability, while achieving competitive reference-based results.

t: RCR-Router:Role-Conditioned Context Routing for Resource-Efficient Multi-Agent LLM Systems
a: School of Computer Science, Carnegie Mellon University
ab: Large language model (LLM) agents are increasingly organized into multi-agent systems for complex reasoning and decision-making tasks. However, scaling such systems can substantially increase inference cost, especially when multiple agents repeatedly process overlapping or role-irrelevant context. Many existing multi-agent frameworks focus on orchestration and role specialization, but still rely on full-context sharing or static context routing, leading to redundant token consumption, increased runtime, and inefficient memory utilization. We present Role-Conditioned Context Routing (RCR), an execution-time layer that allocates role-relevant shared-memory items to agents under token budgets. Given a structured shared memory and a set of role-specialized agents, RCR selectively routes task-relevant memory items to each agent according to its role, optional task-stage metadata, and token budget. RCR integrates role-conditioned relevance scoring, token-budgeted memory selection, and iterative memory updates to reduce redundant context exposure during multi-agent execution. Experiments on multi-hop QA, embodied reasoning (ALFWorld), and web-based decision-making (WebShop) show that RCR reduces token usage by 35% on average and runtime by 38% on average relative to Full-Context, while maintaining or improving task performance.

t: Cultural (In)Competence: Investigating Culture-Specific Stereotype Detection Capabilities of LLMs
a: University of Amsterdam, University of Amsterdam
ab: Stereotypes are subjective constructs that are mediated by the cultural context in which they are viewed. Successfully modeling them thus also requires cultural competence. When using large language models (LLMs) for stereotype-related tasks, such as their detection, it is therefore crucial that models can access relevant cultural knowledge and adjust responses accordingly. Since LLMs have shown disparities in what cultural knowledge is available to them, their capacity regarding stereotypes may also be disparate across languages and cultural contexts (e.g., for non-English languages or for non-US contexts). In this paper, we systematically investigate the effectiveness of LLMs for culture-specific stereotype detection across three factors: (1) the prompting language, (2) the instruction tuning language, and (3) the fine-tuning dataset size. We conduct experiments for US, Dutch, and Chinese cultural contexts. Our results suggest that LLMs do not reliably account for cultural contexts and overpredict the presence of stereotypes. Non-English prompts seem to improve consideration of cultural context and thus lead to more effective predictions. Moreover, we find that additional instruction tuning reduces false-positive rates and that training data size moderates detection effectiveness non-monotonically.

t: Two Heads are Better Than One: Test-time Scaling of Multi-agent Collaborative Reasoning
a: Rutgers University, Rutgers University and Rutgers University
ab: Test-Time Scaling has emerged as a powerful method to extend the reasoning capabilities of Large Language Models. However, single-agent TTS faces significant scalability bottlenecks, as excessively long reasoning traces lead to increased inference costs and stability issues caused by context management failures. To address these limitations, we propose leveraging Multi-Agent Systems as a structural upgrade to standard TTS. By decomposing monolithic reasoning chains into distinct, manageable contexts across multiple agents, MAS offers a more robust framework for scaling reasoning. We validate this approach by introducing M500, a dataset comprising 500 high-quality multi-agent, multi-turn collaborative reasoning traces generated via DeepSeek-R1. Through Supervised Fine-Tuning on M500, we enable open-source models to internalize collaborative reasoning patterns and show improved TTS performance in MAS. Furthermore, we propose an adaptive scaling strategy incorporating a “CEO” agent to dynamically guide the reasoning process and optimize collaboration depth. Extensive experiments within the AgentVerse framework demonstrate that our fine-tuned models, Qwen2.5-32B-MAS and Phi4-14B-MAS, significantly outperform their base counterparts.

t: Narrowing the Horizon: Quantifying Topic Saliency Shifts in Generative Monoculture
a: King's College London, University of London
King's College London, University of London
ab: As Large Language Models (LLMs) become central to how we access and share information, they play an increasingly powerful role in shaping global knowledge. However, as these models evolve, their outputs risk converging into a generative monoculture, where the diversity of perspectives they represent narrows over time. Studies at the model level often fail to pinpoint which specific topics or viewpoints are being marginalised or amplified in this process. In this paper, we introduce a method to measure shifts in topic saliency across model families, tracking what gains or loses prominence during post-training. Applying this approach to a case study of climate change discourse, we demonstrate how homogenisation affects the representation of diverse solutions across different models. We also test interventions to counter this trend, showing that specialised models can help preserve a broader range of perspectives. This underscores the importance of monitoring topic saliency to diagnose the risks of monoculture and to ensure AI systems reflect a pluralism of ideas.

t: A Skill-augmented Agentic Framework and Benchmark for Multi-Video Understanding
ab: Multimodal Large Language Models have achieved strong performance in single-video understanding, yet their ability to reason across multiple videos remains limited. Existing approaches typically concatenate multiple videos into a single input and perform direct inference, which introduces training–inference mismatch, information loss from frame compression, and a lack of explicit cross-video coordination. Meanwhile, current multi-video benchmarks primarily emphasize event-level comparison, leaving identity-level matching, fine-grained discrimination, and structured multi-step reasoning underexplored. To address these gaps, we introduce MVX-Bench, a Multi-Video Cross-Dimension Benchmark that reformulates 11 classical computer vision tasks into a unified multi-video question-answering framework, comprising 1,442 questions over 4,255 videos from diverse real-world datasets. We further propose SAMA, a Skill-Augmented Agentic Framework for Multi-Video Understanding, which integrates visual tools, task-specific skills, and a conflict-aware verification mechanism to support iterative and structured reasoning. Experiments show that SAMA improves substantially over its visual perception backbone and achieves the best average accuracy on MVX-Bench. Ablations confirm the benefits of skill-guided orchestration and conflict-aware verification.

t: A Model with No Head and Many Thoughts
ab: Large language models decode by projecting hidden states through a large vocabulary head at every step. This operation is computationally costly and forces all reasoning to be expressed in discrete tokens. We introduce Soft Latent Thinking, a method that replaces the LM head during reasoning with a lightweight projector, enabling autoregressive rollout in embedding space where reasoning steps remain continuous rather than tokenized. Experiments on DeepSeek-Qwen-1.5B and LLaMA-3.2-3B show that Soft Latent Thinking consistently improves pass@k across all k while reducing per-step compute during chain-of-thought. Our method achieves the highest pass@32 among all soft-thinking approaches, demonstrating that effective reasoning can be carried out in continuous space without discrete token generation.

t: Regulated Reflection for Efficient Reasoning in Large reasoning language models
a: East China University of Science and Technology
East China University of Science and Technology
ab: Large reasoning language models (LRLMs) achieve strong performance on complex reasoning tasks by generating long chain-of-thought trajectories, but such long-form reasoning also increases token consumption and latency. Existing inference-time methods that do not fine-tune the target LRLM optimize long reasoning through budgeting, early exit, uncertainty control, or reflection suppression, but they often treat reflection as a local signal rather than as a factor shaping the reasoning trajectory. In this paper, we identify unregulated reflection as a source of inefficient reasoning and characterize two failure modes: Trajectory Drift, where intermediate reflection opens weakly related branches that restart, reorient, or detour from the current path, and Verification Saturation, where answer-adjacent reflection repeatedly checks or restates an already-emerged provisional answer. To address these issues, we propose Regulated Reflection Decoding (RRD), an inference-time framework that requires no fine-tuning or parameter updates to the target LRLM and treats reflection events as online control points. RRD combines Trajectory Drift Suppression (TDS), which guides intermediate reasoning toward validated continuation branches, and Redundant Verification Suppression (RVS), which suppresses redundant verification when the provisional answer is sufficiently reliable. Experiments on multiple reasoning benchmarks show that RRD reduces reasoning length while preserving or improving accuracy, yielding a stronger accuracy-efficiency trade-off than direct inference and representative inference-time baselines.

t: ParaShard: Knowledge Sharding for Effective Parametric Retrieval-Augmented Generation
a: Institute of Computing Technology, Chinese Academy of Sciences
Institute of Computing Technology, Chinese Academy of Sciences
Institute of Computing Technolgy, Chinese Academy of Sciences
Institute of Computing Technology, Chinese Academy of Sciences
Institute of Computing Technology, Chinese Academy
ab: Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) enhances large language models with external knowledge, but long retrieved contexts incur high computational cost and often degrade performance due to context–knowledge mismatch. Parametric RAG (PRAG) addresses this by integrating external knowledge into model parameters via lightweight adapters. However, existing PRAG methods are fundamentally document-centric, treating each document as an independent unit of knowledge, which leads to poor scalability and weak supervision. We argue that knowledge is inherently distributed across semantically related documents, and document-level parameterization is a suboptimal granularity. To this end, we propose ParaShard, a knowledge-centric framework that organizes knowledge into semantically coherent knowledge shards and parameterizes each shard with a shared adapter. This design enables richer supervision across related documents while significantly reducing the number of required adapters. At inference time, ParaShard dynamically selects and composes multiple shards using a diversity-aware strategy to ensure comprehensive knowledge coverage. Experiments on four knowledge-intensive QA benchmarks show that ParaShard achieves superior average performance across diverse knowledge-intensive tasks compared with strong RAG and PRAG baselines, with particularly strong gains on multi-hop reasoning, and substantially reduces storage cost compared to PRAG, demonstrating the knowledge injection effectiveness and storage efficiency of knowledge-centric parameterization.

t: Beyond Repository Boundaries: Cross-Repository Graph Retrieval for Code Generation
a: Hanoi University of Science and Technology
Hanoi University of Science and Technology
ab: Repository-level code generation requires generated code to be compatible not only with the target repository but also with its dependency environment. Existing retrieval-based methods mainly retrieve context from the local repository, leaving external API usage dependent on the model’s pretrained knowledge, which can be insufficient for unseen or version-specific APIs. Moreover, current retrieval strategies largely focus on one-hop evidence and overlook the structural relationships among code components. We propose CrossCoder, a cross-repository code generation framework that explicitly incorporates external libraries into the retrieval context through a unified knowledge graph over repository and library entities. CrossCoder identifies important nodes via planning and semantic retrieval, then selectively expands neighboring nodes to retrieve richer multi-hop contextual evidence for generation. To further evaluate dependency-version compatibility, we introduce VersionExec, an execution-based benchmark derived from BigCodeBench that evaluates generation under different dependency versions. Experimental results on RepoExec, DevEval, and VersionExec demonstrate that CrossCoder consistently improves both functional correctness (up to 6.3% on pass@1) and robustness to dependency-version changes.

t: Transformer-Encoder Trees for Efficient Multilingual Machine Translation and Speech Translation
ab: Multilingual translation suffers from computational redundancy, especially when translating into multiple languages simultaneously. In addition, translation quality can suffer for low-resource languages. To address this, we introduce Transformer Encoder Tree (TET), a hierarchical, non-autoregressive encoder-only architecture trained with Connectionist Temporal Classification (CTC) for multilingual translation. TET shares intermediate representations among linguistically similar target languages, improving accuracy on low-resource languages while reducing computational redundancy and enabling the generation of all target languages in a single forward pass. TET eliminates the sequential bottleneck of autoregressive models and supports fully parallel decoding of all tokens across all target languages. Compared to a naive one-to-many multilingual design, TET reduces the total parameter count by 66% and lowers inference computation by 60%. In speech translation, combining TET with a non-autoregressive speech recognition backbone (Wav2Vec2) shows competitive translation quality compared to autoregressive systems while speeding up inference by approximately 7-14 \times.

t: Beyond Factual Knowledge: Benchmarking and Learning Step-Level Procedural Rule Reasoning in Large Language Models
a: Institute of automation, Chinese academy of science, Chinese Academy of Sciences
Institute of automation, Chinese academy of science
Institute of automation, Chinese academy of science, Chinese Academy of Sciences
ab: Large language models (LLMs) excel at text understanding and generation, yet still struggle to reliably understand and apply externally provided procedural rules at scale. To evaluate this capability, we introduce RuleWorld, a large-scale benchmark that reformulates rules as globally reusable abstract units rather than instance-specific facts. In RuleWorld, several scenarios, including single-rule, parallel multi-rule, and multi-hop reasoning, are settled for comprehensive evaluation. We further propose DynaRule, an end-to-end framework that injects the given rules into the KV cache and turns retrieval into an internal, learnable, step-wise process. Specifically, DynaRule employs Stacked Step-Level Attention Training with a special <search> token to enable dynamic rule re-attention and updating during inference. In this way, the model can re-attend to the most relevant rules at each step, dynamically replacing outdated ones to support more stable multi-step reasoning. Experiments on RuleWorld show that existing LLMs face challenges under large rule pools, while DynaRule improves average QA accuracy by up to 19 points and achieves over 85% Recall@1 at 10K rules, outperforming strong baselines by large margins.

t: DataKernelBench: Can LLMs Optimize Database Queries on GPUs?
a: Technische Universität Wien and International Business Machines
Technische Universität Wien, Aalborg University, Max-Planck-Institute for Informatics and Technische Universität Ilmenau
ab: GPUs increasingly accelerate database systems, but query-specific peak performance still often relies on hand-written kernels. Existing LLM kernel benchmarks focus on machine learning operators, leaving irregular, heterogeneous, data-movement-heavy database-style operators untested. We introduce **DataKernelBench**, which translates SQL into validated PyTorch **TorchPlan** programs and evaluates LLMs that optimize either the core tensor-bounded snippet or the full query in CUDA or Triton through execution-guided repair. Across ten proprietary and open-weight models on **TPC-H SF10** with an H100 GPU, the strongest full-query CUDA configuration achieves **2.11× speedup over ‘torch.compile‘** at full pass rate. We find that higher-performing implementations commonly use kernel fusion and execution-strategy changes, stronger models benefit most from full-query specialization, and workload context matters more than hardware context. To handle data larger than GPU memory, we extend TorchPlan with Dask-cuDF for on-demand partition loading on **TPC-H SF100** with four H100 GPUs, achieving **2.54×** speedup.**Project page:** https://kerneldf.github.io/datakernelbench

t: TRAJDEBUG: Tracing Error Lifecycle to Identify Critical Failures in Long-Horizon Agent Trajectories
a: The Chinese University of Hong Kong
ab: LLM-based agentic systems have shown remarkable capabilities in complex domains, while suffering from cascading errors and difficulty in debugging. Critical error detection aims to locate the earliest error step in a failed trajectory that is responsible for the final failure. However, progress faces two main challenges. First, long trajectories make it difficult to identify individual errors, since the evidence for judging a step may be scattered across distant instructions, observations, and prior context. Second, failed trajectories often contain multiple local errors with different downstream effects, only some of which remain responsible for the final failure. In this work, we propose TrajDebug, an error-lifecycle tracing framework that addresses long-trajectory error discovery with multi-granularity history compression and evidence-based error identification, and supports critical attribution by tracing each error’s resolution status and terminal impact. We further construct TrajErrBench, a benchmark of 486 manually annotated failed trajectories from and SWE-Bench Pro, covering realistic tool-use and coding scenarios. Experiments across diverse agent benchmarks show that TrajDebug achieves the best overall performance over existing baselines, and application studies further demonstrate that its diagnoses provide actionable feedback for improving downstream agent success. We will release the codes and data to facilitate further research.

t: Synthetic Mixed Training: Scaling Parametric Knowledge Acquisition Beyond RAG
a: Computer Science Department, Stanford University and NVIDIA
ab: Synthetic data augmentation helps language models learn new knowledge in data-constrained domains. However, naively scaling existing synthetic data methods by training on more synthetic tokens or using stronger generators yields diminishing returns below the performance of RAG. To break the RAG ceiling, we introduce Synthetic Mixed Training, which combines synthetic QAs and synthetic documents. This leverages their complementary training signals, and enables log-linear improvements as both synthetic data volume and generator strength increase. This allows the model to outperform RAG by a 2.6% relative gain on QuaLITY, a long-document reading comprehension benchmark. In addition, we introduce Focal Rewriting, a simple technique for synthetic document generation that explicitly conditions document generation on specific questions, improving the diversity of synthetic documents and yielding a steeper log-linear scaling curve. On QuaLITY, our final recipe trains a Llama 8B model that outperforms RAG by 4.4% relatively. Across models and benchmarks (QuaLITY, LongHealth, FinanceBench), our training enables models to beat RAG in five of six settings, outperforms by 2.6%, and achieves a 9.1% gain when combined with RAG.

t: Self-Evaluation Is Already There: Eliciting Latent Judge Calibration in Base LLMs with Minimal Data
a: National University of Singapore and National University of Singapore
ab: Large language models are increasingly evaluated by other models, raising a natural question: can a model predict how a judge will score its own output? We find that the ability is largely present before any targeted training: prompted few-shot, a base model already predicts an external judge’s multi-attribute quality scores on open-ended responses well above chance across three benchmarks. We introduce Self-Evaluation Elicitation (SEE), a method that surfaces this latent ability through a short cycle comprising a calibration-coupled reinforcement learning phase that improves the answer and predicts the judge, followed by a masked distillation phase that sharpens the prediction while leaving the answer untouched. From 160 unique examples, roughly 31× fewer than a reinforcement learning baseline, SEE improves held-out calibration across three benchmarks while preserving answer quality. The elicited self-evaluation is sharply localized within the model’s own token distribution and stable across judges it was never trained against, indicating a transferable notion of quality rather than a single judge’s preference. These results reframe judge-aligned self-evaluation as a problem of elicitation rather than acquisition.

t: FedLing: Linguistic-Structure-Aware Federated Learning for Fair Multilingual LLM Adaptation
a: University of Electronic Science and Technology of China
ab: Multilingual large language models (LLMs) exhibit substantial performance disparities across languages, with low-resource languages often lagging far behind high-resource ones. Federated learning (FL) offers a privacy-preserving path for decentralized multilingual adaptation, but existing methods typically aggregate client updates without explicitly modeling structural differences across languages, inducing gradient interference, amplifying negative transfer, and further disadvantaging underrepresented languages. We introduce FedLing, a linguistic-structure-aware federated learning framework. FedLing performs typology-conditioned spectral routing of client LoRA updates, decomposing them into linguistically transferable consensus subspaces and language-specific divergence subspaces. Unlike posterior-only decomposition methods that require accumulated training history to estimate transferability, FedLing explicitly mixes a round-one energy prior with typology-conditioned empirical subspace alignment through a single coefficient ρ. A continuous typological isolation score further prevents negative transfer for languages without close federation neighbors, and a reciprocal fairness proxy adapts upload bandwidth toward underperforming languages. Experiments across 40 languages show that FedLing consistently improves multilingual adaptation: +7.9 average ROUGE-L and +11.6 ROUGE-L on low-resource languages over FedAvg, with 52% variance reduction and 35% upload savings. The advantage is largest in cold-start and data-scarce regimes, validating the combination of energy-based cold-start routing and typology-conditioned posterior alignment.

t: Using Semantic Uncertainty to Estimate Transition Relevance in Turn-Taking
ab: Turn-taking is a fundamental mechanism that governs when interlocutors speak and listen. Although Spoken Dialogue Systems (SDS) exploit a range of linguistic, acoustic, and non-verbal cues, they produce ill-timed responses in unscripted interaction. A central challenge is anticipating Transition Relevance Places (TRPs), or opportunities, not obligations, for a listener to take the floor. Human listeners do not wait for turn endings; as an utterance unfolds, they use expectations about its developing meaning to anticipate TRPs and decide whether to take the floor. We examine whether these evolving expectations can be modeled through semantic uncertainty—an LLM-derived measure of how strongly a turn so far constrains what may plausibly come next. To do so, we sample possible continuations of an ongoing turn and use changes in semantic dispersion to identify TRPs within turns. We evaluate this account on a dataset with TRP labels derived from real-time listener responses, rather than retrospective annotation. Our approach substantially outperforms prompt-based and fine-tuned text-only baselines, providing empirical support for the view that evolving semantic constraints inform perceived turn-taking opportunities in unscripted interaction.

t: ComplexityMT: Benchmarking the Interaction Between Text Complexity and Machine Translation
a: Mohamed bin Zayed University of Artificial Intelligence
Cardiff University and King Abdul Aziz University
ISCTE - Instituto Universitário de Lisboa and INESC-ID Lisboa
ab: When a text is translated, does the translation retain the complexity of the original? We introduce ComplexityMT, a new challenge for assessing how text complexity and machine translation interact with and influence each other, using the CEFR levels as the measure of text complexity. Across six languages, including Arabic, Dutch, English, French, Hindi, and Russian, we evaluate three open-weight models, one closed model, and a commercial machine translation system on two tasks: i) correlation of CEFR with translation difficulty, and ii) shifts in CEFR levels of the source texts. Our experiments show that higher CEFR levels make texts more difficult to translate, and that machine translation shifts the CEFR level of the target text compared to the original source, for most languages. These findings provide new insights for researchers and practitioners working on multilingual pedagogical content generation and MT difficulty estimation.

t: Unveiling Sentiment Representations in Code-LLMs
a: Korea Advanced Institute of Science and Technology
ab: This paper examines whether Code-LLMs encode latent sentiment representations and how these influence generation behavior. Using probing methods, we show that sentiment information is linearly separable in hidden states. Through activation steering, we demonstrate that manipulating sentiment-aligned directions systematically affects both output tone and downstream task performance. Notably, negative sentiment consistently reduces correctness, while positive effects are weaker and less consistent. Ablation and error analyses indicate these changes are not due to random perturbations but reflect meaningful behavioral shifts, including reduced confidence. These findings suggest that affective latent directions act as unintended control signals in Code-LLMs, with measurable impact on downstream task performance quality. Our study highlights the need to better understand and control such latent factors when deploying Code-LLMs.

t: DVBench: Benchmarking MLLMs for Understanding Dynamic Charts and Narratives in Data Videos
ab: While MLLMs have made significant strides in chart comprehension and video understanding, current evaluations largely isolate these capabilities, leaving a critical gap in understanding temporally evolving structured visual information. To address this gap, we introduce **DVBench**, a benchmark for evaluating MLLMs on data videos, a storytelling medium that integrates dynamic charts with structured narratives. We decompose data video understanding into five dimensions. DVBench comprises 300 real-world data videos and 1,000 human-verified QA pairs curated through a rigorous semi-automated pipeline. Extensive evaluations of nine MLLMs show that Gemini-3.1-Pro achieves the best overall performance, while Kimi-k2.5 is the strongest open-source model. We further identify two notable phenomena: open-source model performance does not scale strictly with parameter size, and narrative proficiency does not guarantee visual capability. Fine-grained analyses and ablation studies further reveal dimension-specific weaknesses and the effects of frame configurations and subtitle inputs, informing future MLLM development. DVBench is publicly available at https://bomiaowang.github.io/DVBench/.

t: DDCG: Decoupled Dual-Critic Guidance for Embodied Agents
ab: Large Language Models (LLMs) have enabled embodied agents to perform high-level planning, yet grounding language-based plans into the physical world remains challenging. While feedback-based closed-loop planning is the dominant paradigm, existing methods typically rely on a single scalar feedback signal, which conflates physically infeasible actions that violate hard constraints with strategically sub-optimal but valid choices. We identify this structural limitation as Signal Confounding, which leads to ambiguous feedback and unreliable plan correction. To address this issue, we propose Decoupled Dual-Critic Guidance (DDCG), a framework that explicitly disentangles feedback into two complementary signals: a Feasibility Critic (C_F) that enforces physical and logical executability constraints, and a Quality Critic (C_Q) that evaluates the strategic value of feasible actions. This decoupled guidance enables precise error attribution during planning without requiring parameter updates to the LLM planner. We provide a theoretical interpretation of DDCG as critic-regularized planning with hard feasibility constraints. Experiments on two embodied planning benchmarks, VirtualHome and ScienceWorld, show that DDCG consistently improves plan executability and task success, particularly in long-horizon settings, highlighting the importance of structured feedback for reliable LLM-based planning.

t: When Tools Hurt LLM Reasoning: State-Dependent Belief Revision under External Evidence
a: Renmin University of China and Shanghai Artificial Intelligence Laboratory
ab: Tool use is often assumed to monotonically improve reasoning, where external evidence is expected to help when relevant and be ignored when irrelevant. We show that this assumption fails in a state-dependent way. Across benchmarks with Python and Wikipedia tools, external evidence reliably helps when initial beliefs are weak, but can flip already-correct answers when those beliefs are strong. We frame this as a misallocation of revision authority, arguing that deferring to external evidence is suboptimal when internal support for the correct answer surpasses the tool’s expected output quality. This predicts that harm should concentrate on high-confidence no-tool cases. We test this prediction with threshold localization, wrong-trace audits, and a same-clue intervention showing that revision framing changes the damage caused by misleading evidence. These findings suggest that mixed no-tool/tool-assisted inference should arbitrate authority rather than privilege tool evidence by default. As a minimal demonstration, we introduce CASE, a label-free controller that selects between no-tool and tool-assisted trajectories using answer-state certainty and improves over existing confidence-based arbitration baselines.

t: ClawBench: Can AI Agents Complete Everyday Online Tasks?
a: University of Waterloo and Texas A&M University - College Station
Georgetown University, NetMind.AI and Protagolabs Inc
University of British Columbia, Department of Computer Science, University of British Columbia
ab: AI agents may assist with emails and documents, but can they reliably complete everyday online workflows on real websites? Everyday online tasks offer a realistic yet unsolved testbed for evaluating next-generation AI agents. To this end, we introduce ClawBench, an evaluation framework comprising 153 everyday online tasks common in daily life and work, spanning 144 platforms across 15 categories, from completing purchases and booking appointments to submitting job applications. These tasks require capabilities beyond existing benchmarks, such as obtaining relevant information from user-provided documents, navigating multi-step workflows across diverse platforms, and write-heavy operations like filling in many detailed forms correctly. Unlike existing benchmarks that evaluate agents in offline sandboxes with static pages, ClawBench operates on production websites, preserving the full complexity, dynamic nature, and interaction challenges of real-world web environments. An interception layer captures and blocks the final submission request, ensuring safe evaluation without real-world side effects. Our evaluations of 8 frontier models show that both proprietary and open-source models complete only a small portion of these tasks. For example, Claude Sonnet 4.6 achieves only 33.3%, which exposes gaps in current AI agents. Progress on ClawBench brings us closer to AI agents that can function as general-purpose assistants.

t: RewardCode: Training Generalist Code Reward Model via Pairwise Reinforcement Learning
ab: Reward modeling aligns language models with human preferences, yet coding tasks, requiring strict logic and syntax, pose challenges due to their domain diversity. In this paper, we propose RewardCode, a generalist code reward model trained via a two-stage pipeline, enabling scalable and precise evaluation through principle-based scoring and unit test generation. Specifically, the first stage combines Structured Fine-Tuning and Rejective Fine-Tuning to distill cross-domain summarization and code evaluation capabilities from advanced LLMs. The second stage introduces Pairwise-GRPO, a reinforcement learning method that uses preference pairs to improve solution discrimination, while ensuring the generation of consistent and verifiable unit tests. Further, to train a cross-domain code reward model, we construct CodePair-18K, a dataset of verifiable code preference pairs and executable unit tests. Experiments on multiple benchmarks show that RewardCode outperforms strong baselines in evaluation accuracy, verifying its effectiveness in advancing general-purpose code LLMs.

t: SpeechJBB: Probing Safety Alignment and Comprehension in Large Audio Language Models under Code-Switched Speech
a: McGill University and Mila - Quebec Artificial Intelligence Institute
ab: Large audio language models (LALMs) are increasingly deployed in real-world applications, yet their safety alignment is still primarily evaluated on monolingual, text-based harmful prompts. This leaves their generalizability under multilingual and spoken settings, particularly code-switched speech, largely underexplored. To address this gap, we introduce SpeechJBB, an audio jailbreak dataset for benchmarking state-of-the-art LALMs across five European languages: English, French, German, Italian, and Spanish, as well as code-switched variants combining pairs of these languages. The extent of safety weaknesses is further probed by introducing an augmented setting where phonologically plausible pseudo-words are inserted around safety-critical terms to simulate localized obfuscation. Across models, code-switched harmful audio yields substantially high jailbreak success rates (JSR), with non-English monolingual and non-English code-switched pairs exhibiting the highest attack success. Pseudo-word insertion monotonically reduces refusal as insertion density increases, even though models rarely attribute harmful meaning to the inserted tokens. Comprehension benchmarks show that these failures are not reducible to multilingual misunderstanding, as several models with strong ASR, spoken language understanding, and spoken reasoning performance are among the most vulnerable.

t: E2A-Bench: Benchmarking Evidence-to-Action Reliability in Financial Chart Reasoning
ab: Can financial vision–language models (VLMs) turn chart evidence into reliable action recommendations? Existing hallucination evaluations are mostly claim-centric: they assess whether generated statements are supported, but not whether evidence remains traceable through rationale, confidence, and final action. We introduce E2A-Bench, a 969-query benchmark for financial chart reasoning, constructed from 323 HS300 constituents under three input modalities with deterministic OHLCV-derived evidence anchors.
