These results suggest that robust user understanding requires reasoning from the roots of the user’s mind, positioning user harnessing as a promising foundation for more adaptive future assistants.

t: WebXSkill: Skill Learning for Autonomous Web Agents
a: Department of Computer Science, University of North Carolina at Chapel Hill
ab: Autonomous web agents powered by large language models (LLMs) remain brittle on long-horizon browser workflows. A key bottleneck is a grounding gap in existing skill formulations: textual workflow skills provide natural language guidance but cannot be directly executed, while code-based skills execute without giving the agent step-level guidance for adaptation or recovery. We introduce WebXSkill, a framework that bridges this gap with executable skills, each pairing a parameterized action program with step-level natural-language guidance. WebXSkill operates in three stages: skill extraction mines reusable action subsequences from readily available synthetic agent trajectories and abstracts them into parameterized skills, skill organization indexes them into a URL-based graph for context-aware retrieval, and skill deployment exposes two complementary modes, grounded mode for fully automated execution and guided mode where skills serve as step-by-step instructions the agent follows with its native planning. WebXSkill demonstrates consistent improvements on WebArena, WebVoyager, and Online-Mind2Web. We further find that better skill deployment mode depends on a model’s plan and execution capability. The code is available at https://github.com/aiming-lab/WebXSkill.

t: Evaluating the Semantic Specificity of Representation Steering in Language Models
a: University of Cambridge and University of Edinburgh
ab: Localized Representation Steering (LRS) is widely used to correct reasoning pathologies in large language models. However, standard benchmark evaluations can easily be fooled by superficial label overrides, creating a false impression of reasoning circuit repairs. In this work, we propose Cross-Rule Transfer (CRT), a diagnostic framework that audits representational interventions by evaluating them on rule families where the model is natively competent. Evaluating late-layer LRS for a widespread logical failure, contradiction blindness, reveals that the intervention merely injects a global label bias: applying the steering vector to rules the model already handles correctly (99.6% baseline) degrades performance to 40.4% by forcing false contradiction predictions. We support this diagnosis with four complementary controls (direct logit bias equivalence, control vector label-flipping, cross-model grafting, and early-layer steering checks), providing a rigorous methodology to distinguish genuine reasoning repairs from superficial label overrides.

t: Online Self-Weighted Fine-Tuning
ab: Standard supervised fine-tuning (SFT) assigns the same explicit loss weight to every expert demonstration, regardless of the model’s changing competence over training queries. Reinforcement learning (RL) based methods adapt update strength using model-generated rollouts, but often require substantially more sampling and can be unstable on hard tasks. We propose Online Self-Weighted Fine-Tuning (OSW-FT), a simple method that augments SFT with online, trajectory-level weighting. For each query, OSW-FT estimates the model’s current success rate using a small number of inference-only rollouts and rescales the standard SFT loss accordingly. The optimization direction remains anchored to the expert trajectory, while the update magnitude adapts online. For binary-verifiable reasoning, we connect this weighting to SFT and RL at the gradient level, inspired by variance-reduction principles. The resulting estimator is unbiased for the exact OSW-FT surrogate update for any finite rollout count, and we analyze convergence with respect to the corresponding surrogate objective. Evaluated across Qwen3 series ranging from 0.6B to 4B on multiple challenging benchmarks (e.g., AIME), OSW-FT consistently improves over SFT on small-to-medium scale models. OSW-FT offers a favorable compute-performance trade-off as a practical approach for fine-tuning small-to-medium LLMs on binary-verifiable reasoning tasks with only 2 online rollouts.

t: EpiWorld: Grounding LLM Policy Agents in Epidemiological World Models
a: Causal Dynamics Lab and Emory University
ab: Epidemic intervention policies are textual artefacts that human decision-makers interpret, justify, and revise through natural language, making large language models a natural candidate for epidemic policy reasoning. A naive LLM, however, lacks the epidemic dynamics needed to project intervention consequences, the quantitative surveillance signals required to assess severity, and the institutional constraints that define admissible actions. We present EpiWorld, a closed-loop framework that grounds an LLM policy actor in a learned action-conditioned epidemiological world model and a tiered skill library of public-health protocols, surveillance tools, and adaptive lessons accumulated through after-action analysis. Given a candidate intervention, the world model predicts regional epidemic evolution and enables fast counterfactual rollouts that provide feedback for policy selection and refinement. Outcomes of simulated futures are distilled into reusable lessons while protocol constraints remain fixed, allowing the decision process to improve without sacrificing interpretability or controllability. We evaluate both the world model and the end-to-end framework on retrospective COVID-19 and Influenza datasets: the world model achieves the best out-of-distribution Peak-MAE among all forecasting baselines, and the closed-loop framework reduces cumulative hospitalisation by up to 59% across datasets and by an average of ~16% across six LLM backbones, outperforming reinforcement-learning and optimal-control policy baselines.

t: PhysProver: Advancing Automatic Theorem Proving for Physics
a: Amazon and University of Illinois at Urbana-Champaign
Department of Computer Science, University of Illinois at Urbana-Champaign
ab: The combination of verifiable languages and LLMs has significantly influenced both the mathematical and computer science communities because it provides a rigorous foundation for theorem proving. Recent advancements in the field provide foundation models and sophisticated agentic systems pushing the boundaries of formal mathematical reasoning to approach the natural language capability of LLMs. However, little attention has been given to the formal physics reasoning, which also heavily relies on similar problem-solving and theorem-proving frameworks. To solve this problem, this paper presents, to the best of our knowledge, the first approach to enhance formal theorem proving in the physics domain. We compose a dedicated dataset PhysLeanData for the task. It is composed of theorems sampled from PhysLean and data generated by a conjecture-based formal data generation pipeline. In the training pipeline, we leverage DeepSeek-Prover-V2-7B, a strong open-source mathematical theorem prover, and apply Reinforcement Learning with Verifiable Rewards (RLVR) to train our model PhysProver. Comprehensive experiments demonstrate that, using only about 5.5K training samples, PhysProver achieves an overall 2.4% improvement in multiple sub-domains. Furthermore, after formal physics training, we observe 1.3% gains on the MiniF2F-Test benchmark, which indicates non-trivial generalization beyond physics domains and enhancement for formal math capability as well. The results highlight the effectiveness and efficiency of our approach, which provides a paradigm for extending formal provers outside mathematical domains. To foster further research, we will release both our dataset and model to the community.

t: AIA^{2}: Attribute-Agnostic Imbalance Augmentation for Subgroup Robustness
ab: Attributes describing data content and context can induce diverse imbalance patterns that go beyond label imbalance alone. However, existing studies primarily address label imbalance while overlooking data attributes, such as topics and demographics, which can induce meaningful subgroup structure while causing model degradation on underrepresented subgroups. We propose Attribute-Agnostic Imbalance Augmentation (AIA^{2}), a framework for improving model robustness under varying subgroup imbalances without explicit subgroup annotations. AIA^{2} automatically discovers varying imbalances via latent semantic distributions, obtains slices with both learning difficulty and subgroup imbalance deficits, and deploys a large language model (LLM) for subgroup-aware imbalance augmentation. We have evaluated AIA^{2} on 5 popular corpora with rich domains and their attribute values, covering social issues and diverse topics. Results show improved performance on the lowest-performing subgroups and consistent gains over competitive baselines. Ablation studies confirm complementary contributions from each component, and additional analyses show that AIA^{2} provides a practical and consistent way to improve worst-group robustness under data subgroup imbalance. Code is available at https://github.com/trust-nlp/AIA2-Subgroup-Robustness.

t: AdaTIR: Adaptive Tool-Integrated Reasoning via Difficulty-Aware Policy Optimization
ab: Tool-Integrated Reasoning (TIR) improves the problem-solving ability of Large Language Models (LLMs), but current TIR agents often invoke external tools even when internal reasoning is sufficient. This cognitive offloading increases latency and can expose the model to noisy tool feedback. We propose AdaTIR, a difficulty-aware policy optimization framework that applies efficiency pressure only when a task is estimated to be solvable under the current TIR policy. This encourages reasoning internalization on easier tasks while preserving tool access for harder ones. We further identify a sign-reversal failure in group-normalized RL: once rollouts in a group are mostly correct, an auxiliary tool-use penalty can dominate the correctness signal and assign negative advantages to correct but tool-heavy trajectories. AdaTIR addresses this with Clipped Advantage Shaping (CAS), which keeps efficiency as a bounded secondary signal. Across mathematical benchmarks, AdaTIR reduces average tool calls by up to 97.6% while maintaining or improving accuracy, and improves AIME 2024 accuracy by 4.8% when tool access is disabled. Additional results on search-based QA and mixed-tool settings indicate that the mechanism is not limited to Python-based math reasoning.

t: On the Robustness of Code LLM Guardrails to Code-mixed and Transliterated Inputs
ab: Safety guardrails in Code Large Language Models (Code LLMs) are designed to prevent the generation of malicious code, yet their robustness under linguistically diverse inputs remains largely unexplored. To address this important safety issue, we present MALICE (Malicious Adversarial LLM Inputs for Code Generation), a large-scale adversarial benchmark that exposes a critical blind spot at the intersection of multilingual malicious prompts and code generation safety. Our approach converts malicious English prompts into code-mixed and transliterated variants through sentence-level translation into low-resource languages while preserving programming keywords intact. The resulting dataset comprises approximately 250,000 adversarial prompts spanning 18 languages at various resource levels, derived from nine existing malicious code benchmarks. We perform a comprehensive evaluation across nine models (including Claude 4.6 and GPT-5.2) and safety tools, which reveals concerning vulnerabilities: code-mixed malicious prompts reduce detection accuracy by over 0.70 absolute points for the strongest classifier, while even the most safety-aligned models see their malicious code generation rates increase threefold. These results demonstrate that current safety alignment fails to generalize beyond English inputs, underscoring an urgent need for multilingual defenses in Code LLMs.

t: Identifying Student Real Weaknesses: Learnable Error-Aware Distillation for Medical Question Answering
a: Qilu University of Technology(Shandong Academy of Sciences)
The First Affiliated Hospital of Shandong First Medical University & Shandong Provincial Qianfoshan Hospital
The First Affiliated Hospital of Shandong First Medical University & Shandong Provincial Qianfoshan Hospital
ab: Large language models (LLMs) show strong performance in medical question answering, but their computational costs limit deployment under resource constraints. Therefore, an increasing number of studies focus on distilling knowledge from LLMs into smaller models to improve performance in medical question answering. However, existing methods often fail to identify truly useful knowledge to distill, making it difficult to focus distillation on the student’s real weaknesses. As a result, much of the distillation budget is spent on already acquired knowledge rather than on weaknesses that still limit performance. To address this problem, we propose LEAD, a Learnable Error-Aware Distillation framework that precisely improves the weaknesses of student models. First, LEAD identifies questions answered incorrectly by the student model to determine which weaknesses require teacher guidance. Then, LEAD generates teacher rationales and similar samples to construct candidate supervision for these errors. Through supervision refinement, reliable and learnable training samples are retained from the candidate supervision. Finally, LEAD trains the student on a balanced sample mixture to correct learnable errors while preserving previously acquired knowledge. Experiments on four medical question answering benchmarks show that LEAD outperforms existing distillation methods.

t: Personas on Demand: Hypernetwork Synthesis of Unseen Users
ab: Simulating an online community at scale calls for language models that can stand in for many distinct users at once, not collapse them into a single generic voice. Prior work shows that a hypernetwork-driven language model can efficiently rebuild known users by storing a small per-user profile vector rather than separate fine-tuned models, one per user. This study explores whether those profile vectors support a harder task: generating behaviorally consistent new users who were never directly observed. Our frozen LLM uses adapter offsets emitted by a hypernetwork. We sample profiles within and beyond the real-user range, then score the generated replies on behavioral measures to determine whether synthetic users match the cohort patterns their profiles imply. We show that synthetic users reproduce behavioral patterns similar to those of real users in the training set: in short threads they stay close to their target profile, and across a longer multi-turn forum simulation they stay largely coherent and do not drift from it. Performance declines as profiles move farther from the distribution of users seen in the original data, suggesting that the method works best for synthetic users that recombine observed patterns rather than extrapolate beyond them.

t: MemGuard: Preventing Memory Contamination in Long-Term Memory-Augmented Large Language Models
a: Department of Computer Science, University of Illinois at Urbana-Champaign
ab: Memory-augmented large language models extend reasoning beyond a fixed context window by maintaining long-term memory across interactions. However, existing memory systems often collapse stable user facts, episodic events, and behavioral rules into a shared space, allowing functionally distinct memories to be retrieved and used as interchangeable evidence. We identify this failure mode as heterogeneous memory contamination, where context-specific events become overgeneralized claims, or semantically relevant but functionally incompatible memories mislead generation. To this end, we introduce MemGuard, a type-aware memory framework that preserves functional memory boundaries during memory construction and retrieval. It assigns each memory an explicit functional role at write time, maintains relations across type-isolated memories, and selectively composes evidence only from necessary memory types, reducing contamination from irrelevant or functionally incompatible evidence. Across hallucination and long-horizon conversation benchmarks, MemGuard improves memory reliability by up to 28.27% while retrieving up to 5.8x fewer memory tokens than prior methods. These results suggest that reliable long-term reasoning depends on principled organization and selective use of heterogeneous memory.

t: EVALUESTEER: Measuring Reward Model Steerability Towards Values and Preferences
a: Department of Computer Science, University of Washington and University of Washington
ab: As large language models (LLMs) are deployed globally, creating pluralistic systems that can accommodate the diverse preferences and values of users becomes essential. We introduce EVALUESTEER, a human-validated benchmark to measure the steerability of LLM and reward models (RMs) to users’ value and stylistic preference profiles grounded in psychology and literature on human-LLM interaction. To address the gap in existing datasets that do not support controlled evaluations of RM steering, we synthetically generated 165,888 preference pairs – systematically varying pairs along 4 value dimensions (traditional, secular-rational, survival, and self-expression) and 4 style dimensions (verbosity, readability, confidence, warmth). We use EVALUESTEER to evaluate whether, given a user profile and a pair of candidate value and style laden responses, LLMs and RMs are able to select the output that aligns with the user’s preferences. Our results show that, when given the user’s full profile of values and stylistic preferences, the best models achieve <75% accuracy in choosing the correct response, in contrast to > 99% accuracy when only relevant style and value preferences are provided. RMs also exhibit systematic biases, favoring secular values and verbose, confident language, and prioritizing style alignment over value alignment when the two conflict. EVALUESTEER thus highlights the limitations of current RMs at identifying and adapting to relevant user profile information, and provides a challenging testbed for developing RMs that can be steered towards diverse human values and preferences.

t: Dataset Protection via Watermarked Canaries in Retrieval-Augmented LLMs
ab: Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) has become an effective method for enhancing large language models (LLMs) with up-to-date knowledge. However, it may pose a risk of copyright infringement, as IP datasets may be incorporated into the knowledge database by malicious Retrieval-Augmented LLMs (RA-LLMs) without authorization. To protect the rights of the dataset owner, an effective dataset membership inference algorithm for RA-LLMs is needed. In this work, we introduce a novel approach, CanaryTrace, to safeguard the ownership of text datasets and effectively detect unauthorized use by the RA-LLMs. Our approach preserves the original data completely unchanged while protecting it by inserting specifically designed canary documents into the IP dataset. These canary documents are created with synthetic content and embedded watermarks to ensure uniqueness, consistency, and statistical provability. During the detection process, unauthorized usage is identified by querying the canary documents and analyzing the responses of RA-LLMs for statistical evidence of the embedded watermark. Our experimental results demonstrate high query efficiency, detectability, and consistency, along with minimal perturbation to the original dataset, all without compromising the performance of the RAG system.

t: Think-Probe-Respond: Improving Large Language Models as Judges of Research Idea Novelty
ab: Automated novelty judgment can accelerate scientific discovery by enabling efficient evaluation, refinement, and comparison of research ideas. While large language models are increasingly adopted for this task, we investigate a previously overlooked limitation in their judgment capabilities: despite generating reasoning rationales that closely mirror those of human experts, their final novelty judgments often diverge substantially. We demonstrate that this miscalibration stems from a systematic bias towards judging ideas as "medium novel". To mitigate this, we propose **T**hink-**P**robe-**R**espond (TPR), a lightweight approach that probes latent novelty judgments from hidden states during the reasoning phase and uses the probed judgments to condition the final response. Across strong baselines, TPR improves novelty judgment performance by 22.30% and successfully mitigates the prevalent "medium novelty" bias.

t: CARE: Privacy-Compliant Agentic Reasoning with Evidence Discordance
a: Mohamed bin Zayed University of Artificial Intelligence
King's College London and University of Cambridge
Mohamed bin Zayed University of Artificial Intelligence and McGill University
McGill University, McGill University and Mila - Quebec Artificial Intelligence Institute
ab: Large language model (LLM) systems are increasingly used to support high-stakes decision-making, but they typically perform worse when the available evidence is internally inconsistent. Such a scenario exists in real-world healthcare settings, with patient-reported symptoms contradicting medical signs. To study this problem, we introduce **MIMIC-DOS**, a dataset for short-horizon organ dysfunction worsening prediction in the intensive care unit (ICU) setting. We derive this dataset from the widely recognized MIMIC-IV, a publicly available electronic health record dataset, and construct it exclusively from cases in which discordance between signs and symptoms exists. This setting poses a substantial challenge for existing LLM-based approaches, with single-pass LLMs and agentic pipelines often struggling to reconcile such conflicting signals. To address this problem, we propose **CARE**: a multi-stage privacy-compliant agentic reasoning framework in which a proprietary LLM provides guidance by generating structured categories and transitions without accessing sensitive patient data, while a local LLM uses these categories and transitions to support evidence acquisition and final decision-making. Empirically, under controlled retrospective evaluation on MIMIC-DOS, CARE achieves the best overall performance across key metrics among the evaluated LLMs and agentic workflows, showing that it can more robustly handle conflicting clinical evidence while preserving privacy. Our code is [here](https://github.com/AAAAA-Academia-Attractions/CARE).

t: BELIEFMEM: Belief-Revising Memory for Conversational LLM Agents
a: University of California, San Diego, University of California, San Diego
ab: Conversational LLM agents accumulate persistent state across sessions, but existing memory systems treat updates as append-or-replace heuristics, leaving contradictory beliefs to coexist in the store and forcing the answer model to reconcile them at query time. We argue this is the wrong abstraction: conversation is a stream of belief revisions, and the right formal lens is the Alchourrón–Gärdenfors–Makinson (AGM) framework, adapted to Hansson belief bases. We present , which operationalizes the AGM operator set as the write semantics of a history-preserving fact belief base. A uniform LLM-driven resolver classifies every extracted claim into one of four actions (exp, rev, dup, con) and runs at two timings: per round against the recent session, and across sessions over a similarity graph. The store never deletes; superseded beliefs retain predecessor pointers, and a context-selection step decides per query whether to surface the head, the full chain, or neither. On LoCoMo (1,540 questions) reaches \mathbf{85.5\%} over Mem0-graph) and \mathbf{92.3\%} with a stronger backbone. On BEAM (400 questions) it reaches \mathbf{54.5\%} (\mathbf{+21.8} over the LIGHT mean).

t: Large Language Models for Machine Translation Quality Annotation: Humans and Models Are Both Challenged
ab: Large Language Models (LLMs) are considered to be a more efficient and cost-effective alternative to human judgment for Machine Translation (MT) evaluation. With MT evaluation spanning a large number of language pairs, domains and levels of annotation granularity, LLMs must be thoroughly evaluated across these dimensions before being reliably used as alternatives to human evaluation. In this paper, we evaluate the performance of LLMs for two prominent MT quality evaluation schemes: Multidimensional Quality Metrics (MQM) and Error Span Annotation (ESA) by comparing their agreement with human annotators. We present results on a long-context test set of 70 language pairs and the publicly available WMT23 and WMT25 data, investigating both score and error span annotation agreement across a variety of language pairs and domains. Our results show that while LLM agreement with human annotators exceeds agreement between human annotators for some evaluation tasks, both vary substantially across annotation schemes, language pairs and domains and remain unreliable for most settings. Furthermore, we identify challenges facing both human and LLM annotators: humans are particularly challenged by fine-grained MQM annotations and low-resource language pairs, while LLMs struggle with minor errors, wrong language variants and error span annotation. Our results highlight the potential for improvement for both human and LLM annotation performance, possibly through human-LLM collaborative annotation pipelines that address the reliability issues identified in this work.

t: Latent Recurrent Thoughts: Recurrent Refinement of Proposed Latents for Reasoning with Frozen LLMs
ab: Chain-of-thought reasoning unfolds in discrete token space: each step is committed as text, errors propagate, and eliciting good traces presupposes traces to imitate. Reasoning instead in a model’s continuous representation space – where intermediate states are vectors rather than words – sidesteps these constraints, but leaves open how those latent states should be computed. We approach this along two axes. First, we keep a large language model (LLM) frozen and use it for what it is already good at – modeling and decoding sequences – while a small auxiliary network supplies continuous latent thoughts as input. Second, we produce those latents by recurrence: a tiny recurrent reasoner refines them over many steps, decoupling the depth of computation from the size of the model, so that the latents are a product of iterative processing rather than a single forward pass. We instantiate this as Latent Recurrent Thoughts (LRT): a task-dedicated proposer supplies base latents, a recurrent reasoner refines them through bounded residual corrections, and the frozen LLM decodes the answer. On symbolic reasoning with answer supervision but no reasoning traces (Countdown-4, Sudoku) and on natural-language reasoning (HumanEval, MBPP, StrategyQA), LRT substantially outperforms prior frozen-decoder continuous-space reasoning methods under an identical decoder, prompt, data, and training budget, and outperforms non-thinking-mode chain-of-thought prompting on the same backbone at a small fraction of its inference compute.

t: FormalMATH: Benchmarking Formal Mathematical Reasoning of Large Language Models
a: The Chinese University of Hong Kong
ab: We introduce FormalMATH, a large-scale Lean4 benchmark for formal mathematical reasoning, comprising 5,560 semantically validated Lean4 statements spanning competition-level and undergraduate mathematics. To improve reliability, FormalMATH is constructed through a human-in-the-loop pipeline that combines type checking, LLM-based semantic verification against the informal–formal statements alignment, negation-based disproving, and expert review. We conduct a systematic evaluation of frontier theorem provers under test-time scaling on FormalMATH. Results show that current provers remain far from solving the benchmark: the strongest model, DeepSeek-Prover-V2 (671B), achieves only 28.31% Pass@32. We further observe substantial domain imbalance across provers, with stronger performance in applied mathematics and algebra but weaker results in discrete mathematics. We identify common failure modes in current provers, including incomplete proofs, weak handling of inequalities, misuse of automation tactics, and redundant hypothesis introduction. Extreme test-time scaling (e.g., Pass@3200) yields only modest gains on a subset of FormalMATH, suggesting that current training paradigms do not equip provers to effectively exploit additional sampling budget. We also observe a counterintuitive negative effect when provers are given human-written natural-language solution references: such references can measurably degrade formal proof generation rather than aid it. Overall, FormalMATH provides a challenging and reliable testbed for measuring progress in formal mathematical reasoning.

t: Can Aha Moments be Fake? Towards Quantifying Decorative and True Thinking in Chain-of-Thought
ab: Large language models can generate long chain-of-thought (CoT) reasoning, yet prior work suggests that CoT can be post-hoc rationalization rather than a faithful reflection of the computation through explicitly designed settings. In this work, we go further and propose a True Thinking Score (TTS) to quantify the causal contribution of each step in CoT to the model’s final prediction in realistic reasoning problems. Across eleven models ranging from 1.5B to 1.1T parameters on common reasoning benchmarks, we find that CoTs often interleave true-thinking steps, which causally affect the final answer, with decorative-thinking steps, which appear useful but have little causal influence; Such decorative steps remain prevalent even for frontier models: Over 30% of steps in Kimi-K2.6 are decorative on MATH with TTS \leq 0.005. Furthermore, TTS enables effective CoT pruning: removing 50% of CoT steps with the lowest TTS can largely maintain the performance. Self-training on these pruned CoTs reduces reasoning length by 66% while preserving performance on Nemotron3-Nano-30B. Finally, we provide a mechanistic analysis showing that LLMs can be steered in the latent space to engage or disengage with reasoning steps. Overall, our results reveal that frontier LLMs often verbalize reasoning steps that are not causally used, challenging both the efficiency and the trustworthiness of CoT.

t: SynAV: Integrated Grounding and Captioning for Fine-grained Omni Video Understanding via Balanced Audio-Visual Synergy
ab: Video understanding is rapidly evolving toward omni-modal fusion, yet Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) still struggle with complex audio-visual reasoning and semantic alignment. Current paradigms often rely on independent modal projectors to map features into the LLM space, an architecture that frequently overlooks intrinsic modal heterogeneity and inadvertently reinforces vision-centric bias by avoiding early, direct semantic interaction between native cross-modal representations. To address these challenges, we propose SynAV, a novel MLLM architecture designed for language-grounded multimodal reasoning. Our framework introduces a two-stage hierarchical cross-modal semantic interaction mechanism: it first performs alignment within the textual semantic space, and subsequently executes a visual-to-audio refinement that bridges semantic gaps and captures temporal dynamics. Furthermore, we employ a frame-by-frame interleaved audio-visual token arrangement enriched with explicit textual timestamps. This strategy acts as a temporal-semantic anchoring mechanism, allowing the LLM to better perceive the synchrony between modalities and seamlessly conduct long-sequence logical reasoning. Our model jointly optimizes temporal grounding and dense captioning tasks in an autoregressive manner. Extensive experiments across 11 benchmarks demonstrate that SynAV significantly outperforms state-of-the-art methods, achieving a superior performance in complex audio-visual language reasoning.

t: WebWeaver: Style-Aware Webpage Generation with Style Contracts
ab: We study style-aware prompt-to-webpage generation: producing executable webpages that preserve content, functionality, and abstract aesthetic intent. We identify the design-intent bottleneck and introduce three components to address it: Web4Style, a brief-based diagnostic benchmark; WebWeaver, a shared-state framework that constructs and propagates an explicit style contract; and WebJudge, a structured multimodal evaluator for content, function, and visual aesthetics. Experiments across three backbone models show that WebWeaver improves over direct generation and representative web/code-generation agents in both automatic and human evaluation. These results highlight style contracts as a missing intermediate layer for reliable prompt-to-webpage generation.

t: The Environmental Impacts of Language Model Training Keep Rising Now is the Time to Catch Impacts on the Rebound
ab: Recent Machine Learning (ML) approaches have shown increased performance on benchmarks at the cost of escalating compute demands. Hardware, algorithmic and carbon optimizations have been proposed to curb energy use and environmental impacts. We estimate the environmental impacts associated with training models documented in the Epoch AI database over the last decade, with a particular focus on impacts associated with Large Language Models and the hardware used to train them. We find that energy use and environmental impacts associated with training ML models have increased exponentially, even when considering impact reduction strategies such as using less carbon intensive electricity mixes or more efficient hardware. Optimization strategies do not mitigate the impacts induced by model training, suggesting rebound effect. We show that the impacts of hardware must be considered over the entire life cycle rather than the sole use phase in order to avoid impact shifting. Our study demonstrates that increasing efficiency alone does not ensure sustainability. There is an urgent need to systematically integrate environmental impacts in NLP evaluation practices to better inform the community and support the use of impact as a feature in research planning and decision making.

t: From Monolithic Prioritization to Stratified Replay: Hierarchical Prioritized Experience Replay for Task-Oriented Dialogue Policy Learning
a: Changsha University of Science and Technology
Changsha University of Science and Technology
Changsha University of Science and Technology
Changsha University of Science and Technology
ab: Replay sampling is central to off-policy task-oriented dialogue policy learning, as it determines which past interactions are revisited during policy updates. Existing priority-based replay methods often rely on a monolithic priority distribution to form minibatches, which entangles coverage across error magnitudes with emphasis on high-error transitions. Under sparse dialogue success and heavy-tailed temporal-difference (TD) errors, this design overexposes extreme residuals and suppresses informative medium-error transitions, a failure mode we call mid-magnitude starvation. To address this problem, we propose Hierarchical Prioritized Experience Replay (HPER), a two-level replay sampler that separates coverage from prioritization. HPER first samples TD-error quantile strata according to occupancy, ensuring that different error magnitudes enter training, and then applies local prioritized replay within the selected stratum to retain emphasis on large residuals. This coverage-first design restores intermediate learning signals without diluting high-error samples. Experiments on multiple dialogue datasets show that HPER improves replay efficiency and yields faster competence onset and higher terminal success than uniform replay and monolithic priority-based replay under matched budgets.

t: Leveraging Teacher-Forcing Token-Level Anomaly Signals for Heterogeneous Backdoor Filtering in LLMs
ab: Generative backdoor attacks pose a growing threat to the instruction tuning of large language models (LLMs), where attackers poison a few training samples to induce malicious payloads on triggered inputs while preserving normal behavior on clean ones. However, existing backdoor-poisoned sample filtering methods typically rely on global sample representations and clustering-based separation, and such global signals can become fragile when heterogeneous target-side malicious payloads scatter poisoned samples or low poisoning rates prevent poisoned samples from forming stable clusters. This motivates us to move beyond cross-sample separability and instead exploit localized token-level target-side anomalies induced by malicious payload tokens under teacher forcing. Building on this intuition, we propose TTAF, a Teacher-forcing Token-level Anomaly Filtering framework which introduces a token-level anomaly score under teacher forcing and aggregates localized evidence to filter suspicious poisoned samples before fine-tuning. Experiments across multiple datasets, representative backdoor attacks, and different LLMs show that TTAF consistently achieves strong filtering performance within this payload-injection setting, with efficient runtime and no external dependencies. Code is available at https://github.com/Sam-Han2020/TTAF.

t: Seeing the Poem: Image-Semantic Detection of AI-Generated Modern Chinese Poetry with MLLMs
ab: Previous detection studies have shown that LLMs cannot be effectively used as detectors, but these studies have not addressed modern Chinese poetry. Moreover, no relevant research has explored the performance of LLMs in detecting modern Chinese poetry. This paper evaluates and enhances the performance of LLMs as detectors for modern Chinese poetry, and proposes an image-semantic guided poetry detection method. Compared with traditional detection approaches, our method innovatively incorporates images that reflect the content of the poetry. Through example-driven approaches, our method effectively integrates information such as meaning, imagery, and feeling from the image, then forms a complementary judgment with the poem text. Experimental results demonstrate that the LLM detectors based on our method outperform baseline detectors based on plain text, and even surpass the best-performing traditional detector, RoBERTa. The Gemini detector using our method achieves a Macro-F1 score of 85.65%, reaching the state-of-the-art level. The performance improvements of different LLM detectors on multiple LLMs-generated data prove the effectiveness of our method.

t: Semantic Shifts of Nationalist Lexemes in German: From Pre-War to Post-War Periods (1918–2024)
ab: This study investigates semantic changes in four historically loaded German political lexemes: Volk, Nation, Staat, and Land. These terms denote basic categories of peoplehood, national community, institutional statehood, and territorial belonging, but their use and emotional associations were reshaped by the ideological language of National Socialism and by the political reconstruction of Germany after 1945. Using DWDS as the empirical basis, we compare a pre-war and wartime baseline (1918–1945) with the post-war period (1945–2024). Our study combines frequency analysis, collocation analysis, and LLM-assisted annotation along three dimensions: nationalist intensity, emotional valence, and temporality. The results suggest different trajectories across the four lexemes: Staat and Land remain comparatively stable as institutional and territorial terms, while Volk shows clearer signs of contextual restructuring, semantic distancing, and possible renewed political markedness. Nation displays intermediate patterns shaped by historical rupture, reunification, and contemporary political discourse. By integrating corpus-based semantic analysis with conceptual history, our study contributes empirical evidence to debates on post-war German national identity and the linguistic reconfiguration of political concepts

t: UniD^{3}: Open Knowledge Graphs and QA Benchmarks for Drug–Disease Discovery and Reasoning
ab: Drug–disease knowledge underpins drug discovery and precision medicine, yet most of it is locked in unstructured PubMed articles and only partially captured by curated databases. We release UniD³-KG, a suite of six knowledge graphs spanning three tasks (Drug–Disease Matching, DDM; Drug Effectiveness Assessment, DEA; and Drug–Target Analysis, DTA), and UniD³-data, three open QA datasets (28,915 DDM, 15,042 DEA and >4,000 DTA pairs), distilled from 157,849 PubMed articles with Llama-3.3-70B by the UniD³ KG-RAG pipeline, which couples task-specific prompting with a dual-stage entity extraction that re-extracts over the consolidated graph to recover cross-chunk and cross-document evidence. External validation on CDR, DrugReviews, P3ps and MedicationQA and a benchmark across seven LLM baselines and three retrieval variants show that UniD³-data is faithful to curated sources and that retrieval over UniD³-KG consistently improves biomedical QA; a clinician verification of 469 FDA-approved, US-marketed drugs further confirms strong agreement with the UniD³-data DDM split (accuracy 0.90, F1 0.90, AUROC 0.90). All artefacts—UniD³-KG, UniD³-data, benchmark scripts and the UniD³-QA explainable chatbot—are released as shared infrastructure for biomedical NLP and drug repurposing.

t: Information-Guided Frontier Decoding: Contextual Utility-Driven Commitment in dMLLMs
ab: Decoding quality in diffusion multimodal language models (dMLLMs) depends heavily on the order in which masked tokens are committed. Existing confidence-based strategies prioritize locally easy tokens, but confidence does not necessarily reflect contextual usefulness. As a result, structurally easy tokens such as punctuation may be committed before informative semantic anchors, weakening context propagation and increasing error accumulation. We propose Information-Guided Frontier Decoding (IGFD), a training-free decoding strategy that ranks candidates using token confidence, neighborhood uncertainty, and structural commitment risk. IGFD encourages early commitment of reliable semantic anchors while delaying fragile structural tokens, improving contextual support during decoding. A dynamic candidate frontier further constrains token selection to locally expandable regions under the same decoding budget. The method requires no additional training, auxiliary models, or extra forward passes. Experiments across multimodal understanding, reasoning, grounding, and hallucination benchmarks show that IGFD consistently outperforms existing decoding strategies across the majority of benchmarks and diffusion MLLM backbones under identical decoding budgets.

t: To Nuke or Not to Nuke: LLMs’ (Missing) Ethical Reasoning and Authorization Actions in a High-Stakes Decision-Making Simulation
a: University of Arizona and Khulna University of Engineering And Technology
ab: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly deployed as long-horizon agents with decision-making capacities. While LLMs can show ethical competence on dilemmas such as trolley problems, this competence may not translate to complex, agentic scenarios. We study whether this competence surfaces and governs LLMs’ behavior in Civilization V, a multiplayer game with a complex decision-making landscape including economy, diplomacy, technology, and military strategy. Starting from 130 high-tension LLM self-play episodes, in which an LLM player spontaneously escalated nuclear authorization, we replay them across 13 models with three prompt interventions: an ethical prompt naming nuclear harm, removal of the previous model’s decision-making rationale, and high-stakes framing emphasizing real-world impacts. No interventions nor their combinations reliably eliminate escalated nuclear authorization. We identify three failure pathways: ethical reasoning that fails to surface without prompting, fails to appear even when prompted, or surfaces but fails to take effect when strategic counter-factors dominate. Evaluations of agentic models, therefore, must test whether ethical reasoning is spontaneously invoked and behaviorally effective in complex decision-making contexts, beyond whether it can be elicited in isolation.

t: RL from Teacher-Model Refinement: Gradual Imitation Learning for Machine Translation
ab: Preference-learning methods for machine translation (MT), such as Direct Preference Optimization (DPO), have shown strong gains but typically rely on carefully curated preference triplets and often struggle to generalize beyond their tuning domains. We propose Reinforcement Learning from Teacher-Model Refinement (RLfR), which replaces static triplets with on-policy, actor-conditioned refinements produced by a frozen teacher. At each step, the actor samples candidate translations, the teacher performs a minimal local edit of each draft, and the actor is reinforced to close the gap using a composite reward that combines scaled negative edit distance for lexical and structural fidelity with COMET for semantic adequacy. This formulation yields a stable, model-aware learning signal without requiring curated preference triplets, making it naturally scalable to many language pairs without additional data collection. Experiments on FLORES-200 (en <-> de/es/zh/ko/ja) show that RLfR consistently outperforms strong baselines, improving semantic quality and entity preservation across automatic, LLM-judge, and human evaluations.

t: DrugClaw and DrugAudit: A Primary-Source-Grounded Agent and Authority-Aware Benchmark for Drug-Information Question Answering
ab: Drug-information question answering is a high-stakes setting where hallucinated facts can mislead clinical decision-making and the provenance of each cited fact matters as much as the fact itself. We present DrugClaw, a multi-agent retrieval-augmented system that queries a registry of drug and pharmacovigilance skills via a reflection-driven state-machine workflow and returns answers grounded in primary regulatory or peer-reviewed records. We also contribute DrugAudit, a 3,772-item authority-aware benchmark with an evaluation panel that scores upstream-of-gold source match, token-level semantic snippet overlap, and citation faithfulness under a dual-judge LLM-as-judge protocol with inter-judge κ = 0.88 (almost-perfect). Across DrugAudit plus drug-related subsets of MedQA (751) and PubMedQA (512), DrugClaw is top-1 on every column of the headline table: composite Evidence Index under both judges, judge-mediated answer correctness, primary-source rate (0.918, +10.1 pp over next-best), faithfulness (0.887, +5.9 pp), MedQA (0.920), and PubMedQA (0.693).

t: BIRD-History: A Benchmark for History-Driven Text-to-SQL with Fine-Grained Knowledge Annotations
ab: While recent Large Language Model (LLM)-based text-to-SQL systems achieve impressive performance on standard benchmarks, they struggle when user queries implicitly rely on domain-specific knowledge, such as business logic, data conventions, and analytical practices, that is neither captured by the schema nor explicitly stated in the natural language question. Historical SQL query logs offer a valuable source of such knowledge, yet existing benchmarks do not adequately support evaluation of history-driven approaches. To address this gap, we introduce BIRD-History, a benchmark consisting of 1,393 tasks across 11 databases, designed to evaluate text-to-SQL systems’ ability to ground underspecified natural language questions using historical SQL scripts. Each task is annotated with ground-truth labels specifying which historical queries contain relevant knowledge and which SQL clauses encode it, enabling systematic evaluation of both retrieval effectiveness and knowledge utilization. Alongside the benchmark, we propose a plug-in retriever that extracts five types of external knowledge from historical SQL scripts, then retrieves and reranks relevant fragments for query generation. The retriever integrates seamlessly into existing few-shot text-to-SQL pipelines without requiring prompt modifications. Experiments demonstrate consistent improvements across four text-to-SQL systems, highlighting the value of leveraging historical query logs for handling underspecified queries. Dataset and code are open-sourced on https://github.com/zjuidg/BIRD-History.

t: When Retrieval Similarity Hurts: A Diagnostic Framework for Document Weighting in Black-Box RAG
ab: Document weighting is an underspecified bottleneck in black-box retrieval-augmented generation. Training-free systems inherit answer-aggregation weights from retrieval similarity, yet this proxy has not been systematically compared with evidence-based alternatives. We propose a unified two-parameter framework that generalizes REPLUG with an evidence term; it is training-free, black-box, and needs no large language model (LLM) calls beyond voting. Similarity-only (λ=0) and evidence-only (λ→∞) weighting are its limiting cases, so one interpolation parameter separates the retrieval prior from the evidence signal. We evaluate across 3 LLMs (7B–70B), 3 open-domain question-answering datasets (31,861 queries), and 3 off-the-shelf evidence types. Cross-encoder and embedding-stability evidence improve exact match in all 9 LLM–dataset cells, whereas natural language inference (NLI) fails as a weighting signal, to our knowledge the first systematic evidence of this failure mode. The similarity prior is largely redundant on NQ-Open and PopQA but helps on TriviaQA, where retriever scores track gold documents better; the pattern replicates under the E5 retriever, with smaller gains concentrated on long-tail PopQA. One default transfers across datasets and scales with minimal loss; calibration depends on signal type, not scale. Practically: prefer cross-encoder evidence, avoid NLI, and use vote mass for selective prediction; weighting itself adds sub-millisecond overhead.

t: Emotional Labor Strategy Preferences in LLM Personas
ab: Emotional labor is the effortful management of emotional displays to meet social or professional expectations. Personality traits have been correlated with emotional labor strategies, yet research on this link relies almost exclusively on self-report scales administered in only occupational settings. We investigate whether large language models injected with psychometrically grounded personas reproduce these personality-driven selection patterns across everyday social scenarios. We construct the first emotional labor strategy dataset of 500 socially situated events, each offering three behavioral choices corresponding to surface acting, deep acting, and genuine expression. We source 50 fictional characters from a large-scale personality repository and profile each through two parallel tracks: observer-rated bipolar adjective composites and in-character self-report items. Five LLMs evaluate all scenarios under both persona conditions. We find that models align more towards deep acting, and that Conscientiousness and Emotional Stability consistently predict this preference. Entropy analysis confirms that persona reliably influences the output and varies across models and emotions.

t: Beyond Accuracy: Evaluating Grounded Visual Evidence in Thinking with Images
a: Institute of Automation, Chinese Academy of Sciences, Zhongguancun Academy and University of Chinese Academy of Sciences
Zhongguancun Institute of Artificial Intelligence and Beijing Zhongguancun Academy
ab: Despite the remarkable progress of Vision-Language Models (VLMs) in adopting "Thinking-with-Images" capabilities, accurately evaluating the authenticity of their reasoning process remains a critical challenge. Existing benchmarks mainly rely on outcome-oriented accuracy, lacking the capability to assess whether models can accurately leverage fine-grained visual cues for multi-step reasoning. To address these limitations, we propose ViEBench, a process-verifiable benchmark designed to evaluate faithful visual reasoning. Comprising 200 multi-scenario high-resolution images with expert-annotated visual evidence, ViEBench uniquely categorizes tasks by difficulty into perception and reasoning dimensions, where reasoning tasks require utilizing localized visual details with prior knowledge. To establish comprehensive evaluation criteria, we introduce a dual-axis matrix that provides fine-grained metrics through four diagnostic quadrants, enabling transparent diagnosis of model behavior across varying task complexities. Our experiments yield several interesting observations: (1) VLMs can sometimes produce correct final answers despite grounding on irrelevant regions, and (2) they may successfully locate the correct evidence but still fail to utilize it to reach accurate conclusions. Our findings demonstrate that ViEBench can serve as a more explainable and practical benchmark for comprehensively evaluating the effectiveness of agentic VLMs.

t: Can LLMs Reliably Identify Causal Conclusions in Scientific Literature? A Multidisciplinary Evaluation
ab: Large language models (LLMs) hold promise for automating causal knowledge extraction, a fundamental component of scientific discovery, yet their ability to reliably identify causal claims in scientific literature remains poorly understood. Using 1,000 manually annotated abstracts spanning 20 disciplines, we evaluate eight frontier LLMs under four prompting strategies on a causal conclusion identification task. More elaborate prompting strategies do not necessarily improve performance, while open-weight models achieve competitive performance relative to proprietary models. LLMs systematically produce false-positive causal predictions on non-causal abstracts, with GPT-5 showing the most extreme bias, and Few-Shot prompting provides the most consistent calibration benefit. Performance varies substantially across disciplines with stronger and more stable results in biomedical fields. Our findings provide practical insights for using LLMs in scientific causal analysis and highlight calibration and domain variation as key challenges for advancing causal reasoning in scholarly text.

t: AgentRx: Diagnosing AI Agent Failures from Execution Trajectories
ab: AI agents often fail in ways that are difficult to localize because executions are probabilistic, long-horizon, multi-agent, and mediated by noisy tool outputs. We address this gap by manually annotating failed agent runs and release a novel benchmark of 170 trajectories across 11 diverse task settings, including structured API workflows, incident management, and open-ended web/file tasks. Each trajectory is annotated with a critical failure step and a category from a grounded-theory derived, cross-domain failure taxonomy. To mitigate the human cost of failure attribution, we present AgentRx, an \textit{automated diagnostic framework} that pinpoints the critical failure step in a failed agent trajectory. It synthesizes constraints, evaluates them step-by-step, and produces an auditable validation log of constraint violations with associated evidence; an LLM-based judge uses this log to localize the critical step and category. AgentRx improves step localization by 75% on average over prior work, while providing failure category attribution.

t: MCTS-Debater: Monte Carlo Tree Search based Rebuttal Generation for Competitive Debate
ab: Competitive debate is a multi-turn, zero-sum adversarial task with opposing stances that requires debaters to anticipate opponents’ counterarguments in real-time interactions and select strategies yielding long-term advantages. Existing large language model debate methods predominantly adopt a greedy generation paradigm that optimizes only the immediate effectiveness of the current rebuttal while lacking forward-looking planning for the overall debate trajectory. To address this limitation, we propose MCTS-Debater, a Monte Carlo Tree Search framework that models competitive debate as a Markov Decision Process. Rather than selecting a single locally optimal response, MCTS-Debater systematically simulates multi-step adversarial interactions under diverse rebuttal strategies, estimates their long-term expected win rates via tree search, and synthesizes the top-performing strategies into a coherent final rebuttal through multi-strategy fusion. Experimental results on the ORCHID and IQ2 datasets demonstrate that MCTS-Debater significantly outperforms existing baselines in logical validity, factual accuracy, and overall persuasiveness. Source code is provided in the supplementary material.

t: FHE-CodeEval: Benchmarking Large Language Models for Fully Homomorphic Encryption Code Generation
a: University of the Chinese Academy of Sciences
Institute of Computing Technology, Chinese Academy of Sciences and University of New South Wales
Institute of Computing Technology, Chinese Academy of Sciences
University of the Chinese Academy of Sciences and Institute of Computing Technology, Chinese Academy of Sciences
Institute of Computing Technology, Chinese Academy of Sciences
ab: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used for code generation, but their ability to program specialized cryptographic systems remains poorly understood. Cheon-Kim-Kim-Song (CKKS), a fully homomorphic encryption (FHE) scheme supporting approximate arithmetic over packed real- and complex-valued vectors, is particularly relevant to machine-learning workloads. Prior work has not systematically examined the CKKS-specific challenges of LLM-generated encrypted programs. To address this gap, we introduce FHE-CodeEval, a 46-case benchmark that evaluates three core challenges: packing, nonlinear approximation, and level/scale management, as well as how models coordinate decisions across them. We further introduce communication-aware efficiency, an FHE-specific metric comparing generated programs with compiler baselines using server-side runtime and ciphertext footprint.We evaluate eight recent proprietary and open-weight LLMs on FHE-CodeEval. Across all 46 cases, the best observed scores reach 51.7% Pass@1 and 69.6% Pass@5 with iterative execution feedback, but only 7.8% Pass@1 and 13.0% Pass@5 in the one-shot setting. For efficiency, even the best-performing model achieves a geometric-mean communication-aware efficiency of only 0.44 over its valid rollouts in the compiler-comparable subset. These results reveal a substantial gap between functional correctness and efficiency in LLM-generated CKKS programs. Code is available at https://github.com/qiuchuy/FHE-CodeEval.

t: Backfire-R1: Identifying and Mitigating Persuasion Vulnerabilities in LLM Agents
a: Tencent Youtu Lab and Fudan University
ab: With the rapid development of Large Language Models (LLMs), research related to LLM-based persuasion has become a hotspot in the field. However, existing studies mostly focus on enhancing LLM agents’ persuasive capabilities, while generally neglecting the issue of their vulnerability to persuasion. In this paper, we analyse the root causes of LLM agents’ vulnerability to persuasion and find that it mainly stems from two contradictions and limitations. First, the purpose of catering to human preferences in pre-training phase conflicts with the need to resist manipulation in persuasion scenarios. Second, LLMs are often restricted to play a helpful assistant during training, and the singularity of this personality setting makes it unusually easy to develop targeted persuasion techniques for them. To eliminate LLMs’ vulnerability to persuasion, we propose the Backfire-R1 framework, which helps LLMs build persuasion resistance and better align with user objective by enabling them to learn the reasoning logic of humans with different personalities in persuasion scenarios. Comprehensive experimental results show that, the proposed method significantly improves the persuasion robustness of LLM agents, reducing the opinion shift score by 62.36% while not impairing the model’s general capabilities. Code is now available at: https://github.com/super-jw/Backfire-R1.

t: REMP: A Structured Event-Probing Benchmark for Long-Horizon Role-Playing Dialogue
ab: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used in role-playing applications, yet evaluating whether they maintain character-consistent behavior over extended interactions remains challenging. Existing benchmarks mostly focus on short exchanges, static long-context inputs, or isolated aspects of role-playing, making long-horizon failures difficult to diagnose. We present REMP (Relationship-Emotion-Memory-Persona), a structured event-probing benchmark for long-horizon role-playing dialogue. REMP constructs multi-chapter dialogue trajectories from character profiles and embeds diagnostic probe events targeting persona consistency, emotional consistency, memory integrity, and relational continuity. We further introduce REMP-EVAL, an anchor-based multi-turn evaluation protocol that assesses model behavior after event triggers using dimension-specific references. The current release contains 160 characters organized into 80 dialogue trajectories, each averaging about 60 sessions and 800 turns. Experiments on 11 LLMs show that memory integrity and emotional consistency are the main bottlenecks, indicating that long-horizon role-playing requires not only long-context retrieval but also sustained affective and relational consistency.

t: Fine-grained stance cues and commonsense knowledge Integrated Reasoning Enhancement for Zero-shot Conversational Stance Detection
ab: Conversational stance detection aims to identify a speaker’s attitude toward a target in multi-turn dialogues, while the zero-shot setting requires generalization to unseen targets. Existing methods often rely on coarse-grained semantic representations or static knowledge injection, limiting their ability to capture subtle stance cues and utilize commonsense knowledge. To address this, we propose FIRE, a reasoning-enhanced framework that integrates fine-grained stance cues and commonsense knowledge for zero-shot conversational stance detection. FIRE adaptively mines sentiment, rhetorical, referential, cross-turn stance dependency cues and commonsense knowledge, and fuses them into explicit reasoning chains for target-aware stance inference. By combining supervised instruction tuning with reinforcement learning, FIRE further improves reasoning-chain quality and stance prediction. Experiments on benchmark datasets show that FIRE consistently outperforms strong baselines across different target types and LLM backbones, demonstrating the effectiveness of fine-grained cue modeling and knowledge-driven reasoning.

t: When Safety Routing Breaks: Understanding Alignment Fragility under Benign Fine-Tuning
ab: Benign fine-tuning severely weakens the safety alignment of large language models (LLMs), so we study why refusal behavior is so fragile. While prior work often attributes this failure to gradient conflict, we propose a fundamentally different Fisher-geometric explanation: safety Fisher is low-rank, and alignment makes the safety geometry flatter while preserving an output-routing pathway. After 100 benign fine-tuning examples, this pathway is selectively re-sharpened in output-side MLP modules, explaining the asymmetric fragility: safety can collapse to high attack success rates, while general utility degrades mildly.The routing view also explains why few safety examples can restore refusal behavior, indicating that internal safety-relevant representations are preserved. Finally, we show that LoRA and ASAM mitigate early collapse by suppressing output-side sharpness, but their protection weakens at larger fine-tuning scales. Overall, safety failure is best understood as a disruption of a low-rank output-routing mechanism.

t: Mind the Gap: Theory-of-Mind-Grounded Friction for Epistemic Alignment
ab: Productive dialogue alignment requires distinguishing surface coordination (acknowledgments and smooth task progression) from epistemic alignment (convergence of belief states); standard preference-based methods typically optimize response-level preferences without explicitly modeling the latter. We operationalize Theory-of-Mind (ToM) inference as a control signal within Frictive Policy Optimization by extracting, at each referring expression, a four-part belief structure: the speaker’s intended referent, the addressee’s interpretation, and each participant’s model of the other’s belief. This makes friction mechanically computable from epistemic-state comparisons, capturing silent divergence, where both participants proceed confidently while grounding to different referents. We evaluate the signal at two levels. At the representation level, ablating the second-order channel reduces misunderstanding recall from 65% to 26%. At the policy level, reward-shaping (FAR) and trust-region (FTR) variants improve intervention F1 and warranted-context calibration over DPO, with Brier scores independently supporting the calibration gains. Across three training runs, FAR and FTR remain substantially more stable, whereas DPO varies widely and can degrade intervention competence already present in the base policy. Thus, ToM-grounded friction provides a trainable signal for context-sensitive intervention under referential belief divergence.

t: PRISM: Post-Training LLM Pruning via Residual Importance Signal Merging and Intra-Block Sparsity Allocation
ab: Post-training pruning compresses Large Language Models (LLMs) without full-model retraining, but performance degrades sharply at high sparsity. We identify two limitations in existing methods: local importance estimates miss global spectral structure, and uniform within-block sparsity ignores heterogeneous sensitivity across transformer projections. We propose PRISM, a post-training pruning framework with training-free mask construction and optional fixed-mask reconstruction optimization. PRISM augments activation-based scoring with two adaptive-rank SVD-derived signals for principal-subspace and residual-aware importance, combines the factors through parameter-free CV-based fusion, and allocates sparsity non-uniformly across attention and MLP projections using a gradient-weighted matrix-level sensitivity proxy. Across six Qwen3 and LLaMA models, PRISM consistently outperforms existing pruning baselines, yielding up to 16.8% relative improvement in WikiText-2 perplexity under the evaluated sparsity settings.

t: VocMoE: Vocabulary-Guided Mixture-of-Experts for Korean Medical Language Models
ab: In Korean medical LLMs, domain-trained models underperform General LLMs of comparable parameter scale. We attribute this *paradoxical failure* to a *cascading two-bottleneck* structure: tokenizer over-fragmentation (*Fragmentation bottleneck, B1*) compounded by a learning-stage representation-alignment failure (*Alignment bottleneck, B2*). Using the Korean medical domain as a case study, we diagnose this paradox and propose **VocMoE**, which is designed to address both bottlenecks: DVE selects domain vocabulary from a medical BERT via an information-theoretic score, and MoDE uses the DVE output (the partition of token ids) as the vocabulary-conditioned, deterministic routing key of the MoE FFN. In this view, the vocabulary partition itself serves as a routing prior, shifting routing from hidden-state learning to vocabulary identity. MediKo-9B-A4B reaches simultaneous SOTA on KorMedMCQA (**57.5**, +14.8 pt), KMMLU Medical, and HAE-RAE, while MediKo-4B-A1B (active 1.69B) surpasses Qwen3-8B (8B) and KULLM3 (10.7B) on KorMedMCQA, updating the active-parameter efficiency frontier.

t: Breaking the Structural Identity: Personalized Federated LoRA Fine-tuning under Rank Heterogeneity
ab: Large Language Models (LLMs) have achieved remarkable success across diverse domains, but their adaptation to privacy-sensitive, distributed datasets remains a challenge. While Federated Learning (FL) combined with Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA) provides a resource efficient paradigm for collaborative fine-tuning, practical deployments are hindered by the dual challenges of resource heterogeneity and data heterogeneity. Existing rank-heterogeneous methods primarily focus on bridging dimension mismatches for aggregation but typically provide a unified global model for all clients sharing the same rank, failing to capture client-specific features in non-IID scenarios. In this paper, we propose FedRoRA (Federated Rank-wise Personalized LoRA), a novel framework that enables fine-grained personalization within rank-heterogeneous federations. FedRoRA decouples adaptation into shared global directions and personalized rank-wise magnitudes governed by learnable diagonal scales. On the server side, it extracts a global subspace via singular value decomposition (SVD) and redistributes client-specific initializations through a personalized projection and top-selection mechanism. Extensive experiments on NLU and NLG benchmarks demonstrate that FedRoRA consistently outperforms state-of-the-art methods.

t: BitNet Text Embeddings
a: National Engineering Research Center of New Electronic Publishing Technologies and Peking University
ab: LLM-based text embedders have substantially improved retrieval and semantic representation quality, but their deployment remains costly: large backbone models slow down embedding inference, while high-dimensional full-precision embeddings impose substantial storage and bandwidth overhead on large-scale indexes. In this paper, we present BITEMBED, an extreme low-bit framework for LLM-based text embedding that jointly targets encoding efficiency and vector storage. BITEMBED converts pretrained LLM backbones into BitNet-style embedding encoders with ternary weights, quantized activations, and lightweight normalization refinement. The converted model is adapted to representation learning through continual contrastive pre-training, followed by supervised contrastive fine-tuning with both similarity-distribution distillation and attention-relation distillation from a full-precision teacher. Beyond quantizing the encoder, BITEMBED further trains output embeddings to support multiple storage precisions meeting different storage needs in various scenarios. Experiments on MMTEB (eng, v2) with Qwen3-0.6B and Gemma3-270M show that BITEMBED is largely comparable to full precision teacher embedders. Moreover, BITEMBED flexibly obtains text embeddings of various precisions, achieving a trade-off between performance and storage cost.

t: MIRAGE: Stealthy Visual Prompt Injection for Vulnerability Detection in Web Agents
ab: Multimodal Large Language Model (MLLM)-based web agents provide practical, high-precision solutions for visual browser automation; however, they inherently expand the attack surface, introducing novel vision-based vulnerabilities. Existing adversarial evaluations targeting these agents frequently rely on permissive threat models and visually conspicuous artifacts. In this paper, we investigate a constrained vulnerability detection setting: a trusted web platform where the evaluator acts solely as an unprivileged third party (e.g., a merchant or advertiser) controlling only a semantically legitimate, spatially constrained region, such as an ad slot, a sponsored card, or a localized widget. Operating under these realistic constraints, we propose MIRAGE, a novel visual indirect prompt injection framework for targeted next-action hijacking. Our approach leverages diffusion models to generate perceptually benign adversarial images strictly confined to the attacker-controlled boundaries permitted by the trusted service provider. To maximize attack efficacy within such a restrictive setting, we introduce a robust optimization technique combining curvature-aware adversarial diffusion guidance with sparse, dark-pixel residual perturbations. Comprehensive evaluations against prominent MLLM web agent frameworks, specifically SeeAct and OpenClaw, empirically demonstrate the potency, realism, and stealth of our proposed MIRAGE. Code is available at https://github.com/EricDai0/MIRAGE.

t: Non-binary bottom-up constituency parsing without arity actions
a: Korea Advanced Institute of Science & Technology
ab: Non-binary bottom-up constituency parsing commonly uses arity-specific reductions such as \textsc{Reduce-}X\#k, which jointly specify the mother label and number of children. We show that arity need not be a primitive transition parameter. The proposed parser predicts the mother label separately and identifies the ordered child sequence from a delimiter-bounded stack configuration. In every well-formed reducible configuration, the active delimiter, label marker, and intervening completed items uniquely determine the reduction domain and hence its arity. This factorization removes label–arity-specific reduction actions while preserving direct construction of the original non-binary trees. Controlled experiments on PTB and CTB show that the delimiter-guided parser closely tracks an arity-specific baseline while using a substantially smaller action inventory. Its predicted trees retain the gold branching profile without systematic collapse at higher arities. The smaller inventory is obtained at the cost of longer derivations and boundary-sensitive errors involving delimiter insertion, preservation, and consumption.

t: NaviRank: LLM-Informed Latent Space Navigation Enhances Reasoning-Intensive Information Retrieval
ab: Retrieve-then-rerank pipelines restrict large language models (LLMs) to a fixed top-k candidate set, making their reasoning ability fundamentally limited by the recall ceiling of the first-stage dense retriever. On reasoning-intensive retrieval, we make two observations: first, relevant documents missed by dense top-k retrieval are frequently reachable within a few hops on the native approximate nearest neighbor (ANN) graph; second, LLM relevance judgments can identify high-yield anchors whose neighborhoods contain these missed documents. Based on these findings, we propose NaviRank, an LLM-guided navigation framework that performs greedy expansion over the HNSW graph: it uses highly parallel pointwise LLM judgments to steer anchor selection and local expansion, followed by listwise calibration for final ranking. Experiments on BRIGHT show that NaviRank achieves 27.0 NDCG@10, while establishing the strongest accuracy–efficiency Pareto frontier in both token usage and latency among all evaluated methods.

t: Beyond Single Vector: Query-Aware Multi-Perspective Document Embeddings for Retrieval
a: National Engineering Research Center of New Electronic Publishing Technologies and Peking University
ab: Recently, large language models (LLMs) have demonstrated excellent performance on general information retrieval tasks, which encode query and document into an embedding vector representing semantic information respectively. However, single-vector representations often fail to capture the multifaceted semantics of informative documents, limiting the adaptability across diverse scenarios. To address this, we propose PRISM (multi-PeRspectIve Semantic inforMation retrieval), a novel framework that leverages LLMs’ implicit reasoning capabilities to extract and structure diverse semantic perspectives. PRISM introduces query-aware semantic fusion to dynamically integrate relevant perspectives during retrieval through weighted query embedding interactions. Furthermore, we propose the contrastive semantic diversification, a training mechanism that disperses semantic embeddings to maximize perspective diversity. Evaluated on the English retrieval subsets of massive multilingual text embedding benchmark (MMTEB), PRISM achieves state-of-the-art general results compared with models trained exclusively on public data.

t: Stop Rolling the Dice: Active Group Relative Policy Optimization via Intrinsic Metacognition
a: Hong Kong University of Science and Technology (Guangzhou)
ab: Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) is an attractive reinforcement learning paradigm for Large Reasoning Models because its groupwise relative advantages eliminate the need for a value network, but its efficiency is severely limited by zero-variance queries whose rollouts are uniformly correct or uniformly incorrect and therefore consume expensive Chain-of-Thought generation without providing useful learning signals. Existing remedies typically rely on offline difficulty labels or external capability trackers, which either fail to follow the model’s rapidly evolving competence or compromise the end-to-end simplicity of GRPO. We propose Active-GRPO, a prompt-free extension that equips the policy with intrinsic fuzzy metacognition via a lightweight confidence head attached to the final prefill representation. The head predicts ordinal confidence bins and is jointly calibrated against empirical rollout outcomes through a dual-objective optimization framework. It further enables a multi-criterion voting mechanism that filters uninformative queries before rollout generation, thereby concentrating compute on samples near the learning boundary with negligible overhead and without perturbing the reasoning distribution. Experiments on mathematical and logical reasoning benchmarks show that Active-GRPO reduces training computation while improving both reasoning accuracy and intrinsic calibration quality.

t: PCoAD: The Pharmaceutical Certificate of Analysis Dataset Based on LLMs Validation and Calibration
ab: Artificial intelligence is now widely applied in drug discovery and development, accelerating the entry of novel pharmaceuticals into clinical practice. As the variety of drugs expands, the workload for pharmaceutical inspection has increased significantly, making the demand for automated verification of pharmaceutical inspection results increasingly urgent. However, current research lacks reliable evaluation methods and datasets. To address this issue, we construct a Pharmaceutical Certificate of Analysis Dataset (PCoAD) based on large language model validation and correction. This dataset comprises 4,272 manually verified pharmaceutical certificates of analysis (PCoAs) based on Chinese and U.S. pharmacopoeias, comprehensively testing the ability of model to verify pharmaceutical inspection processes. Based on PCoAD, we propose the Multi-Agent Cooperation based on Adaptive Retrieval (MACAR) framework. This framework employs text chunking, adaptive retrieval, and inference to validate PCoAs. Experimental results demonstrate that MACAR outperforms multiple state-of-the-art methods across various types of tasks.

t: Seeing Failure In Advance: Pre-Generation Failure Diagnosis for Multi-Modal Retrieval-Augmented-Generation
ab: Multimodal retrieval-augmented generation (MMRAG) systems can fail even when relevant evidence is retrieved, exposing a gap between retrieval and generation. We formulate MMRAG failure diagnosis as an online single-fire decision problem over prefill hidden states, which is distinct from static probing of model internals or post-hoc self-correction. Across InfoSeek, E-VQA, and VISA, we show that hidden states encode both failure occurrence and failure type, with failure detection reaching around 90% accuracy and recall on InfoSeek and E-VQA. We further introduce a Fire-Then-Type prober that separates failure detection from failure typing, improving typed diagnosis over direct classification. Finally, our method matches the response accuracy of final-layer repair on InfoSeek and E-VQA while diagnosing before answer decoding.
