This conflict creates opposing gradients on the same behaviors and can trap training in a local trade-off where further compression harms accuracy while accuracy recovery reintroduces verbose reasoning. At the model-decision level, we refer to the resulting failure mode as entropy conflict: the policy fails to fully collapse onto concise trajectories because accuracy-oriented updates keep restoring broader support over long-correct reasoning paths. To address this issue, we propose an entropy-guided training framework. Instead of forcing a mixed objective to follow an unstable path toward the final efficient-output set, we first contract the policy to a short-output set and then expand from this compact regime to recover accuracy and robustness. Experiments on multiple mathematical reasoning benchmarks show that our method achieves performance comparable to the original model using only about 25% of its reasoning tokens.

t: Write Policy Determines Source Retention in External FIFO Memory: A Delayed-Copy Diagnostic
ab: External hidden-state memories can extend Transformers beyond local attention windows, but the write policy deciding which states enter finite memory is often treated as an implementation detail. We study this factor with a controlled delayed-copy diagnostic using a windowed Transformer augmented with an external FIFO hidden-state memory. Under forced masking, query-to-source attention is blocked, removing this shortcut and making source retention directly testable. We define a capacity boundary as the minimum memory size needed to reach a fixed copy-accuracy threshold. We find that write policy changes this boundary predictably under constrained FIFO memory: an idealized source-only policy, which assumes that relevant states are identifiable at write time, yields an approximately delay-invariant boundary near the source length, whereas an unfiltered prefix-all policy induces a delay-dependent boundary that grows with written non-source content. Intermediate partial-prefix write policies produce intermediate boundaries, while source-pinned controls and memory diagnostics show that prefix-all degradation is dominated by FIFO eviction of source states rather than retrieval interference from retained non-source states alone. A symbolic key–value retrieval diagnostic shows the same qualitative trend. Within this controlled setting, our results highlight write policy as a central variable in evaluating finite FIFO external-memory Transformers.

t: When Does Generating More Help? Disentangling Fixed-Source Synthesis from Source Expansion in Synthetic Data Scaling
ab: Synthetic data can be scaled along two routes: Source Expansion (SE), which enlarges the source by adding seed materials or generators, and Fixed-Source Synthesis (FSS), which holds the source fixed and scales the generation budget. Existing scaling studies typically expand the source as the data grows, conflating SE with FSS and leaving FSS underexplored. We isolate FSS within a standard rejection sampling (RS) pipeline and derive a scaling form for it from how repeated sampling covers a fixed source. Empirically, fit on low budgets, the form predicts performance at the held-out highest budget for every evaluated teacher–student pair. At matched total-sample budgets, SE and FSS are comparable at small budgets, but adding seed questions outperforms spending the same budget on more responses at large budgets. Within FSS, neither synthesizing additional questions from the existing seeds nor varying the synthesis protocol consistently outperforms plain RS across matched budgets. FSS is thus a bounded scaling axis and a controlled setting for comparing synthesis protocols. We will release our code and data to facilitate further research.

t: Efficient Language-to-Vision Feature Injection for Referring Single-Object Tracking
a: University of Chinese Academy of Sciences
University of Chinese Academy of Sciences
University of the Chinese Academy of Sciences
Technology and Engineering Center for Space Utilization, Chinese Academy of Sciences
Technology and Engineering Center for Space Utilization, Chinese Academy of Sciences
ab: Referring single-object tracking enables language-grounded target initialization and subsequent tracking by jointly leveraging semantic cues and visual templates. The core difficulty is to use language differently across stages: it is indispensable for grounding but can induce semantic drift during tracking when overemphasized. Meanwhile, current methods often require costly vision-language alignment training. We present LVTrack, a pure transformer framework that introduces a mode-conditioned Gated Feature Injector to adaptively regulate textual guidance and alleviate semantic drift. Together with targeted adaptations, it directly harnesses a frozen vision-language pretrained model, greatly reducing training cost and preserving strong language understanding. To further improve temporal localization, LVTrack integrates hybrid relative-absolute positional encodings with a lightweight memory mechanism and optimizes autoregressive box prediction using a Gaussian-smoothed KL loss. Extensive experiments on standard benchmarks demonstrate that LVTrack achieves strong performance.

t: CreaMem: A Scene-Aware Memory Architecture for Personalized Agents
a: Mohamed bin Zayed University of Artificial Intelligence
ab: Long-term memory is a core capability for personalized LLM agents. To support it, existing memory systems organize information using various criteria such as topic segments or summary hierarchies. However, we identify two major limitations in these designs. First, they lack scene awareness: memories from unrelated life scenes share the same retrieval space, which inflates the search space and introduces cross-scene interference. Second, they encode each memory from a single perspective, making it difficult to retrieve complementary views of the same event. In this paper, we propose the CreaMem architecture, which enables scene-aware memory organization by partitioning memory into several Life Scene Memories to reduce cross-scene interference at retrieval. Within each memory, entries are dual-coded from both episodic and trait-based perspectives. To go beyond the single perspective and achieve cross-memory synergy, we further devise a per-memory balanced sampling strategy at retrieval time. Extensive experiments on two long-term memory benchmarks show that CreaMem improves QA accuracy across all evaluation metrics, with particularly large gains on multi-hop reasoning performance, validating scene-aware partitioning and cross-memory synergy.

t: ToolDF: Tool-Integrated Reasoning for Mixed-Authenticity Audio Deepfake Detection
a: Korea University and Korea Electronics Technology Institute
National Forensic Service, Republic of Korea
ab: Audio deepfake detection is commonly formulated as clip-level binary classification of single-domain audio. However, real-world manipulated audio can exhibit mixed authenticity, where genuine and manipulated cues coexist across temporal transitions, overlapping sources, or both. This setting requires not only detecting manipulated audio but also localizing the components that provide evidence for the decision. We propose ToolDF, a tool-integrated reasoning framework for mixed-authenticity audio deepfake detection. ToolDF employs an audio large language model as an orchestrator trained with supervised tool-use trajectories. It adaptively analyzes the audio scene, selectively performs source separation, routes components to domain-specific experts, and aggregates their evidence into an interpretable verdict. We further introduce a mixed-authenticity ADD benchmark covering temporal transitions, acoustic overlaps, and hybrid mixtures. Experimental results show that ToolDF achieves the best overall performance on composite-type detection, achieving macro-F1 gains of 3.72 and 14.39 points over the strongest monolithic baseline and a fixed pipeline, respectively, while providing interpretable evidence localized to temporal regions and acoustic sources. Our source code and dataset are publicly available online at https://github.com/rlataewoo/tooldf.

t: CE-GAD: Curriculum-Efficient On-Policy Adversarial Distillation of Large Language Models
a: LinkedIn / Other Research Labs / Research Teams
ab: Generative adversarial distillation (GAD) provides on-policy feedback for black-box distillation by training a discriminator that ranks teacher and student responses to the same prompt. While effective, GAD is also costly: every step pays for a discriminator update, an actor update over the full response, and the indirect cost of recovering whenever the discriminator and the actor progress at incompatible rates. We argue that the right way to make GAD efficient is not to make individual updates cheaper but to decide **when each update is worth its cost**. We introduce **curriculum-efficient GAD (CE-GAD)**, an adaptive recipe that monitors a small set of training signals and uses them to:- (i) skip discriminator updates that would not change the reward, - (ii) constrain actor updates and prune per-token gradients to the subset that actually carries signal, and - (iii) rescale rewards and normalize advantages to preserve within-batch contrast under saturation.Evaluations across four models from two open-source families (Qwen2.5 at 3B/7B/14B and Llama-3.2-3B) demonstrate that CE-GAD matches or surpasses vanilla GAD on quality while winning on 12 out of 16 individual benchmark configurations. Specifically, on Qwen2.5-7B, CE-GAD improves the average score by up to **+3%** relative compared to the base model, while reducing per-step wall-clock time by up to **8x** relative to vanilla GAD.

t: Logic Tree: Topology-Aware Backtracking for DeepResearch Agents
a: Zhejiang Key Laboratory of Intelligent Medical Decision Support and Zhejiang University
Zhejiang University and ZJU-Hangzhou Global Scientific and Technological Innovation Center
ab: Autonomous large language model (LLM) agents have shown strong potential for open-ended information-seeking tasks. However, existing agent frameworks primarily rely on sequential execution, making them vulnerable to error accumulation in long-horizon reasoning. Recent plan-and-execute approaches partially alleviate this issue, but their fixed planning strategies still struggle to recover from intermediate failures. We propose Logic Tree, a non-linear agentic reasoning framework formulated as a Directed Acyclic Graph (DAG). Instead of following a fixed plan with sequential execution, Logic Tree models complex task solving as a dynamically evolving and recoverable graph search process. The framework decomposes queries into parallel execution branches and incorporates a two-level self-correction mechanism. Local backtracking performs targeted rollback to repair failed reasoning states, while global replanning revises high-level execution strategies and preserves verified intermediate conclusions through a knowledge sanitation process. Experiments on BrowseComp, GAIA, and XBench show that Logic Tree consistently outperforms both sequential and plan-and-execute baselines. Further ablation studies demonstrate that combining DAG-based parallel execution with dynamic error recovery substantially improves robustness in long-horizon research tasks.

t: KnowMT-Bench: Benchmarking Knowledge-Intensive Long-Form Question Answering in Multi-Turn Dialogues
a: The Hong Kong University of Science and Technology (Guangzhou)
The Hong Kong University of Science and Technology
The Hong Kong University of Science and Technology (Guangzhou) and Hong Kong University of Science and Technology
ab: Multi-Turn Long-Form Question Answering (MT-LFQA) is a key application paradigm of Large Language Models (LLMs) in knowledge-intensive domains. However, existing benchmarks are limited to single-turn dialogue, while multi-turn dialogue benchmarks typically assess other orthogonal capabilities rather than knowledge-intensive factuality. To bridge this critical gap, we introduce **KnowMT-Bench**, a new benchmark designed to systematically evaluate MT-LFQA for LLMs across knowledge-intensive fields, including medicine, finance, and law. To faithfully assess the model’s real-world performance, KnowMT-Bench employs a dynamic evaluation setting where models generate their own multi-turn dialogue histories given logically progressive question sequences. Our experiments on a diverse suite of LLMs show a clear degradation in both factual capability and information delivery efficiency in multi-turn dialogue. We further probe the underlying causes and investigate mitigation strategies spanning domain-specific finetuning, active context denoising, and RAG. The results show domain-dependent gains from finetuning, while active context denoising and RAG more consistently mitigate these issues, with RAG notably reversing this performance degradation. These findings underscore the importance of our benchmark for evaluating LLMs’ conversational factual capabilities in real-world applications.

t: SCIT: Testing Causal Cache Carriers in Latent Chain-of-Thought Models
a: HKUST(GZ) and The Hong Kong University of Science and Technology
ab: Latent chain-of-thought models move intermediate reasoning into continuous states, obscuring which internal object causally carries a computation. We introduce SCIT, the Suffix Cache Interchange Test, which patches exact source–recipient counterfactuals and crosses cache-segment sufficiency with K/V splits, hidden-state and semantic-source controls, decoded validation, and matched corruption. In GPT-2 arithmetic, counterfactual transfer concentrates in value-cache suffix trajectories rather than hidden states, keys, answer slots, or single-token triggers. Full sufficiency-and-necessity closure holds only for the main CODI-GPT2 checkpoint; the Sim-CoT-style reproduction supports sufficiency and decoded transfer but not necessity. Across broader competent cells, arithmetic-like GPT-2/1B tasks retain latent-tail value/KV transfer, whereas 8B and repaired non-arithmetic tasks shift to prompt-prefix or full-cache K/V; ungated cells receive no call. SCIT thus provides a cache-level diagnostic, a checkpoint-specific arithmetic mechanism, and a competence-gated carrier map—not a universal latent-tail claim. Code: https://github.com/YIDING4869/scit-emnlp-2026

t: CoT-Lock: Embedding Logic Fingerprints into the Chain-of-Thought of Large Reasoning Models
ab: Large Reasoning Models (LRMs) are valuable intellectual property due to their substantial training and alignment costs, creating a need for reliable ownership verification under black-box access, where a verifier can only query a suspect model and inspect its returned output. Existing trigger–response fingerprints are easy to test but are often weakly coupled with Chain-of-Thought (CoT) reasoning and can be fragile under paraphrasing or post-hoc model modifications. We propose CoT-Lock, a reasoning-mediated fingerprinting framework that casts ownership verification as a structured conflict-resolution task. CoT-Lock constructs verification queries in which a default semantic constraint is superseded only by a higher-priority meta-override rule, training the model to resolve fingerprint activation through priority-based arbitration. Our primary ownership test is output-only on confidential held-out probes; when reasoning traces are visible, trace-level verification further checks the expected arbitration process. Experiments on representative reasoning architectures show that CoT-Lock achieves stable black-box verification while preserving reasoning ability with minimal performance degradation, low false positives, and improved robustness against paraphrasing, fine-tuning, pruning, and quantization. Our code is available at https://github.com/acang425/CoT-Lock.

t: Beyond Redundancy: Information-Conserving Semantic Packaging for Vision-Language Models
ab: Vision-Language Models (VLMs) achieve strong multimodal understanding but suffer from high inference costs due to redundant vision tokens. Existing hard-pruning methods discard low-scoring tokens directly, inevitably sacrificing fine-grained visual context. We propose SPack, a training-free token compression method that reframes pruning as information-energy redistribution rather than deletion. Instead of discarding pruned tokens, SPack transfers their semantic mass to retained tokens, enforcing a global principle we term Information Energy Conservation (IEC): the total information contained in redundant tokens is strictly conserved and fully transferred as information gain to the retained components. To realize this conservation, we introduce Optimal Transport (OT) theory, which treats removed energy as mass density and retained tokens as receiver slots. Solving the optimal transport plan under the Wasserstein distance yields a minimum-cost mapping that precisely transfers geometric structure and higher-order moments according to semantic affinity. Concretely, we estimate token importance via relation attention, semantic affinity, and value-space energy, then adaptively route pruned tokens to multiple retained tokens using OT, producing hyper-dense tokens that preserve both local semantics and global context. Extensive experiments demonstrate that SPack consistently achieves a superior accuracy-efficiency trade-off compared to state-of-the-art methods. The code will be released upon acceptance.

t: Lexical Coupling in GUI Element Grounding: Sentence Embeddings Track Labels across Mobile and Web
ab: GUI grounding evaluations often treat high instruction–element embedding similarity as evidence of semantic grounding. Across three mobile and web benchmarks (AndroidControl, MoTIF, Mind2Web), we show this interpretation is frequently confounded by visible-label recovery: no off-the-shelf encoder significantly exceeds a BM25 lexical baseline at top-1, and encoder hit@1 is predictable from lexical rank, candidate-pool size, and label type at AUC 0.85–0.88. On AndroidControl, oracle fusion could lift R@1 by +12.8 pp, but standard reciprocal-rank fusion of the same signals instead degrades it by 1.4 pp. One epoch of in-domain contrastive fine-tuning of a small 22M encoder then beats every lexical and zero-shot baseline by +13.6 pp, localising the failure to off-the-shelf encoders rather than dense retrieval. These results suggest that, on its own, embedding similarity is not sufficient evidence of semantic GUI grounding beyond visible-label recovery; it should be reported against lexical controls and label-type stratification.

t: CAPO-SLT: Confidence-Aware Policy Optimization for Stable Sign Language Translation Generation
ab: Recent sign language translation methods have advanced visual-language alignment, yet autoregressive generation remains vulnerable to unstable policy updates under ambiguous visual evidence. Such instability may cause locally plausible continuations to accumulate into sentence-level semantic deviations, especially when reinforcement learning is used with noisy reward and advantage estimates. Existing PPO-style policy optimization applies confidence-agnostic clipping bounds to all generated tokens, which limits its ability to distinguish between over-amplified confident predictions and low-probability tokens that may still carry useful corrective signals. To address this issue, we propose CAPO-SLT, a reinforcement learning based framework for stable sign language translation generation. CAPO introduces a confidence-aware policy optimization strategy that adapts the upper clipping bound according to old-policy token probability. It applies more conservative updates to high-confidence predictions while preserving update capacity for low-probability positive-advantage tokens. In addition, CAPO caps negative-advantage updates to improve robustness under noisy supervision. This design provides a simple drop-in replacement for standard clipping and stabilizes generation-stage optimization without changing the underlying visual encoder or reward function. Experiments on Chinese and American sign language benchmarks show consistent improvements over pose-based baselines under the same input setting, suggesting that CAPO-SLT provides an effective optimization strategy for stable sign language translation generation.

t: EntangleCodec: A Unified Discrete Audio Tokenizer via Semantic-Acoustic Entanglement
ab: Audio tokenizers serve as the discrete interface between continuous audio and Audio Language Models (ALMs), but existing tokenizers often struggle to support both understanding and generation. Reconstruction-oriented codecs preserve acoustic fidelity but lack rich semantics, while semantic-aware tokenizers typically rely on separate semantic and acoustic streams, introducing redundancy or misalignment.We propose EntangleCodec, a unified discrete audio tokenizer that learns caption-aligned semantic-acoustic representations before quantization. By aligning audio with rich captions rather than ASR transcripts, EntangleCodec captures linguistic content, speaker identity, emotion, prosody, and acoustic scenes within a compact token stream. A flow-matching diffusion decoder further enables high-quality reconstruction across speech, music, and general audio.EntangleCodec achieves reconstruction quality competitive with specialized codecs, outperforms all codec-based baselines on audio understanding by up to +7.4% on MMAR, and supports both TTS and TTA generation in a unified framework. Furthermore, EntangleCodec-based audio language models demonstrate strong scaling behavior: even at 0.6B parameters, the model surpasses specialized continuous-representation LLMs with over 13B parameters across three benchmarks using 22x fewer parameters; scaling to 8B further establishes new state-of-the-art results on MMAR, highlighting that representation quality is as critical as model scale in audio language modeling. Code and model weights are available at https://anonymous.4open.science/r/EntangleCodec-BA01.

t: SCHEDBench: A Benchmark for Evaluating LLM Constraint Faithfulness in Natural-Language Combinatorial Scheduling
ab: This paper introduces **SCHEDBench**, a natural-language benchmark for evaluating **combinatorial scheduling** constraint faithfulness under surface-form variation. Grounded in canonical scheduling instances and solver-derived feasibility and optimality, SCHEDBench assesses whether large language models (**LLMs**) generate schedules with the same constraint-feasible behavior across varied natural-language (NL) surface forms. SCHEDBench spans 1,132 instances across job-shop scheduling problems (JSP), single and multi-mode resource-constrained project scheduling problems (RCPSP), nurse rostering/scheduling, and curriculum timetabling problems of varying difficulty. Instances are templated into natural language problems using domain-specific templates, themed entities, lexical-syntactic template rephrasing, and constraint-level surface-form variation—with reference solutions verified for feasibility and objective optimality. Across thirteen frontier and open-weight LLMs, we find that models are not reliably invariant to semantically equivalent renderings of the same scheduling problem. Surface-form variation reduces feasibility and induces above-noise shifts in per-instance hard-constraint violations on matched instances. Among the tested isolated axes, constraint reordering yields the clearest above-noise sensitivity.

t: Implicit Hierarchical Modeling for Cross-System Legal Case Retrieval
ab: Legal Case Retrieval (LCR) identifies relevant precedent cases to support legal reasoning and sentencing. A core challenge for cross-system LCR is the structural divergence between legal systems: civil-law systems provide explicit statutory hierarchies but lack inter-case citations, while common-law systems offer rich citation networks but lack uniform codified semantic hierarchies. Existing methods exploit only one side of this divide, remaining system-specific. We propose DSLaw, which unifies both systems by implicitly modeling hierarchical semantics through residual quantization and using the resulting discrete representations as semantic anchors for cross-case graph reasoning. By progressively decomposing legal semantics from coarse concepts to fine-grained distinctions, DSLaw constructs implicit connections even without explicit citations. Experiments on COLIEE2025 (common law) and ELAM (civil law) show DSLaw consistently outperforms strong baselines, while joint training further validates cross-system generalization. The implementation is provided at https://github.com/KDEGroup/DSLaw.

t: MCTL: Meta-Cognitive Tool-Learning Framework for Multimodal Fake News Detection
ab: Multimodal fake news proliferates on social media, yet its verification is hindered by context sparsity and analytical heterogeneity: deceptive posts often hinge on implicit social background, while distinct misinformation patterns demand different verification strategies. Existing methods rely on either representation-driven classifiers or LLM-based retrieval-augmented and tool-using pipelines, which act as opaque black boxes or follow rigid, predefined tool chains, failing to adapt reasoning to diverse news and yielding weakly grounded, uninterpretable decisions. To this end, we propose MCTL, a Meta-Cognitive Tool-Learning Framework that reformulates detection from static classification into in-context cognitive orchestration with dynamically planned tool-based reasoning. Specifically, MCTL retrieves cross-modal contextual evidence as external memory to compensate for context sparsity, performs meta-cognitive planning to construct a sample-specific Directed Acyclic Graph (DAG) reasoning blueprint, routes specialized tools along the DAG, and fuses conflicting judgments via consensus-aware arbitration, enabling context-grounded, sample-adaptive, and traceable verification. Extensive experiments demonstrate that MCTL consistently outperforms recent state-of-the-art agentic and RAG baselines, confirming its effectiveness and reliability.

t: Um, Actually: Timely and Calibrated Fact-Checking with DIVER
ab: Fact verification pipelines are often unrealistic: they assume full-input access, operate on isolated atomic claims, and overlook the central question of when a system should act under partial evidence. We introduce DIVER (Deliberative and Iterative fact VERification), an LLM-based framework for calibrated incremental fact-checking. DIVER incrementally extracts verifiable atomic claims from progressively revealed input, retrieves and refines evidence through iterative web search, and triggers a correction as soon as a claim is reliably refuted; if no such trigger occurs, it performs a passage-level revision over the full input to recover missed errors. Across standard fact-checking benchmarks, DIVER outperforms strong LLM-based verification pipelines, with especially large gains on retrieval-intensive settings. We further introduce UmActually, a real-world benchmark built from the Internet game Um, Actually, to evaluate not only whether a system finds an error, but whether it does so at the right time. On UmActually, DIVER reports the strongest end-to-end results while typically buzzing close to the earliest valid decision point, supporting its effectiveness for calibrated incremental fact-checking.

t: Neural Procedural Memory: Empowering LLM Agents with Implicit Activation Steering
a: Institute of automation, Chinese academy of science, Chinese Academy of Sciences
Institute of automation, Chinese academy of science, Chinese Academy of Sciences
Peking University and Beijing Academy of Artificial Intelligence
Institute of automation, Chinese academy of science
Institute of automation, Chinese academy of science, Chinese Academy of Sciences
ab: While Large Language Models (LLMs) excel as static solvers, transforming them into autonomous agents remains challenging. This transition requires continuous environmental interaction, yet current agents lack the necessary persistent procedural memory. Existing approaches predominantly employ Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) to inject explicit textual guidelines into model contexts. However, relying solely on symbolic instructions can introduce a text-action disconnect, frequently failing to activate the internal representations necessary for correct task execution. To address this, the paper introduces Neural Procedural Memory (NPM), a training-free framework that represents agent memory through implicit activation steering rather than explicit instructions. By distilling procedural skills from historical contrastive experiences into steering vectors in the activation space, NPM directly activates the task-relevant neural mechanisms to guide task execution. Evaluations across four agent benchmarks show that NPM performs comparably to baselines using explicit textual instructions. Furthermore, the results show that combining implicit steering with explicit workflows provides complementary advantages, leading to more robust task execution. Representational analyses indicate that these steering vectors encode consistent task logic, forming organized structures within the activation space. These findings suggest that implicit activation steering provides a promising approach for managing agent memory.

t: In-Context Neurofeedback: Can LLMs Control Their Internal Representations through Privileged Access?
a: The University of Tokyo, Tokyo Institute of Technology
ab: Whether large language models (LLMs) can control their own internal representations matters for both machine metacognition and AI safety. A recent study applied neurofeedback to LLMs and claimed that they can control their internal representations. However, the reported control may rely on superficial mechanisms rather than genuine internal access because the control targets in that study are not privileged, meaning that a third party can infer them from the prompt. We redesign the neurofeedback paradigm for LLMs so that the control target satisfies the privileged access requirement, which is closer to neurofeedback experiments in human cognitive neuroscience. Under this stricter setting, the models do not demonstrate reliable control over privileged internal representations, suggesting that previously reported control cannot exclude the possibility that it relies on superficial mechanisms. Our results indicate that rigorous assessments of metacognition in LLMs require evaluation methods that demand privileged access.

t: Scenario-based Probing and Steering Cultural Values in Large Language Models
ab: Evaluation of cultural value alignment in Large Language Models (LLMs) typically relies on direct prompting with survey-style questions, which often elicit neutral or safety-aligned responses and fail to capture the model’s underlying cultural orientation. To overcome these challenges, we propose a framework for probing and steering latent cultural representations in LLMs along the two Inglehart–Welzel axes of the World Values Survey (WVS). By translating social value questions into scenario-based dilemmas, we extract token-level probabilities to measure implicit values and apply activation steering, optionally combined with country-conditioned prompting, to shift model behavior without retraining. Across three 4B-open-weight LLMs, four countries and three social domains, we find substantial variation in steerability. Importantly, we identify latent entanglement, where interventions along one Inglehart–Welzel axis induce a shift along the other. This entanglement is consistent with correlations present in human WVS data and persists across our experimental settings. Our work identifies empirical constraints on cultural alignment in LLMs.

t: EffectMem: Effectiveness-Driven Memory Reuse for Long-Horizon LLM Agents
ab: Recent advances in Large Language Models (LLMs) have stimulated increasing interest in LLM-based agents for long-horizon interactive decision-making. As a lightweight alternative to parameter-level optimization, many studies enhance LLM agents through retrievable experience memory. However, existing retrieval strategies primarily optimize for the relevance of historical memories, leaving the applicability conditions and verifiable execution effects of retrieved trajectories insufficiently captured. To mitigate this executability gap between relevance-driven retrieval and executable reuse, we propose Effectiveness-Driven Memory (EffectMem), a framework that reframes trajectory memory as executable guidance whose applicability and effects are checked during interaction. During memory construction, EffectMem structures successful trajectories into positive executable contracts and localizable failures into negative experience guards. At inference, EffectMem retrieves candidate contracts, verifies their applicability to the current state, executes aligned chunks under guard constraints, and invokes discrepancy-guided correction when observed effects deviate from expected postconditions. Experiments on ALFWorld, ScienceWorld, and WebShop demonstrate that EffectMem outperforms competitive baselines and improves the effectiveness of memory-augmented LLM agents.

t: AdaSpec: Adaptive Routing by Ranking for Speculative Agents
a: University of North Carolina at Chapel Hill
ab: Long-horizon LLM agents execute sequences of reasoning, tool-use, and environment-interaction steps, making end-to-end latency a central deployment bottleneck. Speculative agents reduce this latency by leveraging a faster draft agent to propose the action trajectory while a stronger target agent verifies each action to ensure lossless action trajectories. Recent systems adapt how many future actions a preselected draft agent proposes before verification, but leave the drafter itself unchanged across tasks and episodes. Our experiments show that the best drafter varies across tasks and trajectory prefixes, revealing substantial latency headroom from adaptive drafter selection. This motivates the question: which draft agent should speculate for a given task and target agent to achieve low end-to-end latency? We propose AdaSpec, an adaptive routing framework for speculative agents with an objective distinct from standard model routing: selecting the drafter that minimizes realized speculative-execution latency for a target agent, rather than selecting the model that produces the final answer. AdaSpec profiles a pool of candidate draft-agent configurations for each target agent and trains a lightweight, latency-supervised router to rank them by measured speculative latency. The router supports both query-level routing and episode-level rerouting before each draft-and-check segment, while the target agent remains responsible for verifying actions. AdaSpec improves fixed-drafter baselines across multiple datasets and target-agent settings.

t: From Correctness to Utility: Gain-Based Prefix Evaluation for LLM Reasoning
ab: Reasoning prefixes shape the future trajectory of LLM problem solving, yet existing process reward models usually evaluate them through local step correctness. We argue that correctness is a useful but indirect proxy for the effect we ultimately care about: whether a prefix increases the probability of successful completion. We define this effect as prefix gain, the solve-rate improvement induced by conditioning lightweight student model group on a prefix, and use it to train a Prefix Utility Model (PUM) with a simple pairwise ranking objective. PUM learns outcome-grounded prefix utility and can score both complete trajectories and partial reasoning prefixes. Across Best-of-N selection, beam search, and reinforcement learning on mathematical reasoning, PUM provides a strong prefix-level supervision signal, especially when candidate pools are large, search budgets increase, or rule-based rewards are sparse.

t: MERTA: Multi-Expert Retrieval for Token Allocation in Video Large Language Models
ab: Video Large Language Models (VideoLLMs) excel in video understanding but suffer from significant computational overheads due to extensive visual tokens. Existing mainstream solutions including visual token compression and query-based Retrieval-Augmented Generation (Video RAG), face notable limitations: the former typically pursues task-agnostic compression of global video semantics, lacking query awareness, while the latter fails to optimize visual token construction and relies on costly, rigid annotation data. To address these challenges, we propose MERTA (Multi-Expert Retrieval for Token Allocation), a plug-and-play framework that integrates selective multi-expert collaborative retrieval with query-aware token allocation. MERTA selectively leverages lightweight experts to capture multimodal semantics, adaptively identifying key frames by measuring the relevance among queries, visual content, and auxiliary annotations. It then dynamically allocates the visual token budget, assigning higher budgets to key frames while keeping the total visual token budget constant. MERTA integrates seamlessly without requiring architectural modifications, demonstrating superior efficiency and performance over existing methods across multiple video understanding benchmarks.

t: A Unified Framework to Elicit Structured Feedback for Interpretable Multi-Trait Essay Scoring
ab: Multi-trait Automated Essay Scoring (AES) requires rubric-grounded reasoning across interdependent traits, rather than isolated score prediction. Existing feedback-enhanced methods often decouple feedback from scoring or assess traits independently, weakening score–feedback consistency and rubric alignment. We propose HiFTS, a unified autoregressive framework that generates hierarchical CoT feedback before predicting trait-level and holistic scores. HiFTS distills rubric-grounded hierarchical CoT feedback from a teacher LLM and trains student models to jointly generate feedback and scores. HiFTS further applies Group Relative Policy Optimization with a composite reward balancing score agreement, calibration, feedback quality, and structural validity. At inference, a lightweight global prior provides holistic guidance to reduce drift during long-form reasoning. We also introduce CFMS-34, a Chinese multi-trait AES dataset with 951 essays annotated with holistic scores and 34 rubric-based traits. Experiments on CFMS-34 and ASAP++ show that HiFTS achieves strong holistic and trait-level scoring while producing coherent, rubric-aligned feedback.

t: GAGPO: Generalized Advantage Grouped Policy Optimization
ab: Reinforcement learning (RL) has emerged as a powerful paradigm for post-training large language model (LLM) agents. However, credit assignment in multi-turn environments remains a challenge. Agents typically receive sparse, trajectory-level rewards only at the end of an episode, making it difficult to identify which specific intermediate actions led to success or failure. Consequently, effectively propagating delayed outcomes back to individual steps without relying on costly auxiliary value models remains an open problem. In this paper, we propose Generalized Advantage Grouped Policy Optimization (GAGPO), a critic-free RL method that enables precise, step-aligned temporal credit assignment. GAGPO constructs a non-parametric grouped value proxy from sampled rollouts to compute TD/GAE-style temporal advantages, recursively propagating outcome supervision backward through time. Coupled with group-wise advantage normalization and an action-level importance ratio, GAGPO extracts stable and localized optimization signals directly from multi-turn trajectories. Experiments on ALFWorld and WebShop demonstrate that GAGPO outperforms strong RL baselines. Further analyses reveal faster early-stage learning, improved interaction efficiency, and smoother optimization dynamics, offering a simple yet highly effective framework for multi-turn agentic RL.

t: Estimating Uncertainty from Reasoning: A Large-Scale Study of Multi- and Crosslingual MCQA Performance in LLMs
ab: Uncertainty estimation (UE) enables LLM-powered systems to recognize when to abstain, yet existing research has predominantly focused on English. We present the first large-scale evaluation of UE methods across 22 languages, spanning high-, mid-, and low-resource settings. Using two human-curated Q A datasets, we compare open and closed box UE methods (nine in total) across different model sizes and architectures while eliciting long-form reasoning, avoiding LLM-as-a-judge and embedding-based scoring, which can introduce evaluation noise. We report three main actionable findings. First, we find that prompting models to reason in English while keeping questions in low-resource languages substantially improves UE performance, suggesting that comprehension of low-resource languages is largely intact, and that the reliability bottleneck lies in generation rather than understanding. Second, prompting models to reason in English closes the UE performance gap between low and high-resource languages, demonstrating that generation language matters more than the question language. Third, the choice of UE method should depend on model scale: at smaller scales, open-box probability-based methods outperform alternatives; at larger scales, closed-box self-verbalized uncertainty becomes superior. Finally, we provide an analysis of threshold selection for selective prediction, offering guidance on calibrating abstention in multilingual settings. We publish our code to support further research in multilingual UE. Our code available in Anonymous Github[https://anonymous.4open.science/r/Cross-and-Multilingual-Uncertainty-Estimation-7976/].

t: DisCon4Gen: A Semantic Alignment Framework Through Discriminative Conditioning for Generation
ab: Generative language models (GLMs) excel at text generation and instruction following, while discriminative language models (DLMs) provide strong semantic representations for understanding tasks. Under the manifold hypothesis, natural language semantics can be regarded as lying on a shared latent semantic manifold, while DLMs and GLMs learn different representations of this manifold in their respective latent spaces. However, due to differences in training objectives and modeling strategies, these representation spaces are not naturally aligned, preventing discriminative representations from being directly utilized by GLMs through simple concatenation or linear transformation. To address this issue, a semantic alignment framework through discriminative conditioning for generation (DisCon4Gen) is proposed. From a manifold-based perspective, DisCon4Gen transforms DLM semantics into continuous conditions for GLMs. It further incorporates both global semantic signals and fine-grained discriminative cues to guide generation, enabling GLMs to better exploit external discriminative semantics. Experiments on five downstream datasets show that DisCon4Gen improves over strong supervised fine-tuning baselines and achieves competitive performance across both semantic understanding and generative reasoning tasks.

t: On the Learnability of Antidistillation Reasoning Traces
ab: Unauthorized distillation turns reasoning traces into a conduit for transferring proprietary models’ reasoning behavior to smaller students. Antidistillation Sampling (ADS) perturbs decoding to preserve task utility for legitimate users while obstructing student imitation. Our token-level Metropolis–Hastings diagnosis reveals that current ADS-style defenses leave the trace’s intrinsic learnability largely intact: most tokens still follow the original teacher, while a few teacher-uncertain positions induce extreme loss and dominate optimization. ADS hides learnable reasoning behind a sparse high-loss tail instead of eliminating it. We therefore reformulate reasoning distillation as offline reinforcement learning from imperfect demonstrations, with credit assignment that reinforces high-quality reasoning behavior while suppressing disruptive segments. Across two teachers, six students, and six datasets, the resulting learner extracts reasoning from current anti-distillation traces, outperforming vanilla maximum-likelihood training and eight supervised fine-tuning baselines by up to 21%. We then turn the same principle into an adaptive defense that directly targets high-value reasoning behaviors, exploiting the perceptual gap between humans and models to preserve readability while disrupting model-visible Unicode sequences. This strategy sharply degrades both classical distillation and the adaptive learner, and scales to protect GPT-5.5 traces. These results suggest that robust anti-distillation should optimize for low intrinsic learnability, not merely high token-level surprise.

t: ElementCheck: Complexity-Aware Long-Form Text Factuality Evaluation via Sentence Elements
a: Institute of automation, Chinese academy of science
University of Aberdeen and University of Cambridge
Institute of automation, Chinese academy of science, Chinese Academy of Sciences
Institute of automation, Chinese academy of science, Chinese Academy of Sciences
ab: Existing long-form factuality evaluation relies on the decompose-retrieve-verify pipeline. However, the pipeline suffers from noise from claim decomposition and fixed verification granularity, resulting in unreliable results. We propose ElementCheck, a complexity-aware framework that verifies long-form outputs via sentence elements. Instead of uniformly decomposing sentences into atomic sub-claims, ElementCheck extracts entity pairs that are explicitly linked through verifiable connections in the original sentence as elements, and organizes these into an element graph. The graph topology provides a structural signal for estimating sentence complexity, enabling direct verification for simple sentences and targeted element-level refinement and verification for complex ones. To support fine-grained evaluation, we construct a new benchmark FastFact-Sent by mapping isolated claims from FastFact-Bench back to their source sentences. Experiments on FastFact-Sent and two domain-specific benchmarks show ElementCheck consistently improves factuality verification across five backbone models while maintaining a favorable accuracy-cost trade-off. Further analyses demonstrate that complexity-aware verification reduces unnecessary re-verification and maintains stability across different backbones. The code is available at Here.

t: STQA: A Benchmark for Stock-Focused Tabular Question Answering over Historical and Forecasted Data
a: Beijing Normal University and Beijing Normal-Hong Kong Baptist University
ab: Stock market analysis inherently requires composite reasoning over historical records and future projections, yet existing benchmarks remain fragmented across isolated tasks. We introduce STQA (Stock-focused Tabular Question Answering), an end-to-end benchmark designed to systematically evaluate natural-language question answering over historical data, numerical forecasts, and forecast-based reasoning. Built on a large-scale financial dataset, STQA covers 4,451 stocks and contains 30,500 question–answer pairs derived from expert-crafted templates, accompanied by fine-grained intent and slot annotations. To operationalize this benchmark, we present SQFRS (Stock Query–Forecast–Reasoning System), an agent-based unified framework that orchestrates SQL retrieval and time-series forecasting tools. Experiments demonstrate that while current large language models perform well on historical queries, forecast-based reasoning poses a substantial challenge, revealing critical bottlenecks in tool coordination and reasoning under uncertainty.

t: Beyond Confidence: Test-Time Scaling for Multi-Turn Search Agents via Retrieval Grounding
a: Pohang University of Science and Technology
CMU, Carnegie Mellon University and Facebook
ab: Confidence-based voting aggregates parallel LLM rollouts by weighting each with internal signals such as token log probabilities, and has been actively studied for single-turn reasoning. However, modern LLMs increasingly act as multi-turn search agents that retrieve and condition on external documents. In this paper, we show that confidence-based voting transfers poorly to this multi-turn setting, and identify the underlying failure reason as copy inflation: when retrieved documents are appended to an agent’s context, tokens copied from those documents receive systematically inflated log probabilities. This flattens confidence scores within each question and weakens the resulting weighted vote. To address this issue, we propose Retrieval-Grounded Voting (RGV), which scores each rollout by the lexical overlap between its final answer and the documents it retrieved. By computing the signal outside the contaminated context, RGV sidesteps both token log probabilities and additional LLM calls. Across four search-agent benchmarks and five LLMs, RGV consistently outperforms confidence-based voting, with gains of up to +5.4% accuracy and +35% on minority-correct questions, where the correct answer appears in only 1-2 of 8 rollouts.

t: Hallucination as Exploit: Evidence-Carrying Multimodal Agents
a: Hong Kong University of Science and Technology and Facebook
ab: Multimodal agents increasingly choose tool calls from screenshots, documents, and webpages, where a false perceptual claim can turn hallucination from an answer-quality error into an authorization failure. We formalize this failure as hallucination-to-action conversion (H2AC) and propose evidence-carrying multimodal agents (ECA), in which model text may propose actions but cannot authorize them: constrained DOM/OCR/AX verifiers issue typed certificates for action-critical predicates, and a deterministic gate executes only what the certificates support. Across verifier red-teaming, 7,488 replayed authorization traces, and end-to-end and live-browser evaluations, ECA executes no unsafe action, while GPT-5.4 judge baselines admit 79–99% of unsafe actions under the same threat model; benign actions are occasionally deferred to user confirmation (6.4% on live pages) but never hard-blocked. The guarantee is conditional, extending exactly as far as the verifiers, schemas, and gate implementation that form ECA’s trusted base.

t: Personalizing How Recommendation Agents Reason: Self-Evolving Per-User Skills for Recommendation Agents
a: Harbin Institute of Technology, Shenzhen and Nanjing University
ab: LLM-based recommendation agents personalize what they know through evolving per-user semantic memory, yet how they perform reasoning relies on a universal, static system prompt shared across all users. When a recommendation fails, the agent only updates its memory, but never examines or revises the reasoning that leads to the failure. To close this gap, we propose SAGER (Self-Evolving Agent for Personalized Recommendation), the first framework to equip each user with a dedicated, continuously evolving policy skill. SAGER incorporates three tailored mechanisms for recommendation scenarios: (i) a two-representation skill architecture constrained by a Cognitive Injection Boundary, decoupling a rich evolution substrate from a minimal inference-time injection; (ii) a contrastive differential chain-of-thought engine that diagnoses ranking errors against unchosen near-misses under a refine-not-replace principle; and (iii) skill-augmented listwise reasoning that mitigates the Score-Tie Bottleneck, enabling the slim skill to serve as an active tie-breaker. Evaluated on four public benchmarks, SAGER achieves state-of-the-art accuracy. Furthermore, plugging its policy skill layer into three structurally distinct host agents delivers consistent 9%–12% gains on the H@1 metric. These results indicate that policy skill evolution provides architecture-agnostic improvements that are largely complementary to memory accumulation.

t: When Debate Messages Help or Hurt: Diagnosing Communication in Self-Distillation
ab: Multi-agent debate is widely used to enhance reasoning in language models, yet the exchanged messages are rarely analyzed. We study these messages in a Debate+SFT self-distillation loop by tracking their round-level evolution, intervening on peer messages with T-CIC at inference time, and comparing against matched Solo controls. Across three 5-seed discovery tasks–MATH, GSM-Hard, and 2WikiMultiHopQA–we observe weak refinement on MATH (+0.9pp for Debate versus +9.0pp for Solo), harmful homogenization on GSM-Hard (-11.3pp, with messages 27.5% longer and more self-similar), and mild inflation on 2WikiMHQA (-0.5pp with moderate length growth). A 2-seed T-CIC check on round-4 adapters shows different forms of message dependence: MATH collapses when peer messages are removed, shuffled, or replaced (-16 to -23pp), GSM-Hard is selectively sensitive to mismatched context, and 2WikiMHQA is mostly stable except under cross-problem shuffling. Debate messages should therefore be measured and stress-tested before they are trusted as a training signal.

t: SAMAC: Collaborating with Multi-Disciplinary Team for Adaptive Medical Decision-Making
a: Mohamed bin Zayed University of Artificial Intelligence
Mohamed bin Zayed University of Artificial Intelligence
ab: Multi-agent large language model systems offer a promising paradigm for multidisciplinary medical decision support by integrating heterogeneous expert perspectives. However, existing frameworks often rely on loosely structured interactions, where disagreement is insufficiently diagnosed and discussion may collapse into superficial consensus or parallel opinion aggregation. We propose Structured Adaptive Multi-disciplinary Collaboration (SAMAC), a structured and strategy-aware multi-agent framework for adaptive MDT-style medical reasoning. SAMAC introduces Structured Deliberation to detect opinion disagreement and majority not confident, along with a Consensus Purification mechanism that transforms disagreement into constructive and collaborative refinement. When disagreement arises, SAMAC adaptively selects between Self-refinement and Counter-questioning to enable evidence-grounded negotiation. Experiments on three medical datasets—RADCURE, HANCOCK, and OSCCPI—show that SAMAC consistently improves overall performance and collaborative gains over existing multi-agent baselines. In particular, SAMAC improves the Average Score by 4.29 points on the RADCURE dataset and achieves higher Relative Self-Correction Scores (RSS), indicating more effective resolution of disagreement and stable collective decisions. These results highlight the importance of controlled and diverse interaction dynamics in multi-agent medical reasoning. Code will be released upon publication.

t: DualResearch: Entropy-Gated Dual-Graph Retrieval for Answer Reconstruction in Deep Research Agents
ab: Deep Research Agents (DR-Agents) extend LLMs with multi-step retrieval, tool use, and intermediate computation to solve complex problems. However, their execution logs often contain redundant context, noisy evidence, and brittle dependencies among intermediate decisions. As a result, final answers can be sensitive to irrelevant or weakly verified information. We propose DualResearch, a log-based post-processing framework for answer reconstruction. Given a query and a completed DR-Agent log, DualResearch normalizes the log into event records and constructs two evidence graphs: a breadth semantic graph for declarative evidence and a depth causal graph for procedural provenance. It then retrieves breadth nodes and depth paths, assigns higher weights to retrieval channels with more concentrated retained candidate distributions, and jointly considers relevance and cross-view agreement to select evidence for reconstruction; the concentration measure reflects retrieval confidence rather than factual correctness. Experiments on HLE, GAIA, and GPQA show consistent accuracy improvements over underlying DR-Agents and controlled log-reuse baselines.

t: ESPO: Error-Structured Prompt Optimization via Diagnose, Diversify, and Stabilize
ab: Evolutionary prompt optimizers such as GEPA suffer from prompt bloat: each iteration appends rules and caveats, producing prompts that are 2–3× longer yet no more accurate. We trace this to three deficiencies - incomplete error observation, limited search diversity, and unreliable selection - and propose ESPO (Error-Structured Prompt Optimization), which decomposes prompt optimization into three phases: Diagnose clusters all training errors into structural patterns in one round; Propose generates candidates via four complementary strategies with independent biases; Select applies bootstrap stability selection. On seven public NLP benchmarks - Tweet, MMLU, GSM8K, HotpotQA, ScoNe, HoVer, and PUPA - ESPO wins 6/7 datasets with +3.76% average accuracy over the state-of-the-art (74.67% vs. 70.91% for GEPA), while producing prompts 47% shorter (1,004 vs. 1,878 chars) and faster at inference. Cross-model experiments across four additional student models (Gemma 3 12B, Mistral 14B, Qwen3 32B, Claude Haiku 4.5) show ESPO yields the best average accuracy on every model tested, with the largest gap on Qwen3 GSM8K (15.00% → 91.40%). A generalization bound (Appendix) grounds each phase in a corresponding term of the test-time gap, and the ablation confirms a key prediction: adding diversity without bootstrap selection actually hurts performance (-1.20%).

t: VIBE: Video Instruction-aligned Background music gEneration
ab: Current video-to-music (V2M) models lack semantic control and fail to penalize instruction violations, largely due to their reliance on reconstruction objectives and the representational bottleneck of static cross-modal conditioning in Diffusion Autoregressive (DAR) architectures. To resolve this, we introduce VIBE, a novel text-and-video-to-music (T+V2M) generation model that leverages: (1) Conditioning Connection, a depth-wise cross-layer conditioning mechanism that dynamically bridges the planning and diffusion refinement heads and (2) a comprehensive reward modeling taxonomy, optimizing for both hard, verifiable constraints (e.g., tempo, key) and soft, subjective qualities (e.g., musicality, multimodal alignment) with a structured 5-stage training curriculum. Upon evaluation using audio-visual alignment, instruction following, and audio quality metrics, along with a subjective human evaluation study, we observe that VIBE demonstrates enhanced controllability and instruction adherence while performing comparably to most evaluated baselines on generation fidelity and multimodal alignment.

t: Out-of-Distribution Checkpoint Selection Has a Resolution Problem: Auditing Sparse Exact Match with Token Likelihood
ab: Exact match (EM) can make checkpoint selection ambiguous when a small labeled out of distribution (OOD) validation set leaves several checkpoints tied at zero or at the maximum. Without an explicit tie rule, the reported metric does not identify which checkpoint produced the final test score. We study this validation resolution problem in semantic parsing and morphological reinflection. Our protocol reports the reference budget, token likelihood choice under teacher forcing, and latest tied candidate, while using EM for a unique nonzero maximum. Across 600 draws from 30 runs, 8 references leave every early checkpoint at zero in 48% of draws and the maximum tied in 57%. Within tied draws, mean full split regret falls from 0.063 under random selection to 0.050 with token likelihood. The latest tied candidate performs better on average for mostly monotone trajectories, but token likelihood independently orders candidates that hard EM cannot distinguish. These results support reporting both orderings when small labeled OOD validation sets guide checkpoint selection.

t: Can LLMs Compress Wireless Signals? Physics-Informed Prompting for Training-Free Signal Compression
ab: Wireless signals are a unique form of time-series data that encode rich physical characteristics of the propagation environment. As large volumes of signals are continuously generated in wireless sensing systems, efficient compression is essential for scalable transmission under limited system resources. However, wireless signals exhibit strong variability across environments and time, making it difficult to design universal compression schemes that generalize across domains while preserving the physical fidelity required for accurate reconstruction and sensing. Meanwhile, recent advances in large language models (LLMs) have demonstrated remarkable reasoning and adaptation capabilities across diverse modalities and domains. This raises an intriguing question: can LLMs compress wireless signals in a training-free manner while preserving physical fidelity? To the best of our knowledge, this problem remains unexplored. To answer this question, we propose a physics-informed prompting framework for training-free wireless signal compression. The framework incorporates environmental context and scenario-specific knowledge as physical priors in the prompt. We further introduce a dictionary module with self-learned patterns to stabilize inference and a key prompt module to align the semantics between the LLMs used for compression and reconstruction. Extensive experiments demonstrate that the proposed framework achieves high-fidelity reconstruction under cross-domain settings, highlighting the promise of physics-informed prompting as a new paradigm for processing and compressing low-level physical signals.

t: Node-to-Neighborhood Semantic Consistency: Text-Topology Alignment for TAGs Anomaly Detection
ab: Graph anomaly detection (GAD) on text-attributed graphs (TAGs) is vital for applications such as fraud detection and academic integrity verification. Existing approaches generally fall into two paradigms. GNN-based methods capture structural patterns but struggle to capture fine-grained textual semantics. Methods integrating LLMs with graphs improve semantic understanding yet fail to fully comprehend topological relationships among neighbors. Moreover, both paradigms overlook the correspondence between textual semantics and graph topological relationships, limiting their ability to identify nodes whose semantics are inconsistent with their neighborhoods. In this paper, we formalize TAG anomaly detection as a node-to-neighborhood semantic consistency problem, where anomalies may arise from either textual semantic mismatch or topological deviation between a node and its neighbors. We propose N2NSC (Node-to-Neighborhood Semantic Consistency), a framework that captures the correspondence between graph topology and textual semantics through two complementary fusion paths. The two pathways work synergistically, enabling the LLM to jointly use textual and structural neighborhood information for anomaly detection. Extensive experiments across eight benchmark datasets, with additional validation on two real-world fraud datasets, demonstrate the effectiveness of N2NSC.

t: MedReaMM: Evaluating Large Multimodal Models on Expert-Level Clinical Diagnostic Synthesis
a: Huazhong University of Science and Technology
Huazhong University of Science and Technology
ab: The application of Large Language Models (LLMs) to diagnostic decision-making has garnered growing interest. However, existing benchmarks largely focus on textual reasoning or isolated visual question-answering (VQA) tasks, lacking holistic integration of clinical narratives and medical imaging, and thus failing to assess the multimodal diagnostic synthesis capability central to expert clinical judgment. To bridge this gap, we introduce **MedReaMM**, a benchmark specifically designed to evaluate models’ ability to synthesize heterogeneous clinical evidence consisting of detailed patient histories alongside multiple medical images into accurate differential diagnoses under a complete-information paradigm. Constructed from case reports sourced from top-tier medical journals and curated clinical case databases, MedReaMM comprises 625 expert-validated cases with an average of 2.79 medical images per case and a total of 1,042 standardized diagnoses annotated with ICD-11 codes. These cases predominantly represent rare, atypical, or multi-system presentations that demand expert-level evidence integration beyond routine pattern recognition. We evaluate 23 Large Multimodal Models (LMMs) and find that most achieve diagnostic accuracy scores below 50%, underscoring a substantial gap in multimodal diagnostic synthesis capability. Further analysis reveals that medical knowledge proficiency, medical image understanding, and evidence integration are all highly correlated with diagnostic performance.

t: CoCoA: Context-Conditional Cultural Alignment for Large Language Models
ab: Large Language Models (LLMs) often favor Western-associated entities across cultural contexts. Conventional debiasing methods aim for uniform neutrality, but cultural bias mitigation demands context-conditional behavior, preferring culturally appropriate entities when cultural cues are present and remaining neutral when they are absent. We propose CoCoA (Context-Conditional Cultural Alignment), a framework that learns this behavior through dual-context training on the same entity pairs under contexts with and without cultural cues. CoCoA combines a contrastive alignment objective with calibration and drift regularization, optimized through goal-aware gradient reconciliation. We evaluate CoCoA on CAMeL and Camellia, two entity-centric cultural bias benchmarks, across ten language settings and four LLMs. CoCoA reduces the Cultural Bias Score from 43 to 24 on average while maintaining near-neutral preferences at 50.2, with minimal impact on general performance across five standard benchmarks. These findings highlight that effective cultural alignment requires context-conditional modeling rather than uniform debiasing, and establish a new direction for mitigating entity-centric cultural bias in LLMs.

t: Think Before You Score: Pedagogical Chain-of-Thought Annotation and Reinforcement Learning for Low-Resource Multilingual Essay Evaluation
ab: Automated Essay Scoring (AES) in low-resource, non-English educational settings faces a compounded challenge: existing corpora record only a final holistic score, discarding the rich intermediate reasoning that human examiners rely on. We argue this annotation gap may contribute to Rubric Drift—the observed tendency of LLMs to apply scoring norms misaligned with the target curriculum, potentially reflecting Anglocentric defaults. To address this, we introduce MPEAB-2430, a multilingual AES benchmark spanning Malay, Hindi, and Arabic curricula, annotated with Pedagogical Chain-of-Thought (P-CoT) trajectories that capture sub-dimensional analyses, explicit error attribution, and curriculum-conformant feedback, derived entirely from independent, language-specific expert practice. Leveraging this rich but modest-scale supervision, we propose RL-CRAF++, a sample-efficient pipeline combining CoT-SFT with Constrained GRPO. Crucially, our RL formulation relies entirely on human-annotation-derived rewards, completely bypassing the potential biases of external LLM judges. Evaluated independently per language, a 4B parameter RL-CRAF++ model consistently surpasses zero-shot frontier models (including GPT-5 and DeepSeek-V3.2) on in-domain test sets. Ablation analysis reveals that P-CoT supervision accounts for approximately 78.1% of the alignment gain over standard SFT, providing strong evidence that, in this culturally situated evaluation setting, process-level structural supervision contributes substantially more than RL-stage calibration alone. Our code is available at https://github.com/TW-NLP/MPEAB

t: Distilling LLM Reasoning into an Interpretable Policy Tree for Human-AI Collaboration
ab: Constructing efficient and reliable policies to assist humans is indispensable for human-AI collaboration. Existing methods mainly follow two lines of work. The majority of prior work relies on multi-agent reinforcement learning (MARL) to learn black-box policies, which limits interpretability and raises safety concerns. Recent methods query large language models (LLMs) at each decision step, causing slow responses and high inference costs. We propose Co-\pi-tree, a closed-loop method that learns an executable policy tree consisting of a partner-behavior prediction tree and an agent-action selection tree. Co-\pi-tree constructs a policy through distilling LLM reasoning into policy tree code. It then evaluates the policy through partner interaction, obtains feedback, and uses natural language summaries of interaction feedback to improve problematic branches. Experiments in Overcooked-AI show that Co-π-tree improves average reward by 6.4% over the strongest LLM baseline, while reducing the number of LLM queries by 77.7% and test-time latency by 97.1%. Project page: https://beiwenzhang.github.io/Co-pi-tree/.

t: IndicDetect: Evaluating Cross-Lingual LLM-Generated Text Detection for Hindi, Telugu, and Tamil
ab: The rapid proliferation of LLMs has further heightened the necessity to develop dependable AI-generated text detection, especially beyond English. Nevertheless, current benchmarks pay little attention to Indic languages and test detectors in idealized settings that do not represent the real world. We present a generalized benchmark for AI-generated text detection in Hindi, Telugu, and Tamil, which we name IndicDetect is a benchmark designed to assess the robustness of detectors under realistic distribution shifts. IndicDetect comprises highly curated human-written texts matched with LLM-generated counterparts across various domains and generators, and systematically evaluates detectors in the presence of domain shift, generator shift, and adversarial perturbation. Using a single and repeatable evaluation scheme, we evaluate a wide range of statistical and neural detectors. We find substantial robustness failures: supervised neural detectors perform well in-distribution, but most training-free methods fail catastrophically on unseen generators and adversarial attacks, with larger failures observed for Telugu and Tamil than for Hindi. These results highlight that the primary weakness of existing detectors in Indic settings lies in their robustness, not peak accuracy. IndicDetect provides standard data splits, an evaluation protocol, and baselines to establish a robust, language-aware foundation for AI-generated text detection in Indic scripts.

t: Distilling Multimodal Evolution with Adaptive Anchors for Cloud-Edge Collaborative MLLMs
a: Shandong University of Finance and Economics
Shandong University of Finance and Economics
Shandong University of Finance and Economics
Beijing University of Post and Telecommunications
Shandong University of Finance and Economics
ab: Cloud-edge collaboration provides a practical paradigm for deploying MLLMs on resource-constrained devices, where compact edge-side models are improved with supervision from stronger cloud-side models. However, existing cloud-edge distillation methods mainly rely on pseudo labels or static feature alignment, overlooking how the teacher progressively transforms multimodal inputs into answers. In this paper, we propose A^2-MED, Adaptive Anchor-Guided Multimodal Evolution Distillation for cloud-edge MLLMs. Our key idea is to organize the teacher’s layer-wise multimodal evolution into functional stages through adaptive teacher-side anchoring, and transfer the resulting stage-wise evolution as process-level supervision. Specifically, we adaptively identify functional anchors from the teacher according to layer-wise indicators of cross-modal binding, semantic integration, and answer prediction, and then project these anchors to the student to establish corresponding functional stages. Under these teacher-defined stages, we align teacher-student anchor states and distill inter-stage multimodal evolution relations, enabling the student to learn how the teacher progressively transforms multimodal inputs into answers. Experiments on A-OKVQA and VizWiz show that our method consistently improves over representative cloud-edge and distillation baselines, with further analyses validating the effectiveness of adaptive anchors and evolution distillation.

t: Doc-CoB: Enhancing Document Understanding with Visual Chain-of-Boxes Reasoning
ab: Document understanding aims to perform question answering and information extraction over document images, where the visual content is highly information-dense and most queries rely on only a few relevant layout regions. However, existing methods either adopt a one-pass strategy that implicitly assumes all layouts are equally important, or focus excessively on small regions at the cost of losing critical layout information. To address these limitations, we introduce Doc-CoB (Chain-of-Boxes), a simple-yet-effective framework that integrates coarse-to-fine layout-aware visual reasoning into multimodal large language models. Instead of directly zooming into small regions, Doc-CoB progressively focuses on query-relevant layouts while preserving global document information. Specifically, it first selects key layout boxes and then focuses on them for further understanding with visual prompting. To support this paradigm, we introduce two reasoning tasks for box recognition and box reasoning, with an automatic pipeline that constructs 249k training samples with intermediate visual supervision. Experiments on seven benchmarks with four popular models show that Doc-CoB significantly improves performance, demonstrating its effectiveness and wide applicability. The code and the data are available at https://github.com/Doc-CoB/Doc-CoB.

t: FORGE: Fine-grained multimodal evaluation for manufacturing quality assurance
a: The Chinese University of Hong Kong (Shenzhen)
Université Claude Bernard (Lyon I) and University of Waterloo
University of Sydney, University of Sydney
ab: The manufacturing sector is increasingly adopting Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) to move from low-level perception toward higher-level reasoning and decision support, yet current evaluations rarely reflect the fine-grained precision that real-world manufacturing demands. Progress is further hindered by data scarcity and a lack of fine-grained domain semantics in existing datasets. To bridge this gap, we introduce FORGE, a benchmark for three core quality-assurance tasks of discrete manufacturing: workpiece verification, structural surface inspection, and assembly verification. We first construct a high-quality multimodal dataset spanning real-world 2D images and 3D point clouds, annotated with fine-grained domain semantics such as standardized model numbers. We then evaluate 18 state-of-the-art MLLMs on these three tasks, revealing significant performance gaps. Counter to conventional understanding, our bottleneck analysis on five representative models indicates that visual grounding is not the primary limiting factor. Instead, insufficient domain-specific knowledge is the key bottleneck. Beyond evaluation, we show that our structured annotations can serve as an actionable training resource: supervised fine-tuning of a compact 3B-parameter model on our data yields up to 90.8% relative improvement in accuracy on held-out manufacturing scenarios, providing preliminary evidence for a practical pathway toward domain-adapted manufacturing MLLMs.

t: Skill-as-Pseudocode: Refactoring Skill Libraries to Pseudocode for LLM Agents
a: School of Computer Science and Engineering, Nanyang Technological University
ab: Markdown skill libraries for LLM agents ship as free-form prose, forcing the agent to re-derive both the input schema and the concrete invocation syntax on every retrieval. This produces a "confused → re-retrieve → still confused" loop: the agent issues a partially-correct action, receives uninformative feedback, and re-retrieves the same prose. We propose Skill-as-Pseudocode (SaP), an automatic conversion of markdown skill libraries into typed pseudocode with deterministic quality control. From each cluster of similar procedural passages, SaP extracts a typed contract and filters it through a four-check deterministic verifier (coverage, binding, replacement, risk). Promoted contracts are inlined into a rewritten skill skeleton alongside restored action templates, giving the agent two complementary signals: a typed signature for what a skill does and a concrete template for how to invoke it. On the ALFWorld unseen split (134 games, gpt-4o-mini, three seeds), SaP wins 82/402 paired games versus 47/402 for the Graph-of-Skills (GoS) baseline (pooled McNemar p = 8.2 × 10⁻⁵), at −22.8 ± 6.4% input tokens and −14.5 ± 4.1% LLM calls per game. A bundle-component ablation attributes the gain to the pairing of typed contracts with concrete action templates: the contract alone falls below the prose baseline.

t: AEGIS-D: Multi-Agent Debate for High-Precision Verification of Hard Competition Mathematics
a: University of Illinois, Urbana Champaign and Princeton University
ab: Fluent but subtly wrong mathematical solutions can contaminate training, evaluation, and reward-labeling data. We present AEGIS-D (Assessment- and Evidence-Gated Inspection System via Debate), a precision-first multi-agent pipeline for blind verification of competition-level mathematics. Five same-model, role-prompted agents exchange structured arguments, while an assessment gate accepts a candidate only when at least three report positive confirming evidence rather than mere non-refutation. On 195 hard-to-verify variants from 58 IMO/USAMO/Putnam-level problems, a single judge achieves 55.1% precision; AEGIS-D achieves 92.5% precision and 63.8% recall, reducing false positives from 24.7 to 3.0 per run (8.2-fold). A repeated two-by-two factorial associates role prompting with the largest observed false-positive reduction and finds a smaller conditional benefit from gating. Paired round and threshold analyses expose the cost-precision trade-off, and single-run transfers to Omni-MATH and OlymMATH provide preliminary evidence beyond the constructed stress test.

t: STARS: Skill Triage via Activation Risk Scoring for LLM Agents
ab: The risk of an agent skill call depends not on the skill alone but on the invocation context: the same file-reading skill is benign when listing logs, yet dangerous when tainted content steers the agent toward secret exfiltration. We formalize invocation-time auditing: intercept a proposed skill call before execution and score its risk from the user request, the candidate skill, and the runtime context. STARS implements this as a three-stage pipeline that fuses a static capability prior with a request-conditioned invocation scorer. The primary configuration, STARS-LLM, uses an LLM judge; STARS-Rules is a deterministic, API-free alternative. On SIA-Bench, a 3,000-record synthetic benchmark with a 180-record human check at Fleiss κ = 0.709, request-conditioned scoring improves high-risk retrieval on held-out indirect prompt injection, where static metadata cannot see the attack. On a frozen 500/100 scoring subset, STARS-LLM raises rules-only HR-AUPRC from 0.297 to 0.728 in-distribution and from 0.504 to 0.757 on held-out IPI. That gain is in ranking: under frozen thresholds, held-out classification accuracy does not improve. SIA-Bench is a ranking stress test, not an estimate of real-world prevalence.

t: CoopAgent: Training Multi-Agent Cooperation from Single-Agent Execution Trajectories
