ab: Layer pruning aims to accelerate the inference of Large Language Models on general hardware by removing less important Transformer layers. However, naively deleting layers typically degrades model performance. To reduce this degradation, prior work approximates removed layers with replacement components such as linear layers. These approaches often require large datasets and heavy replacement modules, which increase computational and memory costs. Their time complexity also restricts them to static, consecutive-layer pruning. In this work, we introduce a novel method, Superior layer Pruning performance by Super-fast Recovery (SPSR), which uses Pearson correlation coefficients to quantify a layer’s recovery ability and applies a super-fast fine-tuning procedure with a lightweight replacement component. SPSR readily extends to non-consecutive pruning and to dynamic pruning. Experimental results show that SPSR achieves performance competitive with state-of-the-art methods while substantially improving recovery efficiency.

t: HyperSU: Corpus-Driven Semantic-Unit Hypergraph for Retrieval-Augmented Generation
a: University of Sydney and University of New South Wales
ab: Recent Hypergraph-based retrieval-augmented generation (HyperRAG) methods use hyperedges to connect multiple entities simultaneously, enabling more efficient multi-entity evidence organization than pairwise graph structures. However, existing HyperRAG methods often rely on LLM-generated summaries to construct hyperedges, which can introduce hallucinations while also incurring high indexing costs. In addition, during retrieval, existing methods typically rely on either one-hop neighbor expansion or PageRank diffusion. The former may miss useful multi-hop evidence, while the latter can suffer from uncontrolled propagation over excessive hub nodes, leading to semantic drift and noisy reasoning chains. To address these challenges, we propose HyperSU, a novel hypergraph-based RAG framework featuring semantic-unit hyperedges and clue-guided bidirectional retrieval. During construction, HyperSU formulates hyperedge construction as an entity-aware minimum-description-length (MDL) optimization problem, inducing source-grounded semantic-unit hyperedges that balance sentence-level semantic coherence and entity compactness. It then constructs a hypergraph by modeling each semantic unit as a hyperedge over its co-mentioned entities. During retrieval, HyperSU performs clue-guided bidirectional expansion over the semantic-unit hypergraph, enabling both multi-hop evidence discovery and evidence-anchored noise reduction. Experiments show that HyperSU consistently improves answer accuracy over standard, graph-based, and hypergraph-based RAG baselines, raising average accuracy on GraphRAG-Bench by 5.5 points over the strongest baseline (68.7 vs. 63.2), with larger gains on reasoning-intensive tasks, where the relative improvement reaches 14.1%. Our code is available at https://github.com/RAIDSLab/HyperSU.

t: Conditional Perturbation Generators for Probing and Mitigating Recovery Risks in Multimodal Large Language Models Unlearning
ab: Multimodal large language models (MLLMs) trained on image-text data may retain sensitive information in textual memories, visual representations, and cross-modal associations, creating a need for reliable unlearning. Although existing unlearning methods can reduce target disclosure under clean queries, suppressed knowledge may remain recoverable under adversarial conditions. We introduce a new perspective on this vulnerability by assessing post-unlearning recovery through conditional perturbation generation, where a learned generator maps each image-text input to perturbations that promote recovery of the suppressed response. This framework is instantiated with two generators: CEPG injects conditional soft tokens into the multimodal input embedding sequence, while CPPG generates pixel-space perturbations under CLIP-based semantic conditions. Experiments across five unlearning methods show strong recovery risks. CEPG achieves average recovery ratio (Rec) scores of 60.19% on MLLMU-Bench and 46.74% on CLEAR, while CPPG attains 34.28% and 29.47%, respectively. Both attacks remain effective with limited or no direct access to forgotten samples, highlighting that current unlearning offers insufficient robustness guarantees. To mitigate this vulnerability, we introduce Adversarially Robust Unlearning (ARU), which integrates conditional recovery attacks into unlearning with attribution-guided parameter selection, significantly reducing recovery rates while preserving utility on retain sets.

t: HiGraph: Explicit Discrepancy Reasoning with Hierarchical Graph Propagation for Joint Pronunciation Assessment
ab: Automated pronunciation assessment predicts pronunciation quality at the phone, word, and utterance levels. Recent joint models use both canonical and realized phone representations, but their mismatch is often encoded implicitly rather than preserved as a separate scoring path. This makes it difficult to trace how local phone errors affect word- and utterance-level scores. We propose HiGraph, which explicitly computes canonical-realized mismatch and propagates it through a hierarchical phone-to-word-to-utterance graph. This creates a structured discrepancy path from phone-level mismatch evidence to higher-level score representations. Under the same pipeline as our reproduced HMamba baseline, HiGraph improves word stress and utterance completeness on SpeechOcean762 (SO762). The learned word-level trace score also aligns with mispronunciation detection and diagnosis (MDD) ground truth. When words are ranked by this trace score, the top-ranked word contains a true mispronunciation in 81.5% of test utterances, and at least one of the top two words does so in 93.8% of test utterances. These results show that explicit discrepancy propagation can improve selected assessment dimensions while supporting feedback localization grounded in annotated mispronunciations.

t: ProRAC: A Neuro-symbolic Method for Reasoning about Actions with LLM-based Progression and Search
ab: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used in agentic systems, where reliable planning requires tracking how actions change the world over long horizons. This capability is central to reasoning about actions and change (RAC), which involves checking action executability, updating states, and preserving unaffected facts. However, recent RAC and planning benchmarks show that LLMs still struggle with these basic abilities. Effective neuro-symbolic methods for improving RAC and planning directly over natural language remain underexplored. In this paper, we propose ProRAC (Progression-based Reasoning about Actions and Change), a neuro-symbolic framework that leverages LLMs to tackle RAC and planning problems through an agentic, modular design. Central to ProRAC is a unified framework that operates in two modes: a reasoning mode that sequentially executes actions to validate states and answer queries, and a searching mode that integrates this progression into an A* search guided by a fine-tuned heuristic model to find plans. Extensive evaluations across multiple RAC and planning benchmarks show that ProRAC achieves competitive performance across different model backbones and task types.

t: CapGeo-Bench: Decoupling Visual Perception from Reasoning and Evaluating Geometric Understanding
ab: While Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) have achieved remarkable success in difficult purely textual mathematical reasoning tasks, even advanced closed-source models such as GPT-o3 still struggle with geometric problems. This discrepancy motivates us to investigate the root cause: is the bottleneck of multimodal geometric reasoning rooted in reasoning itself, or in the perception of geometric information from diagrams? To answer this question, we conduct an exploratory experiment and find that providing high-quality captions consistently and substantially boosts performance of MLLMs, empirically validating the visual perception bottleneck in geometric reasoning. However, MLLMs’ capabilities in visual geometric perception remain insufficiently evaluated. To fill the gap, we propose CapGeo-Bench, a benchmark of 4,641 high-quality figure–caption pairs equipped with a fine-grained keypoint-based evaluation metric. Specifically, CapGeo-Bench encompasses three geometric classes and is devided into four difficulty levels according to the complexity of geometric primitives. Captions are scored at a fine-grained level by extracting keypoints along three dimensions-geometric elements, spatial relationships, and numerical attributes. CapGeo-Bench provides a reliable instrument and guideline for evaluating and advancing MLLMs’ geometric perception capabilities. Our code and data are publicly available at: https://github.com/YuYingLi0/CapGeo.

t: Why This and Not That? A Collaborative Reflection Approach for Understanding Thought Coverage in Decision Making Support Dialog
ab: Conversational agents that support reflection for decision-making often rely on adaptive dialog policies that map observed user behavior to actions such as probing, deepening, or redirecting. Yet the same pattern can reflect a range of different reasons such as deliberate prioritisation or limited self-access. By modeling the observable pattern rather than the user’s reason for it, current policies risk premature assumptions about the user state and inappropriate next actions. To address this gap, we introduce a human-centered method for surfacing this hidden inference step. In a user study with 62 users and 232 collaborative moments, we pause a reflection-support agent when it would normally redirect the conversation, surface its observation, and ask users to interpret the pattern and decide how to proceed. We derive a taxonomy of nine interpretation categories and show that similar reflective states can call for substantially different follow-up actions. Our findings challenge the assumption that adaptive dialog policies can rely on observable behavior alone, and suggest how user-provided interpretations can inform more appropriate conversational actions.

t: Using Grounded Theory for Agent Behavior Analysis at Scale
a: University of Texas at El Paso
Department of Computer Science, Whiting School of Engineering
ab: Understanding agent behavior requires methods that scale to thousands of trajectories and surface new patterns in long, often unfamiliar tasks where pre-built classifiers fall short. We propose to bring grounded theory into agent trajectory analysis: a six-decade-old qualitative method from the social sciences, with a principled saturation criterion and an auditable trail from data to theory. We propose AutoTraceGT (Automated Trace analysis through Grounded Theory), the first multi-agent pipeline that automates grounded theory on agent trajectories. It iteratively performs open, axial, and theoretical coding until saturation, producing a behavioral taxonomy tailored to each task. Across six trajectory corpora, AutoTraceGT produces codebooks that recover 73–91% of the failure modes in human-annotated taxonomies and surface additional patterns that those taxonomies miss. The emergent theoretical narrative aligns with prior expert accounts. Used as a deductive feature space, the codebook outperforms zero-shot and few-shot LLM baselines on downstream failure prediction. These results suggest Grounded Theory offers a scalable analytic tool for ML researchers and agent developers studying what agents actually do.

t: D2C-Routing: Dimension-to-Composition Evidence Routing for Mixed-Origin AI-Generated Text Detection
a: School of Artificial Intelligence, Beihang University and Institute of Computing Technology, Chinese Academy of Sciences
ab: AI-generated text detection is commonly framed as a binary document-level judgment about whether a text is human-written or machine-generated. This framing breaks down for mixed-origin writing, where content origin and expression origin may differ. We cast mixed-origin detection as dimension-to-composition source attribution, inferring content origin and expression origin before composing them into four collaboration types. We propose *Dimension-to-Composition Routing* (**D2C-Routing**), which routes content-side and expression-side evidence to supervised dimension heads before a learned gated composition layer predicts the final label. On MixD2C, a reconstructed split derived from the HART mixed-origin benchmark, our disclosed D2C-Routing-based detector system reaches 0.8603 four-way Avg TPR@1%FPR, 6.5 points above the same-split RACE-local rerun. Core ablations support the routing design, while error analysis shows that distinguishing AI-content/human-expression from fully AI-generated text remains the hardest boundary. Code is available at https://github.com/bystander563/d2c-routing-artifact.

t: OmniDA: Grounding Agentic Multimodal Data Analysis with Evidence-Aware Process Rewards
a: The Chinese University of Hong Kong and Department of Computer Science and Engineering, The Chinese University of Hong Kong
College of Computer Science and Technology, Zhejiang University
ab: Real-world data analysis often requires joint reasoning over heterogeneous artifacts such as tables, charts, and textual reports. Training reliable multimodal large language model (MLLM) agents for this setting remains challenging, as large-scale aligned training data are scarce, and outcome-only rewards are too coarse to distinguish grounded cross-source analysis from spurious success. We introduce OmniDA, a training recipe that addresses these two challenges with a scalable multimodal data-synthesis pipeline and an Evidence-Aware Process Reward (EAPR) that supervises both evidence recovery and procedural validity. Through this pipeline, we construct OmniDA-11K, a high-quality training corpus for multimodal data analysis. When instantiated with Qwen3-VL-8B, OmniDA improves over the corresponding agentic baseline by 19.2 points on average across five challenging benchmarks and achieves the strongest overall performance among existing open-source data-analysis agents. These results highlight the value of supervising evidence recovery and analytical procedure beyond final-answer correctness.

t: Learning to Think in Blocks: A Prior-Guided Reinforcement Learning Framework for Deep Research
a: United Automotive Electronic Systems Co., Ltd.
United Automotive Electronic Systems Co., Ltd.
ab: Reinforcement learning (RL) for multi-turn deep research agents suffers from a granularity mismatch: token-level methods incur high variance over long reasoning horizons, while sequence-level methods ignore the internal decision structure of multi-turn interactions. We introduce Block-wise Geometric Policy Optimization (BGPO), which treats each assistant turn—packaging reasoning and tool invocation into one semantically coherent unit—as an optimization-level macro-action and aggregates block-averaged log-importance ratios with equal weights across blocks. We prove that block-equal weighting minimizes a covariance-robust upper bound on ratio variance under weak inter-block coupling, with the approximation gap relative to sequence-length weighting bounded by block-length imbalance. To improve exploration efficiency, we expose human-defined rewrite operators—including decomposition, keyword extraction, synonym replacement, and HyDE—as a prompt-level exploration prior during RL rollouts. On seven knowledge-intensive QA benchmarks, our 7B system achieves an average judge score of 0.715 ± 0.010 over three training seeds, compared with 0.664 for Search-R1-7B. A controlled fixed-prior attribution study further confirms that block-level optimization independently improves answer quality, achieving 0.527/0.395 F1/EM compared with 0.482/0.350 for GRPO. Our code is publicly available at https://github.com/meiotoufa/Learning-to-Think-in-Blocks.

t: Don’t Lose Entities from Retrieval to Generation: Dual Entity Recovery RAG for multi-hop QA
a: Ulsan National Institute of Science and Technology
Ulsan National Institute of Science and Technology
ab: Retrieval-augmented multi-hop question answering (QA) decomposes a query into sub-questions and decomposes the corpus into smaller retrieval units such as sentences. Both forms of decomposition improve the pipeline, but we show that both share the same vulnerability, the loss of entity information, and that this loss breaks the pipeline at two separate points. The first point is retrieval, where a sub-question loses the entity resolved at the previous hop, leaving the retriever with nothing to match against. The second point is harder to see, because retrieval still appears to succeed. Once a passage is split into sentences, an isolated sentence loses the context that grounds its pronouns, so even with the correct sentence in hand the LLM cannot tell which entity the sentence is about. We isolate this second point as a distinct failure mode that we call lost-in-generation, and a retrieval-controlled experiment shows that it degrades answers even when the gold evidence is fixed in the context. We then propose Dual Entity Recovery RAG (DER-RAG), which keeps the grounding entity explicit from retrieval through to generation with two lightweight components, a two-way query decomposition that carries the resolved entity across sub-questions and a subject entity prefix attached to each sentence at generation time. DER-RAG needs no graph construction, no corpus modification, and no fine-tuning, yet on three multi-hop QA benchmarks it matches or exceeds strong baselines, including graph-based methods that depend on costly offline structures.

t: Scalable Supervision for Software Agents via Patch Reasoning
a: Xiaohongshu and The Chinese University of Hong Kong, Shenzhen
Tencent and University of Edinburgh, University of Edinburgh
The Chinese University of Hong Kong, Shenzhen
ab: While language model agents have advanced software engineering, existing test-based supervision is limiting its scalability on real-world issues. The reason is twofold: (1) high-coverage tests are naturally rare in the wild, and (2) building and running test sandbox is heavy and fragile. To unlock supervision scaling, we propose R4P, a reasoning-based method that provides scaffold-agnostic rewards. R4P uses a group-wise training objective, enabling it to verify multiple patches against each other’s modification and gain a dense reward for supervising agents without executing tests or relying on specific agent trajectories. R4P achieves 72.2% Acc. for verifying patches from SWE-bench, competitive with proprietary models. To show the downstream practical utility of R4P, we design and train an execution-free scaffold, Mini-SE, with pure RL via R4P. Mini-SE achieves 26.2% Pass@1, showing a 10.0% improvement over the original Qwen3-32B, and can be further improved to 32.8% with R4P for test-time scaling on patch selection. The stable scaling curves illustrate that though imperfect, R4P can still reliably support downstream tasks at scale.

t: GD^2PO: Group-Dynamic Reward-Decoupled Policy Optimization for Mitigating Multi-Reward RL Conflicts
a: The Chinese University of Hong Kong
Beijing Institute for General Artificial Intelligence
ab: Post-training large language models often require optimizing multiple objectives simultaneously, motivating multi-reward reinforcement learning (RL) methods that model different objectives as separate reward signals. Existing methods like Group reward-Decoupled Policy Optimization (GDPO) compute group-normalized advantages separately for each reward dimension and then aggregate them for policy updates. However, this aggregation process can cause cross-reward advantage conflict: the same rollout may have positive advantages on some reward dimensions but negative advantages on others, causing positive and negative signals to cancel each other during aggregation. To address this issue, we propose GD^2PO, short for Group-Dynamic Reward-Decoupled Policy Optimization, a conflict-aware multi-reward policy optimization method. Before advantage aggregation, GD^2PO uses conflict-aware criteria to identify and filter rollouts with severe reward-wise disagreement, reducing the influence of unreliable update signals. It further introduces query-level reweighting to dynamically adjust the update strength of each query according to its overall reward consensus. Experiments on tool calling and helpfulness-safety alignment show that GD^2PO outperforms existing methods. Our code is available at https://github.com/Qwen-Applications/GD2PO.

t: DailyReport: An Open-ended Benchmark for Evaluating Search Agents on Daily Search Tasks
a: University of Science and Technology of China
Institute of Automation, Chinese Academy of Sciences
University of Science and Technology of China
ab: Search Agents (SAs) typically leverage large language models (LLMs) to support complex information-seeking tasks by autonomously exploring web sources and synthesizing information into comprehensive responses. For SAs evaluation, prior benchmarks mainly focus on specialized tasks that are unlikely to arise in real-world user scenarios. Moreover, their reliance on coarse task-level rubrics often limits evaluation interpretability. To bridge this gap, we introduce DailyReport, an open-ended benchmark to evaluate SA capabilities on daily search tasks. It contains 150 open-ended tasks with 3,546 associated rubrics, capturing widely discussed and timely information demands of real-world users. Each task is decomposed into subtasks and evaluated with cascade rubrics across disentangled dimensions. Through cascade performance attribution and user-centric aggregation, we derive highly interpretable scores for each dimension, along with a user preference score. Our results on 17 agentic systems show that current systems still fall short of users’ expectations. DailyReport will be open-sourced to facilitate future research.

t: JPhonABX: Japanese Phonological Discrimination Dataset for Moraic and Accentual Minimal Pairs
a: NII, The University of Tokyo and AIST, National Institute of Advanced Industrial Science and Technology
ab: Self-supervised speech models are known to encode phonological information, yet it remains underexplored whether they capture phonological properties characteristic of Japanese, such as mora and pitch accent. This paper introduces JPhonABX, a Japanese phonological discrimination dataset targeting moraic and accentual contrasts. It consists of 192,000 moraic and 98,000 accentual ABX test items, covering various types of contrasts such as those involving moraic nasal, geminate consonant, vowel length, and pitch accent. Our human evaluation by native Japanese speakers shows high discrimination accuracy and inter-rater agreement, validating the quality of the dataset. We further evaluate several self-supervised speech models and find that while almost all of them show no significant difference from humans in mora discrimination, they perform significantly worse in accent discrimination, and even models trained on Japanese fail to reach human-level performance.

t: LLMBridge: An LLM Pipeline for End-to-end Referential Bridging Resolution in English
ab: In this paper, we introduce LLMBridge, a new LLM based system for the task of end-to-end referential bridging resolution in English. Our bridging resolution pipeline combines heuristic pre/post-processing with the natural language inference ability that comes from LLMs. We evaluate our bridging resolution pipeline on three datasets which have been used for referential bridging resolution evaluation in English: ISNotes, BASHI, and GUMBridge. Comparison to previous bridging resolution systems shows that the performance of LLMBridge surpasses previous state-of-the-art (SoTA) systems for all three datasets in the challenging End-to-end Evaluation Setting, as well as the Basic Bridging Resolution Evaluation Setting (gold bridging anaphor given). We also conduct a thorough error analysis of the LLMBridge performance, examining what varieties of bridging remain difficult for LLM based systems to identify. With this paper, we release the code for the LLMBridge pipeline.

t: Efficient Diffusion Language Models: A Comprehensive Survey
a: City University of Hong Kong and Institute of automation, Chinese academy of science
Institute of Automation，Chinese Academy of Sciences
Department of Computer Science and Engineering, The Chinese University of Hong Kong
The Chinese University of Hong Kong
Institute of automation, Chinese academy of science, Chinese Academy of Sciences
The Chinese University of Hong Kong
Institute of automation, Chinese academy of science, Chinese Academy of Sciences
ab: Diffusion language models (dLLMs) have recently emerged as a promising alternative to autoregressive (AR) language models, offering competitive performance with a fundamentally different generation paradigm. Instead of producing tokens strictly left-to-right, dLLMs iteratively refine partially masked sequences, enabling bidirectional context modeling and supporting parallel token updates. This design creates new opportunities for accelerating generation and improving controllability. However, practical deployment of dLLMs remains challenging due to the high cost of training at scale and the lack of mature inference optimizations such as cache-friendly decoding and robust parallel sampling. In this work, we provide a comprehensive overview of recent progress on efficient dLLMs. To reflect how efficiency bottlenecks arise across the full lifecycle of dLLMs, spanning training, decoding, and deployment, we organize existing approaches into five categories: Training, Inference, Context, Framework, and Multimodality. For each category, we summarize representative methods and highlight their motivations, key techniques, and empirical trade-offs. Finally, we discuss open challenges and outline promising directions for future research toward high-throughput, robust, and practically deployable diffusion language models.

t: Don’t Scroll Back: Missing-Evidence Memory for Streaming Dialogue Summarization
a: Korea Advanced Institute of Science & Technology
Korea Advanced Institute of Science and Technology
ab: Users of modern platforms repeatedly need summaries of recent dialogue, but the window rarely contains enough context to be interpreted on its own. We formalize this setting as streaming dialogue summarization, where a system must summarize a current window using selective memory from an unbounded history under a fixed budget. We show that the central challenge is not how much history is accessed, but whether memory recovers the evidence that the current window presupposes. We construct a benchmark and evaluation protocol that separately assesses whether memory contains gap-resolving evidence and whether the generated summary reflects it. We propose ReMEMBER, a missing-evidence memory framework that conditions retrieval on unresolved window dependencies and refines retrieved chunks into evidence-dense memory under a fixed budget. Experiments on dialogues with histories up to 160K tokens show that ReMEMBER improves memory recall and gap-resolution completeness over memory construction baselines under the same budget. The code and benchmark will be released upon publication.

t: DPA-MoE: A Runtime Precision Control Framework for MoE Inference
a: Agency for Defense Development and Yonsei University
ab: Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) models reduce computation by routing each token to a small set of experts, but each selected expert is still used at a fixed precision. We present DPA-MoE, a runtime precision control framework that makes routed experts any-precision. DPA-MoE encodes expert feed-forward weights as prefix-decodable chunks using SharedScale AnyBCQ, profiles per-expert reconstruction residuals offline, and allocates chunks at inference time using live router gate scores. This post-routing allocation lets a single encoded MoE checkpoint operate at multiple effective weight budgets without retraining or re-encoding. Experiments on Qwen3-30B-A3B and DeepSeekMoE-16B show that DPA-MoE improves KL divergence and downstream accuracy over uniform chunk allocation at matched budgets, with modest steady-state throughput overhead in our prototype.

t: PDOS: Widening the Safety Overton Window Through Persona-Driven Generation
ab: Safety in large language models is often framed as requiring a single correct response, even in safety-sensitive contexts where multiple perspectives may exist. Existing approaches largely ignore Overton pluralism (inclusion of multiple reasonable viewpoints for a single query) and reduce complex context to monolithic judgments that fail to capture the range of reasonable viewpoints. Moreover, existing frameworks are not grounded in safety settings, which limits their ability to capture the diversity of perspectives required in safety-critical situations. Existing safety datasets do not provide Overton-style annotations, limiting their ability to represent multiple harm perspectives within the same safety-critical situation. To address this, we construct **SOS**, the safety-focused Overton dataset of 1,770 real-world safety situations annotated across 14 harm taxonomy. We further propose **PDOS**, a lightweight, training-free framework that retrieves personas from a synthetic pool and integrates their perspectives to generate unified Overton safety responses. PDOS achieves the highest average NLI coverage of 0.4226 among several baselines, and outperforms the strongest baseline by 13.3%. Our findings show that Overton-based safety pluralism requires adaptable, context-aware approaches, providing insights into how these methods can better capture diverse perspectives.

t: EmoDistill: Offline Emotion Skill Distillation for Language Model Agents in Adversarial Negotiation
a: University of Cambridge and University of Cambridge
ab: Post-trained LLMs are often optimized to produce helpful, polite, and accommodating responses. In adversarial negotiation, however, such behavior can become a vulnerability: emotionally framed language may influence an agent’s bargaining decisions in ways that conflict with its user’s objectives. We therefore introduce EmoDistill, an offline framework for distilling emotional negotiation skills from LLM–LLM interactions into smaller language-model agents. Here, an emotional negotiation skill is a state-conditioned behavior that determines which explicit emotion to invoke in a bargaining state and how to realize that emotion as an effective negotiation utterance. EmoDistill learns these two components separately: an Implicit Q-Learning (IQL) selector learns which emotion to express in each bargaining state, while a LoRA-adapted 7B policy learns the emotion-conditioned expression through Supervised Fine-Tuning (SFT) and Judge Policy Optimization (JPO). Across four emotion-sensitive negotiation domains, the full EmoDistill policy achieves competitive Utility and improves over vanilla and IQL-only baselines in most settings. Emotion-free ablations show that removing the explicit emotion channel substantially reduces overall negotiation utility, while transfer experiments reveal partial, domain-dependent transfer and robustness to unseen LLM counterparties. The code is available at https://github.com/Yunbo-max/EmoDistill.

t: Confident but Wrong: A Constrained Decoding Diagnostic for Low-Resource Automatic Post-Editing
ab: Automatic Post-Editing (APE) for low-resource languages (LRLs) often fails to improve Machine Translation (MT), and the score alone cannot say why: whether more training would help, or whether the training data is too inconsistent to learn from. We introduce a black-box, inference-time diagnostic that tells these two cases apart without retraining or annotation. It varies an edit-distance penalty \lambda that drives the model from free editing towards copying the MT, and reads two signals: (1) the shape of the Translation Edit Rate (TER)-vs-\lambda curve, U-shaped if edits from the model reduce error and monotonically decreasing if none does; and (2) the ordering of constraint variants that trust model confidence to increasing degrees, which shows whether confidence tracks edit quality. Across decoder-only and encoder–decoder models on English–Sinhala, the diagnostic exposes two failure modes consistent with a heterogeneous post-edit signal as the underlying cause: Binary Collapse, where the model copies the MT or makes off-target edits, and Confident Miscalibration, where the confidence signals we test do not separate useful edits from unnecessary ones. The pattern holds on English–Marathi and English–Tamil, with the failure modes tracking the post-edit distribution rather than MT quality or language family. Beyond diagnosis, the curve shape prescribes a concrete next step for practitioners; in the favorable case, a static constraint yields a free inference-time accuracy gain. We release the first English–Sinhala ({\sim}66k) and a new English–Tamil ({\sim}39k) APE datasets with all code.

t: Do Vision-Language Models Understand Visual Persuasiveness? A Diagnosis via Visual Persuasive Factors
a: Pohang University of Science and Technology
Pohang University of Science and Technology
ab: Visual persuasion uses images to shape cognition, emotion, and behavior, with its effects depending on both visual attributes and semantic context. Despite recent progress, it remains unclear whether Vision-Language Models (VLMs) understand visual persuasiveness. This motivates us to ask: can VLMs assess whether an image persuasively supports an intended message, which visual factors shape this judgment, and do they align with human judgments? Through empirical analyses on image-message pairs where human raters consistently agree on the persuasiveness judgment, we show that VLMs exhibit a recall-oriented bias: they over-predict images as persuasive while achieving high recall. We introduce Visual Persuasive Factors (VPFs), a taxonomy informed by cognitive psychology for quantifying visual cues that shape persuasive judgments. Our factor-level analysis reveals that VPFs distinguish human persuasiveness judgments, whereas VLMs only partially reproduce these patterns, often generating false positives by treating persuasion-relevant cues as sufficient evidence. Building on this insight, we evaluate VPF-guided interventions and find that properly framed VPF knowledge can improve performance, but merely specifying visual cues or adding step-by-step reasoning is insufficient. By analyzing model rationales at the level of functional reasoning steps, we further identify a central bottleneck in connecting object identification to semantic message alignment.

t: VEN-VL: A Visual Ensemble MoE Framework for Effective and Efficient Multi-Modal Understanding
ab: Despite the remarkable progress achieved by recent efficient methods in accelerating multimodal understanding, they still suffer from noticeable performance degradation. Their emphasis on the high compression ratio of a single visual clue and reliance on the heuristic pruning strategy with coarse attention alignment incurs a bottleneck on the information *capacity* and *density* of visual tokens. Addressing this limitation, we propose VEN-VL, a visual ensemble MoE framework for effective and efficient perception following the *enrich then compact* principle. Specifically, we first enrich the information capacity by unifying the visual representations of different perspectives, and then progressively compact it with adaptive routers in specialized visual experts to enhance the information density. Furthermore, we incorporate the reconstruction ability of vanilla structure via explicit visual supervision, facilitating crucial information preservation. Experimental results demonstrate our superiority in complex visual tasks with few information-condensed tokens, which effectively bridges the gap between performance and efficiency. Code will be available.

t: A Unified Per-Token Gating Family for On-Policy Distillation: FKL/RKL Mixing with Multi-Channel and Bias Coefficients
ab: Per-token gating of forward/reverse KL losses has emerged as a key technique for on-policy distillation (OPD), but existing methods such as EOPD (Agarwal et al., 2024) and ToDi (Jung et al., 2025) each commit to a single gating signal and a single direction. It is unclear which signal works best for a given task, or whether gating helps consistently. We introduce a unified analysis framework: a four-coefficient parameterization \sigma(a, h_t + b, u_x + c + d, \text{gap}_t) in which EOPD and ToDi appear as 1D restrictions, exposing multi-channel composition and an explicit bias term as additional structural degrees of freedom. On TweetEval emotion and hate, our framework improves over the matched-magnitude 1D restrictions in 33 of 36 comparable configurations (91.7%). A 26-configuration mean-match isolation experiment shows that dynamic OPD outperforms effective-KL-matched static baselines in 19 of 26 cases, with no configuration falling below the -1\sigma noise band relative to its matched static counterpart. The optimal (a,b,c,d) is task-conditional: emotion favors entropy, hate favors prompt-level uncertainty.

t: Knowing but Not Doing: Discourse-level Constraints Adherence of Large Language Models
a: Large Model Data Technology Lab, Huawei Technologies Ltd.
ab: Instruction following in large language models (LLMs) is commonly evaluated at the sentence or surface level, leaving discourse-level constraints underexplored. We study discourse-level instruction following by formalizing it as a structured constraint adherence problem and constructing both explicit and implicit benchmarks for evaluation. Experiments are conducted across models of different scales, revealing a systematic recognition–adherence gap: models can identify discourse constraints but frequently fail to adhere to them during generation with specific failure modes. This failure stems from a fundamental misalignment between standard training objectives and global structural integrity. Importantly, models show substantially improved adherence when discourse-level structural objectives are explicitly optimized.

t: ASP: Adaptive Semantic Preservation for Context Compression
ab: Context compression has emerged as a vital approach to mitigate both performance degradation and resource consumption for large language models (LLMs) in long context scenarios. Current state-of-the-art methods allocate the compression budget at fixed-size block granularity, either uniformly or with adaptation across blocks. Both strategies fragment sentence-level semantic units and overlook the relevance variation within each block. In this paper, we propose the Adaptive Semantic Preservation (ASP) compressor, built on two innovations: (1) To preserve semantic units, our Semantic-Preserving Segmentation partitions context along natural sentence boundaries while maintaining the morphological atomicity of words. (2) To prioritize critical information, our task-aware Adaptive Budget Allocation dynamically assigns compression budget based on each sentence’s informational salience for the task instruction. Extensive experiments across diverse long-context scenarios show that ASP outperforms strong task-aware and task-agnostic compression baselines on both Llama-3-8B-Instruct and Qwen-2.5-7B-Instruct. In particular, ASP delivers stronger robustness compared with other baselines even at the extreme 16\times high compression ratio.

t: SCOPE-RL: Optimizing Reasoning Paths Before and After Success
a: Beijing University of Post and Telecommunications
ab: Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) optimizes LLMs using sparse verifiable final-answer rewards. This sparse anchor reliably verifies whether a trajectory succeeds but provides no direct feedback on the reasoning path that produced it. Before success, prerequisite progress on hard problems receives no reward signal; after success, outcome rewards cannot distinguish well-organized correct trajectories from redundant or locally flawed ones. We introduce SCOPE-RL (Scaffolded Chain Optimization with Process Efficiency), a two-stage framework that densifies this anchor while retaining the GRPO update: Adaptive Scaffolded RL adds prefix-decomposed verifiable rewards on answer-hidden sub-question chains before success, and Quality-Aware Process RL applies correctness-gated process-shape rewards to refine correct trajectories after success. An expert-validated Step-Quality Evaluation Protocol evaluates useful-step density, error localization, and token efficiency beyond final-answer accuracy. On Qwen3-8B-Instruct trained on DAPO-Math and Big-Math, SCOPE-RL improves average accuracy by up to 11.2 pp and reduces reasoning tokens by up to 27.1% over outcome-only GRPO; the gains hold under GSPO and on Qwen3-0.6B-Instruct, indicating that reward-signal densification is complementary to policy-update-level RLVR advances.

t: Generating Complete Court Judgments with Large Language Models: A Study on CMML
ab: Given the criminal fact, a complete legal judgment usually contains two parts: Court View Generation (CVG) for the case and Legal Judgement Prediction (LJP) for each defendant. However, existing studies still cannot support unified modeling and evaluation of complete legal judgments. First, at the data level, existing legal datasets mostly cover either single-defendant scenarios or multi-defendant scenarios, and the attributes predicted by LJP are not rich enough, making it difficult for models to generalize to real-world complete legal judgments. Second, CVG and LJP are usually modeled independently, ignoring their intrinsic connection. Third, the role of auxiliary articles has not been explored. To address these issues, we build CMML (Chinese Mixed-Defendant Multi-Attribute Legal Judgment Dataset), a large-scale dataset that mixes single- and multi-defendant cases with multi-attribute annotations. Based on CMML, we propose a new task, LJP-x, which extends LJP with additional prediction attributes. We further systematically study the interaction between CVG and LJP-x, and explore how auxiliary articles influence both tasks. Our dataset is available at: https://github.com/magicalpig2003/CMML.

t: Dive: Accurate and Efficient Video Large Language Models for Lifespan Question via Head-wise Visual KV Cache Compression
ab: Given a Video Large Language Model (VLLM) and a pre-recorded video, how can we minimize the cumulative inference latency over future questions? Addressing this is crucial since VLLMs not only serve a massive volume of questions over the video’s lifespan but also incur substantial latency for each question. Existing methods compress visual tokens generated from a video to accelerate inference for each question. However, under aggressive compression ratios, prior approaches suffer from severe accuracy degradation, still resulting in high inference latency on each question. In this paper, we propose Dive, a visual KV cache compression method that preserves accuracy even under aggressive compression ratios. To maintain accuracy, Dive conserves the temporal context of the input video by evicting KV pairs after the prefill stage, rather than filtering out visual tokens before the VLLM processes the tokens through attention mechanisms. Dive significantly reduces per-question decoding latency by carefully evicting KV pairs, thereby achieving low cumulative latency over a massive volume of questions. Experiments show that Dive retains 98.2% of accuracy, using only 5% of the KV cache in Qwen2.5-VL.

t: Reinforcing Traceable Medical Reasoning with Critical Evidence Graph
a: Shanghai Innovation Institute and Shanghai Jiao Tong University
Shanghai Jiaotong University, Shanghai Artificial Intelligence Laboratory and Sensetime
ab: Large language models (LLMs) with reasoning capabilities have shown impressive performance in clinical applications, yet the readability and traceability of their reasoning processes remain limited, as reasoning quality is often overlooked during training. To address this, we propose MedCEG, a framework that augments medical language models with clinically traceable reasoning by explicitly supervising the reasoning process through a critical evidence graph (CEG). Specifically, we curate challenging clinical cases and algorithmically construct a CEG for each sample via multi-model consensus as a high-quality, traceable reasoning pathway. The CEG reformulates the reasoning process for supervised fine-tuning and underpins a traceable reasoning procedure reward that evaluates generated reasoning against the CEG through deterministic graph operations measuring semantic matching, triplet recall and connected-component analysis. Experiments show that MedCEG surpasses existing methods among open-source medical models of comparable scale while producing clinically readable and traceable reasoning chains. Code and models are available at https://github.com/LinjieMu/MedCEG.

t: Bridging the English-Arabic Medical Knowledge Gap: Targeted Low-Rank Adaptation via Causal Layer Selection
ab: Large Language Models (LLMs) perform strongly in English medical tasks but degrade substantially in Arabic, a gap widely attributed to limited training data. We systematically investigate this assumption via tuned lens probing and causal activation patching, and find that Arabic medical knowledge is present in intermediate model representations but fails to surface at the output. This mechanistic insight motivates a targeted adaptation strategy. Rather than fine-tuning the full network, we propose Targeted Low-Rank Adaptation (TLoRA), restricted to the layer window where cross-lingual representations diverge, upstream of the output layers where the failure manifests. We evaluate TLoRA on multiple-choice medical QA, where our approach outperforms full-network LoRA, zero-shot, and few-shot baselines. We further evaluate it on short-answer generation and multi-turn clinical dialogue, where it performs competitively without the need for task-specific finetuning. We additionally introduce AraClinicDialog, a clinician-constructed Arabic medical dialogue benchmark in MSA with validated variants across four Arabic dialects. Together, these contributions demonstrate that mechanistic diagnosis can serve as a practical guide for targeted adaptation in underrepresented-language medical LLMs.

t: TUX: Measuring Human–AI Tacit Understanding
ab: As large language models (LLMs) increasingly act as collaborative partners, human–AI alignment is often evaluated through explicit task success, accuracy, or reward optimization. Yet many collaborative settings depend on tacit understanding: whether an agent can align with a human’s evaluative stance or representational priors without clear objectives, communication, or feedback. To study this capacity, we develop a spectrum-placement task inspired by the social party game Wavelength, in which humans and agents independently place concepts along subjective spectra. We operationalize the Tacit Understanding Index (TUX) as a pairwise behavioral measure of similarity between human and agent judgments, and evaluate it with 241 human participants and 200 profile-conditioned LLM agents across four models. We find that nearest human–agent pairs in trait space achieve significantly higher TUX, suggesting that tacit alignment is associated with person-level characteristics rather than reflecting only random similarity. Regression analyses show that TUX becomes more explainable as predictor sets become richer, with individual traits, decision-making styles, and confidence improving over aggregate trait-distance baselines. These findings suggest that TUX provides a measurable behavioral signal of human–LLM tacit understanding, while revealing the limits of profile-based conditioning for capturing deeper representational alignment.

t: PSR: Efficient Knowledge Graph Question Answering via Plan-Guided Schema-Level Reasoning
ab: Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) enhances Large Language Models (LLMs) in Knowledge Graph Question Answering (KGQA) by retrieving reasoning paths from external Knowledge Graphs (KGs). However, the practicality of existing methods is often limited by their reliance on iterative retrieval, where the number of required LLM calls increases with retrieval depth, leading to expensive interaction costs. To address this, we propose Plan-guided Schema-level Reasoning (PSR), a training-free and efficient RAG framework for KGQA that requires only three LLM calls. First, PSR generates a retrieval plan from the input question (the first LLM call). It then performs Plan-Regularized Monte Carlo Tree Search to extract a compact set of schema-level paths from the KG, which are subsequently filtered by the LLM (the second LLM call). Finally, PSR grounds the chosen schema-level paths into instance-level reasoning paths to augment the LLM’s answer generation (the third LLM call). Experimental results on three datasets demonstrate the high efficiency and competitive accuracy of PSR.

t: SCENE: A Scenario Completion Benchmark for Measuring Social Bias in Large Language Models
ab: Most existing benchmarks evaluate social bias in large language models (LLMs) using multiple-choice questions (MCQ) grounded in stereotypical contexts. While MCQ formats enable straightforward quantification, how LLMs manifest social bias in task-specific contexts and under different output constraints remains underexplored. We introduce SCENE, a benchmark for measuring the social bias shown by LLMs in scenario-completion tasks. Given short scenarios involving social groups, models must complete key elements of the situation through two tasks: (i) Character Specification, which asks models to assign social attributes to characters, and (ii) Plot Continuation, which asks models to select the most plausible narrative continuation. Combining templates adapted from prior benchmarks with newly collected templates through a university-wide competition, we construct a dataset of over 75,000 Korean instances. Experiments show that bias measurements are highly sensitive to task context and output constraints, even for identical underlying scenarios, suggesting that widely used MCQ-based evaluations may not fully capture certain manifestations of stereotypes. SCENE is publicly available at https://github.com/DSAIL-SKKU/SCENE-EMNLP-2026.

t: Performance of Grapheme-Based Tokenizers on Word-level and Natural Language Understanding tasks for Indic Languages
a: Indian Institute of Technology, Madras, Dhirubhai Ambani Institute Of Information and Communication Technology and FLAME University
ab: Tokenization is one of the factors which influences the multilingual downstream performance of a language model. This paper demonstrates that vocabulary constrained grapheme cluster based tokenization leads to improved performance on Natural Language Understanding and Word-level tasks. We assess three different grapheme cluster based tokenizers, which are the Grapheme Cluster tokenizer, the Grapheme Pair Encoding, and a vocabulary constrained version of Grapheme Pair Encoding, across eleven Indic languages, namely Assamese, Bengali, Gujarati, Hindi, Kannada, Malayalam, Marathi, Odia, Punjabi, Tamil, and Telugu. We present the intrinsic performance of three grapheme cluster based tokenizers using Fertility, Rényi Efficiency, and Percentile Frequency. We also compare the performance of these grapheme based tokenizers with seven popular multilingual and Indic-focused tokenizers on downstream tasks. We find that the vocabulary constrained Grapheme Pair Encoding tokenizer exhibits competitive and sometimes superior downstream performance in comparison to other grapheme cluster based tokenizers.

t: A MultiModal Autoregressive Transformer Framework for Social Popularity Prediction
ab: Understanding and predicting the temporal popularity of social media content is critical for digital marketing and recommendation systems. Existing methods often rely on static feature concatenation, struggling to capture complex multimodal interactions and strict sequential dependencies in long-term popularity evolution, frequently underestimating viral content. To address these limitations, we propose a MultiModal Autoregressive Transformer Framework (MMATF). Our framework extracts and refines key representations from video covers, texts, category tags, and numerical statistics. A dynamic modality interaction module adaptively fuses these inputs to capture evolving content dynamics, establishing a solid foundation for temporal relevance. Furthermore, an autoregressive temporal encoding module strictly prevents future information leakage. Extensive experiments on SMTPD and ICIP datasets demonstrate MMATF significantly outperforms advanced baselines across 7-, 14-, and 30-day horizons. Specifically, compared to the strongest baseline, our model reduces Mean Absolute Error by 3.8% and 4.3%, and improves Spearman’s Rank Correlation by 0.3% and 0.4% for 30-day predictions on SMTPD and ICIP respectively, proving consistent long-term forecasting accuracy.

t: From Separation to Entanglement: Dissecting Feed-Forward Network Functional Organization in Vision–Language Models for Ancient Chinese Documents
a: Nanjing Agricultural University and Nanjing Agricultural University
China Mobile Communications Company Limited Research Institute
ab: While Vision-Language Models (VLMs) have demonstrated strong capabilities in general multimodal tasks, they face significant challenges in low-resource, cross-temporal settings such as ancient Chinese documents, where models must overcome complex visual noise and leverage deep linguistic priors. The functional organization of task-relevant components in existing VLMs remains understudied from a computational interpretability perspective. To address this, we introduce AncientVision-3T, an intervention-oriented diagnostic benchmark designed for mechanistic interpretability experiments on VLMs, organized across OCR, image classification, and image understanding tasks of increasing abstraction. Based on this benchmark, we propose the Ancient Chinese Target-Conditioned Gradient-based Neuron analysis framework (AC-TCGN), which identifies and validates task-relevant neurons for dissecting functional organization in general and domain-specific VLMs. Our experiments demonstrate that AC-TCGN effectively identifies neurons that are critical for model predictions. Moreover, our experimental results reveal a transition from separation to entanglement in the functional organization of decoder feed-forward networks: general VLMs show stronger task-wise separability, whereas the ancient Chinese domain-specific VLM shows greater cross-task neuron sharing and reduced task-wise separability. This suggests enhanced coupling between visual form and historical-semantic processing in ancient Chinese document image-text tasks.

t: When and What to Teach: Budget-Aware Online Adaptation for Web Agents
a: University of Electronic Science and Technology of China
Hefei University of Technology and Institute of Software Chinese Academy of Sciences
University of Electronic Science and Technology of China
Xi'an University of Architecture and Technology
University of Electronic Science and Technology of China
University of Electronic Science and Technology of China
ab: Web agents have achieved significant success in automating complex internet tasks but deploying them in real-world environments requires continuous online adaptation. Given that deploying powerful proprietary models remains commercially cost-prohibitive, practitioners must rely on lightweight local models that evolve post-deployment via online teaching from a stronger teacher. However, standard interactive feedback imposes prohibitive costs. We show that conventional trajectory-level preference optimization wastes budget on both unresolvable episodes and redundant execution turns. To resolve these inefficiencies, we propose Score-Guided Online Teaching with Budgeted Trajectory Trimming, a budget-aware framework that systematically orchestrates when and what to teach. Specifically, our framework integrates a solvability-aware teacher gate to dictate when to query the teacher model and a score-guided turn selection mechanism to decide what informative turns to retain. Extensive experiments on MiniWoB and TimeWarp demonstrate that our method achieves comparable first-pass success while reducing teacher calls by 22.6% and student training compute by 52.1% on average. Our code is available at https://github.com/zjw131f1fc/budgeted-online-teaching.

t: Mining or Synthesis? Rethinking Exploration Efficiency in Iterative Alignment of Mathematical Reasoning
a: Huawei Technologies Ltd. and Tsinghua University
Large Model Data Technology Lab, Huawei Technologies Ltd.
Harbin Institute of Technology, Shenzhen and Harbin Institute of Technology
ab: Iterative Direct Preference Optimization (DPO) has emerged as a widely used paradigm for aligning Large Language Models on reasoning tasks. Existing approaches typically rely on Best-of-N sampling (N\geq8) to mine positive trajectories from the distribution tail. In this work, we show that in mathematical reasoning, increasing N yields diminishing returns while increasing verifier-induced false-positive risk and the distribution shift required for policy updates. To address this, we introduce PACE (Proximal Alignment via Corrective Exploration), a generation-based corrective framework that replaces exhaustive mining with low-budget exploration (2\leq N\leq3). Rather than searching for increasingly rare positive samples, PACE synthesizes high-fidelity preference pairs from failed explorations through corrective hindsight refinement and verification-guided filtering. Empirically, PACE matches or exceeds the performance of DPO-R1 (N=16) while using about 1/5 of the compute, and remains robust under 20% label corruption, where high-N baselines exhibit substantially higher noise exploitation.

t: Scientific Knowledge-driven Decoding Constraints Improving the Reliability of LLMs
ab: Large language models (LLMs) have shown strong knowledge reserves and task-solving capabilities, but still face the challenge of severe hallucination, hindering their practical application. Though scientific theories and rules can efficiently direct the behaviors of human manipulators, LLMs still do not utilize these highly-condensed knowledge sufficiently through training or prompting. To address this issue, we propose **SciDC**, an LLM generation method that integrate subject-specific knowledge with strong constraints. By adopting strong LLMs to automatically convert flexible knowledge into multi-layered, standardized rules, we build an extensible framework to effectively constrain the model generation on domain tasks. Experiments on scientific tasks including industrial formulation design, clinical tumor diagnosis and retrosynthesis planning, consistently demonstrate the effectiveness of our method, achieving a 12% accuracy improvement on average compared with vanilla generation. We further discuss the potential of LLMs in automatically inductively summarizing highly-condensed knowledge, looking ahead to practical solutions for accelerating the overall scientific research process. All the code of this paper can be obtained.

t: HSPMark: Desynchronization-Resilient Multi-Bit LLM Watermarking via Semantic Anchoring
a: Huazhong University of Science and Technology
ab: Reliable multi-bit watermarking is essential for tracing the provenance of large language model (LLM) outputs. However, existing high-capacity schemes typically synchronize pseudo-random functions through discrete token n-gram matching, which makes them vulnerable to desynchronization under semantics-preserving paraphrasing attacks. To address this issue, we propose HSPMark, a hierarchical semantic projection marking mechanism for context-aware multi-bit watermarking, which shifts watermark synchronization from brittle token histories to continuous semantic anchors. HSPMark extracts stable contextual features using a pre-trained sentence-level encoder and a lightweight Robust Semantic MLP, then projects these features into context-conditioned pseudo-orthogonal bias matrices for multi-bit payload injection. To balance payload capacity and generation quality, HSPMark introduces an entropy-adaptive embedding mechanism that modulates logit bias according to predictive uncertainty. Extensive evaluations demonstrate that HSPMark improves robustness against paraphrase-induced desynchronization and local perturbations while maintaining a competitive trade-off among bit accuracy, payload capacity, and text quality compared with existing high-capacity baselines.

t: GUI Agents for Continual Game Generation
ab: Generating a game is not the same as making one playable. Existing code-generation approaches often translate a prompt directly into an artifact, leaving interaction-level failures undetected. We argue that game generation requires a player and study two roles for graphical user interface (GUI) agents. First, we introduce PlaytestArena, an evaluation environment containing 200 browser-based game-generation tasks across eight genres, each paired with rubrics of expected in-play behaviors. An independent GUI judge loads and plays each build to adjudicate these rubrics. Second, we propose Play2Code, in which a game agent and a rubric-blind GUI playtester iteratively generate, play, and refine games through shared memory. The playtester provides gameplay traces and actionable feedback, while a separate GPT-5.5 judge assigns final benchmark scores. Across three frontier backbones, Play2Code achieves a 66.8% rubric pass rate, outperforming single-pass and agentic-coding baselines by 37.1 and 14.6 points, respectively. Its scores also improve monotonically across refinement rounds. Further analysis shows that GUI-agent feedback is more traceable than human reports yet exhibits similarly idiosyncratic priorities. These results establish GUI playtesting as an evaluation and refinement signal for interactive code generation. Our project website is available at https://continual-game-generation.vercel.app/.

t: MedEQ: A Clinical Emotional Intelligence Benchmark and Rubric-Guided Reinforcement Learning for Patient-Centric Medical LLMs
ab: Patient-facing medical LLMs are typically evaluated for clinical knowledge and safety, but clinically correct answers can still fail patients by missing fear, mishandling uncertainty, or offering emotionally unsafe reassurance. We introduce MedEQ, a benchmark for clinical emotional intelligence in medical communication. MedEQ includes 413 clinically grounded consultation scenarios across 51 specialties and 7,336 expert-refined rubric items over 21 core dimensions. These expert-validated rubrics operationalize emotional cue recognition, empathic adequacy, ethical emotional regulation, and affective safety, enabling diagnostic evaluation rather than a single holistic empathy score. Using an LLM-as-judge rubric pipeline, we find that strong contemporary models often handle surface compassion, safety, and response structure, yet remain weak on deeper emotional inference, personalization, mixed emotions, cultural context, and real-time responses to illness-related distress. We further conduct a proof-of-concept rubric-guided reinforcement learning study, showing that MedEQ-derived rubric signals can transfer to an independent emotional intelligence benchmark: rubric-guided training of Qwen3-32B improves EQ-Bench performance from 42.42 to 81.49 while preserving or slightly improving standard medical benchmark scores. MedEQ therefore makes clinical emotional intelligence measurable and decomposable, and provides evidence that expert-refined rubrics can support the evaluation and improvement of patient-facing medical AI.

t: AgenTRIM: Tool Risk Mitigation for Agentic AI
a: Fujitsu Research and Development Center Co. Ltm.
Fujitsu Research and Development Center Co. Ltm.
Fujitsu Research and Development Center Co. Ltm.
Fujitsu Research and Development Center Co. Ltm.
ab: AI agents combine LLMs with external tools to solve complex tasks. While tools extend agents’ capabilities, improper permissions introduce risks such as indirect prompt injection and tool misuse. We characterize these failures as unbalanced tool-driven agency, a unified view in which agents either retain unnecessary permissions (excessive agency) or fail to invoke required tools (insufficient agency), increasing risk and reducing performance. We introduce AgenTRIM, a framework that addresses this imbalance without altering agent reasoning, through complementary offline and online stages. Offline, it reconstructs the agent’s tool interface from code and validates tool behavior via controlled executions and trace analysis. At runtime, it enforces per-step least-privilege access through adaptive capability filtering and isolated validation of tool calls, implicitly decomposing tasks without explicit planning. On the AgentDojo benchmark, AgenTRIM substantially reduces attack success while improving task performance over the baseline, unlike other leading defenses. To assess robustness beyond prompt injection, we conduct additional experiments covering description-based attacks and policy enforcement. Together, these results establish AgenTRIM as a general, capability-preserving framework for mitigating tool-driven risks in LLM-based agents.

t: Why Prompt-Injection Detectors Fail on XPIA: A Latent-Space Explanation
a: Microsoft and Indian Institute of Technology, Delhi
BITS Pilani, Birla Institute of Technology and Science
ab: Prompt-injection detectors often fail on **cross-prompt-injection attacks (XPIA)**, where the adversarial instruction is hidden inside a document, email, webpage, or tool output. This paper argues that the failure is not only a **distribution-shift problem**, but also a **representation-level problem**. Inside the hidden states of frozen detector backbones, user prompt-injection attacks (UPIA) and XPIA are encoded along **distinct, weakly aligned directions**. A detector whose readout is primarily aligned with the UPIA direction can therefore miss the XPIA signal, even though both signals are present in the same model’s representation. A **two-axis linear-discriminant probe** recovers this missing signal: UPIA attacks fire the UPIA axis in **99.9%** of caught cases, while XPIA attacks fire the XPIA axis in **97.3%** of caught cases. Axis ablations and activation-level steering suggest that these directions are not only predictive but may also be behaviorally relevant under controlled perturbations. The geometry persists across model families, training stages, scales, and external prompt-injection benchmarks, suggesting that **XPIA should be treated as a distinct threat axis rather than as a harder version of UPIA**.

t: DIAG: Diagnostic Iterative Alignment and Generation for Data-Efficient Mathematical Preference Distillation
a: Okinawa Institute of Science and Technology (OIST)
Huawei Technologies Ltd. and Tsinghua University
ab: Iterative preference optimization is essential for aligning Large Language Models on mathematical reasoning tasks, yet its efficiency is often throttled by signal scarcity: as the model improves, static problem sets become increasingly mismatched to the model’s evolving competence, producing rollouts that are either too easy or too hard and therefore non-informative, which leads to a scarcity of valid preference pairs. We propose DIAG, a Diagnostic Iterative Alignment and Generation framework that adaptively reshapes the practice distribution to increase informative supervision and focus training near the student’s current competence boundary. DIAG consists of two phases: (1) diagnosing valid preference-pair yield to calibrate the exploration-exploitation trade-off and allocate topic quotas via an Empirical Bayes shrinkage estimator, thereby prioritizing high-yield concepts; and (2) generating targeted practice, where a teacher synthesizes variants from the student’s failure traces. We further provide a theoretical view interpreting DIAG as a teacher-mediated approximation to KL-regularized reweighting of the practice distribution toward the student’s competence boundary, where valid preference-pair yield is maximized. Experiments show that DIAG boosts yield across iterations and delivers stronger reasoning performance under an iso-effective training budget, demonstrating that it can distill more informative preference supervision for mathematical reasoning.

t: Multilingual Medical Reasoning for Question Answering with Large Language Models
a: University of the Basque Country. UPV/EHU.
ab: Large Language Models with reasoning capabilities have recently shown strong promise for medical Question Answering. Current approaches report competitive results on English benchmarks through knowledge distillation from large models, yet multilingual coverage remains limited. We extend this line of research by presenting a method to generate multilingual reasoning traces that enrich the distillation paradigm with factual information from Wikipedia. Using a retrieval-augmented generation pipeline over WikiProject Medicine, we produce 500k reasoning traces in English, Italian, and Spanish. The traces are generated to solve medical questions drawn from MedQA and MedMCQA, both of which we extend to Italian and Spanish. We evaluate our approach across in-domain and out-of-domain Medical QA benchmarks, demonstrating consistent performance gains in both few-shot in-context learning and supervised fine-tuning settings, achieving state-of-the-art results among 8B-parameter models across multiple model families. With the aim of fostering the development of multilingual clinical decision-support tools, we release the complete suite of resources: reasoning traces, translated datasets, Medical Wikipedia, and fine-tuned models.

t: VeriTrace: Evolving Mental Models for Deep Research Agents
a: University of Cambridge and University of Cambridge
ab: Deep research agents face vast, interdependent, and pervasively uncertain information. Existing systems explore what evolving intermediate representations should look like, but leave their evolution to the LLM’s implicit reasoning. Without explicit regulation, the intermediate layer is easily contaminated by mixed-quality information, and errors propagate along its dependencies, so model scale often ends up substituting for absent regulation. We argue that an agent’s mental model should instead evolve through explicit feedback that continuously aligns task understanding with reality, and identify three regulatory loops: interpretive update, deviation feedback, and schema revision. We realise this in VeriTrace, a cognitive-graph framework that explicitly implements the three loops. Using matched Qwen3.5-27B backbones, VeriTrace improves over the strongest matched baseline by an average of 4.82 pp on DeepResearch Bench (DRB) Insight (1.83 pp Overall) and by 5.9 pp Overall win rate on DeepConsult. With Config-DeepSeek, it achieves the strongest reproducible open-source result on DRB.

t: LLM Knows, Speaks Not: Extracting Decoder-State Representations for Column Type Annotation
ab: Column Type Annotation (CTA) enriches tables with semantic column types that are often missing or incomplete in real-world data, aiding multiple downstream table tasks. Yet CTA remains challenging because sparse or noisy column values often require table-level context for disambiguation. Prior work either flattens tables into encoder inputs, losing structure and semantics, or follows a description-then-encoding pipeline that separates encoding and adds generation cost. We propose D2R, a decoder-based framework that obtains column representations directly from the hidden state that initiates column description generation. Specifically, D2R first encodes the table context once as a shared prefix KV cache, providing table-level context for all target columns. For each column, we append its sampled values and a description trigger token, then extract the trigger’s hidden state as the column embedding, preserving semantics without producing text. A decoder-attached classifier, trained via contrastive learning aligned with the CTA objective, predicts column types directly from this embedding. Across four CTA benchmarks, D2R achieves the best Micro-F1, outperforming TURL, a strong table PLM, by up to 12.57 points, while retaining efficient inference. The code is available at https://github.com/IvesCheung/cta.

t: CompassJudger-2: A Holistic Approach Towards Generalist Judge Model
ab: Recently, the role of LLM-as-judge in evaluating large language models has gained prominence, emerging as an important method to partially replace costly human assessment. However, current judge models suffer from narrow specialization and limited robustness, undermining their capacity for comprehensive evaluations. In this work, we decompose the ability of a generalist and generative judge model into three levels: objective verification, subjective evaluation, and rubric refinement. We present CompassJudger-2, a novel generalist judge model that overcomes these limitations via a task-driven, multi-scenarios data curation strategy. We conducted large-scale data collection for each type of task and designed tailored rejection sampling strategies to filter the data, ensuring data diversity, accuracy, and effectiveness. Empirically, CompassJudger-2 achieves superior results across multiple judge and reward benchmarks, demostrating its excellent robustness and generalization ability. These contributions advance robust, scalable LLM judgment and establish new performance and evaluation standards.

t: BioELX: Context-Aware Cross-lingual Biomedical Entity Linking without Task-Specific Supervision
a: University of Stuttgart and University of Southampton
ab: Cross-lingual biomedical entity linking (BEL) maps mentions in any language to unique identifiers in a biomedical knowledge base, supporting clinical and biomedical NLP applications. We identify two issues affecting current systems. First, the UMLS aliases used to train cross-lingual BEL retrievers are heavily skewed toward English, so retrievers generalize poorly to non-English mentions. Second, although context is often necessary for disambiguation, naively injecting context into retrievers trained only to align aliases severely degrades retrieval. We propose BioELX, a retrieve-rerank framework that addresses both issues. For retrieval, we continue training SapBERT_{\mbox{multi}} using Wikidata-derived cross-lingual alias supervision, forming shared concept neighborhoods across languages. For reranking, we adapt pretrained LLM rerankers to entity linking through mention-anchored prompting, which marks the target mention so that rerankers score candidates with respect to the intended mention rather than other salient tokens in the context. Experiments show that BioELX achieves new state-of-the-art results on four cross-lingual BEL benchmarks, improving Recall@1 by 4.8 to 18.2 percentage points over prior best results, without any task-specific BEL annotations.

t: Med-Chain: An Adaptive Clinical-Chain Retrieval Framework for Evidence-Grounded Medical Question Answering
ab: Large Language Models (LLMs) have shown strong potential in medical question answering, but their reliance on static parametric knowledge limits their ability to handle rapidly evolving clinical evidence. The retrieval system mitigates this issue by incorporating external medical knowledge, but flat retrieval can return lexically relevant but clinically misaligned evidence. We propose Med-Chain, a training-free medical evidence retrieval framework that reformulates retrieval as inspectable and repairable clinical evidence paths. Med-Chain first routes each question through a clinical topic tree to progressively narrow retrieval from broad domains to specific guideline sections. It then verifies whether the retrieved path matches the clinical intent and performs level-aware refinement to repair mismatches. Experiments on seven medical QA benchmarks show that Med-Chain consistently improves backbone LLMs and outperforms existing medical Retrieval-augmented generation baselines, highlighting the value of clinically structured and repairable evidence retrieval.

t: HW-GNN: Homophily-Aware Gaussian-Window Constrained Graph Spectral Network for Social Network Bot Detection
a: Zhejiang Lab, Zhejiang Lab and Hangzhou Yugu Technology Co., Ltd.
ab: Social bots are increasingly polluting online platforms by spreading misinformation and engaging in coordinated manipulation, posing severe threats to cybersecurity. Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) have become mainstream for social bot detection due to their ability to integrate structural and attribute features, with spectral-based approaches demonstrating particular efficacy due to discriminative patterns in the spectral domain. However, current spectral GNN methods face two limitations: (1) their broad-spectrum fitting mechanisms degrade the focus on bot-specific spectral features, and (2) certain domain knowledge valuable for bot detection, e.g., low homophily correlates with high-frequency features, has not been fully incorporated into existing methods.To address these challenges, we propose HWGNN, a novel homophily-aware graph spectral network with Gaussian window constraints. Our framework introduces two key innovations: (i) a Gaussian-window constrained spectral network that employs learnable Gaussian windows to highlight bot-related spectral features, and (ii) a homophily-aware adaptation mechanism that injects domain knowledge between homophily ratios and frequency features into the Gaussian window optimization process. Through extensive experimentation on multiple benchmark datasets, we demonstrate that HWGNN achieves state-of-the-art bot detection performance, outperforming existing methods with an average improvement of 4.6% in F1-score, while exhibiting strong plug-in compatibility with existing spectral GNNs.

t: From Proprietary to Public: Dataset Declassification for Question Answering
ab: Training Question Answering (QA) systems on real customer interaction data is often infeasible to reproduce or share due to privacy and intellectual property constraints. We introduce dataset declassification, a framework that replaces proprietary QA datasets with public, semantically equivalent counterparts that preserve training and evaluation utility while satisfying typical legal and privacy requirements. The approach maps proprietary questions to public equivalents via large-scale retrieval and reconstructs answers from domain-matched corpora using LLM-based annotation. Experiments on four QA benchmarks show that models trained and evaluated on declassified datasets achieve performance within \Delta \approx 0 of the original data. The method targets datasets whose underlying information needs already exist in public knowledge sources (e.g., knowledge available on the web and used by public-facing services). We further provide explicit applicability conditions showing that declassification succeeds when sufficient semantic overlap exists between proprietary and public corpora, and degrades predictably when it does not.

t: TimeSage-EV: A Live Benchmark for Agentic Time Series Analysis in Evolving Environments
