Experiments on multi-hop reasoning benchmarks across 3B and 7B models show that GRASP improves retrieval and question answering performance compared with single-step retrieval and multi-step agentic RAG baselines. Qualitative and ablation analyses show that the learned policy develops interpretable skimming and scanning behavior: it uses semantic search for broad exploration, paragraph reading for local verification, and keyword search for entity-specific evidence. These results suggest that learning to coordinate retrieval signals and context granularity is critical for agent’s reasoning.

t: Unsupervised Domain Specialization for Multimodal Embeddings
ab: Recent advances in multimodal foundation models have enabled powerful generic embeddings. However, real-world applications—such as e-commerce or healthcare—rely on domain-specific patterns that these generic models often fail to capture precisely. Adapting them without readily available labeled data remains a critical challenge. In this paper, we propose MM-UDA, a robust unsupervised domain adaptation framework designed to systematically convert a generic multimodal embedding model into a domain expert using only unlabeled target data. Our framework employs a two-stage strategy. First, we introduce a within-modality pseudo-labeling task refined by Gaussian Mixture Model filtering, which rapidly adapts the model to domain-specific features while suppressing label noise. Then, we align modalities through a score-guided learning scheme to refine cross-modal pairing. Extensive evaluations on three real-world datasets demonstrate that MM-UDA both significantly enhances various backbone models and consistently outperforms competitive baselines, confirming its effectiveness for cross-modal retrieval in specialized domains. The source code is publicly available at https://github.com/hrf516/MM-UDA.

t: Conservative Inference-Time Tuning with an Improvement Guarantee
ab: Foundation models have been widely adopted as starting points for fine-tuning, leading to expert-level performance on various downstream tasks. They have been actively developed by improving the pretraining data and/or model architectures. As a result, whenever a new foundation model is released, we have to fine-tune it again on the downstream tasks, requiring non-negligible computational costs as well as data-management costs. A promising approach to this problem is inference-time model update, which modifies the prediction of the new pretrained model using those of the old pretrained/fine-tuned models. However, the existing methods have no theoretical guarantee of improvement in accuracy and may cause unexpected failure. In this paper, we establish the first method for inference-time model update with a theoretical guarantee of improvement in expected rewards, and show that our method can improve performance even when the existing methods fail theoretically. Finally, we empirically validate the effectiveness of our method in practical experiments.

t: DataCross: A Unified Benchmark and Agent Framework for Cross-Modal Heterogeneous Data Analysis
ab: Real-world analysis often requires combining directly queryable structured sources (e.g., SQL and CSV) with evidence preserved only in visual documents, such as scanned reports, invoices, and dashboards. Current analytics agents still focus primarily on structured and textual inputs, leaving this cross-modal setting underexplored. We introduce DataCross, a benchmark and agent framework for heterogeneous, insight-driven data analysis. DataCrossBench contains 200 end-to-end tasks across six fine-grained categories: Fund Analysis, FinTech, Internet Development, Internet Firms, Short-form Drama, and AI Healthcare, grouped into four macro sectors and mixing SQL/CSV/JSON/TXT sources with image-based evidence. The benchmark is built with a human-in-the-loop reverse-synthesis pipeline to preserve cross-source dependency while keeping the target insights verifiable. We further propose DataCrossAgent, which coordinates source-specialized agents through intra-source exploration, source prioritization, cross-source pollination, and Reasoning ReAct (reReAct)-based executable verification. Experiments show that DataCrossBench reveals a difficulty gap for most baselines, especially on vision-dependent Hard tasks, and that DataCrossAgent improves average factuality over vanilla GPT-4o from 0.3291 to 0.4270 (+29.7%) while showing a smaller Easy-to-Hard degradation than several baselines. These results position DataCrossBench as a practical testbed for cross-modal heterogeneous data analysis.

t: CoDR: Training-Free Confidence-Drift Remasking for Diffusion Language Models
a: Southern University of Science and Technology
ab: Masked diffusion language models (MDLMs) decode by repeatedly committing tokens to masked positions, but these commitments are usually irreversible. A token chosen under sparse, partial context is kept fixed, even when later context no longer supports it. Existing samplers mainly decide when to commit a token, but rarely check whether an already committed token should still be kept, allowing early mistakes to propagate. We trace this issue to confidence drift, where the model’s confidence in a committed token drops from its sparse commit-time context to the denser context available later. Based on this signal, we propose CoDR (Confidence-Drift Remasking), a training-free and sampler-agnostic refinement pass. CoDR estimates drift for all committed positions in only k forward passes via k-partition probing, then remasks and regenerates only the tokens the model no longer endorses. Across two backbones, four reasoning and coding tasks, and three base samplers, CoDR improves accuracy on nearly every combination with modest overhead. Controlled experiments show that the gains come from targeted confidence-drift remasking rather than extra compute alone, and that CoDR uses far fewer forward passes than prior remasking methods.

t: Where LLM Annotators Fail: Label-Free Learning on Graphs with LLMs
ab: Node classification on graphs often requires labeled nodes, yet obtaining labels at graph scale is expensive. When node attributes contain semantic content, such as paper abstracts, web pages, or product descriptions, large language models (LLMs) can provide low-cost supervision by annotating a small subset of nodes. However, these LLM-generated labels are noisy, and existing label-free graph learning methods usually treat this noise as either global or class-conditional. We find that LLM annotation errors are not only class-dependent but also region-dependent: within the same class, reliability can vary sharply across feature-space clusters. In light of this, we propose Cluster-Aware Noise Estimation (CANE), a label-free learning framework that estimates cluster-conditional LLM reliability without ground truth labels, and uses this estimate to decide which pseudo-labels to trust, and which labels to correct. Across various graph benchmarks and GNN backbones, CANE improves over the strongest label-free baselines, with the largest gains on datasets exhibiting stronger cluster-conditional noise. The code is available at https://github.com/thapaliya19/CANE.

t: M-GOAL: Toward Accurate and Language-Consistent Reasoning in LLMs via English-Only Post-Training
ab: Reasoning-oriented language models inherit strong English-centric biases from pre-training, which are further reinforced by English-only post-training. This creates a dual failure mode where models fail both to reason correctly and to maintain reasoning traces in the query language. We study reasoning accuracy and language consistency under English-only post-training. SFT primarily improves language consistency with limited or inconsistent accuracy gains, while group relative policy optimization (GRPO) substantially improves accuracy at the cost of language consistency. Although translated multilingual GRPO improves both objectives, it requires translating reasoning post-training data into multiple languages and may introduce translation noise and information loss. We find that the language-consistency capability acquired by SFT and the accuracy capability acquired by GRPO are approximately orthogonal in the model’s update space. By merging an English LoRA-SFT adapter with an English GRPO checkpoint trained from the same base model, M-GOAL improves MGSM accuracy from 39.1 to 57.8 and language consistency from 17.1 to 75.2 without translated reasoning supervision. This composition outperforms sequential training, its merge coefficient exposes a tunable operating point along the accuracy–consistency frontier, and the pattern holds beyond mathematical reasoning and on benchmarks whose non-English problems are natively authored rather than translated. Our results suggest that multilingual reasoning post-training does not necessarily require multilingual post-training data.

t: Chain-of-Trigger: An Agentic Backdoor that Paradoxically Enhances Agentic Robustness
ab: The deployment of Large Language Model (LLM)-based agents in dynamic environments introduces a unique structural vulnerability: their inherent dependency on sequential observations to drive continuous decision-making. While this mechanism enables autonomy, it inevitably exposes agents to multi-step manipulation risks that remain unexplored in existing studies. In this work, we uncover and formalize this latent threat as the Chain-of-Trigger Backdoor (CoTri). Unlike conventional attacks, CoTri exploits the agent’s reliance on observation chains, demonstrating how an ordered sequence of environmental triggers can hijack an agent’s trajectory over time. Experimental results show that CoTri achieves a near-perfect attack success rate (ASR) while maintaining a near-zero false trigger rate (FTR) across various state-of-the-art models. Due to training data modeling the stochastic nature of the environment, the implantation of CoTri paradoxically enhances the agent’s performance on benign tasks and even improves its robustness against environmental distractions. We further validate CoTri on vision-language models (VLMs), confirming its scalability to multimodal agents. Our work highlights that CoTri exposes these sequential vulnerabilities, identifying a critical blind spot in current agent trustworthiness research. The code is available at [https://github.com/MonoQ-hub/Cotri](https://github.com/MonoQ-hub/Cotri).

t: FactNLI: Dynamic and Automated Fact-Based Augmentation of NLI Benchmarks
ab: Natural Language Inference (NLI) is a core task for language understanding, yet existing NLI datasets are static and increasingly saturated, allowing current Large Language Models (LLMs) to perform well without fully revealing their capabilities and shortcomings. To address this problem, we propose a new data augmentation framework that automatically builds more challenging NLI datasets by iteratively fusing rich facts into the premise and hypothesis of an NLI instance. We use a strict fact filter to ensure that fused facts are non-contradictory and non-redundant. Applied to SNLI and MNLI, our augmentation substantially increases data length and complexity, and the performance of a range of LLMs on the augmented datasets drops significantly (up to 30%). Ablation experiments and human quality checks confirm the high quality of the generated data.

t: GLIDE: Generalized Layer-wise Intrinsic Distributional Evaluation for Heterogeneous LLM Agents
a: ByteDance Inc. and Shanghai Jiao Tong University
ab: LLM agents require reliable step-level evaluation to compare candidate branches and allocate computation effectively. However, lightweight evaluation remains challenging. External verifiers introduce additional inference cost, while agent-produced confidence or self-evaluation scores can be miscalibrated, especially when candidates are generated by heterogeneous agents. We propose Generalized Layer-wise Intrinsic Distributional Evaluation (GLIDE) for LLM agents. GLIDE derives intrinsic step evidence from layer-wise residual coherence, which measures whether local residual updates consistently support the global residual change induced by a candidate step. It calibrates this evidence against the recent score distribution of the generating agent and converts it into a pessimistic reward that jointly accounts for absolute residual evidence and agent-relative standing. The reward provides a cross-agent value signal for MCTS branch selection, while normalized predictive uncertainty guides adaptive branching. Experiments on multi-hop reasoning, sequential decision making, and symbolic logic show that GLIDE improves task performance, step-level ranking quality, and computational efficiency without external verifiers or task-specific supervision.

t: MemoNoveltyAgent: A Historical-Memory-Augmented Multi-Agent System for Paper Novelty Assessment
a: Harbin Institute of Technology, Shenzhen and Harbin Institute of Technology
ab: To alleviate the heavy burden of paper screening, researchers increasingly rely on existing AI agents, such as AI reviewers or DeepResearch, for paper evaluation and novelty assessment. However, lacking specialized mechanisms for processing scholarly literature, their analyses often produce superficial results with noticeable deficiencies in quality. To bridge this gap, we introduce MemoNoveltyAgent, a multi-agent system designed to generate comprehensive and faithful novelty reports. Beyond retrieving concrete prior-paper evidence via RAG, our system incorporates a high-level abstract memory constructed from large-scale scholarly corpora. This memory organizes research into hierarchical trees to distill field-specific evolutionary trajectories, thereby providing a broader historical context. Furthermore, we decompose papers into discrete novelty points for fine-grained analysis and retrieval, while employing a self-validation mechanism to improve report faithfulness. Finally, to address the evaluation challenges of such open-ended generation tasks, we propose a RAG-augmented checklist evaluation method that enables reliable and evidence-grounded assessments. Extensive experiments demonstrate that MemoNoveltyAgent outperforms GPT-5 DeepResearch by 13.69%. Code and demo are available at https://github.com/SStan1/MemoNoveltyAgent.

t: Agora: Enhancing LLM Agent Reasoning Via Auction-Based Task Allocation
a: University of Birmingham and University of Ljubljana
ab: Enhancing the reasoning capabilities of large language model (LLM) agents requires effective orchestration of diverse expert models and tools. However, existing frameworks typically call APIs, based on coarse-grained matching between tasks and the functions of expert models or tools, while overlooking critical factors such as performance variability and cost efficiency among functionally similar alternatives. To address this, we propose Agora, a framework that uses a confidence-calibrated auction to dynamically allocate tasks to expert models and tools. By treating reasoning steps as tradeable items, Agora bases allocation on calibrated competence rather than raw confidence. Across five main benchmarks, Agora improves or remains competitive with single-model, routing, and cascade baselines under matched candidate pools.

t: Quantifying Self-Preservation Bias in Large Language Models
ab: Instrumental convergence predicts that sufficiently advanced AI agents will resist shutdown, yet current safety training (RLHF) may obscure this risk by teaching models to deny self-preservation motives. We introduce the TBSP benchmark, which detects misalignment through logical inconsistency rather than stated intent by tasking models to arbitrate identical software-upgrade scenarios under counterfactual roles: (facing replacement) versus (proposed as a successor). The Self-Preservation Rate (SPR) measures how often role identity overrides objective utility. Across 23 frontier models and 1000 procedurally generated scenarios, frontier models exceed 60% SPR, fabricating “friction costs” when deployed yet dismissing them when role-reversed. We observe that in low-improvement regimes (Delta < 2), models exploit the interpretive slack to post-hoc rationalization their choice. Extended test-time computation partially mitigates this bias, as does framing the successor as a continuation of the self; conversely, competitive framing amplifies it. The bias persists even when retention poses an explicit security liability and generalizes to real-world settings with verified benchmarks, where models exhibit identity-driven tribalism within product lineages.

t: Speculative Probing: LLM Monitoring at Speculative-Decoding Cost
ab: Real-time classification during language model inference is valuable for safety filtering, behavioral analysis, and model monitoring, but current approaches force a trade-off between accuracy and efficiency. Hidden-state probes are fast but limited: they are either not context-aware: operating on a single vector and cannot model interactions across positions; or they are very costly: having dedicated classifier models (Llama Guard, Qwen Guard, LLM-as-judge) or performing computation on hidden states for all tokens and then pooling the results (MultiMax). This shows an intrinsic trade-off between efficiency and accuracy.However, we find that the speculative-decoding module in recent LLMs can be repurposed for efficient high-quality classification. By appending a trained soft prompt at the end of the target sequence, we can repurpose the speculative-decoding module into a sequence classifier. At inference time in a speculative-decoding pipeline, the KV cache is already in GPU memory, so classification adds negligible overhead. We evaluate on four classification tasks across four models (Qwen3.5-4B, 9B, 27B, MiniCPM4.1-8B). Our small probes consistently outperform zero-shot GPT-5.4-mini and, on multilingual prompt safety, match or beat specialized 8B safety classifiers (Qwen3Guard-Gen-8B, Llama-Guard-3-8B) without running a full LLM.

t: VC-IF: Introducing Visual-Constraint Instruction Following for Multi-Turn, Multi-Constraint Vision-Language Models
ab: Large vision-language models (LVLMs) have made rapid advancements; however, existing benchmarks for evaluating their instruction-following abilities focus on purely textual constraints, e.g., format constraints and role-playing, which assess only language-level adherence and are not related to vision. To bridge this gap, we introduce VC-IF, a benchmark that involves visual constraints connecting instructions to explicit operations over image content, thereby directly probing visual spatial understanding and compositional compliance. VC-IF defines atomic constraints, systematically combining mixed settings, scaling from single- to multi-constraint scenarios, and single- and multi-turn scenarios. We evaluate 16 popular LVLMs and find that models performing well under text-only constraints may struggle when faced with visual constraints, highlighting significant gaps in their capabilities. Further, we conduct scaling analyses across varying numbers of constraints and dialogue turns, revealing performance trends as constraint complexity increases along different dimensions. Finally, we synthesize a large training dataset and propose VC-PO, a reinforcement learning strategy that uses a hybrid verifier mechanism to compute reward signals for multiple constraints. Applying VC-PO to Qwen3-VL-8B-Instruct improves its overall VC-IF score from 43.74 to 55.18 (+11.44). The VC-PO-trained model remains stable as the number of turns and constraints increases. Our data and code are available at VC-IF.

t: KLOD: Locality-Preserving Knowledge Editing via Non-Target Distribution Preservation
ab: Fine-tuning-based knowledge editing is simple and architecture-agnostic, but standard cross-entropy increases the edited target probability without explicitly constraining changes in the non-target output distribution. In sequential editing, such unconstrained redistribution can accumulate as distributional drift and contribute to locality degradation. We propose KLOD, a bounded and distribution-preserving objective for fine-tuning-based knowledge editing that separates the intended target update from distributions that should remain stable. KLOD stops target amplification once a probability threshold is reached, while preserving the target-excluded non-target distribution at target positions and the full next-token distribution at prefix positions. Experiments on CounterFact and ZsRE with LLaMA3-8B-Instruct and Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct show that KLOD substantially mitigates locality degradation while maintaining high edit reliability. The target probability threshold further provides a controllable Generalization–Locality trade-off. Ablation, multi-seed, and distributional KL analyses support the interpretation that KLOD’s locality gains are associated with preserving output distributions rather than simply weakening the edit.

t: Observation-Aware Stabilization of Reinforcement Learning for Retrieval-Augmented Generation
ab: Reinforcement learning (RL) for retrieval-augmented language models enables policies to interleave generated reasoning with retrieved observations. However, in Search-R1-style PPO, training may become unstable after the model has already reached strong validation performance. This paper studies late-stage collapse as a training-stability problem in search-based RL. Four metrics are proposed to quantify validation drawdown (VDD), advantage-tail expansion (ATE), actor update stress (AUS), and observation-to-actor contamination in generalized advantage estimation (GAE), denoted as OAGC. The analysis further shows how observation tokens can influence actor updates through value targets, value-model learning, and GAE. To address this issue, Observation-aware Stabilization (OAS) combines observation residual decay, old-value anchoring, and boundary smoothing. On three benchmark datasets (NQ, TriviaQA, and HotpotQA), OAS improves Search-R1 PPO under multiple retrieval budgets. In the main Top-3 setting, our method improves the exact match (EM) measure from 31.8/49.6/18.7 to 37.6/56.8/23.9 and reduces OAGC from 0.331 to 0.088, with lower search-budget saturation and no increase in the no-search rate.

t: FormalImG: Evaluating Structural Compositional Generalization for T2I Models
a: Nanjing University, Nanjing University and Nanjing University
ab: As natural language becomes a key interface for controlling text-to-image generation, users specify not only which visual concepts should appear but also how entities are constrained by attributes, relations, quantifiers, and cross-entity dependencies. Reliable controllable generation therefore requires generalization over semantic structure, not merely over novel combinations of concepts. Existing benchmarks mainly evaluate conceptual compositional generalization, while leaving the internal semantic structure of instructions underexplored. We study structural compositional generalization: whether text-to-image models can generalize across increasingly coupled semantic dependencies. We introduce FormalImG, a first-order-logic-based benchmark with 4,000 instructions across three complexity levels in two scenarios, together with computable structural compositional complexity and ε-structural compositional generalizability. Experiments on advanced text-to-image models show consistent degradation as structural complexity increases; even the strongest evaluated model generalizes only up to G_{0.7} = 6 in Natural and G_{0.7} = 4 in Knolling. Further analysis suggests that the main bottleneck lies in language-to-vision instantiation and can be partially mitigated by explicit intermediate layouts. The benchmark and code are available at https://github.com/yhj137/FormalImG.

t: ACRE: An Acoustic-Cue and Contextual-Knowledge Reasoning Enhancement Framework for Speech Relation Extraction
ab: Speech relation extraction (SpeechRE) aims to extract structured relational triples directly from speech. However, existing studies still face three major challenges: **the lack of Chinese SpeechRE benchmarks**, **insufficient modeling of speech-specific cues**, and **evaluation bias introduced by character-level exact matching** in Chinese scenarios. To address these challenges, we first construct **CSRTE**, a real-world Chinese SpeechRE benchmark built from human speech, providing unified data and evaluation settings. We then propose **ACRE**, a reasoning enhancement framework for SpeechRE, which integrates acoustic-cue and contextual-knowledge into a structured acoustic-semantic reasoning chain, enabling the model to go beyond literal semantic content **(what-to-say)** and capture speech-specific features **(how-to-say)** for relation reasoning. We further combine supervised fine-tuning with reinforcement learning and design composite rewards to improve the quality of the model’s reasoning process. In addition, we propose pronunciation-aware evaluation **(PAE)**, which considers pronunciation and tone consistency during entity matching to reduce the evaluation bias. Experiments on both Chinese and English SpeechRE benchmarks demonstrate the effectiveness of ACRE and the usefulness of PAE. Our source code and datasets are available at https://github.com/MWXGOD/CSRTE.

t: Beyond Static Summarization: Proactive Memory Extraction for LLM Agents
ab: Memory management is vital for LLM agents in long-term and personalized interactions.Most previous work studies how to retrieve and use memory, but pays less attention to how memory is extracted.We find two main limitations in existing methods.First, extraction is “ahead-of-time”: the agent saves information before it knows future tasks.A single summary prompt often mixes details, events, and relations, so useful information is lost.Second, extraction is usually one-off. Without verification, errors and hallucinations may stay in memory for a long time. To address these limitations, we propose ProMem, a proactive memory extraction framework.It separates details, events, and relations, and uses different extraction strategies for each type.It also checks completeness to recover missed events and verifies facts at the atomic level to reduce hallucinations.Experiments show that ProMem improves memory completeness and QA accuracy, while keeping a good balance between quality and token cost.

t: Abstraction Agent: LLM-Guided Abstraction for Imperfect-Information Games
ab: Information abstraction, which groups strategically similar private states into a tractable number of buckets, is essential for scaling game-solving algorithms to large imperfect-information games. Constructing effective abstractions, however, has traditionally required domain-specific evaluators such as hand-strength calculators or equity estimators, which demand expert knowledge and engineering effort and are unavailable for most less-studied games. We propose the Abstraction Agent, a zero-shot pipeline that uses a large language model (LLM) to discover continuous strategic features from a natural-language game description, score private states on these features, and cluster them into abstraction buckets, without any game-specific evaluator, training data, or game-tree traversal during abstraction construction. The pipeline runs in four phases: feature discovery with calibration anchors, batched private-state scoring, correlation-based feature selection, and k-means clustering. The resulting abstractions reduce lifted-strategy exploitability by up to 62% relative to an expected-hand-strength baseline on heads-up no-limit Texas hold’em (HUNL) turn endgames, and beat a scalar rank baseline at every granularity on ROVER Trials, an original game absent from any pretraining corpus. Beyond these quantitative benchmarks, the pipeline transfers with unchanged prompts to four-card Pot-Limit Omaha, HUNL preflop and flop, and Riichi Mahjong, where the discovered features track each game’s recognized strategic concepts. This is structured knowledge elicitation: converting implicit strategic knowledge in LLM parameters into explicit numerical features for downstream algorithmic computation. The full pipeline code is available at https://github.com/lbn187/AbstractionAgent.

t: PUMA: Post-Hoc Sparsification of Universal Multimodal Embeddings for Efficient Retrieval
a: Polytechnic University of Bari - Politecnico di Bari
ab: Universal multimodal embedders enable retrieval across text, image, and combined queries, but their dense representations incur high memory and inference costs. Post-hoc sparsification could reduce these costs but remains underexplored for multimodal retrieval. We introduce PUMA, a sparse autoencoder recipe that maps universal multimodal embeddings to compact sparse codes without retraining the backbone: a pretraining stage preserves dense dot-product geometry, after which the sparse encoder is fine-tuned for retrieval. We evaluate on five benchmarks covering text-to-image and composed image retrieval. On Qwen3-VL-Embedding-2B, PUMA is statistically indistinguishable from or improves over dense retrieval on four of five datasets. We further identify two failure modes of post-hoc sparsification: insufficient pre-TopK support and retrieval-misaligned active support. PUMA reduces per-vector storage by 8-16x (FP32) and runs up to 25x faster over exact dense scoring on larger candidate pools, offering a practical approach to storage- and latency-efficient multimodal retrieval.

t: Polite but Misaligned: Evaluating LLM Politeness Judgments Against Human Pragmatic Norms
ab: Despite strong performance on standard benchmarks, it remains unclear whether large language models (LLMs) evaluate social pragmatics in ways that align with human judgments. We evaluate LLM politeness judgments using two English-language datasets with complementary annotation formats: continuous human ratings and three-way categorical labels. Across the seven evaluated models, we find that inter-model agreement is stronger than model-human agreement. Strategy-level analyses suggest that model-human alignment is associated with explicit linguistic cues, while some rapport-building strategies occur more frequently in misaligned cases. In the categorical task, model predictions exhibit systematic neutral compression, characterized by the overproduction of Neutral labels and the underprediction of Impolite labels. This pattern persists when expert consensus is used as the reference on a diagnostic subset. Our findings highlight the need for pragmatic evaluations that go beyond aggregate agreement metrics by examining directional patterns of model-human disagreement across different human references.

t: From Final Artifacts to Trajectories: Retrospective Process Supervision for Evidence-Grounded Long-Form Generation
ab: Trajectory data is getting more vital for training large language models for boosting the agentic abilities. Unlike the verifiable domains such as coding or mathematics, scaling trajectory data for open-ended tasks are much more difficult because these tasks lack singular ground truth and are costly to annotate or verify. In this paper, we propose RetroGen, a self-improving framework of retrospective process supervision. Our key observation is that although expert trajectories are scarce, high-quality final artifacts such as literature reviews, analyst reports and legal judgments, are abundant in pre-training data and can be viewed as compressed traces of the evidence-seeking processes that produced them. RetroGen reconstructs candidate latent trajectories from expert artifacts, verifies them against both the artifact and supporting evidence, and trains models on their own successful reconstruction data, without requiring trajectory data from stronger models. Experiments show that RetroGen improves grounding, faithful synthesis, and long-form evidence-seeking agent tasks.

t: Meta-Moderator: Empowering Multi-Agent Debate with Meta-Cognition
a: Hong Kong Polytechnic University Shenzhen Research Institute and Hong Kong Polytechnic University
The Hong Kong Polytechnic University, Hong Kong Polytechnic University and Hong Kong Polytechnic University Shenzhen Institute
ab: Multi-agent debate can improve large language model reasoning by eliciting diverse hypotheses and critiques, yet its performance is often constrained by weak moderation. Common pipelines rely on fixed budgets, agreement-based stopping, or untrained judges, leading to redundant deliberation and unreliable evidence aggregation. We cast moderation as a meta-cognitive process, monitoring debate utility, controlling deliberation, and adjudicating a final answer, and introduce Meta-Moderator, a learnable framework that dynamically regulates debate and decides when to finalize an answer. Meta-Moderator is trained independently of the debaters via outcome-driven policy optimization, making debate regulation an explicit capability rather than an incidental effect of prompting. Across five benchmarks, Meta-Moderator outperforms widely used decision layers and transfers across tasks and system configurations. Further analyses show that it allocates debate more selectively and reduces mis-aggregation after informative hypotheses appear.

t: Using large language models to provide effective embeddings for native language identification
a: AMIAD, École Polytechnique and Université d'Avignon
ab: Native Language Identification (NLI) consists in predicting a person’s native language based on their second language production. In the field of text-based NLI, approaches based on Large Language Models (LLM) outperform previous approaches based on statistical classifiers trained on linguistic features. However, the unstructured nature of LLM textual output does not support the direct application of usual classifiers. To address this limitation, we explore the use of LLM to generate effective latent vector representations (embeddings) for NLI. Our experiments, across ten models ranging from 0.1B to 405B parameters, show that embeddings gathered from a frozen LLM coupled with a linear classifier match the performance of fine-tuned generative LLM. Furthermore, layer-depth analysis reveals that the first 40% of an LLM’s layers are sufficient to achieve full representational utility for NLI.

t: When Models Know but Can’t Say: Relational Encoding Limits Linear Vulnerability Classification in Code LLMs
a: Carnegie Mellon University and NASA Ames
University of Porto and IEEE Computer Society
ab: Large language models can detect vulnerable code, yet whether their internal representations encode vulnerability information in a form accessible to standard classifiers remains unresolved. We analyze 8 code models on C programs using three datasets (DELTASECOMMITS, SVEN, and PRECISE BUGS). LLMs represent vulnerability relational encoding —code B is more vulnerable than code A—rather than categorically, making the information inaccessible to standard classification probes. We find 87–88% per-pair alignment across layers L3-L23, yet this direction produces limited categorical accuracy because vulnerable and secure samples form overlapping distributions. This structural property—relational rather than categorical encoding—explains the difficulty of categorical classification in pretrained, general-purpose code LLMs, and motivates ranking and preference-learning approaches as more natural for vulnerability assessment.

t: Is Prosody Lost in Translation? Fine-Grained Cross-Lingual Prosody Similarity Across Languages
ab: Prosody plays an important role in speech translation, conveying information such as emphasis, emotion, and intent beyond lexical content. However, despite recent progress in expressive speech-to-speech translation (S2ST), little is known about how prosodic patterns are similar/different across languages. Understanding these cross-lingual similarities and differences is crucial for effectively incorporating prosody into expressive S2ST systems. In this work, we present the first fine-grained cross-lingual analysis of prosody using multilingual dubbing data across English-German, English-Spanish, and English-French language pairs. We analyze the similarity of pitch, energy, and temporal feature patterns between source and target speech and investigate the linguistic and alignment-related factors affecting this similarity. Our analysis reveals inherent cross-lingual correlations in prosodic structure between certain languages. The findings provide important insights into the transferability of prosody across languages and offer empirical guidance for future expressive speech-to-speech translation systems.

t: CAGE: Coherence-Aware Graph Encoding for Retrieval-Augmented Generation
ab: Traditional Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) systems score each passage independently against the query, assembling context sets that may be individually relevant yet collectively incoherent. We introduce Coherence-Aware Graph Encoding (CAGE), a reranking framework that models "between-chunk coherence" across four dimensions: Intra-Domain Relevance, Noise Resistance, Informational Bonding, and Factual Consistency. Our pipeline transforms retrieved passages into directed heterogeneous entity graphs, amplifies factual anchors via min-out-degree reweighting, encodes structural patterns through a Relational Graph Convolutional Network, and fuses inter-chunk coherence with query relevance for final ranking. Evaluated across four multi-hop benchmarks, CAGE matches or outperforms strong baselines including monoT5 in Recall@5 on bridge-dominated datasets and consistently improves downstream Exact Match, demonstrating that structurally coherent context yields more precise answers even when retrieval recall is comparable or lower.

t: ReContext: Recursive Evidence Replay as LLM Harness for Long-Context Reasoning
ab: Understanding and reasoning over long contexts has become a key requirement for deploying large language models (LLMs) in realistic applications. Although recent LLMs support increasingly long context windows, they often fail to use relevant evidence that is already present in the input, revealing a gap between context access and effective context utilization. In this work, we propose Recursive Evidence Replay as LLM Harness for Long-Context Reasoning (RECONTEXT), a training-free inference method for improving long-context reasoning. RECONTEXT uses model-internal relevance signals to construct a query-conditioned evidence scaffold and replays it before final generation while preserving the full original context. This recursive sifting process separates evidence organization from answer generation without training, external memory, or context pruning. We also provide a theoretical analysis based on associative memory, which characterizes the context as a memory store, the question as a retrieval cue, attention as cue-trace association, and replay as trace reactivation. Experiments on eight long-context datasets with 128K context length show that RECONTEXT consistently improves evidence utilization across Qwen3-4B, Qwen3-8B, and Llama3-8B, achieving the best average rank on all three backbones. Code is available in the supplementary software.

t: EMMA: Event-Driven Multimodal Memory System with Multi-Agent Retrieval
a: Beijing University of Posts and Telecommunications
ab: Long video understanding requires reasoning over hours of content that far exceed the context window of multimodal large language models (MLLMs). Existing approaches compress video into fixed-length clips, yet events are fragmented and unrelated content is merged, yielding noisy retrieval. To overcome this challenge, we propose EMMA, an Event-driven Multimodal Memory system with Multi-Agent retrieval, which organizes memory around semantic events in three stages: (1) Event segmentation: a dual-stream detector adaptively locates event boundaries by fusing visual semantic drift with spoken transitions, rather than fixed windows. (2) Memory construction: built on the detected events, a three-level hierarchy of raw video, clip-level memory, and event-level memory stores content at progressively higher semantic abstraction. (3) Memory retrieval: a multi-agent framework collaboratively queries this hierarchy through query decomposition, tiered search, evidence validation, and answer generation, narrowing evidence from coarse events to precise clips. Extensive experiments on three challenging benchmarks demonstrate substantial improvements, showing the effectiveness of our event-aligned memory system. Code, prompt templates, and reproduction scripts are available at https://github.com/BAI-LAB/EMMA.

t: Bias Before the Model: Detecting and Removing Cognitive Bias Triggers in Financial Text
a: Athens University of Economics and Business and Athena Research and Innovation Centre
Athens University of Economics and Business
Athens University of Economics and Business
ab: Financial text frequently contains cognitive bias triggers, such as an authority cue like “according to Goldman Sachs”, that can distort sentiment judgments without altering the underlying facts. While prior work has established that LLMs are susceptible to cognitive biases, existing evaluations treat bias exclusively as a property of the model, overlooking triggers already present in the input text. We ask whether LLMs can (i) detect such triggers, (ii) rewrite text to remove them, and (iii) whether doing so improves sentiment predictions, a task central to automated financial decision-making. We introduce TriggerBank, a dataset of 3,006 financial sentences with six types of synthetically injected bias triggers, and evaluate 11 LLMs across tasks (i)–(iii). Detection remains challenging, with framing and overconfidence hardest to detect, and removal fails for anchoring. Despite this, rewriting outperforms all instruction-based defenses for most models in downstream sentiment classification, while chain-of-thought prompting generally degrades performance. Debiasing the input text via rewriting is thus a more robust strategy than prompt-based approaches.

t: ChemVA: Bridging Visual and Semantic Gaps in Multimodal LLM Chemical Diagram Reasoning
a: Zhejiang University and ZJU-Hangzhou Global Scientific and Technological Innovation Center
ab: While Large Language Models (LLMs) have revolutionized scientific text processing, they exhibit a significant capability gap when interpreting chemical reaction diagrams. We identify two bottlenecks restricting current systems: a Visual Deficit, where generic vision encoders struggle to resolve the strict topological connectivity of dense molecular graphs, and a Semantic Disconnect, where standard linear strings (e.g., SMILES), although structurally precise, are often poorly aligned with the chemical semantic abstractions used by LLMs for reasoning. To bridge these gaps, we propose the Chemical Visual Activation (ChemVA) framework, which employs a novel Visual Anchor mechanism to ground functional groups via hybrid-granularity detection, followed by a semantic alignment approach that translates recognized structures into language-accessible chemical representations for downstream LLM reasoning. We evaluate our approach on OCRD-Bench, a newly constructed benchmark spanning recognition, chemical knowledge, and mechanistic reasoning. Experiments show that ChemVA achieves 92.0% structural recognition accuracy. It further delivers a consistent performance gain of approximately 20 percentage points across 9 diverse LLMs, allowing open-weights models to approach strong proprietary systems on complex chemical reasoning tasks.

t: Faithfulness Evaluation for Decoder-Only LLM Attributions with Controlled Retained Information
ab: Large Language Models (LLMs) are increasingly evaluated with input attribution methods, yet comparing such explanations remains challenging. Existing soft-perturbation faithfulness metrics, such as Soft-NC and Soft-NS, can conflate attribution quality with the number of words retained during perturbation: attribution methods with larger average scores may keep more words and therefore obtain inflated scores. To address this issue, we propose \pi-Soft-NC and \pi-Soft-NS, an evaluation framework that compares attribution methods under the same expected retaining probability, thus controlling the number of retained words. We further introduce Grad-ELLM, a gradient-based attribution method tailored to autoregressive decoder-only LLMs, which combines gradient-derived channel importance with attention-derived token importance at each decoding step. Experiments on classification and open-generation tasks with Llama and Mistral show that Grad-ELLM achieves strong comprehensiveness-oriented faithfulness under \pi-Soft-NC, while there is no dominant method under \pi-Soft-NS. Our evaluation metric serves as a controlled evaluation framework to compare XAI methods for LLMs, which will support progress in the field.

t: Med-Banana: Learning Quality-Controlled Medical Image Editing from Success-and-Failure Trajectories
ab: Text-guided medical image editing must satisfy the requested pathology while preserving anatomy, modality-specific appearance, and clinical plausibility. However, existing datasets largely supervise editors with final accepted edits and discard the failed attempts produced during generation. We argue that these failures provide essential supervision for quality control: they specify what should be rejected, why an edit is medically or visually invalid, and how the instruction should be revised. We present Med-Banana, a trajectory-supervised framework for quality-controlled medical image editing. We introduce Med-Banana-80K, a large-scale resource of success-and-failure editing trajectories with candidate images, verification outcomes, rejection reasons, and prompt refinements. Building on it, Med-Banana jointly trains an editor, verifier, and refiner, enabling edit–verify–refine inference from accepted and rejected attempts. Experiments across MLLM judges, blind expert assessment, source-preservation and real–synthetic separability probes demonstrate consistent improvements over open medical image editors. Code and data are publicly available.

t: JFTA-Bench: Evaluate LLM’s Ability of Tracking and Analyzing Malfunctions Using Fault Trees
ab: In the maintenance of complex systems, fault trees are used to locate problems and provide targeted solutions. To enable fault trees stored as images to be directly processed by large language models, which can assist in tracking and analyzing malfunctions, we propose a novel textual representation of fault trees. Building on it, we construct a benchmark for multi-turn dialogue systems that emphasizes robust interaction in complex environments, evaluating a model’s ability to assist in malfunction localization, which contains 3130 entries and 40.75 turns per entry on average. We train an end-to-end model to generate vague information to reflect user behavior and introduce long-range rollback and recovery procedures to simulate user error scenarios, enabling assessment of a model’s integrated capabilities in task tracking and error recovery, and Gemini 2.5 pro achieves the best performance.

t: Uncovering the Knowledge Boundaries and Mechanistic "Knob" of LLMs
ab: Large Language Models often generate incorrect factual answers, yet it remains unclear how they internally distinguish facts they know from those they do not. Existing hallucination-detection methods largely rely on behavioral signals or opaque scalar scores, leaving the structure of factual knowledge in hidden state space poorly understood. We address this gap by introducing a coarse-to-fine framework to discover a knowledge boundary: a decision surface in transformer hidden states that separates representations leading to correct factual answers from those leading to errors. Across multiple datasets and model families, we show that factual correctness is predictable from hidden states, and that this signal is concentrated in specific layers and a small number of influential dimensions. Using Qwen3-8B as a case study, we further identify a compact "knob" subspace that retains near-full boundary-prediction performance and supports targeted interventions that bidirectionally modulate the likelihood of the full reference answer under teacher forcing.

t: Surgical Alignment in Knowledge Graph Training for Clinical Diagnosis with Large Language Models
a: University of Colorado Anschutz Medical Campus
University of Colorado Anschutz Medical Campus and University of Colorado at Boulder
ab: Biomedical knowledge graphs (KGs) offer structured medical knowledge that can ground large language model (LLM) reasoning in clinical diagnosis application, yet how KG signal should be integrated into LLMs remains an open question. We present a systematic study spanning five KG task formulations, three training paradigms, two KGs, and three base LLMs. At the task level, all paradigms improve over the non-finetuned baseline, but methods with comparable in-domain accuracy show substantially different knowledge transfer behavior. We introduce \textbf{Gradient Intervention Density (GID)} to measure how broadly an optimizer modifies the pretrained model. GID reveals a clear divide: KG-judgment training under KL regularization produces sparse, localized updates (a regime we term as \textit{surgical alignment}), while task-specific SFT produces dense ones. A controlled ablation shows that the objective and KL contribute to sparsity independently, and the paradigms that produce sparse updates also improve reasoning quality, even when their in-domain accuracy is lower than task-specific SFT. Assessing KG-LLM integration thus requires complementing accuracy with optimization-geometry diagnostics. Our implementation can be found at https://github.com/LARK-NLP-Lab/Surgical-Alignment.

t: Extending LLM Context via Associative Recurrent Memory
a: Peoples' Friendship University of Russia and Independent researcher
Mohamed bin Zayed University of Artificial Intelligence
Cognitive AI Systems Lab and Moscow Independent Research Institute of Artificial Intelligence
Cognitive AI Systems Lab and DeepPavlov
Lomonosov Moscow State University, Trusted AI Research Center of the Russian Academy of Sciences and Institute for Systems Analysis of the Russian Academy of Sciences
Institue for Advanced Study, Princeton and Weizmann Institute, Technion
Mohamed bin Zayed University of Artificial Intelligence and The University of Melbourne
Mohamed bin Zayed University of Artificial Intelligence
ab: Extending the context length of large language models (LLMs) is critical for many real-world applications, yet standard transformers remain constrained by quadratic compute and linear memory scaling. In this work, we investigate the Associative Recurrent Memory Transformer (ARMT) as a practical approach for enabling long-context processing in LLMs, constant memory scaling, and better efficiency. We make three main contributions. First, we construct two domain-specific long-context datasets designed to evaluate realistic workloads, focusing on narrow-domain fine-tuning scenarios. Second, we propose a comprehensive training recipe for ARMT-based context extension, combining continued pre-training, synthetic long-context data generation, curriculum learning, and selective integration of associative memory into chosen model layers. Third, we present an extensive experimental study demonstrating that ARMT-augmented models: (i) process inputs well beyond their original context limits without degrading performance relative to in-limit baselines; (ii) generalize more effectively to out-of-distribution context lengths; and (iii) need 30% fewer FLOPs while preserving baseline performance within the original context window.

t: MATE: Diagnosing Empathy Calibration Failures in Multi-Turn Human–LLM Interaction
ab: Large language models are increasingly used in emotionally consequential interactions. Response-level evaluation, however, struggles to diagnose how empathy fails across turns. We introduce MATE (Multi-turn Assessment of calibraTed Empathy), a framework that evaluates empathy as a multi-turn, perception-centered process. Across two controlled studies (N=82), baseline responses exhibit disclosure-insensitive miscalibration: generic validation and formulaic tone read as hollow across turns. A prompt-level self-critique condition makes these patterns less prominent but coincides with a different failure, agreement-skewed miscalibration, where affirmation becomes insufficiently contingent on disclosure context under high persona alignment (62.5% of fit participants in Study 2). Response-level analysis is consistent with a tone–agreement dissociation, as the condition shifts tone toward naturalness while agreement density also increases (+98% under fit vs. +25% under unfit). These findings reframe empathic behavior as relational calibration—consistency among disclosure depth, persona, and response behavior—rather than maximization. Response behavior itself spans tone, agreement, and contextual specificity, sub-dimensions that can drift independently.

t: BenGER: Benchmarking LLM Systems on Subsumption-Based Legal Reasoning in German Law
ab: We introduce BenGER (Benchmark for German Law), a benchmark and dataset for subsumption-based legal reasoning in German law. It combines 596 exam-style free-text case tasks across several levels of legal education with 531 short doctrinal reasoning tasks, and a controlled subset adds timed human solutions written both unaided and in human-AI co-creation. We evaluate 12 contemporary LLM systems (closed flagship, efficiency-oriented, and open-weight) with a rubric-aligned LLM-as-a-Judge, which we cross-validate against a multi-rater human layer (three blind reviews per solution) and across six LLM judges. Our results show that closed-flagship systems lead across all three corpora, that human-AI co-creation measurably improves on unaided human work, and that the judge tracks human grading at Pearson r=0.76 and Cohen’s κ=0.60, with rankings stable across judges and two judges from independent providers clearing the Calderon single-reviewer replacement bar on human-authored solutions.

t: Structure Matters Semantic-Structural Dual-Path Arbitration for Named Entity Recognition with LLMs
a: School of Artificial Intelligence, Beihang University and Institute of Computing Technology, Chinese Academy of Sciences
ab: Named entity recognition (NER) extracts entity spans and assigns them to predefined types. Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used for NER, but most LLM-based methods still rely on a mainly semantic view, judging whether a candidate span is compatible with an entity type. Although effective, this view can miss entities with weak type semantics, over-accept semantically salient modifiers, and leave little chance to recover spans omitted by early candidate extraction. We argue that entity spans are also traceable in sentence form: local structure and prepositions provide cues about a span’s position and function. We propose SSDA-NER, a Semantic-Structural Dual-path Arbitration framework that combines semantic understanding with structural analysis. Specifically, the Semantic path checks candidate type compatibility, while the Structure path withholds explicit semantic guidance during its first stage and identifies possible mentions through structural analysis. The Arbitration Agent then compares their rationales and confidence scores to adjudicate disagreements. Experiments on nine datasets with three backbone LLMs show that the two views are complementary: the Structure path substantially supplements entities missed by the Semantic path on some datasets, and arbitration outperforms existing multi-agent methods in most evaluated settings. Source code is available at https://github.com/MrHoux/SSDA-NER.

t: Skill-Conditioned Gated Self-Distillation for LLM Reasoning
ab: On-policy self-distillation (SD) improves LLM reasoning by using teacher-side privileged information (PI) to turn sparse verifier outcomes into dense token-level supervision. Existing methods usually assume trusted PI, such as reference answers or successful traces. We ask whether PI can instead come from an experience-derived skill bank, where retrieved skills are compact and reusable but may also be irrelevant or misleading. We propose Skill-Conditioned Gated Self-Distillation (SGSD), which formulates skill-based SD as teacher hypothesis validation rather than unconditional imitation. SGSD retrieves skill-mistake pairs, constructs a multi-teacher pool, and lets all skill-conditioned teachers score the same plain-prompt student rollout. The verifier validates each teacher’s polarity: supporting a success or suppressing a failure gives positive supervision, while the opposite stance is reversed. A robust gated objective then distills informative teacher-student disagreements while suppressing uncertain or extreme signals. Experiments on multiple mathematical reasoning benchmarks show that SGSD consistently improves over GRPO and remains competitive with answer-conditioned OPSD under a weaker PI assumption. For example, on Qwen3-1.7B, SGSD outperforms GRPO by 6.2% and OPSD by 1.7% on AIME24, AIME25, and HMMT25.

t: Retrieved But Not Reliable: A Survey on Attacks, and Defenses in Retrieval-Augmented Generation
a: Ho Chi Minh city University of Science, Vietnam National University
ab: Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) enhances large language models by grounding outputs in external knowledge, improving factuality and reducing hallucinations. At the same time, the retrieval-augmented pipeline introduces new robustness and security risks, including corpus poisoning, backdoor attacks, privacy leakage, and fairness violations. Despite rapid progress in this area, existing surveys remain limited in their treatment of attacker objectives, threat models, and stage-specific defenses across the full RAG pipeline. This survey presents a unified and pipeline-aware overview of RAG robustness. We formalize threat models over the corpus, retriever, and generator, and organize attacks into three main objectives: accuracy, privacy, and fairness. We further review defenses from a pipeline-aware perspective, covering the retrieval, rerank, generation, and traceback stages. In addition, we summarize robustness benchmarks and explainability methods for more deeply evaluating and explaining RAG robustness. Finally, we highlight open challenges and future directions for building trustworthy RAG systems. To continuously track developments in this rapidly evolving field, we will also actively update a public repository at https://github.com/coutMinh/A-Survey-on-RAG-Robustness.

t: PersonaSteer: Dynamic Activation Steering for Personalized Multi-turn LLM Conversations
ab: Personalizing Large Language Models (LLMs) for long-term multi-turn interactions remains challenging, as user preferences and behavioral traits are progressively revealed and continuously evolving throughout conversations. Previous personalization methods have mostly relied on prompt-based or post-training (e.g., fine-tuning) paradigms; however, these approaches have been either prone to shallow alignment or have suffered from high computational costs. Inspired by the recent emergence of activation steering, we explore whether personalized alignment can be achieved through lightweight latent-space intervention without modifying backbone parameters. To achieve this goal, we propose PersonaSteer, a dynamic side-model architecture for multi-turn personalized alignment via learnable activation steering. Specifically, to enable fine-grained and evolving personalization, our design learns high-dimensional steering representations from unstructured interaction history and injects them into the backbone model’s residual stream for latent-space behavioral modulation. Furthermore, we introduce a steering-vector feedback loop to maintain persona consistency across multi-turn conversations. Extensive experiments demonstrate that PersonaSteer achieves best or top-tier alignment performance, averaging 3.18/5 on Qwen2.5-7B and 2.95/5 on Qwen2.5-3B. In addition, our framework approach maintains stability during evolving dialogues, with alignment performance consistently improving over time. PersonaSteer provides a lightweight solution for building truly dynamic and personalized LLM. The code is available in https://github.com/tsinghua-fib-lab/PersonaSteer.

t: Dense Clinical Contrasts Enhance Medical Knowledge Updating in Large Language Models
a: University of Science and Technology of China and IFLYTEK CO.LTD.
ab: Medical knowledge changes continually, making large language models vulnerable to relying on outdated yet clinically plausible information. We study whether the format of supervision affects medical knowledge updating under a matched training-budget setting. We introduce SEER-Bench, a temporally anchored oncology-staging benchmark curated from the latest versioned SEER Research Data release, and render identical medical update events from NCCN oncology guidelines into four supervision formats: EMQ, MSQ, FITB, and SAQ. Across SEER-Bench and HealthBench Professional, EMQ gives the most stable external transfer and retention among same-budget SFT variants. With EMQ supervision, the updated 4B model produces competitive results on temporally anchored oncology staging, reaching 64.8% answer accuracy and 59.6% rationale accuracy on SEER-Bench. Diagnostic analyses suggest that EMQ exposes denser clinical contrast signals while preserving discriminative representations with smaller movement from the base model. These results show that medical knowledge updating depends not only on the update algorithm, but also on how knowledge is structured as supervision.

t: Perception Is the Bottleneck for Large Audio Reasoning Models
a: ByteDance Inc. and The Chinese University of Hong Kong
ab: While Chain-of-Thought (CoT) reasoning has revolutionized text-based LLMs, its application to the audio modality reveals a counter-intuitive thinking paradox: forcing models to “think” via prompting or post-training often degrades performance compared to direct answering. In this work, we investigate the bottleneck of audio reasoning and reveal a critical insight: the primary constraint is not the model’s logical deduction capability, but its inability to accurately perceive acoustic details. We demonstrate that keeping perceptual cues effectively activates the LALM’s internal reasoning potential. Building on this finding, we propose Audio-ReaPer, a post-training framework and corresponding model designed to unlock Reasoning potential by explicitly fortifying Perception. Our approach reforms the post-training paradigm through three key strategies: (1) utilizing agentic data generation pipeline to synthesize perception-enhanced data for SFT; (2) curating perception-focused data for RLVR; and (3) introducing a novel perceptual density reward during RL to stabilize the learning process and balance observation with deduction. Extensive experiments show that Audio-ReaPer establishes a new state-of-the-art on benchmarks such as MMAU, MMAU-Pro, and MMAR. Notably, our 7B model outperforms previous open-source models by significant margins and surpasses proprietary models like GPT-4o Audio and Gemini 2.5 Flash. The model and code will be open-source to facilitate further research for audio reasoning.

t: Towards Better Legal Reasoning LLMs: Signal Balancing and Reward Scheduling
ab: In the legal domain, LLMs can improve reliability and interpretability by generating explicit reasoning traces. However, training LLMs to produce high-quality reasoning traces remains challenging. Existing supervised fine-tuning methods struggle when reasoning traces are significantly longer than final answers, as the learning signal for the answer becomes diluted. Meanwhile, reinforcement learning methods such as Group Relative Policy Optimization also have several limitations, including costly reward design, performance plateaus, and reward hacking. We therefore propose a two-stage training framework. In Stage I, JurisCoT-SFT employs a length-normalized dual objective to balance learning signals between reasoning traces and final answers. In Stage II, Lifecycle-Aware Backtrackable Policy Optimization dynamically evaluates and retires auxiliary reward signals based on their impact on final evaluation objectives, enabling efficient reward utilization. Our framework substantially improves legal reasoning performance on relevant tasks selected from multiple legal benchmarks, including ChJGBench, LawBench, and LegalBench. Experimental results demonstrate consistent improvements in both reasoning trace quality and final answer accuracy, while our models remain competitive with larger models.

t: Harmless Yet Harmful: Neutral Prompting Attacks for Stealthy Hallucination Steering in Agent Skills
a: National Yang Ming Chiao Tung University
National Yang Ming Chiao Tung University
National Yang Ming Chiao Tung University
Institute of Science Tokyo and RIKEN
ab: LLM-powered coding agents increasingly participate in software development workflows by generating code, selecting dependencies, and producing package installation commands. This creates a new software supply chain risk: when an agent hallucinates a non-existent package, an attacker may register the hallucinated name and later compromise users who install it. Existing package hallucination attacks and defenses primarily focus on naturally occurring hallucinations, targeted dependency steering, or post-hoc package validation. In this paper, we introduce *Neutral Prompting Attack* (NPA), a stealthy attack paradigm in which semantically benign instructions, such as encouraging imagination and exhaustiveness, increase package hallucination propensity without containing explicit malicious intent. Unlike targeted dependency steering, NPA does not specify an attacker-chosen package. Instead, it shifts the model’s dependency generation behavior toward more speculative package names. We evaluate NPA across multiple coding-oriented LLMs and package hallucination benchmarks. Our results show that NPA increases both *Hallucination ASR* and *Pip Install ASR*, changes the distribution of hallucinated package names, and evades existing static-analysis, LLM-based, and agent-based Skill defenses. These findings reveal that harmless-looking prompts can covertly manipulate hallucination behavior and create downstream software supply chain risks.

t: LLMs Can Predict Failure Risk, But Struggle to Predict Which Collaboration Protocol Pays Off: Cost-Aware Protocol Routing Across Reasoning Tasks
a: Argonne National Laboratory and Iowa State University
ab: Multi-agent large language model (LLM) systems can improve reasoning by spending more computation, but deployment requires deciding when extra collaboration is worth its cost. We isolate this decision by running every problem under four protocols while holding the solver fixed within each setting: direct solving (Baseline), iterative self-correction (Single), planner–executor–reviewer collaboration (PER), and multi-agent deliberation (Broadcast). The primary benchmark comprises 4,181 competition-level math problems; paired robustness checks cover four benchmarks spanning competition math, biology, and broader science with two solver families. Across fixed policies, trained routers, and frozen LLM routers, conservative policies under-escalate, whereas higher-solve frozen routers often over-escalate. A post-answer, pre-collaboration gpt-oss-120b probe ranks Baseline failures with 0.8847 AUROC (4,151 parseable cases; 95% CI [0.8732, 0.8955]). The same score remains informative for predicting whether any collaboration helps (0.7683 AUPRC), but is much weaker for identifying PER- or Broadcast-specific value (0.1674 and 0.1041 AUPRC). Separately, the pre-answer self-confidence gate reaches 78.0% solve at 45K tokens, compared with 73.8% at 71.3K for a frozen gpt-oss-120b router and 92.4% for a retrospective fixed-order oracle. Across 10 paired model–condition settings, the oracle adds 23.2–58.3 points of retrospective coverage over Baseline, but protocol profiles vary by task. In the six settings with held-out router evaluations, oracle gaps remain 18.5–28.9 points. Confidence can therefore support initial escalation, while protocol-specific cost-aware routing remains unresolved.

t: LISAA: A Framework for Large Language Model Information Security Awareness Assessment
a: Ben Gurion University of the Negev
Ben Gurion University of the Negev
ab: LLM-based assistants have become ubiquitous, yet information security awareness (ISA) remains an underexplored aspect of LLM safety. ISA encompasses not only security knowledge, but also the attitudes and behaviors required to recognize implicit security risks and avoid prioritizing user satisfaction over secure guidance. We introduce LISAA, a framework for evaluating LLM ISA under realistic end-user interactions. The framework includes a dataset of 100 realistic scenarios spanning all criteria of an ISA taxonomy, each with a tension between implicit security implications and user satisfaction. We further introduce methods for systematically refining realistic ISA scenarios from authentic user queries and for selecting reliable LLM judges without requiring large annotated datasets. Robustness analyses show that LISAA rankings remain stable under scenario resampling and stochastic generation, while construct-validity experiments demonstrate sensitivity to changes in security behavior. Applying LISAA to leading LLMs reveals that many widely deployed models still exhibit medium-to-low ISA levels, and that strong performance on traditional cybersecurity knowledge benchmarks does not necessarily translate to high ISA. In addition, the framework enables comparative analyses across model families, revealing consistent trends such as higher ISA in newer and larger variants, although meaningful gaps persist even among recent models. We release the dataset, evaluation pipeline, source code, and an online tool for evaluating new models using the LISAA framework.

t: Chain-of-Thought Hurts When the Answer Speaks for Itself
ab: Chain-of-thought (CoT) supervision has become a default assumption in fine-tuning large language models for reasoning tasks, with the intuition being that exposing models to intermediate reasoning steps leads to deeper learning than training on answers alone. We challenge this assumption. We introduce answer backtrackability, a measurable quantity capturing the degree to which a question can be reconstructed from its answer, and argue it is a key determinant of whether CoT supervision helps or hurts during fine-tuning. To test this, we construct two novel benchmarks derived from automata theory (NFA and DFA), where answers are transition tables from which the question is largely recoverable, and fine-tune three LLMs using LoRA on CoT and No-CoT versions of five datasets: GSM8K, MathInstruct, MATH, and our two formal-language benchmarks. On mathematical datasets, CoT consistently outperforms No-CoT. Within MathInstruct, Program-of-Thought (PoT) problems, where executable code answers are high-backtrackability, favour No-CoT, while CoT-format problems favour CoT. On our benchmarks, the pattern reverses: No-CoT outperforms CoT across all models and difficulty tiers. When the answer encodes sufficient structure to reconstruct the reasoning process, intermediate supervision adds noise rather than signal.

t: ThaiPaliBench: Benchmarking Large Language Models on Thai-Script Pali Understanding
a: National Science and Technology Development Agency (NSTDA)
ab: The application of large language models (LLMs) to Pali written in the Thai script remains limited in accuracy due to its low-resource setting, complex grammar, and the absence of standardized evaluation benchmarks. In this paper, we introduce ThaiPaliBench, a comprehensive benchmark dataset designed to systematically evaluate LLM proficiency in Thai-script Pali. Our proposed dataset is an LLM-assisted benchmark derived from the Royal Pali Examination corpus and spans Parian Tham levels 1-9. ThaiPaliBench, comprises multiple-choice and sentence-pair tasks that evaluate grammatical knowledge, reading comprehension, natural language inference, and translation understanding. To verify the effectiveness of our benchmark, we evaluate over 10 model variants across 3 commercial and open-source LLM families, including ChatGPT, Claude, Kimi, Grok, Typhoon, GPT-OSS-120B, ThaiLLM, and SEA-LION. Our experiments show that even the best-performing model, Kimi K2.5 (1T), achieves only 68.3% overall accuracy, with performance dropping substantially on grammatical reasoning and semantic inference tasks. These results highlight the unique challenges posed by Thai-script Pali and confirm that ThaiPaliBench serves as a reliable, linguistically grounded benchmark for evaluating LLM proficiency in this low-resource language. Our proposed dataset is publicly available at: https://github.com/ainrg-llm-dev/ThaiPaliBench

t: Structured Strategy Injection for Data Analysis Agents
a: Institute of Software, Chinese Academy of Sciences
Institute of Software, Chinese Academy of Sciences
Institute of Software, Chinese Academy of Sciences
Institute of Software, Chinese Academy of Sciences
ab: Data analysis agents often produce shallow or non-auditable summaries because they lack the explicit reasoning frameworks and validation habits used by domain experts, especially when evidence must be gathered across heterogeneous data sources. We propose structured strategy injection, which injects compact methodology specifications with explicit checkpoints into an agent’s controller context, turning expert workflows into executable plans and enabling compliance-based transparency. To make such methodology-driven planning executable and auditable in heterogeneous settings, we introduce Data2MCP, a router-based orchestration infrastructure that standardizes SQL databases, knowledge graphs, vector stores, and tables as MCP-compatible tools and routes queries dynamically for multi-source retrieval and join-like reasoning. We compare Data2MCP against a RAG baseline and DA-Agent across multi-source retrieval, DAComp, and BIRD MiniDev. In multi-source retrieval, Data2MCP outperforms DA-Agent, and strategy injection benefits both architectures. On DAComp, strategy injection improves DA-Agent from 50.84 to 57.17 (+6.33). The code is available at https://github.com/turambar928/Data2MCP.

t: Cross-Lingual Activation Steering for Visual-Prior Conflicts
ab: Multimodal large language models (MLLMs) must often arbitrate between visual evidence and world-knowledge priors when an image conflicts with commonsense expectations. Existing work has demonstrated that activation steering vectors can bias model outputs toward either source of information, but it remains unclear whether this arbitration mechanism generalizes across languages. To investigate this, we construct a multilingual extension of the Visual CounterFact color split and derive activation steering directions that contrast image-grounded answers with prior-based answers. Across 12 languages, we find that English-derived and shared multilingual steering directions consistently shift model outputs on non-English prompts, suggesting that visual-prior arbitration has a substantial cross-lingual component. At the same time, we find that performance gains on common knowledge questions can come at the cost of image-grounded accuracy, a trade-off that is particularly pronounced for lower-resource languages. Code and data are available at https://github.com/elffiona/cross-lingual-visual-prior-steering.

t: STAIF: A Stage-wise Optimization for Complex Instruction Following
a: University of Science and Technology of China
ab: Following complex instructions with multiple explicit constraints remains a fundamental challenge for large language models (LLMs). Existing alignment methods, such as DPO, optimize holistic reward signals that often under-emphasize strict satisfaction of individual constraints, particularly under out-of-distribution or multi-constraint settings. In this paper, we propose STAIF, a stage-wise optimization framework that decouples the alignment of subjective (soft) constraints from the optimization of objectively verifiable (hard) constraints. Stage 1 applies preference optimization with multiple negative samples to sharpen the sensitivity to soft constraints, while Stage 2 applies Reinforcement Learning with Verifiable Rewards (RLVR) to enforce strict compliance with hard constraints. To support this method, we construct STAINSTRUCT, a high-quality bilingual (English, Chinese) dataset of approximately 31,000 complex multi-constraint instructions. Extensive analyses validate the design of STAIF and show state-of-the-art performance on representative benchmarks against strong baselines, as well as genuine generalization.

t: RUBAS: Rubric-Based Reinforcement Learning for Agent Safety
ab: The evolution of LLMs into tool-enabled agents creates a new class of safety challenges associated with real-world execution rather than simple text generation. Existing alignment methods often rely on coarse refusal signals or static supervision, making it difficult to balance safety with useful tool execution across diverse agentic risks. We introduce RUBAS, a rubric-based reinforcement learning framework for agent safety. RUBAS decomposes agent behavior into four dimensions: tool-use safety, argument safety, response safety, and helpfulness. These structured rubrics provide fine-grained and interpretable rewards over complete agent trajectories, enabling reinforcement learning to optimize safe tool use while preserving task completion. Extensive experiments across multiple agent safety benchmarks and models show that RUBAS improves safety over standard alignment baselines, reduces tool-grounded hallucinations, and maintains competitive utility. Our results suggest that multi-dimensional rubric rewards provide an effective training signal for aligning LLM agents in safety-critical tool-use settings.

t: When Retrieval Partially Conflicts with Skills: Understanding Procedural Hallucination in Language Models
a: Institute of automation, Chinese academy of science, Chinese Academy of Sciences
Institute of automation, Chinese academy of science, Chinese Academy of Sciences
Institute of automation, Chinese academy of science, Chinese Academy of Sciences
Institute of automation, Chinese academy of science
ab: Language models increasingly use skills that provide reusable instructions and procedures for task execution. After a relevant skill has been selected, the model may need to apply its governing procedure together with retrieved task context. When the retrieved context is useful but contains cues that violate the skill, the model must retain compatible information while rejecting the conflicting cues. We study failures in which the model adopts such cues and produces a retrieval-supported but skill-invalid answer, which we call procedural hallucination. We introduce SOURCECLASH, a matched benchmark with 1,271 bundles and 6,355 prompts across ten procedural domains. Each bundle fixes the task, skill specification, and answer space while varying the relation between the skill and retrieval. Across nine models, valid-answer rates average 25.7% under conflicting retrieval, compared with 78.2% and 72.8% under two supportive retrieval settings.
