MASkills presents a new agent-optimization pipeline that integrates skill-conditioned credit assignment, hierarchical credit aggregation, and momentum-smoothed optimization, enabling agent skill libraries to evolve through refinement, induction, consolidation, and pruning. Experiments on HotpotQA, LoCoMo, and GAIA demonstrate the effectiveness of MASkills across multiple agentic tasks.

t: Can Multimodal Large Language Models Generate and Detect Multimodal Social Media Fake News?
ab: The rapid advancement of generative AI raises concerns about the misuse of Multimodal LLMs (MLLMs) for large-scale disinformation campaigns on social media. Despite existing research on textual disinformation, a fundamental question remains unanswered: can MLLMs be exploited to fabricate realistic multimodal fake news, and can they reliably detect it? We introduce a multi-agent framework in which a story agent, an image agent, and a critic agent collaborate to produce fake social media posts that plausibly counter true news. We apply the framework to generate over 9,000 paired multimodal news posts across science, health, and entertainment domains, and benchmark 16 open- and closed-source MLLMs for automated detection. We find that most models fall substantially short of human-level accuracy and fail critically on identifying image authenticity. Our research provides a foundation for developing robust defenses against social media fake news. Code and data are available at https://github.com/xiuzhenzhang/Multimodal.

t: Beyond Prompts: Measuring and Optimizing LLM Tool-Agent Harnesses
ab: LLM tool agents can be improved without retraining by modifying the runtime harness around a fixed model: prompts, tool interfaces, middleware, state handling, and recovery logic. We study this setting as resource-bounded harness selection for fixed-model multi-turn tool agents, with the search surface scoped to prompts and tool-boundary middleware: edits are guarded intercepts at the tool boundary, not arbitrary rewriting of agent execution logic. Our optimizer-agnostic protocol reports mean held-out lift, worst-condition lift, repeatability, logged cost diagnostics, and RelLift95(B), a conservative estimate of the held-out gain of the harness selected under budget B. We instantiate the protocol with prompt-only and prompt-plus-middleware optimizers, including PRISM, which clusters failures and routes repairs to prompt, tool-boundary middleware, or joint edit surfaces within a Pareto search. On BFCL multi-round, tau2-Retail, and tau2-Telecom, PRISM obtains mean held-out lifts of 14.2, 14.9, and 10.1 percentage points and positive empirical RelLift95 on all three benchmarks, and a component ablation attributes the margin chiefly to failure-surface routing and the edit-pattern constraint. Across optimizers, the results show that some search procedures can occasionally find large gains but still choose brittle updates, so the reliability of the chosen harness should be reported alongside average held-out lift.

t: What Gets Unmasked First? Trajectory Analysis of Diffusion Models for Graph-to-Text Generation
a: University of Texas at Arlington, University of Texas at Arlington
ab: We present the first systematic study of masked diffusion language models (MDLMs) for graph-to-text generation. We analyze MDLM generation trajectories—the order in which tokens are unmasked during iterative decoding—and find that, unlike autoregressive LLMs which generate text linearly, MDLMs naturally prioritize entities first, followed by relational and function words, with structural tokens resolved last. We further identify a previously undocumented failure mode of supervised fine-tuning: SFT disrupts this strategy by prematurely anchoring structural sentence-ending tokens early in the decoding trajectory, effectively fixing the output length which can lead to omitted or hallucinated information. To address this, we propose \lambda-scaled structural decoding, a training-free inference-time modification that downweights structural token confidence and recovers +9.4 BLEU-4. Finally, we introduce Graph-LLaDA, which integrates a Graph Transformer encoder into LLaDA’s decoding process to explicitly incorporate relational graph structure. Cross-dataset evaluation on LAGRANGE reveals that previous baselines overfit to dataset-specific patterns, while LLM- and MDLM-based approaches generalize significantly better. All code and datasets used in our experiments are publicly available at https://github.com/idirlab/Graph_LLaDA.

t: SVE-Loom: Improving Session-Level Reliability for Natural-Language-to-SVE Code Generation with Bounded Feedback
a: University of the Chinese Academy of Sciences
University of the Chinese Academy of Sciences
ab: Architecture-specific vector programming remains a difficult frontier for language models: an implementation can satisfy surface syntax yet fail because of a hallucinated intrinsic, an invalid predicate shape, a sizeless-type misuse, or a subtle tail-handling error. This work studies NL2SVE, a function-level code generation problem that maps natural-language specifications and fixed C/C++ signatures to ARM Scalable Vector Extension (SVE) implementations. We introduce SVE-Loom, a model-agnostic generation-and-repair framework that operates within a bounded compile-and-run feedback session. SVE-Loom combines ACLE schema repair, execution feedback, and reference-assisted Regional Semantic Bootstrap when scalar semantics are available. From an initial prompt under a bounded feedback budget, wrapped models using SVE-Loom achieve higher success rates, producing more legal and correct SVE implementations across evaluation benchmarks. We further mitigate the scarcity of public SVE supervision by constructing a NL2SVE corpus from GitHub-mined SVE code, template-generated kernels, and SVE-Loom-guided API-model candidates. This third layer makes the corpus extensible: scalar references or capability gaps can be converted into NL-to-SVE examples, while candidate SVE implementations are retained only after schema checks, compilation, execution testing, speedup measurement, and human audit.

t: Notes2Skills: From Lab Notebooks to Certainty-Aware Scientific Agent Skills
a: Southern University of Science and Technology and Shenzhen Loop Area Institute
Southern University of Science and Technology
The Hong Kong University of Science and Technology (Guangzhou)
Southern University of Science and Technology
Southern University of Science and Technology
ab: Scientific discovery workflows rely heavily on lab notes, where researchers record observations, interpret uncertain results, and plan follow-up experiments. Unlike polished publications, lab notes preserve evolving scientific reasoning, tacit scientific knowledge, and author uncertainty, giving AI agents access to the process of science. However, most prior work on scientific text focuses on papers, protocols, or structured databases, leaving informal laboratory notes underexplored as inputs to AI agents for science. This gap matters because tacit knowledge in lab notes is not written as a clean set of instructions: validated observations, tentative judgments, and possible experimental next steps often appear in the same passage. If these signals are conflated, an AI agent may mistake uncertain scientific judgments for confirmed conclusions or executable actions. To this end, we present Notes2Skills, a two-stage framework for turning lab notebooks into verifiable skills for scientific AI agents while preserving the author’s certainty. Across three wet-lab sessions and seven original downstream configurations, Notes2Skills is the only tested configuration that avoids both observed regime-level failures: over-acting on uncertain notes and missing firm directives. We show that certainty preservation is a key missing piece between lab notebooks and reliable agent skills, opening a path toward safer AI co-scientist systems.

t: What Does Layer-Importance Reveal About Transformers and State-Space Models?
a: École Polytechnique de Montréal and Mila - Quebec Artificial Intelligence Institute
ab: Transformers and state-space models (SSMs) are the two dominant families of sequence models, and a central open question is how far the analytical knowledge built for transformers transfers to SSMs. We address this through the lens of layer importance which underpins compression, selective fine-tuning, and interpretability across both families. We decompose layer importance into two distinct notions. Necessity captures how much the pretrained model depends on a layer’s existing contribution, measured by the loss increase from bypassing it. Plasticity captures where the model absorbs new information during fine-tuning, measured by the magnitude of task-specific weight updates. Our analysis reveals that transformers and SSMs behave fundamentally differently: in residual transformers, Necessity and Plasticity anti-align across depth, whereas in Mamba-style SSMs they point to overlapping regions. The sign of this alignment also predicts downstream adaptation behavior. In transformers, the updates are in the most plastic layers, which increases catastrophic forgetting, while this tier-dependent effect disappears in Mamba-style SSMs

t: SHARD: Safe and Helpful Alignment via Self-Reframing Distillation
a: University of North Carolina at Chapel Hill
University of North Carolina at Chapel Hill
Department of Computer Science, University of North Carolina at Chapel Hill
ab: Large language models often struggle with sensitive prompts. They may refuse outright, provide generic safety boilerplate, or fail to address the user’s legitimate informational needs that can be answered safely. We introduce SHARD, a self-reframing distillation method to improve safety-helpfulness. It first rewrites sensitive prompts to surface benign intent using philosophical guidelines, then reframes its original responses into safe, more helpful ones, and finally fine-tunes the model on its self-reframed responses. Across DNA and the English subset of LINGUASAFE, SHARD improves helpfulness for most model families while preserving safety. It also remains competitive with distillation from a larger teacher model, suggesting that models can internalize safe and helpful behavior elicited from the models themselves.

t: Empowering LLM Agents with Geospatial Awareness: Toward Grounded Reasoning for Wildfire Response
a: New York University and University of Maryland, College Park
ab: Effective disaster response is essential for safeguarding lives and property. Existing statistical approaches often lack semantic context, generalize poorly across events, and offer limited interpretability. While large language models (LLMs) provide few-shot generalization, they remain text-bound and blind to geography. To bridge this gap, we introduce a Geospatial Awareness Layer (GAL) that grounds LLM agents in structured Earth data. Starting from raw wildfire detections, GAL automatically retrieves and integrates infrastructure, demographic, terrain, and weather information from external geodatabases, assembling them into a concise, unit-annotated perception script. This enriched context enables agents to produce evidence-based resource-allocation recommendations (e.g., personnel assignments and budget allocations), further reinforced by historical analogs and daily change signals for incremental updates. We evaluate the framework in real wildfire scenarios across multiple LLM models, showing that geospatially grounded agents can outperform baselines. The proposed framework can generalize to other hazards such as floods and hurricanes.

t: RoboTrustBench: Benchmarking the Trustworthiness of Video World Models for Robotic Manipulation
ab: Video world models are increasingly used in robotic manipulation, yet existing benchmarks mostly evaluate them under valid, feasible, and safe instructions. We introduce RoboTrustBench, a benchmark for evaluating the trustworthiness of video world models under four scenarios: Normal, Constraint-Sensitive, Counterfactual, and Adversarial. Built from real-world DROID episodes, RoboTrustBench contains 1,207 expert-validated instruction–image pairs and a six-dimensional evaluation protocol with 13 fine-grained criteria. Evaluating seven representative video world models with human and MLLM assessment, we find that current models often generate visually coherent videos, but struggle with constraint reasoning, counterfactual grounding, physical interaction, and unsafe-instruction suppression. These results show that visual quality and surface-level instruction following are insufficient for trustworthy robotic video world modeling.

t: FedLoRAGuard: Federated Dynamic Graph Neural Networks with Differential-Privacy Certificates for LoRA Adapter Integrity Verification
ab: Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA) is now the dominant parameter-efficient fine-tuning method for large language models, but the resulting open marketplace of adapters has become a supply-chain attack surface: backdoored adapters merge silently with arbitrary task adapters while preserving benign utility, and existing centralized integrity tools require marketplaces to share raw weights, which is incompatible with proprietary fine-tuning. We present FedLoRAGuard, a federated dynamic-graph framework that verifies adapter integrity without weight sharing. The LoRA ecosystem is modeled as a heterogeneous continuous-time dynamic graph with four node types and six edge types; a federated dynamic GNN is trained per-client with client-update-level (ε, δ)-DP Gaussian noise, secure aggregation, and FLTrust scoring. We prove a sensitivity bound for federated heterogeneous-GNN client updates and a certified poisoning-radius theorem that converts the per-round inference-time smoothing budget ε_r into an analytical bound on the size of a bounded-update colluding coalition k*. On 13,500 benign and backdoored adapters across four base-model families and ten attack types, FedLoRAGuard obtains 96.4% macro-F1 and a certified coalition bound k* = 25 from N = 50 marketplaces at the inference-time smoothing budget ε_r = 0.5, and empirically tolerates label-flipping Byzantine coalitions up to ρ ≤ 0.33 without certificate degradation. The DP-SGD training-time mechanism, calibrated at σ = 1.1 and Poisson subsampling q = 0.2 over T = 100 rounds, achieves a cumulative privacy budget ε_T ≈ 13.6 at δ = 10⁻⁵ under the Opacus PRV accountant, with sub-second per-adapter verification latency on A100-class hardware. The full DP + secure-aggregation stack adds a measured median per-round wall-clock overhead of ≈ 4% (pooled median across three runs of 20–60 measurement rounds on identical CPU hardware) over non-private FedAvg; the released runtime ships the instrumentation so operators can re-measure in place on their target hardware.

t: When Models Hear What They Expect: Diagnosing Prosodic Heuristics in Multimodal Sarcasm Detection
a: MTRI Tokyo Technology Research Institute and University of Groningen
PRAII Foundation, MTRI Tokyo Technology Research Institute and IEEE
ab: Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) process speech and text jointly, yet whether they exploit prosodic cues for pragmatic inference or rely on surface acoustic patterns has received little systematic investigation. We address this through sarcasm detection, evaluating Qwen2.5-Omni and Qwen3-Omni on Mandarin Chinese and English under five modality conditions that decompose the contributions of lexical content, vocal semantics, and prosodic structure. Adding audio systematically inflates false positives without improving true positive detection. Acoustic error diagnosis reveals that model errors cluster on a shared stereotype of expressive prosody, namely elevated pitch and irregular pausing, that diverges from the actual cues marking sarcasm in both languages. Targeted manipulation of only these two dimensions causally confirms the heuristic, inducing false positive rates of up to 60%. Applying the same manipulation template to Gemini 3 Flash Preview without modification replicates the effect, suggesting that the stereotype extends beyond the Qwen Omni family rather than arising from a single model architecture.

t: BudgetThinker: Empowering Budget-aware LLM Reasoning with Control Tokens
a: Mohamed bin Zayed University of Artificial Intelligence and Tsinghua University
Institute for AI Industry Research (AIR), Tsinghua University
Institute for AI Industry Research, Tsinghua University
ab: Scaling test-time computation improves the reasoning ability of large language models (LLMs), but the resulting latency and cost limit its use in latency- and cost-sensitive scenarios. We present BudgetThinker, a framework for reasoning-budget adherence that provides online control of chain-of-thought (CoT) length during decoding. Rather than relying on a one-shot prompt instruction, BudgetThinker periodically inserts specialized tokens that communicate the remaining reasoning budget. A two-stage training pipeline, consisting of supervised fine-tuning and curriculum-based reinforcement learning, teaches the model to interpret these signals and adapt its reasoning pace. Across the evaluated 1.5B and 7B text backbones, a 7B multimodal backbone, and a 1.5B code-reasoning model evaluated on HumanEval, BudgetThinker improves budget adherence and accuracy–efficiency trade-offs over competitive baselines. The controlled comparisons isolate the contribution of online ratio signaling from the shared training pipeline. Code is available at https://github.com/MobileLLM/BudgetThinker.

t: Does Thinking Help Fairness? Reasoning Tokens Resolve Some Biases but Create More
ab: Thinking in reasoning language models (RLMs) has been subject to debate on whether it resolves or amplifies bias. Prior works have shown competing conclusions in both directions. Using a within-model thinking-vs.-non-thinking ablation across QwQ-32B, DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-32B, and Qwen3-32B on three high-stakes decision tasks (Adult, COMPAS, Credit), we show that thinking has an asymmetric dual effect on counterfactual fairness: it both resolves counterfactual flips produced by the non-thinking baseline and creates new flips at near-saturating model confidence. In all nine (model, dataset) combinations, the created flips outnumber the resolved flips by roughly 5\times. To explain the effect, we treat the thinking trace itself as a measurable site of fairness change and study it through two dynamic instruments: 1) We propose Counterfactual Depth Probability Gap (CDPG) to track bias evolution along thinking depth, and observe that bias propagates and amplifies with thinking. 2) We also formulate Bias Transition Matrices (BTM) to show how predictions of counterfactual pairs change from non-thinking to thinking, and find that the asymmetric dual effect originates in the pair-state joint transition.

t: AdaCultureSafe: Adaptive Cultural Safety Grounded by Cultural Knowledge in Large Language Models
a: Jiangxi University of Finance and Economics
ab: With the global proliferation of Large Language Models (LLMs), cultural safety, defined as the ability to generate respectful and appropriate responses across diverse cultures, becomes critical for responsible AI deployment. However, existing research often treats cultural safety and cultural knowledge in isolation. It remains unclear whether cultural safety is grounded in understanding varying cultural knowledge to enable LLMs to adaptively yield respectful and appropriate responses across diverse cultures, which triggers ethical concerns in cross-cultural scenarios.In this work, we introduce AdaCultureSafe, a dataset designed to jointly evaluate cultural safety and knowledge. Through AdaCultureSafe, we reveal a critical insight: a significant decoupling exists between cultural safety and cultural knowledge proficiency. Although LLMs possess rich cultural knowledge, they fail to leverage it to improve cultural safety. LLMs tend to rely on generic safety rather than safety based on culture-specific knowledge. Motivated by this, we propose a knowledge-grounded method that elicits internal cultural knowledge in LLMs during response generation. Experimental results demonstrate that our approach effectively improves cultural safety. Our work can aid better understanding the landscape of cultural safety of LLMs.

t: SDRAG: Sub-question Dependency-Aware Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Multi-hop Question Answering
ab: Multi-hop question answering (QA) requires integrating evidence across multiple documents and reasoning over interdependent intermediate steps, posing significant challenges for retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) systems. While recent RAG-based approaches interleave retrieval and reasoning to improve factual grounding, they often struggle with complex multi-hop questions due to retrieval–reason mismatch, ignored dependencies among sub-questions, and error propagation during decomposition. In this work, we propose SDRAG, a sub-question dependency-aware RAG framework that explicitly models the intrinsic logic of multi-hop questions as a dependency graph. SDRAG first decomposes the question into fine-grained sub-questions and explicitly models their dependency relations, then refines the graph by pruning unreliable or redundant nodes, and finally traverses the pruned graph to coordinate retrieval and reasoning. To improve graph construction quality, we further introduce a supervised fine-tuning strategy that independently trains task-specific LoRA adapters for decomposition, dependency prediction, and pruning. Experiments on three common multi-hop QA benchmarks show that SDRAG consistently outperforms strong RAG-based baselines, while additional analyses demonstrate the effectiveness of dependency modeling, graph pruning, and fine-tuning.

t: ParaThinker: Native Parallel Reasoning for Scaling LLM Test-Time Compute
a: Institute for AI Industry Research (AIR), Tsinghua University
Mohamed bin Zayed University of Artificial Intelligence and Tsinghua University
Institute for AI Industry Research, Tsinghua University
ab: Test-time scaling improves the reasoning capability of large language models by generating longer sequential chains of thought. While effective, this approach reaches a bottleneck as computation increases, resulting in a “test-time scaling plateau” where further computation provides only marginal gains. We argue that this ceiling reflects a limitation of the scaling strategy rather than model capability, a phenomenon we term Tunnel Vision, where imperfect early steps can lock the model into a suboptimal reasoning path. Motivated by this observation, we propose ParaThinker, an end-to-end parallel reasoning framework that trains LLMs to generate multiple reasoning paths in parallel and aggregate them into a final answer within a single architecture. By exploring different lines of thought, ParaThinker sidesteps the Tunnel Vision issue and unlocks the model’s reasoning potential. On challenging reasoning benchmarks, ParaThinker achieves accuracy improvements (e.g., 6.5%–20.7% on AIME-24 with a 1.5B model) over sequential-reasoning LLMs under the same budget of decoding tokens. Under matched decoding token budgets and with KV-cache reuse, ParaThinker achieves 38.7%–66.8% lower inference latency than sequential decoding via batched parallel generation. The code is available at https://github.com/MobileLLM/ParaThinker.

t: Orchestrating Hidden-Intermediate Pruning-and-Distill for MoEs Slimming
ab: The remarkable performance of Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) models often comes with substantial architectural scale and resource overhead. Prior structural compression mainly focuses on expert-level or FFN intermediate pruning. However, we identify an emerging architectural trend that the FFN expansion ratio in state-of-the-art MoEs has steadily decreased, making intermediate-only pruning less effective and motivating us to explore other redundancies. Motivated by this, we propose an orchestrated hidden-intermediate prune-and-distill framework that, to the best of our knowledge, is the first to jointly prune expert FFNs along both intermediate and hidden dimensions. It includes Budget-Constrained Coordinate Descent to efficiently search expert-specific pruning ratios across the two dimensions, and attention relation transfer distillation to provide stable supervision under hidden misalignment. Extensive experiments across diverse benchmarks validates that hidden-dimension pruning is a promising direction for compressing modern MoEs.

t: Towards Reliable Truth-Aligned Uncertainty Estimation in Large Language Models
a: Korea Advanced Institute of Science & Technology
ab: Uncertainty estimation (UE) aims to quantify uncertainty in large language model (LLM) outputs to flag potential hallucinations and support reliable deployment. However, UE metrics often exhibit unstable performance across models and datasets, limiting their practical utility. We formalise this phenomenon as proxy failure, arising because UE metrics are derived from model behaviour rather than being explicitly grounded in factual correctness. We show that when mutual information between a UE score and correctness is low, the score’s discriminability must be close to chance. To address this, we propose Truth AnChoring (TAC), a lightweight post-hoc calibration method that maps raw UE scores to truth-aligned correctness probabilities. Even with noisy and few-shot supervision, TAC continues to improve calibration, providing a practical calibration protocol. Our findings highlight the limitations of treating heuristic UE metrics as direct indicators of uncertainty about factual correctness, and position our TAC as a principled step toward more reliable uncertainty estimation for LLMs.

t: ProEvent: An Event-centric Benchmark for Proactive Agents
ab: Proactive agents are expected to anticipate user needs and provide autonomous assistance by perceiving environmental context without explicit instructions. A fundamental capability of such agents is to identify and track users’ upcoming events, enabling continuous and event-specific assistance. For example, by recording the time and location of a planned hike, an agent can deliver weather reminders in advance or provide navigation support before departure. However, existing works on proactive agents largely overlook event-centric assistance, and the open-ended nature of proactive assistance poses challenges for reliable evaluation.To bridge these gaps, we introduce ProEvent, the first event-centric benchmark designed to assess an agent’s ability to proactively maintain a user’s timetable based on ongoing instant messaging chats. ProEvent provides synthesized yet realistic chats that consider the dynamic interaction among users, concurrent chat threads, and noise in the real world, and evaluates proactive agents on response timing, single-step response correctness, and multi-step response correctness. Experiments on eight LLMs and pipelines reveal that current agents frequently overact and struggle with event cancellation. Notably, even the state-of-the-art GPT-5.1 provides redundant assistance in 30% of cases and achieves only 26.7% recall in event cancellation scenarios. Further qualitative analysis reveals fundamental limitations of current LLMs as proactive agents, particularly in detecting implicit events and reasoning from the user’s first-person perspective.

t: FCPRAG: Fusion-Controller Parametric Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Stable Multi-Passage LoRA Injection
a: HKUST(GZ) and The Hong Kong University of Science and Technology
ab: Parametric retrieval-augmented generation (PRAG) injects retrieved evidence into a large language model (LLM) through passage-specific LoRA adapters, reducing reliance on long in-context prompts. When multiple passages are retrieved for the same query, however, evidence-level fusion becomes a bottleneck: equal-weight merging can amplify weak or conflicting evidence, and translating retrieval signals into fusion weights often requires fragile global tuning. We propose FCPRAG, a fusion-controlled parametric RAG framework that adds a lightweight controller for retrieval-conditioned, sample-level adapter fusion. The controller predicts per-passage fusion scores together with sample-level calibration signals, including a mixing gate and an adaptive temperature, enabling fusion that stays selective under informative retrieval signals and conservative under uncertainty. FCPRAG is trained with merge-aware supervision derived from each adapter’s marginal contribution within a multi-adapter merge, using training data only. We further show that a single dataset-level temperature is suboptimal under heteroscedastic retrieval uncertainty, motivating sample-level adaptation. Experiments on HotpotQA, 2WikiMultiHopQA, PopQA, and ComplexWebQuestions (CWQ) across three LLM backbones show that FCPRAG consistently improves F1 over standard RAG and parametric RAG baselines, with gains of up to 4.65% on 2WikiMultiHopQA and 7.55% on CWQ, while also reducing tuning cost and improving robustness under retrieval perturbations. Code is available at https://github.com/ReinerBRO/FCPRAG.

t: Critical Positions in LLM Reasoning: A Metacognitive Lens on Intervention-Sensitive Locations
ab: Large Language Models (LLMs) achieve strong reasoning performance by generating intermediate reasoning trajectories through autoregressive decoding. Existing approaches such as self-consistency, tree-based reasoning, and critical token analysis improve reasoning by exploring diverse trajectories or identifying influential tokens. In this work, we identify a distinct phenomenon in LLM reasoning: **critical positions** — locations where re-sampling continuations disproportionately influences the final outcome, independent of the specific token at that position. Motivated by this, we propose **Metacognitive Influence Tracing (MIT)**, the first unsupervised framework for identifying critical positions from a single reasoning trace using only attention structure. MIT models reasoning trajectories as influence graphs and estimates propagated influence through a diffusion process, enabling the discovery of structurally important reasoning positions without supervision or contrastive trajectories. Building on these insights, we further propose **Adaptive Critical Sampling (ACS)**, an intervention framework that selectively re-samples at critical positions instead of regenerating entire reasoning traces. Across six benchmark tasks and five models, ACS improves accuracy by an average of **7.78 points** over CoT while reducing computational cost by **59.83%** over Self-Consistency.

t: TopoEval: A Comprehensive Benchmark for Topological Reasoning in Foundation Models
a: Beijing Institute of Mathematical Sciences and Applications
Beijing Institute of Mathematical Sciences and Applications
Beijing Institute of Mathematical Sciences and Applications
ab: Topological reasoning—the ability to identify structural invariants under continuous deformations—is a cornerstone of human visual cognition, yet it remains under-explored in modern AI systems. Existing benchmarks provide limited coverage of mathematical topology as a discipline and rarely probe the depth of topological reasoning. To bridge this gap, we introduce TopoEval, an 800-item benchmark suite for topological reasoning. TopoEval centers on a 400-item answer-based Core track and includes a 400-item Proof track for reference-grounded informal proof assessment. The suite spans four major topology branches, twelve fine-grained subfields, and three difficulty levels. On Core, we investigate model scaling, reasoning depth, prompt strategies, image dependency, and academic tiers. The strongest Core configuration reaches 73.0% overall and 54.1% on all 85 K12 items. For context, topology-trained graduate-student solvers reach 96.3% under the audited protocol in Appendix B.2. On Proof, pass-plus-borderline rates are low across the selected conditions, indicating difficulty in producing reference-aligned natural-language topology proofs. TopoEval profiles these capabilities across academic level, image dependency, and proof quality.

t: Old Memories Die Hard: Unveiling Shallow Forgetting and Ripple Effects in Privacy Unlearning
ab: Large language models (LLMs) often memorize personally identifiable information (PII) during training, raising serious privacy concerns. While machine unlearning has emerged as a promising mitigation, its effectiveness against privacy attacks remains unclear. We introduce PrivUn, an evaluation framework for privacy unlearning under recovery attacks, paired with three measurement tools: forgetting scores, association metrics, and layer-wise analysis of forgetting depth. This framework studies not only whether a model forgets, but also how forgetting propagates and where it fails.Using PrivUn, we make two findings. (i) The PII ripple effect is gradient-driven, not semantic. Graph-based proximity is uncorrelated with PII forgetting, while gradient-based association is more strongly correlated. (ii) Label-based unlearning is typically shallow, while PII is stored across deeper layers. Layer-wise evidence suggests that label-based methods mainly change the final layers, explaining why they reduce direct retrieval but remain vulnerable to stronger recovery attacks.

t: ReCite: Agentic Reasoning for Faithful Citation
ab: Accurate citations are the foundation of academic writing, tracing intellectual origins and substantiating core claims. However, manually navigating the growing volume of scientific literature is increasingly difficult, prompting reliance on automatic citation recommendation. While modern retrieval-augmented architectures have largely mitigated the fabrication of non-existent papers, current systems relying on semantic similarity struggle with misattribution, often citing authentic papers that fail to logically support the author’s claim. To address this challenge, we argue that accurate citation requires a shift from similarity-based search to active, claim-level reasoning. We propose ReCite, a decoupled agentic framework that orchestrates location perception, intent-aware query planning, and reflective verification. Trained on synthesized reasoning trajectories, our agent verifies claim-evidence consistency and triggers self-correction loops when retrieved candidates lack logical support. Experiments demonstrate that our lightweight framework outperforms state-of-the-art massive generative models in strict citation accuracy. By grounding literature matching in verifiable logic rather than semantic overlap, ReCite establishes a reliable foundation for automated academic writing.

t: Silence over Error: Risk-Averse Navigation Landmark Extraction via Progressive MLLM Alignment
ab: Existing pedestrian navigation systems often provide direction-only instructions with limited visual confirmation at complex intersections or along long straight paths. We study coordinate-free landmark extraction from dashcam image sequences. The model returns a set of landmarks with structured attributes (e.g., category and description), or abstains when visual evidence is insufficient. Although general MLLMs can recognize street-scene objects, they do not reliably follow expert rules for filtering ambiguous candidates. Moreover, a false landmark can mislead a pedestrian, making precision more important than exhaustive coverage in this task. We therefore develop a progressive alignment framework, supported by a landmark annotation and augmentation pipeline that converts navigation experts’ selection criteria into staged supervision signals. We further propose a hard-gated bipartite matcher for box-free evaluation and a navigation-aware risk-sensitive reward that penalizes false positives more heavily than abstentions without inducing blanket silence. On the held-out benchmark, our model achieves 92.29% precision while maintaining practical coverage, outperforming strong MLLM baselines. A 30-day A/B test with 2M users on the Amap platform further shows that landmark-augmented instructions reduce departure-confirmation latency by 23.5%. Together, these results demonstrate that risk-aware alignment enables reliable, abstention-capable landmark extraction for navigation.

t: HarmProfile: Characterizing Harmful Distributions in Frontier LLMs
ab: Frontier large language models (LLMs) safety evaluation has largely treated harmful generation as an attack outcome rather than an object of analysis. Consequently, little is known about the outputs themselves, partly because large-scale, high-quality collections of frontier-model misbehavior are difficult to obtain. To address this gap, we introduce **HarmProfile**, a content-centric benchmark dataset that collects model misbehavior across diverse harm categories and model families, and defines the resulting content distribution as a model-level risk profile. The premise is that, just as linguistic behavior can be characterized from an utterance corpus, model risk can be characterized from the content, severity, and variation of its safety failures. HarmProfile contains over 80,000 validated artifacts from 23 frontier LLMs across 13 model families, organized into 15 harm categories and 57 subcategories. Using this corpus, we find that frontier LLMs reliably produces harmful content at scale, yet exhibit distinct risk profiles; both harmfulness and diversity grow with model capability, suggesting that frontier LLMs may appear safe yet harbor increasingly dangerous knowledge beneath the alignment surface. The code and dataset resources are publicly available at https://github.com/fresh-ma/HarmProfile.

t: ClinTraceBench: Source-Verifiable Longitudinal Clinical Reasoning over EHR-Derived Dialogues
a: Jarvis Research Center, Tencent YouTu Lab
The Chinese University of Hong Kong
ab: Clinical LLM assistants must reason over multi-visit patient trajectories, yet whether the compact history representations used to scale them—retrieval, structured timelines, LLM summaries, agentic memory—preserve the longitudinal signal clinical reasoning needs has not been measured. We introduce ClinTraceBench: 385 MIMIC-IV-derived verified dialogues with event-ID provenance, a nine-task taxonomy (T1–T9), and L0–L4 deterministic + L5 human-audit validation (98.92% agreement). We evaluate eight history representation strategies—a no-context floor, last-visit-only, full-context, BGE-M3 dense-retrieval, two compression schemes, and two agentic-memory systems (Mem0, A-Mem)—across four backbones (DeepSeek-V3, GPT-4o-mini, Haiku 4.5, Sonnet 4.6) on 6,271 questions: 32 cells, 200,672 predictions. Four findings emerge: (F1) compressed strategies pay an aggregation tax on multi-visit trends and cross-patient comparisons; (F2) the blind-to-full gap spans +29.8 percentage points (GPT-4o-mini) to +62.7 (Haiku); (F3) abstention scales non-monotonically with context length; (F4) a controlled T3 injection probe isolates compression-induced relation loss—with the attribution sentence present before construction, Mem0, A-Mem, and llm-summary still recover only 0–5.3% of the injected positives. On the Pareto frontier Haiku dominates Sonnet under full-context (25.76 vs. 106.21), inverting the “biggest backbone wins” heuristic.

t: ACE: Affective Continuous Editing via Object–Atmospheric Control for Fine-Grained Image Editing
a: University of Science and Technology of China
University of Science and Technology of China
University of Science and Technology of China
University of Science and Technology of China
ab: Affective image editing aims to transform an image toward a target emotional state. Existing emotion-based editing methods typically represent emotion as a global condition, which often leads models to produce templated edits, limiting their ability to control fine-grained affective variations. To address these limitations, we propose Affective Continuous Editing Framework (ACE), an object–atmospheric framework for modeling visual emotion. To reduce templated editing, our framework employs an Affective Disentanglement Agent (ADA) to translate abstract affective intent into region-level editing instructions and counterfactual supervision signals. Guided by this data, we de-sign a decoupled regional LoRA module with two independent lightweight branches, Object LoRA (OB-LoRA) and Atmosphere LoRA (AT- LoRA), which respectively learn object and atmospheric editing directions. In addition, we introduce a counterfactual regional suppression loss, encouraging the model to learn disentangled regional features and continuous, fine-grained affective variations. Experiments demon-strate that ACE achieves better identity preservation, region-level controllability, and fine-grained emotional expression than existing emo-tion-conditioned editing methods. Quantitative analyses further confirm that the two learned control directions are monotonic and largely confined to their intended regions. The dataset and code are available at https://github.com/xixixixixxxx/ACE.

t: Factual Decoding via Head Coordination Graphs in Large Language Models
ab: Hallucinations remain challenging for large language models (LLMs), especially in factual generation. Existing mitigation methods often rely on retrieval, supervision, representation editing, or output-level decoding, while paying limited attention to how factual support is internally coordinated across attention heads. In this work, we study factual decoding from a head-level coordination perspective and find that unreliable generations are often associated with fragmented and unstable use of factual anchors across heads. To improve such coordination, we propose Head Coordination Graphs (HCG), a plug-and-play inference-time framework that models attention heads as interacting nodes. HCG uses explicit factual anchors as observable support signals to construct sparse head graphs and applies risk-gated propagation to adaptively regulate cross-head influence without parameter updates, additional training, or external knowledge. Experiments across multiple factuality and hallucination benchmarks demonstrate broad improvements in factual consistency across open-source LLMs, while analyses and ablations demonstrate the importance of head-level coordination, sparse graph construction, and risk-gated propagation.

t: MIS-Bench: Benchmarking Multimodal LLMs for Psychotherapeutic Interpersonal Skills Assessment
ab: Multimodal large language models (MLLMs) are increasingly used as evaluators, yet their reliability in professional assessment tasks that require expert judgment remains unclear. We investigate this challenge in the context of assessing psychotherapeutic interpersonal skills and introduce MIS-Bench, a Multimodal Interpersonal Skills (MIS) benchmark comprising 996 psychotherapy response videos annotated across 8 dimensions of Facilitative Interpersonal Skills. Across 9 MLLMs with multiple modality and prompting settings, we find that current models show only modest agreement with human experts, inconsistent gains from multimodal input, and limited benefits from reasoning-based prompting. To mitigate this gap, we propose MIS-RAFT, a regression-aware fine-tuning method inspired by RAFT and tailored to fine-grained interpersonal skill scoring at one-decimal precision. MIS-RAFT addresses the mismatch between autoregressive token prediction and scalar-valued expert assessment, significantly improving agreement with human ratings. Overall, MIS-Bench reveals a clear gap between general multimodal capability and expert-level interpersonal judgment, while MIS-RAFT offers a promising path toward more reliable model-based assessment.

t: MegaCode: A Repository-Level Dataset for Long-Context Code Reasoning
ab: Code reasoning is essential for building AI systems that can understand, generate, and verify complex software. Yet most open-source code corpora focus on isolated snippets or single functions, failing to capture the long-range dependencies and cross-file interactions that define real-world repositories. We introduce MegaCode, a 300B repository-level corpus designed to support structured code reasoning and long-context modeling. MegaCode preserves full project structure—including build scripts, configuration files, and inter-file links—and is constructed through a multi-stage curation pipeline combining deduplication, rule-based filtering, and model-based quality assessment. Models pretrained on MegaCode demonstrate consistent gains on code reasoning and long-context benchmarks compared with those trained on flattened code datasets. Also, we validate the effectiveness of adding repo relevent infomation such as LSP, repo structure and repo summary. These results highlight the importance of maintaining repository structure for next-generation code intelligence. We release the dataset, curation pipeline, and evaluation suite to facilitate research on large-scale code pretraining and repository-level understanding.

t: CAMFT: Conflict-Aware Mergeable Fine-Tuning for Large Language Models
a: Institute of automation, Chinese academy of science, Chinese Academy of Sciences
ab: Model merging has emerged as a promising paradigm for integrating multiple task-specific capabilities into a single large language model. However, existing methods predominantly focus on post-hoc processing of independently fine-tuned models, overlooking how the training phase itself impacts cross-task compatibility. Resolving parameter conflicts after fine-tuning is inherently sub-optimal. To address this, we propose CAMFT, a Conflict-Aware Mergeable Fine-Tuning method that makes task adaptation both efficient and merge-aware. CAMFT treats mergeability as a property shaped during fine-tuning, rather than only a problem to be solved after fine-tuning. By guiding each task to update sparse coordinates with lower cross-task conflict, CAMFT produces task updates that are efficient to train and more compatible for downstream model merging. Extensive experiments demonstrate that CAMFT outperforms standard fine-tuning baselines in multi-task merging scenarios. The code will be made publicly available.

t: Avoidance Learning of Failure Modes Produces Robust Tool Planners
ab: Multi-step tool planning is vulnerable to structural errors that propagate across dependent calls: a wrong argument, broken dependency, or mis-ordered operation can invalidate an otherwise plausible trajectory. We introduce FORTE, a framework that makes these failure modes explicit training targets. FORTE defines a nine-error taxonomy for multi-step plans, constructs taxonomy-grounded contrastive corpora by injecting minimally edited failures into gold trajectories, and trains a lightweight judge to recognize and score these errors. The same frozen judge then provides dense reward for GRPO planner optimization and verification for Best-of-N inference. Across ToolHop and NESTFUL, FORTE achieves the highest Judge Success Rate across all six open-weight backbone-dataset configurations and the highest observed end-task execution accuracy among the evaluated methods in all six settings. With Qwen2.5-7B, FORTE reaches 96.6 JSR and 99.5 dependency accuracy on ToolHop, and 98.6 JSR and 89.0 dependency accuracy on NESTFUL. Under a matched five-sample selection budget, FORTE-Qwen2.5-7B also outperforms GPT-5.5 across JSR, functional match, parameter accuracy, and dependency accuracy on both benchmarks. Ablations show that taxonomy-grounded contrastive negatives are essential for both judge discrimination and effective inference-time selection. These results demonstrate that explicitly learning which planning failures to avoid provides a strong supervision signal for robust multi-step tool planning.

t: REIGN: Refurbished Embeddings with Integrated Guidance Networks for Efficient Context-Length Scaling
ab: Dense retrieval over long documents is expensive. Token-level encoders scale quadratically in sequence length, and most long-context embedding models reach 32K tokens only through architectural workarounds or by stretching billion-parameter LLMs. We propose REIGN (Refurbished Embeddings with Integrated Guidance Networks), a contrastively trained bi-encoder that operates on sequences of contextualised chunk embeddings from a frozen Guidance Network (GN) rather than on raw tokens. REIGN targets multi-chunk inputs and primarily document-to-document retrieval; single-chunk inputs stay with the GN. Decoupling token-level processing from document-level reasoning, and caching the GN embeddings to disk, cuts per-document training cost by roughly four orders of magnitude relative to chunked Transformer fine-tuning. We also release a synthetic long-document retrieval benchmark for contrastive training and evaluation at long context lengths. Across an in-distribution Wikipedia benchmark, the LoCo out-of-distribution suite, and a real-world patent retrieval case study, REIGN matches dense long-context retrievers at smaller parameter budgets per regime. A paired significance test puts it on par with models 1.6–4.3× larger on the patent task, and it stays within 0.65 nDCG@10 of a 20×-larger model on LoCo.

t: When 2D Tasks Meet 1D Serialization: On Serialization Friction in Structured Tasks
ab: In the LLM era, many symbolic and structured problems are presented to models through 1D text serialization. Yet some such problems are natively two-dimensional: their relevant relations, such as row–column correspondence or spatial adjacency, are defined by position in a 2D layout rather than by sequential order. This raises a representational question: does preserving the same symbolic entries in a 1D sequence also preserve the relational structure needed for computation? We study this issue through the lens of serialization friction: the representational mismatch in which the same underlying task instances and entries are still present, but relations that depend on layout become implicit under 1D serialization. The study uses a controlled synthetic testbed of three tasks: matrix transpose, Conway’s Game of Life, and LU decomposition. In each task, the same instances are presented either as 1D text serialization or as their native 2D layout rendered as an image. Across this testbed, 1D serialization degrades more sharply as task size grows, and errors under serialization exhibit spatially structured patterns, suggesting that this presentation choice is consequential within our testbed. To assess whether the gap is merely due to routing inputs through a visual pathway, we add a within-visual probe that renders the 1D serialized content as an image; this layout-disrupted rendering performs worse than native 2D rendering. These findings suggest that, for layout-defined tasks, reducing inputs to 1D serialization is not a neutral choice of representation.

t: Benchmarking Argument Identification and Ellipsis Recovery in Chinese Comparative Constructions
ab: Ellipsis in comparative constructions provides a challenging test of semantic interpretation because comprehenders must reconstruct implicit constituents that are not overtly expressed. This study investigates whether large language models (LLMs) can capture the structured semantic inferences required for understanding Chinese comparative constructions. We introduce a linguistically motivated evaluation framework targeting two essential components of comparative interpretation: (i) identification of comparative arguments and (ii) recovery of elliptical constituents. Based on 2,076 naturally occurring Chinese bi-comparative sentences, we construct an annotated resource with comparative argument boundaries, recovered elliptical constituents, and five comparison dimensions representing distinct semantic bases of comparison. We evaluate several representative LLMs, including DeepSeek-V3.1, GPT-4o, and Gemini-2.0-Flash. While all models reliably identify overt comparative arguments, they exhibit substantial degradation when reconstructing implicit constituents. These results suggest that current LLMs can capture surface-level structural regularities but still face challenges in recovering implicit semantic representations required for human-like interpretation. Our resource provides a controlled linguistic testbed for studying the relationship between linguistic structure, semantic inference, and computational models of language understanding.

t: OPE: Overcoming Information Saturation in Parallel Thinking via Outline-Guided Path Exploration
ab: Parallel thinking has emerged as a new paradigm for large reasoning models (LRMs) in tackling complex problems. Recent methods leverage Reinforcement Learning (RL) to enhance parallel thinking, aiming to address the limitations in computational resources and effectiveness encountered with supervised fine-tuning. However, most existing studies primarily focus on optimizing the aggregation phase, with limited attention to the path exploration stage. In this paper, we theoretically analyze the optimization of parallel thinking under the Reinforcement Learning with Verifiable Rewards (RLVR) setting, and identify that the mutual information bottleneck among exploration paths fundamentally restricts overall performance. To address this, we propose Outline-Guided Path Exploration (OPE), which explicitly partitions the solution space by generating diverse reasoning outlines prior to parallel path reasoning, thereby reducing information redundancy and improving the diversity of information captured across exploration paths. OPE are implemented with an iterative RL strategy that optimizes outline planning and outline-guided reasoning independently. Extensive experiments across multiple challenging mathematical benchmarks demonstrate that OPE effectively improves reasoning performance in different aggregation strategies, enabling LRMs to more reliably discover correct solutions.

t: Beyond Similarity: Coverage-Aware Prompt Selection for Time Series Forecasting with LLMs
ab: Similarity-based retrieval is the dominant rule for conditioning large language models (LLMs) in in-context learning, retrieval-augmented generation, and prompt-based time series forecasting. The rule concentrates on near-duplicate candidates, an issue that has motivated diversity-aware retrieval but remains unexamined in other retrieval-conditioned pipelines. We study this issue using prompt-based time series forecasting as a test bed, where a learned prompt pool is retrieved by similarity. Dominant methods in this setting retrieve top-K entries by cosine similarity without redundancy control, producing a bias toward dominant temporal patterns while overlooking rare but informative events. We propose CASP-LLM, a coverage-aware semantic prompting framework that addresses this prompt selection bias by combining usage-tracking and saturating-gate techniques into a coverage regularizer that adds no learnable parameters. On six long-term benchmarks and the M4 short-term benchmark, CASP-LLM matches or improves on similarity-based LLM forecasters on most dataset-horizon settings, with the exceptions of Electricity, M4-Monthly, and the few-shot long-horizon setting. A controlled study locates the failure mode at the cross-batch usage level rather than per-retrieval redundancy: within-retrieval diversification such as MMR does not help, whereas regularizing anchor usage across training does.

t: BlockBatch: Multi-Scale Consensus Decoding for Efficient Diffusion Language Model Inference
a: Georgia Institute of Technology and National University of Singapore
ab: Diffusion language models (dLLMs) generate text by iteratively denoising multiple token positions in parallel, offering an attractive alternative to strictly autoregressive decoding. In practice, however, block-wise dLLM inference exposes a difficult granularity trade-off: small blocks preserve local conditioning but require many denoising steps, whereas large blocks expose more parallelism but can make premature commitments. Existing block-wise acceleration methods either use a fixed block size or adapt block boundaries along a single decoding trajectory, leaving the complementarity among concurrently executed block-size trajectories unused. We show that block-size diversity provides a useful branching dimension. Different block sizes induce related but non-identical KV-cache trajectories: branches often share an initial prefix, bifurcate at semantically decisive positions, and later agree on syntactically lightweight tokens. Motivated by this structure, we propose BlockBatch, a training-free online inference framework that executes multiple block-size branches for the same request inside a batched forward pass. BlockBatch coordinates these branches through confidence-gated token merging, leader-based synchronization, and periodic full-sequence refreshes that re-anchor local block updates to a globally consistent KV state. Across three representative dLLMs and four datasets, BlockBatch reduces denoising NFEs by 26.6% on average and achieves a 1.33\times average end-to-end speedup, with comparable average accuracy.

t: AMDKernelVault: Large-Scale Datasets and Agentic Training for AMD GPU Kernel Optimization
a: Advanced Micro Devices and Stanford University
ab: We introduce AMDKernelVault, an open corpus and training framework for optimizing HIP and Triton kernels on recent AMD CDNA GPUs. Existing LLM-based kernel agents are predominantly designed for CUDA and NVIDIA hardware and often rely on repeated calls to frontier models for generation, reflection, and optimization. To address this gap, we develop HIPKernelGen and TritonKernelGen, agent-driven pipelines that translate PyTorch references into GPU kernels, compile and validate candidates under ROCm, and profile their latency on AMD hardware. AMDKernelVault contains 62,153 execution-verified HIP kernel samples, 2,377 production-grounded ROCm Libraries QA entries, and 39,893 Triton kernels. To demonstrate the corpus’s utility, we specialize Qwen3-8B through supervised fine-tuning and execution-aware reinforcement learning. Under fixed evaluation budgets and identical agent settings, the resulting model achieves the highest correctness among the evaluated models on PyTorch-to-HIP (34.0% Pass@1), TritonBench-G (33.2% Corr@3), and ROCmBench (41.94% Corr@3), while running locally on AMD hardware. These advantages are specific to the reported correctness metrics and do not extend uniformly to compilation accuracy or execution speed. The corpus and documentation are publicly available at https://huggingface.co/datasets/amd/AIG-Datasets.

t: KGFlow: Enhancing Large Language Model Reasoning with Multi-Graph Alignment for Knowledge-Intensive Medical Question Answering
ab: Medical question answering (QA) is a knowledge-intensive task demanding evidence-based reasoning across diverse sources. Despite the demonstrated efficacy of augmenting large language models (LLMs) with domain-specific knowledge graphs (KGs) for QA tasks, the prevailing single-KG paradigm neglects the benefits of multi-KG complementarity. This paper introduces KGFlow, a novel multi-KG reasoning paradigm that mitigates the incomplete coverage and fragmented evidence of single-KG approaches through three LLM agents. Given a query, Knowledge Explorer extracts relevant knowledge triples in parallel from heterogeneous sources. Graph Aligner then semantically harmonizes these triples into global reasoning paths, which are filtered by Contextual Pruner to preserve the most valuable paths for inference. Extensive experiments show that KGFlow achieves promising performance improvements compared to state-of-the-art techniques on five medical QA datasets. We further observe by cases that the plug-and-play nature of our framework enables its application to diverse KG combinations and multilingual scenarios, resulting in broader knowledge coverage than single-KG approaches.

t: CWF: A Collaborative Writing Framework for Personalized and Reliable Long-Form Popular Science Writing
a: Huazhong University of Science and Technology
Huazhong University of Science and Technology
Huazhong University of Science and Technology
ab: We introduce Personalized and Reliable Popular Science Writing, a novel task that requires adapting scientific explanations to audiences with different cognitive levels while preserving factual accuracy. However, improving personalization often introduces simplifications that increase the risk of hallucination and factual distortion. To address these challenges, we first construct a dataset of 39,134 entries and a reader-centric Personalized Science Communication Benchmark (PSCB) that jointly evaluates audience adaptation and factual accuracy. To reduce data and computational requirements while improving generalization across domains and audiences, we introduce DA-MoE, which explicitly decouples audience adaptation from domain knowledge through separate modeling. To enable robust verification and revision in evidence-scarce scenarios, a multi-agent fact-checking mechanism that augments limited evidence with role-specific agent debate and propagates confidence over a graph is proposed. Experiments on PSCB show that our approach achieves state-of-the-art performance.

t: Compositional Generalization with Outcome-Level Optimization
a: Heidelberg University and Heidelberg Institute for Theoretical Studies
ab: Compositional generalization refers to correctly interpret novel combinations of known primitives, which remains a major challenge. Existing approaches often rely on supervised fine-tuning, which encourages models to imitate target outputs. This token-level training paradigm fails to capture the global compositional structure required for generalizing to unseen combinations. In this work, we investigate whether compositional generalization can instead be improved through outcome-level reinforcement learning. We adopt Group Relative Policy Optimization to optimize models based on feedback on their final outputs. Within this framework, we explore both a simple binary outcome reward and a composite reward that provides additional composition feedback. Experiments on multiple compositional benchmarks show that reinforcement learning improves compositional generalization compared to supervised fine-tuning. Further analysis reveals that supervised models tend to overfit frequent training compositions, whereas reinforcement learning improves compositional generalization by reshaping the output distribution, particularly for more complex composition types.

t: From Perception to Simulation: Unveiling and Empowering Mental Spatial Dynamics in MLLMs
a: Institute of Automation, Chinese Academy of Sciences
Institute of automation, Chinese academy of science, Chinese Academy of Sciences
Institute of automation, Chinese academy of science
ab: Spatial reasoning is a fundamental component of world understanding for Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs). While existing research has advanced the perception of spatial relations in static scenes, the domain of dynamic spatial simulation remains relatively unexplored. To bridge this gap, we introduce MentalGrid, a benchmark focused on spatial reasoning tasks that require models to simulate evolving spatial states without intermediate visual feedback. Extensive evaluation on our benchmark reveals a significant deficiency in the spatial simulation capabilities of existing models. Specifically, we find that performance is constrained by perceptual limitations in simple simulation scenarios and hindered by inadequate multi-step reasoning as complexity increases. To address these challenges, we propose a three-stage curriculum learning framework utilizing 16k specialized spatial reasoning samples. This approach yields SpatialWalker, which achieves a 33.8% average improvement over its base model, surpassing proprietary models like Gemini-3-Flash in spatial simulation. Furthermore, SpatialWalker demonstrates robust generalization, maintaining a 4.9% average gain on out-of-domain benchmarks, demonstrating the pivotal role of spatial simulation as a fundamental building block for broader spatial intelligence.

t: SteganoBackdoor: Evading Data-Poisoning Defenses via Steganographic Backdoors
ab: Transformer-based models are highly susceptible to backdoor attacks via supervised fine-tuning (SFT). To red-team existing data-poisoning defenses, prior work has increasingly focused on stylized triggers, synthetic artifacts, and token-level perturbations designed to evade detection. However, this trend has shifted threat models away from naturally occurring semantic triggers and realistic low-budget poisoning settings. Addressing this gap, we introduce SteganoBackdoor, an optimization-based framework that transforms semantic-trigger seeds through autoregressive token replacement, sequentially minimizing embedding overlap with the inference-time trigger while preserving a strong per-sample training-time payload. The resulting SteganoPoisons maintain linguistic fluency and encode the payload across ordinary tokens, such that no individual token carries a concentrated signal and the full payload instead emerges from their exact combination and ordering. Across 18 encoder-based and decoder-only models spanning 120M to 14B parameters, SteganoBackdoor achieves high attack success under sub-percent poisoning budgets and exposes limitations in existing data-poisoning defenses. Project page: github.com/exruiec/SteganoBackdoor

t: Vendi-RAG: Adaptively Trading-Off Diversity And Quality Significantly Improves Retrieval Augmented Generation With LLMs
a: Upwork Inc and Department of Computer Science, University of Toronto
ab: Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) for multi-hop question answering is limited by retrieving semantically redundant documents, when reasoning instead needs diverse, complementary sources. We introduce Vendi-RAG, which treats set-level semantic diversity as a first-class retrieval objective. It combines an eigenvalue-based diversity score (the Vendi Score) with query relevance into a single Vendi Retrieval Score, embedded in an iterative loop that uses an LLM-based answer-quality signal to adaptively rebalance diversity and relevance. On HotpotQA, MuSiQue, and 2WikiMultiHopQA, Vendi-RAG improves accuracy by +2.4, +1.6, and +2.4 points over the strongest diversity-aware iterative baseline (Adaptive Retrieval + MMR). A fixed-s variant captures most of the gain at no extra inference cost, while the LLM-judge loop adds a smaller but significant gain on hard queries. Results hold across five instruction-tuned backbones and two dense retrievers, identifying set-level retrieval diversity as a primary, controllable axis for improving multi-hop RAG.

t: Which Language Should a Skeleton Speak? Language Choices in Multilingual Reasoning
a: Korea Advanced Institute of Science & Technology
Korea Advanced Institute of Science & Technology
Korea Advanced Institute of Science & Technology
ab: Skeleton-based reasoning prompting is a promising training-free approach for structuring LLM reasoning, but prior work largely assumes an English-centric setting. We propose the Language-Aware Skeleton Exploration Framework () to study skeleton-language choice in multilingual mathematical reasoning. Across math benchmarks, model scales, and languages, we show that English skeletons yield a small positive tendency on average, most visible for smaller models and low-resource languages. However, few language-level gains remain significant after correction, and English is not universally optimal. Combining greedy decoding, multi-rollout evaluation, translation ablation, and cross-benchmark validation, we further find three patterns of skeleton-language effects: directionally consistent, evaluation- and benchmark-dependent, and asymmetric negative. These effects cannot be fully explained by generation quality alone. Overall, skeleton language is a context-dependent design variable that requires multi-level exploration. All resources are released[<https://github.com/lhsstn/LASEF>].

t: When Helpfulness Becomes Scientific Sycophancy: Triggering and Mitigating LLM Failures on Flawed Scientific Premises
ab: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used as scientific assistants, but their helpfulness can become harmful when they validate or build upon a user’s flawed scientific premise instead of challenging it. We study this failure mode as scientific sycophancy and introduce SciSycEval, a trap-based benchmark that tests whether LLMs reject, ambiguously qualify, or sycophantically operationalize flawed but plausible premises. Using trap assertions constructed from evidence abstracts across six domains and three reasoning-error types, we evaluate high-performing models under controlled task and authority settings. We find that scientific sycophancy decreases sharply across stronger GPT models, but persists as a trigger-dependent failure mode: generative tasks, high-authority framing, domain-specific evidential gaps, and overgeneralized premises substantially amplify sycophantic behavior. Critical-evaluation prompts reduce but do not eliminate the failures, showing that scientific LLMs must be evaluated and safeguarded for epistemic robustness under the interaction pressures that trigger sycophancy, rather than for factual accuracy alone.

t: SciTrace: Trajectory-Aware Safety Reasoning for Scientific Discovery Agents
a: Allen Institute and CMU, Carnegie Mellon University
Carnegie Mellon University and University of Chinese Academy of Sciences
ab: LLM-based scientific agents have shown strong capacity for autonomous research, yet their safety layers remain structurally divorced from core reasoning: they inspect pipeline outputs rather than shaping the deliberation that produces them. This separation opens two failure modes: safety signals accumulated at one stage are discarded before the next, and sequences of individually benign tool calls can compose into harmful outcomes that no single-step filter detects. To address these challenges, we introduce **SciTrace**, a framework that weaves safety reasoning into every stage of the scientific agent pipeline. SciTrace couples two complementary mechanisms: a *Safety-Intrinsic Reasoning Loop* (SIR) that maintains a cumulative risk state across the Thinker, Experimenter, Writer, and Reviewer stages through joint task-and-safety deliberation, and a *Compositional Tool-Chain Verifier* (CTV) that performs trajectory-aware safety checks before execution, catching risks that surface only across multi-step tool sequences. Evaluated on 240 high-risk research tasks and 120 tool-related risk tasks spanning six scientific domains, SciTrace achieves state-of-the-art (**SOTA**) safety among compared frameworks across four backbone models: it consistently improves tool call safety and adversarial robustness while preserving scientific output quality, and it uncovers **78.8%** of the compositional tool-chain escapes that single-step monitors miss. The project website is available at [https://opensciagent.github.io/SciTrace/](https://opensciagent.github.io/SciTrace/).

t: Beyond Task-Based Evaluation: Toward Situated Benchmarks for Educational LLMs
a: Shanghai Innovation Institute and East China Normal University
ab: This paper argues that evaluation of educational LLMs should move beyond decontextualized task-based benchmarks toward situated benchmarks centered on pedagogical action. Prior work in human-computer interaction and the learning sciences has long emphasized situated use, user context, and interaction processes; our focus is narrower and complementary: how these concerns should reshape benchmark design for educational LLMs. Existing evaluations already cover question generation, knowledge answering, error diagnosis, feedback generation, and teaching analysis, but their dominant unit remains the single input-output episode, making it difficult to compare whether a model genuinely supports learning progress, instructional judgment, or subsequent revision in context. Educational activity is processual, context-dependent, and development-oriented, so explanations, feedback, and hints can only be evaluated properly in relation to learner state, interaction history, and pedagogical goals. We review a landscape still dominated by task-based paradigms and argue, from educational conceptions, educational values, and research methodology, that next-generation educational benchmarks should make pedagogical function in context a core target. We further propose layered, scalable, and benchmarkable situated protocols built through simulation-first development and follow-up empirical calibration, extending evaluation beyond task quality to contextual fit and downstream consequences for learning and teaching decisions.

t: KREL: Automatic Medical Coding via Knowledge-Guided Reasoning over Clinical Evidence with LLMs
ab: Automatic Medical Coding (AMC), which assigns standardized International Classification of Diseases (ICD) codes to clinical notes, is essential for medical reimbursement, quality reporting, and clinical research. Existing pre-trained language model (PLM)-based methods typically formulate AMC as an extreme multi-label classification problem over a predefined code set, while recent large language model (LLM)-based approaches instead frame it as generation or multi-step reasoning. However, key challenges remain, including the extreme length of clinical notes that hinders effective interpretation, the vast ICD label space, and complex coding rules that are not explicitly captured by LLMs. In this work, we propose Knowledge-Guided Reasoning over Clinical Evidence with LLMs (KREL), a framework that leverages LLMs for clinical text understanding and reasoning while integrating selected structured coding relations as external knowledge. This design enables tight coupling between domain knowledge and LLM reasoning, reducing hallucinations and supporting rule-aware verification. Experiments on benchmark datasets show that KREL consistently outperforms strong PLM-based and state-of-the-art LLM-based baselines.

t: Mitigating Object Hallucinations in Vision-Language Models via Head-Level Attribution and Counteractive Pruning
ab: Large vision-language models (LVLMs) excel at multimodal tasks but often generate instance-level object hallucinations, describing nonexistent objects. Yet most mitigation strategies rely on output-level or coarse-grained interventions, limiting their ability to identify and selectively regulate attention heads associated with faithful versus hallucinatory generation, often at the cost of descriptive coverage. To address this limitation, we propose HACP, a training-free framework that integrates head-level semantic attribution with instance-adaptive counteractive pruning. HACP introduces InfoSpectralScore to summarize spectral changes in head-perturbed representations and identify heads associated with hallucination or grounded generation, which are then selectively suppressed or reinforced during decoding. Across multiple LVLMs and benchmarks, HACP consistently reduces hallucinations while preserving descriptive coverage; on a 1000-image multi-label COCO subset, it lowers CHAIR-s/i from 66.7/18.0 to 43.4/8.6 and improves F1 from 73.0 to 77.0. These findings suggest that head-level attribution provides an actionable signal for fine-grained inference-time hallucination control in LVLMs, while helping preserve descriptive coverage. The official project repository for HACP is available at https://github.com/S1yang/HACP.

t: Can LVLMs Uncover the Truth Behind Visual Illusions? An Analysis of Perceptual and Reasoning Capabilities
a: Renmin University of China and Alibaba Group
Institute of Computing Technology, Chinese Academy of Sciences
ab: Large Vision Language Models have integrated reasoning capabilities, elevating cognitive performance to new levels. However, existing evaluations either focus solely on perception or rely on specific domains such as maths or coding. Evaluation for reasoning capabilities that align with an open-world environment is still required, especially one that considers perception and reasoning jointly. To bridge this gap, we propose to evaluate LVLMs by exploiting visual illusions as a diagnostic tool. Visual illusions are phenomena in which the human visual system misinterprets objective signals, resulting in an understanding that deviates from reality. We constructed IllusionReasoning, a benchmark of illusion images collected from the real world, incorporating diverse annotated question-answer pairs. Based on IllusionReasoning, we show that the reasoning capabilities of a wide range of LVLMs are not as advanced as claimed. Our work provides new insights into LVLMs and offers future direction for optimisation.

t: Graph Neural Networks for Automatic Term Generation: Defining and Exploring Terminological Graph
a: Graduate School of Education, The University of Tokyo
ab: Despite the advance in automatic term acquisition (ATA) research, the use of ATA in terminology work is limited. One of the main reasons is that most ATA research focuses on automatic term extraction (ATE) from textual corpora and does not consider terminologies. This paper introduces automatic term generation (ATG), a new method of ATA, which explores existing terminologies, in which timeline information is also considered. We propose a new way of representing the structure of a terminology as a graph, which consists of nodes that represent constituent elements of terms and two types of links that represent intra-term dependency between constituent elements and term closure between the first and the last constituent element of terms. ATG is then defined as a set of link prediction tasks, i.e. predicting two types of links. Cliques of the graph represent the new generated terms. They are determined in a backward fashion by first selecting nodes for which term closure links are predicted and then by walking backward to term nodes for which intra-term dependency links exist. Experiments showed that our approach gives high performance in predicting new terms.

t: Implicit Personality Representations in Humans and LLMs
a: University of Melbourne and Carnegie Mellon University
Eberhard-Karls-Universität Tübingen and University of Melbourne
ab: A century of psychology has found that the trait words people use to describe one another vary, but the relational structure among those traits, which ones go together and which oppose, is strikingly consistent across raters and cultures. We test whether the LLM (Qwen 2.5-7B-Instruct) reproduces this structure in its internal trait representations. From millions of crowd-sourced personality ratings of fictional characters, we build a human implicit-personality matrix over hundreds of traits; from contrastive model activations, we build a matching matrix over the same traits. The two relational structures align strongly (Mantel r = 0.77), and the agreement holds trait by trait as well as in aggregate. Two dominant axes of the model’s trait representations recover the social and intellectual dimensions long known to organize human personality impressions, social warmth and intellectual competence. On held-out dialogue, projecting model activations onto these directions yields personality profiles that agree with human ratings. This work establishes a framework that enables comprehensive, human-grounded comparison between internal model trait geometry and the shared structure of human personality impressions.

t: Behavior2Trip: Towards Personalized Travel Planning via User Behavior Trajectory
