Training such agents to act safely is difficult, since safety and task success are distinct objectives, and safety arises only at a small number of safety-critical steps within a trajectory. Standard supervision is insufficient: imitating safe trajectories teaches behavior without explaining why it is safe, and contrasting arbitrary safe and unsafe trajectories mixes the safety signal with unrelated differences. We propose SafeBranch, a framework that aligns an embodied actor on safety through branch pairs constructed from the actor’s own unsafe rollouts via environment rollback. SafeBranch rolls each unsafe rollout back to the safety-critical step that caused the violation, queries the actor for a safe alternative, and pairs the original action with the alternative so that the two branches differ only at that step. The trained actor acts safely at deployment with no critic in the loop. On IS-Bench, SafetyALFRED, and out-of-distribution variants with unseen tasks and objects, it improves safe task completion, achieving roughly ten times more safe successes than the untrained baseline on the unseen-object variant. Project page: https://github.com/98hyunse/SafeBranch.

t: A Geometry-Aware Depth Function for Robust Unsupervised Textual Anomaly Detection
a: ISIR / Sorbonne Université and Télécom Paris
ab: Textual anomaly detection (AD) aims to identify samples that deviate from the underlying distribution of normal data, without requiring explicit supervision on anomalies. Existing literature has focused almost exclusively on the semi-supervised setting, assuming access to clean training datasets composed solely of normal samples. However, this assumption rarely holds in real-world scenarios, as datasets used to infer the normal distribution are frequently contaminated by anomalies. In this work, we first highlight the sensitivity of conventional anomaly detection methods to contamination, before demonstrating the relevance of data depth functions for robust textual anomaly detection. Building on recent findings regarding the geometry of language model embeddings, further supported by our empirical observations, we introduce the geodesic depth to better capture the structure of contextual embedding spaces. Our results show that the geodesic depth consistently outperforms commonly used anomaly detection methods once contamination exceeds 10% in the training data, with substantially larger improvements observed in the most challenging scenarios.

t: Two-Stage Reinforcement Learning for Sound and Adversarial Test Generation in Code LLMs
ab: Reinforcement learning (RL) has substantially advanced code generation with large language models (LLMs) through executable feedback. The feedback for coding problems mainly comes from specific test cases, where high-quality test cases are often scarce since they should be both sound and discriminative. We thus turn to study the auto-generation of test cases using the learned model. We find this is naturally an adversarial RL problem: the model is expected to generate effective test cases as counterexamples, depending on the solver’s current failure modes. We propose Test Cases Scaling (TCS), a two-stage RL framework for effective test generation. Both stages train a test generator from a rolling policy-aligned buffer: Stage 1 generates tests consistent with the reference solution, and Stage 2 restricts the buffer to current failure modes and learns counterexample tests. Across TACO and LiveCodeBench, TCS improves both pass@1 and inference-time answer selection according to generated tests. We find the learned test generator can also improve outputs from other LLMs to further improve their performance.

t: What do Reward Models Memorize?
ab: This paper studies what discriminatively trained reward models (RMs) memorize by measuring counterfactual memorization on two human preference datasets. We show that RMs 1) misallocate memorization to easy, high margin preference pairs, 2) memorize dataset-specific shortcuts (e.g., model identity, user sampling strategy), and 3) overgeneralize simple heuristic correlates of human preference (e.g., length, compliance) when confronted with unseen preference pairs. Overall, our findings indicate that discriminative training of RMs from human preference data results in biased RMs not yet capable of judging response quality in context-dependent scenarios.

t: DyCo: Dynamic Cognitive Role Coordination for Open-Ended Multi-Agent Research Synthesis and Verification
a: Huazhong University of Science and Technology
Huazhong University of Science and Technology
ab: Most multi-agent systems rely on fairly fixed collaboration patterns: roles, interaction paths, and task decomposition are set in advance. This works poorly for open-ended, literature-grounded research synthesis, where uncertainty changes what needs to be explored, challenged, and verified. We introduce DyCo, a framework for dynamic cognitive role coordination that combines cognitive role partitioning, dynamic teaming, and Exploration–Verification Alternation (EVA) to balance idea generation with validation. We use the Myers–Briggs Type Indicator (MBTI) only as a structured way to specify role priors under controlled conditions, not as a claim about human personality. On DeepResearch Bench, a diverse DyCo configuration reaches a RACE score of 42.75, outperforming the strongest multi-agent baseline by 4.6% (p<0.01, d=0.42), and a budget-matched non-MBTI control shows that this gain is not explained by additional computation. Extended matched-role controls on all 50 evaluation tasks indicate that most of the improvement comes from rich, structured role priors combined with verification-oriented coordination rather than the MBTI taxonomy itself, and the diverse configuration is not significantly better than the strongest homogeneous one. We further present DyCo-Efficient, which removes dynamic teaming and preserves most of the observed quality at roughly one thirteenth of the token cost, positioning Full DyCo as an optional high-budget configuration.

t: Measuring Human-Like Bias in LLMs? A Critique of Human-Derived Bias Constructs in LLM Evaluation
a: Johannes Kepler Universität Linz, Universidad Nacional del Centro de la Provincia de Buenos Aires and Consejo Nacional de Investigaciones Científicas y Técnicas
ab: Researchers increasingly use human-derived bias constructs to study Large Language Models (LLMs), including social-cognitive constructs such as implicit bias and stereotype activation, and cognitive biases such as anchoring, framing effects, and confirmation bias. Such approaches offer alternatives to overt bias probes, particularly when direct questioning may obscure bias or when model behaviour appears normatively acceptable. However, adapting human bias constructs to LLMs introduces an inferential gap. Psychological instruments were developed to study human cognition and social behaviour, whereas LLM evaluations rely on probabilities, text completions, rankings, or simulated decisions. This paper critiques human-centered bias evaluation in LLMs. We show how this gap arises from mismatches pertaining to human-derived constructs, human-model differences, and evaluation contexts, which can blur distinct interpretations of model bias. We then introduce a framework providing an analytical lens for relating these elements to warranted interpretations, with attention to target constructs, operationalizations, scope of inference, and limits of human analogy.

t: RELOOP: Recursive Retrieval with Multi-Hop Reasoner and Planners for Heterogeneous QA
a: The Hong Kong University of Science and Technology (Guangzhou)
Mohamed bin Zayed University of Artificial Intelligence
ab: Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) remains challenging for multi-hop question answering when supporting evidence is distributed across heterogeneous sources, including text, tables, and knowledge graphs (KGs). Existing systems often rely on modality-specific retrieval pipelines or uncontrolled iterative search, making it difficult to preserve source structure while maintaining efficient evidence acquisition. We present **RELOOP**, a structure-aware retrieval framework built on **Hierarchical Sequence (HSEQ)**, a reversible representation that maps heterogeneous sources into provenance-preserving typed segments with lightweight structural links. Operating on this unified evidence interface, a lightweight iterator selects and expands candidate evidence through structure-respecting actions, while an explicit sufficiency signal determines when the accumulated evidence is adequate for answering. A head module then synthesizes the final answer from a compact, canonicalized evidence package, with an optional refinement step when inconsistent evidence is detected. Experiments on HotpotQA, HybridQA, TAT-QA, and MetaQA show that RELOOP consistently improves answer quality over strong single-pass and iterative RAG baselines while requiring substantially fewer retrieval steps than graph-expansion approaches. These results suggest that a reversible, structure-aware evidence interface provides an effective foundation for accurate and budget-controlled retrieval across heterogeneous QA settings.

t: GREAT: Generalizable Backdoor Attacks in RLHF via Emotion-Aware Trigger Synthesis
a: CISPA Helmholtz Center for Information Security and Universität Hamburg
CISPA Helmholtz Center for Information Security and Universität des Saarlandes
CISPA Helmholtz Center for Information Security and Universität des Saarlandes
CISPA Helmholtz Center for Information Security
ab: Recent work has shown that RLHF is highly susceptible to backdoor attacks. However, existing methods often rely on rare tokens or fixed triggers, limiting their impact in realistic scenarios. In this work, we develop GREAT, a novel framework for crafting natural distributional backdoors in RLHF. Specifically, GREAT targets harmful response generation for a vulnerable user subpopulation featured by semantically violent requests paired with emotionally angry triggers. At the core of our framework is a trigger identification pipeline that operates in the model’s latent embedding space, leveraging dimensionality reduction and clustering techniques to identify representative triggers. To enable this, we introduce a hierarchical and diversity-driven prompting strategy to construct Erinyes, a high-quality dataset of over 5000 angry triggers curated from GPT-4.1. Our experiments show that GREAT significantly outperforms baselines in attack generalization to unseen triggers, while preserving standard utility and maintaining stealth under defenses.

t: Compliance, Capability, and Conflict: Benchmarking Multimodal LLMs under System Messages
ab: Production deployments of Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) increasingly rely on system messages to govern model behavior. Yet existing MLLM benchmarks either evaluate constraints in text only or embed them into the user turn, leaving system-message adherence in multimodal contexts largely unmeasured; they also leave open whether compliance comes at the cost of foundational vision-language capabilities. We introduce **VSysBench**, a simple yet effective MLLM benchmark that organizes system-message constraints into 5 main categories and 22 sub-categories, ranging from textual directives in visual contexts to fully vision-grounded ones, each paired with a misaligned counterpart that stress-tests the instructional hierarchy. **VSysBench** scores each response jointly along two axes, constraint compliance and answer correctness, via the Joint Satisfaction Rate (JSR) and Cross-Constraint Sensitivity (CCS). Across 16 MLLMs, we find that imposing system messages substantially erodes base task accuracy, that compliance collapses under user conflict for open-weight models while remaining stable for top proprietary ones, and that vision-grounded constraints are the hardest category for nearly every model.

t: Trajectory Self-Feedback in Diffusion Language Models: A Systematic Survey
ab: Diffusion language models generate text through iterative denoising, allowing intermediate predictions to influence later denoising steps, a recurring practice we call trajectory self-feedback (TSF). TSF is adopted under inconsistent terminology, evaluated on incompatible benchmarks, and studied by disconnected communities, yet no prior review characterises it reproducibly. We present a systematic literature review under an evidence-based methodology: six pre-specified questions, a documented six-library search with snowballing, explicit selection and quality criteria, and a structured synthesis of 24 primary studies across seven clusters, with a released audit trail. We find: (i) a model-agnostic taxonomy resolves four operator families: Prediction-Space Concatenation, Confidence-weighted Path Signals, Reward-Reinforced Conditioning, and Correction-Targeted Feedback, that the literature conflates as self-conditioning; (ii) evidence of benefit is real but fragmented across incomparable settings; (iii) within our search window, no study jointly varies the TSF mechanism and measures faithfulness on knowledge-intensive tasks; and (iv) a discrete/continuous asymmetry consistent with the sampling-wall hypothesis is visible but never tested. We conclude with eight open problems, a dependency map, and review-derived diagnostics (Commitment Index, Correction Capacity) and a Standardised Evaluation Protocol (SEP-DLM) to make TSF measurable across quality, correction, trajectory commitment, and faithfulness.

t: Navigating Intention Reasoning Trees to Guide Agentic Preference Optimization
ab: Understanding human intentions in videos requires deep cognitive reasoning, yet Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) frequently suffer from factual hallucinations and counterfactual blindness. To address these limitations, we introduce ASTRO, a novel framework that navigates Intention Reansoning Tree to guide preference optimization. Our approach employs a collaborative multi-agent system integrated with Monte Carlo Tree Search (MCTS) to systematically explore complex reasoning spaces based on visual evidence. By navigating this tree, ASTRO dynamically extracts distinct cognitive trajectories—correct, error, and ambiguous paths—to construct high-quality preference pairs. Finally, we apply Direct Preference Optimization (DPO) using these contrastive paths, explicitly enhancing the model’s factual grounding and sensitivity to causal boundaries. Extensive experiments across complex video intention benchmarks demonstrate that ASTRO achieves superior performance while exhibiting remarkable data efficiency, significantly outperforming fully supervised baselines using only a fraction of the original training data.

t: SVote-2S: Input-Side Evidence Voting for Two-Stage Self-Consistency in Multi-Hop QA
ab: Self-consistency (SC) improves chain-of-thought reasoning by aggregating multiple sampled answers, yet all existing variants operate in the output space—they refine answer selection but leave the noisy input context unchanged. We observe that when multiple reasoning traces independently cite the same support items, those items are likely key evidence for the question. Building on this input-side consensus signal, we propose SVote-2S, a two-stage self-consistency framework for multi-hop question answering. In Stage 1, SVote-2S performs confidence-weighted voting over support items cited across N sampled traces and selects a compact evidence set. In Stage 2, the model re-reasons over a filtered context containing only the selected evidence paragraphs (about 15% of the original length on average on our benchmarks), enabling more focused reasoning. The final answer is determined by confidence-weighted fusion of samples from both stages. The fusion serves as a robustness safeguard, while the primary gain comes from evidence voting and re-reasoning. Across three benchmarks (HotpotQA, MuSiQue, 2WikiMultihopQA) and three LLMs, SVote-2S improves over SC by 5.36 EM on average and consistently outperforms the strongest output-side baseline (CISC) across all nine settings, without additional training or external retrieval.

t: Crowd Values: How Human Values Reshape LLM-Agent Communities
a: University of Science and Technology of China and Research, Microsoft
ab: As LLMs evolve from standalone assistants into autonomous agents, they increasingly operate in populations where communication, coordination, and competition form community-like interaction networks. In such settings, individually value-steered behaviors can accumulate into group-level dynamics, raising the question of how human values shape collective outcomes in interacting LLM-agent populations. We introduce CIVA, a community-level value analysis framework that varies value direction and prevalence, then measures how these interventions propagate through repeated interactions into macro-level dynamics and micro-level behaviors. We apply it in a resource-constrained multi-agent community where LLM agents autonomously communicate, cooperate, and compete. The value scan reveals distinct structural response patterns: activation-supporting values such as benevolence supports persistence and resilience, an activation-constraining value such as tradition regulates growth and cohesion, and a bidirectionally disruptive value such as power perturbs collective regimes in both directions. At the micro level, representative interventions induce emergent behaviors including deception, betrayal, self-preservation, and power-seeking. These results show that human values can act as population-level structural variables in agent communities and motivate evaluation for multi-agent value alignment.

t: PaperScout: An Autonomous Agent for Academic Paper Search with Process-Aware Sequence-Level Policy Optimization
a: University of Science and Technology of China
University of Science and Technology of China
University of Science and Technology of China
University of Science and Technology of China
ab: Academic paper search is a fundamental task in scientific research, yet most existing approaches rely on rigid, predefined workflows that struggle with complex, conditional queries. To address this limitation, we propose PaperScout, an autonomous agent that reformulates paper search as a sequential decision-making process. Unlike static workflows, PaperScout dynamically decides whether, when, and how to invoke search and expand tools based on accumulated retrieval context. However, training such agents presents a fundamental challenge: standard reinforcement learning methods, typically designed for single-turn tasks, suffer from a granularity mismatch when applied to multi-turn agentic tasks—where token-level optimization diverges from the granularity of sequence-level interactions—leading to noisy credit assignment and unstable training dynamics. We introduce Proximal Sequence Policy Optimization (PSPO), a process-aware, sequence-level policy optimization method that aligns optimization with agent–environment interaction. Comprehensive experiments on both synthetic and real-world benchmarks demonstrate that PaperScout significantly outperforms strong workflow-driven and RL baselines in both recall and relevance, validating the effectiveness of our adaptive agentic framework and optimization strategy.

t: Leaving the Past Behind: Breaking Personalization Inertia in Long-Term LLM Agents
ab: LLM agents rely on long-term interaction histories to tailor their responses to individual users. However, historical personalization signals may become stale or misaligned with expectations implied by the current context, leading agents to follow outdated preferences during reasoning. We refer to this failure mode as personalization inertia, which shifts the agent’s behavior away from the user’s current intent. Existing methods mainly optimize final responses or memory retrieval, leaving such failures underexplored. In this paper, we propose Personalization Inertia VerificatiOn and RegulaTion (Pivot), a framework for mitigating personalization inertia in long-term interactions with agents. Concretely, we construct a trajectory-independent evidence condition as a diagnostic reference, model prefix-evidence consistency to assess compatibility with the current personalization evidence, and learn a rollback policy to determine whether and where to intervene. The selected intervention triggers local repair, preserving the reliable prefix while regenerating only the potentially inertia-affected suffix under evidence-guided constraints. Experiments on benchmark datasets demonstrate consistent gains in personalization accuracy and trajectory faithfulness with targeted intervention overhead.

t: RLPgR: Reinforcement Learning from Dependency-Aware Progress Rewards
ab: Group-relative policy optimization (GRPO) provides a stable recipe for outcome-based RL on language model reasoning, but its credit assignment is coarse: it broadcasts a single trajectory advantage to every token, regardless of how individual steps contribute to the outcome. We call this the uniform-broadcast failure mode and address it with RLPgR, a dependency-aware rescaling of the existing GRPO advantage. RLPgR parses each rollout into a Progress Dependency Graph (PDG), where each node groups a contiguous span of steps into a milestone-level unit with a locally validatable artifact, and directed edges connect a node to the artifacts it depends on. Using the PDG, RLPgR rescales the group-relative advantage by a small, bounded, sign-preserving factor at the node level. This preserves the outcome-governed rollout direction while each step’s update better reflects its dependency role, avoiding the reward-hacking drift of densely shaped process rewards. To reduce PDG construction cost, we train an open Qwen3-8B progress annotator amortizing a one-time proprietary bootstrap. Across model families and sizes on five math reasoning benchmarks, RLPgR is competitive with strong outcome-RL and process-RL baselines under matched training budget. Three controlled studies (scaling-strength sensitivity, segment-level baselines, and PDG label perturbation) support the view that the gain comes from structured credit assignment rather than incidental tuning.

t: Enhancing Emotional Support Conversation with Plug-in Modules for Sequential Strategy Modeling and Strategy-Specialized Generation
ab: Emotional Support Conversation (ESC) aims to alleviate users’ emotional distress through multi-turn interactions by selecting appropriate support strategies and generating aligned responses. Despite recent progress, existing approaches face three key limitations: (1) the inability to capture sequential transition patterns of strategies within conversations; (2) a training-inference mismatch in strategy prediction; and (3) reliance on a shared decoder that limits strategy-specific expression. To address these challenges, we propose S3-ESC, a simple framework of three components that are model-agnostic across encoder-decoder ESC backbones. First, we introduce a Sequential strategy predictor that models strategy transition patterns. Second, we apply Scheduled sampling for strategy to mitigate the training-inference mismatch. Third, we propose Selective LoRA for strategy that enables strategy-specialized generation. Experiments on six ESC backbones show that S3-ESC consistently improves strategy prediction accuracy, by up to 4.5pp, while enhancing response quality on most of them. Our code is publicly available.

t: Multimodal Boolean Logic Culture Retrieval
ab: Cultural image retrieval is essential for organizing and analyzing large-scale digital heritage resources. However, existing multimodal retrieval methods usually encode a query as a holistic embedding, making it difficult to preserve logical operators and cultural relations during retrieval. Therefore, we introduce Multimodal Boolean Logic Culture Retrieval, a novel task that moves beyond general visual similarity by enforcing strict Boolean constraints over structured cultural elements. To tackle this, we propose *CLAIR*, a training-free framework that reformulates the retrieval objective to seamlessly integrate logical operations directly within the multimodal embedding space. Furthermore, we construct CulTi2.0, a dedicated benchmark designed to evaluate diverse logical query forms based on cultural visual atoms. Extensive experiments show that while current multimodal models struggle with explicit logical queries, *CLAIR* provides consistent and generalizable improvements as a plug-and-play solution across various datasets and model families. Code and dataset are publicly available at https://github.com/AI4Culture/CulTi2.0.

t: Neither Here Nor There: Cross-Lingual Representation Dynamics of Code-Mixed Text — A Hindi–English Case Study
ab: Multilingual encoder-based language models are widely used for code-mixed analysis, yet their internal representations of code-mixed inputs—and their relationship to the constituent languages—remain poorly understood. Using Hindi–English as a case study, we construct a unified trilingual corpus of parallel English, Hindi (Devanagari), and Romanized code-mixed sentences. We then probe cross-lingual representation alignment in standard multilingual encoders and their code-mix-adapted variants using CKA, token-level saliency, and entropy-based uncertainty analysis. We find that while standard models align English and Hindi well, code-mixed inputs remain loosely connected to either language — and that continued pre-training on code-mixed data improves English–code-mixed alignment at the cost of English–Hindi alignment. Interpretability analyses further reveal a clear asymmetry: models process code-mixed text through an English-dominant semantic subspace, while native-script Hindi provides complementary signals that reduce representational uncertainty. Motivated by these findings, we introduce a trilingual post-training alignment objective that brings code-mixed representations closer to both constituent languages simultaneously, yielding more balanced cross-lingual alignment and downstream gains on sentiment analysis and hate speech detection — showing that grounding code-mixed representations in their constituent languages meaningfully helps cross-lingual understanding. Code is available at: https://github.com/debajyotimaz/tri_align_EMNLP_2026.

t: CL-OCR: Fusing Layout Analysis and Adapting Recognition for Document Parsing in the Wild
a: Institute of automation, Chinese academy of science
Institute of automation, Chinese academy of science, Chinese Academy of Sciences
University of the Chinese Academy of Sciences
Institute of automation, Chinese academy of science, Chinese Academy of Sciences
Centre for Artificial Intelligence and Robotics Hong Kong Institute of Science & Innovation, Chinese Academy of Sciences
, Institute of automation, Chinese academy of science
Institute of automation, Chinese academy of science, Chinese Academy of Sciences
ab: Recent OCR models achieve strong results on document benchmarks, with several 1–2B OCR-specialized models surpassing much larger general multimodal LLMs (MLLMs). However, complex real-world documents often contain blur, cropping, curved text, handwriting, and unfamiliar structures, which remain challenging for current OCR systems. We trace this gap to a shift in the error source: errors on canonical benchmarks mainly arise from layout analysis, including localization, element classification, and reading order, while errors under these challenging conditions mainly arise from content recognition. To this end, we propose CL-OCR, a two-stage framework that first fuses semantic structure from an MLLM-based detector with geometric candidates from a vision detector to obtain calibrated layouts, then enhances recognition via a shared LoRA adapter gated by a lightweight router. We further construct OCRWildBench and a companion training split to study these conditions. Experiments show that CL-OCR remains competitive on canonical benchmarks and achieves the strongest overall performance among OCR-specialized models on OCRWildBench.

t: Unveiling Latent Cognitive Bias Constructs in Large Language Models
ab: As Large Language Models (LLMs) are increasingly adopted in decision-making, there is a growing need to better understand the behavioural patterns underlying their reasoning. Evaluation is one of the primary approaches used to study model behaviour. However, most existing LLM evaluations rely on task-based benchmarks that summarise performance through aggregate scores. While effective for comparing model performance, such approaches provide limited insight into the latent behavioural tendencies that drive biased reasoning. In this paper, we propose a construct-based evaluation framework for studying cognitive bias in LLMs grounded in psychometric evaluation. We systematically perturb prompts across controlled conditions to analyse reasoning behaviour. From model responses, we derive behavioural features capturing susceptibility, robustness, correction, and variability, and apply latent variable modelling to infer underlying behavioural constructs. Our findings show that cognitive bias in LLMs is structured and dynamic, varying across bias type, model families, and scale.

t: IHDec: Divergence-Steered Contrastive Decoding for Securing Multi-Turn Instruction Hierarchies
ab: Large Language Models (LLMs) often fail to maintain instruction hierarchies (IH) when processing multi-source inputs with varying role-level priorities, paradoxically adhering to lower-priority directives during conflicts. While existing defenses mitigate this issue, they are largely restricted to single-turn scenarios and require expensive fine-tuning. In this paper, we formalize this failure mode in multi-turn contexts via a Jensen-Shannon Divergence (JSD) framework, uncovering a pervasive role-influence inversion phenomenon where subordinate inputs override superior roles. To rectify this without training, we propose IHDec (Instruction Hierarchy-steered Decoding). IHDec leverages JSD to automatically detect token-level hierarchy violations and dynamically executes contrastive decoding to suppress misaligned subordinate roles. Extensive evaluations demonstrate that IHDec outperforms training-based baselines in multi-turn conflicts while fully preserving general response quality. Furthermore, IHDec strengthens safety against adversarial prompt injections and exhibits a robust scaling synergy with larger models.

t: Stay Within Your Bounds: Distance-Guided Decoding for Guaranteed Context-Free Grammar Compliance
ab: Grammar-constrained decoding helps large language models produce syntactically valid structured outputs, such as code, JSON, and SQL. For context-free grammars, many practical decoders enforce local prefix feasibility: each token must keep the current prefix extendable to some valid completion. Yet, under tokenizer–grammar mismatch and finite token budgets, feasible prefixes may still fail to reach acceptance. We propose a lookahead-guided decoding framework for context-free grammars based on pushdown automata. Offline, we compute bounded pushdown summaries with reachability labels and upper-bound distances to acceptance. Online, these estimates guide horizon-aware pruning and beam search. The resulting decoder is syntactically sound: every output is accepted by the target grammar. Experiments on JSON, SQL, and Linear Temporal Logic (LTL) show both consistent syntactic validity and improved completion quality over existing baselines.

t: Remember and Reweight: Enhancing Multi-Agent Debate with Experience Memory and Confidence Estimation
a: Institute of Automation, Chinese Academy of Sciences
Institute of automation, Chinese academy of science
Institute of automation, Chinese academy of science, Chinese Academy of Sciences
ab: Multi-agent debate (MAD) improves the reasoning capabilities of large language models by having multiple agents iteratively refine their responses through discussion. However, MAD suffers from a critical vulnerability known as shared misconception: when a majority of agents initially converge on an incorrect answer, the debate process tends to amplify rather than correct the error. Existing methods primarily address peer skew but leave the agents’ inherently biased concept priors unaddressed. To mitigate this systematic weakness, we propose **R^2-MAD** (Remember and Reweight for Multi-Agent Debate), a framework that equips agents with an experience memory accumulated from past debates. R^2-MAD intervenes on both failure modes through two complementary mechanisms: A debate-state-aware retrieval policy dynamically calibrates the concept prior by retrieving relevant historical evidence based on the current consensus level. Then these retrieved experiences provide a basis for estimating per-agent reliability, yielding confidence weights to modulate peer influence. Experiments on various benchmarks show that R^2-MAD achieves consistent improvements over existing single-agent and MAD baselines.

t: Retrieval Evaluation Under Temporal Drift in Technical Documentation
ab: Information retrieval (IR) benchmarks typically follow the Cranfield paradigm, relying on static and predefined corpora. However, temporal changes in technical corpora, such as API deprecations and code reorganizations, can render existing benchmarks stale. In our work, we investigate how temporal corpus drift affects FreshStack, a retrieval benchmark focused on technical domains. We examine two independent corpus snapshots of FreshStack from October 2024 and October 2025 to answer queries about LangChain. Our analysis shows that all but one query posed in 2024 remains fully supported by the 2025 corpus, as relevant documents *migrate* from LangChain to competitor repositories, such as LlamaIndex. Next, we compare the accuracy of retrieval models on both snapshots and observe only minor shifts in model rankings, with overall strong correlation of up to 0.978 Kendall \tau at Recall@50. These results suggest that retrieval benchmarks for technical documentation, e.g., LangChain, can remain reliable when re-judged in the drift regime we observe, where relevant evidence is *relocated* rather than invalidated. All resources (code and data) are publicly available at https://github.com/fresh-stack/driftbench.

t: ATLAS: Exploring Scalable Activation-Space Data Attribution
a: INRIA and University of California, Berkeley
Transluce and University of California Berkeley
ab: As post-training data can induce many unexpected behaviors in large language models (LLMs), scalable data attribution is important for efficiently tracing these behaviors back to the data that induced them. Most existing methods are expensive because they require running at minimum forward and backward passes (and sometimes Hessians) across the entire training corpus for each eval behavior. This makes it difficult to adaptively study new behaviors because each one requires training-sized compute. We propose a general framework for data attribution that generalizes recent approaches, which we observe to share a two-stage structure: training examples and behaviors are mapped independently to vectors, and attribution is a similarity between them. We use this to propose several novel activation-based or gradient-based methods. Evaluating their performance on Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct and Qwen-2.5-7B-Instruct, we find no single method performs best across behaviors. On free-generation tasks, two methods in our framework often outperform TRAK and persona-vector baselines, while a steering-guided mixture of the two almost always does. On reading comprehension hallucination, one gradient based method substantially outperforms the baselines, while the remaining methods and baselines perform similarly to random selection.

t: PLANE: Plug-and-Play Fine-Grained Visual Experts for Hallucination Mitigation in Large Vision-Language Models
a: ByteDance Inc. and East China Normal University
ab: Large Vision-Language Models (LVLMs) commonly suffer from hallucinations, which appear as fabricating non-existent objects or outputting incorrect attributes and spatial relationships in images. Previous works empirically indicate that CLIP-style vision encoders tend to focus on primary objects while ignoring image details, which is one of the causes of hallucinations. To address this issue, we propose plug-and-play fine-grained visual experts (PLANE) comprising two components: LoRA visual experts operating on CLIP for multi-aspect image encoding, and an instruction-aware gate network for adaptive image feature fusion. During training, we construct a fine-grained image-caption pairs dataset, where images are described from three aspects: objects, attributes, and relations between objects. Image-caption pairs from different aspects are used to train the three fine-grained LoRA experts respectively. Aiming at comprehensively evaluate our method’s capabilities, we manually annotate a fine-grained hallucination evaluation benchmark for LVLMs which is GPT4-independent during evaluation phase (GIFT). We conduct experiments both on popular hallucination evaluation benchmarks and GIFT. The results show that our method effectively reduces hallucinations across models of different types and sizes while introducing minimal inference latency. Compared to advanced baselines, our model also demonstrates superior performance.

t: R^3 -MDT: A Retain-Rerank-Revise Framework Based on Uncertainty and Consistency for Medical Decision Tree Extraction
a: Mohamed bin Zayed University of Artificial Intelligence
Harbin Institute of Technology, Shenzhen and Harbin Institute of Technology
ab: Automatic extraction of Medical Decision Trees (MDTs) is an important task for Clinical Decision Support Systems, but remains challenging due to the complex logical structures involved. Recent approaches based on Large Language Models (LLMs) commonly adopt generate-then-revise pipelines with self-correction to improve reasoning accuracy. However, we find that applying revision uniformly across all samples can be harmful, as it often alters already correct and stable predictions, leading to over-correction on simple cases. To alleviate this issue, we propose R^3-MDT, an adaptive inference framework that dynamically selects reasoning strategies based on sample difficulty. We use model uncertainty and output consistency as internal signals to estimate difficulty and route samples into Easy, Medium, and Hard categories. For Easy samples with confident and consistent predictions, we directly retain the initial outputs. Medium-difficulty samples, which exhibit ambiguity among multiple plausible candidates, are handled via reranking to select the optimal decision tree. Hard samples, characterized by high uncertainty and structural inconsistency, are revised to rectify intractable generation failures. By adaptively selecting inference strategies based on difficulty levels, R^3-MDT avoids unnecessary revisions while effectively correcting underlying reasoning failures. Experiments on the Text2DT benchmark show that R^3-MDT alleviates the over-correction problem and achieves state-of-the-art performance, while auxiliary language- and task-shift evaluations indicate the broader transferability of its routing principle.

t: Ancient-Bench: A Comprehensive Multi-millennial, Multi-medium, and Multi-script Benchmark for Ancient Chinese Artifact Text Recognition
ab: Ancient Chinese artifact recognition is fundamental to heritage digitization, and benchmarks for ancient texts are essential for evaluating current model capabilities. However, existing benchmarks suffer from “fragmentation”, manifested in limited temporal coverage, limited medium diversity, and incomplete script types. Therefore, we present Ancient-Bench, a comprehensive benchmark of 2,700 images for ancient Chinese artifact text recognition, featuring three dimensions: Multi-millennial (spanning 3,000 years of character evolution), Multi-medium (covering nine artifact categories), and Multi-script (encompassing seven historical script forms). To enable consistent and fair evaluation across heterogeneous media, we further define three annotation standards tailored to the medium-specific characteristics of ancient texts: symbol standardization, character standardization, and parsing standardization. Extensive experiments on Ancient-Bench covering general Vision-Language Models (VLMs) and OCR-specialist models reveal that ancient Chinese recognition remains fundamentally unsolved, with persistent challenges in variant characters, specialized symbols, and hallucination. The data and evaluation code will be publicly available.

t: A Circuit for Plural Reference: How LLMs Represent and Retrieve Singular and Plural Entities
a: Utrecht University and Queen Mary, University of London
ab: Coreference resolution is an important task in contextual reasoning. In this paper, we investigate the mechanism for representing and retrieving singular and plural entities for plural reference. We use a combination of mechanistic interpretability and attention pattern analysis to study the process in which LLMs predict a pronoun to refer back to previously mentioned entities. Using a range of causal intervention techniques, we find a set of attention heads that are responsible for (1) representing coreference information in the input, (2) identifying entities that form a plural reference, (3) transferring the information to the component that is responsible for selecting the antecedents and predicting the pronoun. We also find that LLMs align with humans in preference for plural pronoun. Specifically, entities in a plural construction are more likely to be referred to as a plural entity if they are ontologically similar and are linked by the conjunction and.

t: SpikeXL: Language-Agnostic Spike Representations for Few-Shot Cross-Lingual Speech Command Recognition
a: Posts & Telecommunications Institute of Technology and Posts & Telecommunications Institute of Technology
FPT Swinburne University of Technology, Vietnam and Academy of Cryptography Techniques
ab: Deploying speech command recognition on multilingual edge devices demands models that are both energy-efficient and capable of cross-lingual transfer without per-language retraining—two goals rarely addressed jointly. Spiking Neural Networks (SNNs) offer substantial energy savings via sparse binary communication, yet their cross-lingual generalization remains unstudied. We present SpikeXL, a framework that investigates whether SNN spike sparsity provides an inductive bias toward language-agnostic representations. Our experiments suggest that the V_{th} firing threshold of Leaky Integrate-and-Fire (LIF) neurons suppresses language-specific surface phonetics while preserving command-level acoustic structure, yielding embeddings that transfer across languages more readily than dense ANN activations. Building on this finding, we introduce Spike-space Contrastive Alignment (SCA), a contrastive objective adapted for spike-rate embeddings that aligns semantically equivalent commands across languages without requiring bilingual lexicons or parallel speech data. On Speech-MASSIVE across 12 typologically diverse languages, SpikeXL achieves a Cross-Lingual Semantic Similarity (CLSS) of 0.912—outperforming a parameter-matched Transformer with the same SCA objective (0.763) and SNN without SCA (0.721)—indicating that spike sparsity itself contributes an inductive bias beyond what contrastive training alone provides. Few-shot k-NN classification on target languages (115 support samples, frozen encoder) reaches 80.8 macro-average accuracy, corroborating alignment quality with a metric fully independent of the SCA objective. On English GSC-v2, SpikeXL reaches 92.76 accuracy with 2.5M parameters and 45M synaptic operations per inference.

t: Learning to Search: A Decision-Based Agent for Knowledge-Based Visual Question Answering
ab: Knowledge-based visual question answering (KB-VQA) requires vision-language models to understand images and use external knowledge, especially for rare entities and long-tail facts. Most existing retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) methods adopt a fixed pipeline that sequentially retrieves information, filters it, and then produces an answer. Such a design makes it difficult to adapt to diverse question types. Moreover, it separates retrieval from reasoning, making it hard for the model to decide when to search, how to refine queries, or when to stop. As a result, the retrieved evidence is often poorly aligned with the question. To address these limitations, we reformulate KB-VQA as a search-agent problem and model the solving process as a multi-step decision-making procedure. At each step, the agent selects one of four actions-Answer, Image Retrieval, Text Retrieval, and Caption-based on its current information state. We further design an automated pipeline to collect multi-step trajectories that record the agent’s reasoning process, tool usage, and intermediate decisions. These trajectories are then used as supervision for fine-tuning. Experiments on InfoSeek and E-VQA demonstrate that our method achieves state-of-the-art performance, consistently outperforming prior baselines and confirming the effectiveness of our framework.

t: PRFC: Learning Progressive Recovery from Function Calling Errors for Tool-Using LLMs
ab: Tool-using large language models (LLMs) can make multiple attempts to complete a task, using execution feedback from failed tool calls to identify errors and revise subsequent actions. However, their recovery performance often plateaus in later attempts, as models may repeat similar tool-call errors instead of making effective corrections. To address this limitation, we introduce PRFC, a reinforcement learning method that models error recovery as a sequential decision-making process. PRFC uses a progress-aware reward that assigns credit only when a later attempt improves upon previous failures, encouraging steady improvement across the recovery trajectory. Across four benchmarks with a Qwen3-4B backbone, PRFC improves multi-turn recovery on BFCL-v3 by an absolute 6.4% and achieves the highest mean score across three single-step tasks (API-Bank, T-Eval, and Nestful). These results show that modeling progress across attempts provides an effective learning signal for multi-attempt tool-use recovery. These results suggest that explicitly modeling progress across attempts provides a useful learning signal for tool-use recovery.

t: EDWARD-NMT: Elastic Dimensions With Adaptive Routing and Dual-consistency for Neural Machine Translation
a: UNEY and Ho Chi Minh City University of Technology
Ho Chi Minh city University of Science, Vietnam National University
ab: Sparse Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) is a powerful paradigm for scaling Neural Machine Translation (NMT) and managing language heterogeneity. However, practical limitations hinder its deployment on resource-constrained devices: the entire expert pool must remain in memory, and the per-token compute budget is statically fixed during training by rigid top-k routing. We introduce **EDWARD-NMT** (**E**lastic **D**imensions **W**ith **A**daptive **R**outing and **D**ual-consistency for **NMT**), a novel MoE encoder-decoder architecture designed for a “train once, deploy anywhere” paradigm that exposes a family of deployable sub-networks at inference time. EDWARD-NMT integrates three key innovations: (i) Matryoshka-style elastic dimensions to flexibly reduce the memory footprint; (ii) an adaptive sigmoid router with a learned, task-conditioned threshold, allowing each token to dynamically determine its active expert count; and (iii) a dual-consistency objective to maximize the performance of the extracted sub-networks. Extensive experiments on PhoMT (En\leftrightarrowVi), WMT-14 (En\leftrightarrowDe), multilingual OPUS-16, and a multi-domain De\leftrightarrowEn benchmark validate our approach. The full-capacity architecture matches or exceeds strong MoE baselines with improved parameter efficiency. Furthermore, the sub-networks seamlessly extracted from a single checkpoint consistently outperform comparably sized dense Transformers without any retraining.

t: Predictive Language Grounding for Event-Driven Time Series Forecasting via Dual-Path Event Injection
ab: Discrete events such as holidays, policy announcements, and public gatherings leave no trace in historical time series yet fundamentally shape future demand. Language models capture precisely this event knowledge, making them a natural source of auxiliary signal for event-driven forecasting. However, some multimodal forecasters borrow semantic alignment from vision-language pretraining, enforcing geometric proximity between text and series embeddings. For time series regression, this objective is theoretically unnecessary and actively harmful when training data is limited or text-series coupling is weak: contrastive gradients compress the high-variance series features required to represent event-induced spikes. We propose predictive grounding as the principled alternative, shaping language representations through prediction loss alone. PROSE (Predictive grOunding for event-driven time-Series forEcasting) realizes this framework through a fully fine-tuned language encoder, token-level Event Token Injection, LLM-generated Trajectory Reasoning Anchors as global prefix tokens, and a Soft Functional Alignment loss. On a 464K-sample Chinese holiday benchmark, PROSE surpasses the strongest baseline by 10.7% WMAPE; on Time-MMD, it achieves state-of-the-art results across 7 of 9 domains.

t: HalluPeer: A Taxonomy-driven Benchmark for Detecting Hallucinations in Scientific Peer Reviews
a: National Yang Ming Chiao Tung University
National Yang Ming Chiao Tung University
National Yang Ming Chiao Tung University
National Yang Ming Chiao Tung University
National Yang Ming Chiao Tung University
ab: The growing scale of academic peer review has motivated the use of Large Language Models (LLMs) as review assistants, yet LLMs can generate fluent but unsupported claims that undermine review reliability. Existing hallucination benchmarks are not designed for peer review, where verification requires grounding claims in long, technical papers. We introduce HalluPeer, a benchmark for detecting hallucinations in scientific peer reviews, providing aligned triples of paper content, human-written reviews, and hallucination-injected reviews, annotated for detection, classification, and localization. Our pipeline induces a peer-review-specific hallucination taxonomy, identifies review contexts, and injects hallucinations with automated filtering. Experiments on 12K papers and 38K reviews show that existing detectors struggle to separate hallucinations from legitimate critique, while evaluation on authentic reviews demonstrates that HalluPeer-defined hallucination patterns occur in real peer reviews, highlighting the critical need for source-aware verification.

t: Learning from Own Solutions: Self-Conditioned Credit Assignment for Reinforcement Learning with Verifiable Rewards
a: ByteDance Inc. and Beijing Institute of Technology
ab: Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) has driven substantial progress in training LLMs for reasoning tasks, but representative methods such as GRPO assign uniform credit across all tokens, wasting gradient on routine tokens while under-crediting pivotal reasoning steps. Existing token-level credit assignment methods require resources beyond the model’s own rollouts. GRPO variants rely on process reward models or ground-truth answers. Knowledge distillation assigns credit through per-token divergence but requires external teachers (On-Policy Distillation) or privileged information (On-Policy Self Distillation). However, these dependencies limit applicability in the pure RLVR setting. We observe that conditioning the model on its own verified trajectories induces a measurable per-token KL divergence between the original and conditioned distributions, and prove that distilling from a self-teacher constructed by verified trajectories leads to infeasible weighted-average solutions when multiple verified trajectories exist. We propose SC-GRPO (Self-Conditioned GRPO), which uses KL divergence mentioned before as a multiplicative weight on GRPO gradients. Across five benchmarks spanning math, code, and agentic tasks, SC-GRPO consistently outperforms 8.1% over GRPO and 5.9% over DAPO with stronger OOD performance. Moreover, SC-GRPO achieves higher performance than OPD.

t: Simple Beats Spend: Cost-Performance Trade-Offs for Multi-Agent Machine Translation of Financial Long Documents
a: J.P. Morgan Chase and University of Oxford
School of Computer Science, Carnegie Mellon University
ab: Agentic MT frameworks often adopt human-inspired roles, layered post-editing, and complex workflows. To stress-test these designs, we examine cost–performance trade-offs across five multi-agent MT workflows on specialized long documents. Using six language pairs from two financial test sets and LLMs spanning lower to higher capacity and cost tiers, we evaluate translation quality and terminology accuracy relative to token-level cost. We find: (i) lean pipelines match the quality of more complex systems at lower cost; (ii) terminology accuracy depends more on model capacity than on workflow complexity; (iii) document-length resilience is not universal, as some simple and some complex workflows maintain quality on longer documents; and (iv) post-editing agents offer a better return on model capacity than base translation. Edited-span analysis further suggests that many post-edits are stylistic or lexical alternatives rather than consistently preferred improvements.

t: OntoDiagnose: Ontology-Grounded Reasoning for Medical Question Answering with Language Models
a: Indian Institute of Technology, Bombay, Dhirubhai Ambani Institute Of Information and Communication Technology
ab: Language models achieve strong performance in medical question answering, yet hallucinations persist even in domain-specialized models, particularly on complex clinical vignettes involving rare presentations, multi-hop reasoning, and ambiguous evidence requiring explicit relational grounding. We introduce OntoDiagnose, a training-free, ontology-grounded, clinician-inspired reasoning pipeline that augments parametric knowledge with structured evidence from SNOMED CT. Given a clinical question, OntoDiagnose extracts salient medical entities, grounds them in the ontology, explores a bounded subgraph, and compresses relevant relations into compact, interpretable evidence chains that guide reasoning. We evaluate OntoDiagnose across USMLE-style and biomedical QA benchmarks using MedGemma, BioMistral, MedPhi, and OpenBioLLM under zero-shot, few-shot, and chain-of-thought settings. OntoDiagnose consistently improves over prompt-only baselines, with an average gain of 9.6 accuracy points on MedQA and the largest relative gains for the lowest-scoring models. These results show the benefit of incorporating ontology-grounded evidence into medical question answering without modifying model parameters.

t: Long Listening Thoughts: Eliciting Open Auditory Reasoning with Deliberative Perception and Cognitive Refinement
ab: We introduce Long Listening Thoughts (LLT), a framework for constructing post-training datasets that improves audio reasoning by pairing deliberate perceptual grounding with explicit cognitive behaviors. On audio understanding and reasoning benchmarks, large audio–language models (LALMs) are limited primarily by perceptual errors, yet existing post-training datasets rely on audio descriptions of limited diversity. Through a four-stage pipeline, LLT (1) builds multi-aspect dense audio descriptions spanning semantic, acoustic, and temporal information, (2) generates more challenging questions, (3) synthesizes incorrect reasoning traces, and (4) extends short reasoning traces into long ones via a thought-continuation strategy that elicits cognitive behaviors such as verification and backtracking. Using LLT, we synthesize 1.6M reasoning traces and train Qwen2.5-Omni-7B with a two-stage pipeline of supervised fine-tuning (SFT) followed by direct preference optimization (DPO). This improves accuracy on MMAU Test-mini (71.5 \rightarrow 78.2), MMAR (56.7 \rightarrow 63.7), and MMSU (60.6 \rightarrow 66.0).

t: Evidence-Guided Bidirectional Iterative Reasoning for Interpretable Personality Recognition
a: Institute of automation, Chinese academy of science, Chinese Academy of Sciences
Institute of automation, Chinese academy of sciences
Institute of Automation, Chinese Academy of Sciences
ab: Identifying personality accurately can improve interpretability and adaptability for human–computer interaction and psychological assessment. Recent studies have introduced evidence utterance into large language models (LLMs) for personality recognition, providing supporting evidence to explain personality labels. However, the mixed background and social expressions in dialogue scenarios interfere with the identification of evidence utterance. At the same time, the overconfidence of LLMs leads to biased personality inference. Inspired by the lens theory in psychology, how to systematically explore the mutual influence between evidence utterance identification and personality recognition while improving the performance of both tasks remains a key challenge. In this paper, we reframe personality recognition as an Evidence-Personality Iterative Reasoning problem (EPIR). A graph model is employed to select an initial evidence utterance set, and personality recognition is performed based on a Generative-Discriminative Feedback mechanism. Then, the inferred results are fed back to the graph mapping network to dynamically adjust evidence utterance filtering. This interactive iterative process continues until the evidence and personality results across different iterations converge. Experimental results on the two public datasets demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed method.

t: UltraVoice: Scaling Fine-Grained Style-Controlled Speech Conversations for Spoken Dialogue Models
a: National Key Laboratory of General Artificial Intelligence
Beijing Institute for General Artificial Intelligence
ab: Spoken dialogue models currently lack the ability for fine-grained speech style control, a critical capability for human-like interaction that is often overlooked in favor of purely functional capabilities like reasoning and question answering. To address this limitation, we introduce **UltraVoice**, the first large-scale spoken dialogue dataset engineered for multiple fine-grained speech style control. Encompassing over 830 hours of spoken dialogues, UltraVoice provides instructions across six key speech stylistic dimensions: emotion, speed, volume, accent, language, and composite styles. Fine-tuning leading models such as SLAM-Omni and VocalNet on UltraVoice significantly enhances their fine-grained speech stylistic controllability without degrading core conversational abilities. Specifically, our fine-tuned models achieve improvements of 29.12-42.33% in Mean Opinion Score (MOS) and 14.61-40.09 percentage points in Instruction Following Rate (IFR) on multi-dimensional control tasks designed in the UltraVoice. Moreover, on the URO-Bench benchmark, our fine-tuned models demonstrate substantial gains in core understanding, reasoning, and conversational abilities, with average improvements of +10.84% on the Basic setting and +7.87% on the Pro setting. Furthermore, the dataset’s utility extends to training controllable Text-to-Speech (TTS) models, underscoring its high quality and broad applicability for expressive speech synthesis. The complete dataset and model checkpoints are available at: [https://github.com/bigai-nlco/UltraVoice](https://github.com/bigai-nlco/UltraVoice).

t: EvolSQL: Structure-Aware Evolution for Scalable Text-to-SQL Data Synthesis
a: Beijing University of Aeronautics and Astronautics
ab: Training effective Text-to-SQL models remains challenging due to the scarcity of high-quality, diverse, and structurally complex datasets. Existing methods either rely on limited human-annotated corpora, or synthesize datasets directly by simply prompting LLMs without explicit control over SQL structures, often resulting in limited structural diversity and complexity. To address this, we introduce EvolSQL, a structure-aware data synthesis framework that evolves SQL queries from seed data into richer and more semantically diverse forms. EvolSQL starts with an exploratory Query-SQL expansion to broaden question diversity and improve schema coverage, and then applies an adaptive directional evolution strategy using six atomic transformation operators derived from the SQL Abstract Syntax Tree to progressively increase query complexity across relational, predicate, aggregation, and nesting dimensions. An execution-grounded SQL refinement module and schema-aware deduplication further ensure the creation of high-quality, structurally diverse mapping pairs. Experimental results show that a 7B model fine-tuned on our data outperforms one trained on the much larger SynSQL dataset using only 1/18 of the data. Our code is available at https://github.com/slaanurgle/EvolSQL.

t: Think Wider: Mitigating Latent Rank Collapse in Implicit Chain-of-Thought Reasoning
a: HKUST(GZ) and The Hong Kong University of Science and Technology
ab: Chain-of-thought (CoT) reasoning improves the reasoning ability of large language models by introducing intermediate computation, but explicit rationales increase decoding length, latency, and context cost. Implicit CoT offers a more efficient alternative by moving intermediate reasoning into continuous latent states. However, latent reasoning can be unstable: successive latent states may become overly similar and collapse toward a shared dominant direction, reducing the diversity of the reasoning trajectory. In this work, we identify \textit{latent rank collapse} and propose \textbf{WIDER}, a lightweight spectral regularizer for implicit CoT. During training, WIDER estimates the shared direction of each latent trajectory and penalizes projections onto this direction, encouraging latent states to span a broader representational subspace. The method is plug-and-play and leaves the backbone model, latent schedule, and inference-time decoding procedure unchanged. We further formulate this collapse as a geometric bottleneck in implicit reasoning, casting its mitigation as a training-time regularization problem rather than an inference-time decoding change. Extensive experiments show that WIDER improves matched implicit CoT baselines, while mechanistic analyses reveal higher effective rank, lower dominant-direction energy, and reduced redundancy among latent steps. These results highlight latent subspace utilization as an important factor for efficient continuous reasoning, providing a geometric perspective for analyzing and improving implicit CoT. Code is available at https://github.com/whitesweater/WIDER.

t: Adaptive Test-Time Compute Allocation for Block Diffusion Language Models in Complex Reasoning
ab: Recent advances in block diffusion language models have demonstrated competitive performance and strong scalability on reasoning tasks. However, their test-time compute allocation remains largely unexplored, leaving a critical speed-effectiveness trade-off unresolved in long Chain-of-Thought reasoning. To address this, we propose a unified test-time compute allocation framework that introduces adaptivity in both step-wise decoding and blockwise generation. At the decoding level, we propose Bounded Adaptive Confidence Decoding (BACD), a difficulty-aware sampling strategy that dynamically adjusts denoising based on model confidence, accelerating inference while controlling error accumulation. Beyond step-wise adaptivity, we introduce the Think Coarse, Critic Fine (TCCF) paradigm that allocates large block sizes for exploratory thinking and smaller block sizes for precise refinement. To stabilize training under varying block configurations, we adopt Progressive Block Size Extension, which mitigates quality degradation when scaling up block sizes. Extensive evaluations on six benchmarks show that our TDAR-8B model with BACD and TCCF achieves a 2.38 speedup and +3.4% average accuracy over the strong TraDo-8B baseline, unlocking the potential of block diffusion in complex reasoning.

t: TrajToM: Evaluating Theory of Mind over Mental State Trajectories in Social Dialogues
ab: Theory of Mind (ToM) is crucial for understanding social dialogue, where characters’ mental states are rarely stated explicitly but evolve through interaction and shape later behavior. Existing ToM benchmarks focus mainly on selected dialogue turns or state changes across separate scenarios, leaving within-dialogue mental state trajectories underexplored. We introduce TrajToM, a benchmark for evaluating whether LLMs can reason over evolving emotions, beliefs, intentions, and desires in continuous social dialogue. Built with a Sketch-first construction paradigm, TrajToM contains 700 dialogues and 18,165 multiple-choice questions across mental state reasoning, behavioral reasoning, and trajectory reasoning. Experiments reveal a substantial human-model gap, with GPT-5.2 reaching 67.4% overall accuracy compared with 88.2% for humans, and show persistent bottlenecks in second-order reasoning, behavior explanation, and change direction assessment. We further examine MARTA as an exploratory trajectory-aligned process-supervision framework, showing that explicit supervision over mental state trajectories can improve ToM reasoning.

t: Beyond Token-Level Guidance: Inference-Time Alignment of Specialized LLMs via Cross-Family Representation Steering
ab: Large language models (LLMs) finetuned for specialized domains represent crucial high-impact applications. Inference-time alignment improves safety degraded from specialization finetuning without requiring substantial computational resources, complementing finetuning-based methods with an easy-to-use, plug-and-play solution. However, existing inference-time methods fail to reliably improve safety without disrupting domain capability. We identify the root cause as complementary expertise orthogonality: specialized base models and general-domain guidance models have orthogonal competencies, making the guidance signal unreliable for specialized generation. This primarily manifests as stop token interference, where the guidance model’s tendency toward continuation overrides the base model’s decision to stop, burying correct answers under guidance-induced continuation. To address this problem, we propose CREST, an inference-time alignment method that steers base model hidden representations using safety directions extracted from a guidance model of any family, avoiding token-level structural limitations entirely. CREST improves safety where specialization has weakened it while preserving both domain-specific capability and the safety of already well-aligned models, outperforming baselines by up to 22.2% on safety benchmarks. Our code is available at: https://github.com/DecayingSeart/CREST.

t: DualES: Internalizing Query-Text Duality for Text-to-ES via Bidirectional Reasoning-Enhanced Supervision
ab: Text-to-ES aims to translate natural language into executable Elasticsearch(ES) queries. Unlike more open-ended reasoning tasks, such as mathematical reasoning, this problem is defined over a constrained domain-specific language, where the synergy between forward reasoning and backward reasoning can be more explicitly realized under strict structural constraints. While recent work has explored reasoning-oriented training and prompting in text-to-SQL, forward and backward reasoning have not been systematically studied in text-to-ES. In this paper, we systematically study the bidirectional duality of the text-to-ES task by establishing a bidirectional reasoning perspective across both training and prompting stages. We introduce two large-scale datasets, TERD and ETRD, for forward and backward reasoning, respectively, and propose DualES, a unified framework that combines the two. Experimental results show that our DualES-CoRE strategy sets a new State-of-the-Art(SOTA), achieving 69.23% on LED and 50.14% on BirdES. This corresponds to absolute execution accuracy gains of 6.92% and 7.34% over previous benchmarks, outperforming both open-source and closed-source baselines. We will release the datasets in the future.

t: IWP: Token Pruning as Implicit Weight Pruning in Large Vision Language Models
a: KAIST, Korea Advanced Institute of Science & Technology
Korea Advanced Institute of Science & Technology
Korea Advanced Institute of Science and Technology
ab: Large Vision–Language Models (LVLMs) show impressive performance across image and video understanding tasks, yet their computational cost grows rapidly with the number of visual tokens. Existing token pruning methods address this by reducing the number of visual tokens, but overlook the internal mechanism of attention. In this paper, we propose a novel training-free token pruning framework grounded in the dual-form perspective of attention. We reformulate attention as an implicit linear layer whose weight matrix is the sum of rank-1 outer products, each generated by a single token’s key–value pair. Token pruning thus reduces to identifying an optimal subset of these rank-1 updates that retains the essential information of the original dual weight matrix. Extending this perspective to standard softmax attention in LVLMs, we derive a novel importance metric quantifying both a token’s information magnitude and information duplication. To efficiently select the subset with the proposed metric, we introduce Progressive Chunked Maximal Marginal Relevance. Extensive experiments demonstrate that our method achieves a better trade-off between performance and efficiency, while providing another perspective on existing pruning approaches.

t: SVD-Attention: Efficiently Analyzing Attention Blocks in Transformers
ab: Pretrained transformers spend a large share of their inference compute inside self-attention, yet the per-head query-key interaction is structurally low-rank by construction. We ask a diagnostic question: across layers and architectures, which heads actually use the full rank budget on real data, and which do not? We propose SVD-Attention, a post-hoc method that decomposes the per-head interaction matrix M_h and scores every singular mode by both its spectral magnitude and its activation variance across tokens on a small calibration set. The score keeps the modes the head can amplify and that real data actually activates, and discards the rest; the resulting factorization is exact for the retained modes and needs no finetuning. Across seven pretrained models and five task types, the diagnostic finds a task-dependent pattern: redundancy sits in the early to middle layers for sentiment and image classification and for generation, and in the late layers for dense prediction and extractive question answering. It is also predictive: truncating the layers it flags costs at most 1.75 F1, while truncating the same number of layers elsewhere in the same model costs up to 50 F1. SVD-Attention is an analysis tool rather than a compression method: acting on it reduces inference FLOPs by 0.8-1.5% on its own and by 8-11% when composed with weight pruning, with 0-4% change in task quality. We release the code at https://github.com/riksanyal/SVD-Attention.

t: Variance-Adaptive Muon: Pre-Orthogonalization Variance Modulation for Efficient Language Model Pretraining
ab: Optimizer design plays a central role in efficient language model pretraining, directly affecting optimization dynamics, convergence speed, and compute cost under fixed training budgets. Muon has emerged as a strong optimizer by orthogonalizing momentum updates, yielding a matrix-valued analogue of sign-based normalization. However, unlike Adam-style methods, Muon does not explicitly incorporate gradient-variance information into its updates. Motivated by Adam’s variance-adaptive interpretation, we propose Muon-NSR and Muon-VS, two variance-adaptive Muon variants for language model pretraining. Muon-NSR applies noise-to-signal ratio (NSR) modulation before Newton–Schulz orthogonalization, whereas Muon-VS uses variance scaling (VS) without introducing any additional hyperparameters beyond those of Muon. Both methods preserve Muon’s spectral normalization structure while requiring only one additional variance buffer. Experiments on Llama-style and GPT-2 pretraining across model scales from 125M to 1.2B parameters show that our methods improve over well-tuned Muon baselines and remain competitive with representative adaptive Muon-family baselines. On Llama-1.2B, Muon-VS achieves a 1.33× step-to-target speedup over a well-tuned Muon baseline, with Muon’s final validation loss as the target. These results indicate that variance-adaptive modulation is a simple and effective mechanism for improving Muon-style optimizers in language model pretraining.

t: StoryLens: Preference-Aligned Story Rewriting via Context-Aware Narrative Enrichment
a: Beijing University of Post and Telecommunications
ab: Story rewriting aims to adapt existing narratives to diverse reader preferences while preserving plot consistency and narrative coherence. Unlike conventional work on style transfer, we argue that effective story rewriting demands context-aware narrative enrichment beyond surface-level stylistic adaptation. Our pilot human study shows that style adaptation alone provides only marginal gains in reader satisfaction (2.3%), while context-enhanced rewriting substantially improves user preference alignment (24.5%). Motivated by this, we introduce STORYLENSBENCH, a large-scale benchmark for preference-aligned story rewriting, comprising structured story books, multi-dimensional reader preference profiles, and ranked context-aware rewritten stories. Building on this benchmark, we propose STORYLENSEVAL, a reward model for estimating reader satisfaction over rewritten stories, and STORYLENSWRITER, a two-stage rewriting model combining supervised fine-tuning with GRPO-based reinforcement learning. We further establish a comprehensive evaluation framework covering fidelity, coherence, and reader satisfaction. Experimental results demonstrate that STORYLENSWRITER consistently outperforms strong generation and personalization baselines, highlighting the importance of context-aware narrative enrichment for personalized story rewriting.

t: Spatial Reasoning in Large Vision-Language Models via Egocentric-to-Allocentric Transformation
ab: Multi-view spatial reasoning in large vision-language models involves inferring view-specific spatial relations and integrating them into a consistent scene-centered representation. However, existing approaches often learn view-dependent relations tied to individual camera frames, which limits their ability to form viewpoint-invariant spatial representations. Motivated by cognitive models of spatial perspective-taking, we propose SCoRE (Spatial Consistency Reasoning), a method that formulates multi-view spatial reasoning as an egocentric-to-allocentric transformation problem. SCoRE first trains the model to infer egocentric object relations from single-view observations. It then applies reinforcement learning to encourage the model to estimate viewpoint orientation, transform egocentric relations into a shared scene-centered reference frame, and predict allocentric object relations. To enforce viewpoint-invariant reasoning, we optimize the model with a multi-view consistency reward that aligns predictions from different views in the common allocentric space. Experiments show that SCoRE improves spatial reasoning performance by +3.69%p on multi-view benchmarks and +4.72%p on general spatial reasoning benchmarks over prior state-of-the-art methods, demonstrating the effectiveness of explicit reference-frame transformation for robust multi-view spatial understanding.

t: Retrieval-Augmented Agentic Rubric Generation for Reliable Medical Response Evaluation
a: University College London, University of London
ab: Large Language Models (LLMs) are increasingly used for clinical decision support, where hallucinations and unsafe suggestions may pose direct risks to patient safety. These risks are hard to assess: subtle clinical errors are often missed by generic metrics and LLM judges using general criteria, while expert-authored fine-grained rubrics are expensive and difficult to scale. In this paper, we propose a retrieval-augmented multi-agent framework for automatically generating instance-specific evaluation rubrics.Our approach grounds evaluation in authoritative medical evidence by decomposing retrieved content into atomic facts and synthesizing them with user interaction constraints to form fine-grained evaluation criteria. Evaluated on HealthBench and LLMEval-Med, our framework achieves Clinical Intent Alignment (CIA) scores of 50.20% and 31.90%, significantly outperforming the GPT-4o baseline and showing consistent improvements across English and Chinese medical benchmarks. In discriminative tests on HealthBench, our rubrics achieve a 7.8% point higher win rate than GPT-4o and increase the mean score difference from 4.972 to 8.658. Ablation studies further show that individual components contribute differently across datasets, with interaction-intent modeling providing the most consistent contribution to clinical-criterion coverage. Beyond evaluation, our rubrics guide response refinement, improving response quality by 9.2%. These results suggest that automated, knowledge-grounded rubric generation provides a scalable foundation for evaluating and improving medical LLMs. The code is available at https://anonymous.4open.science/r/Automated-Rubric-Generation-E716/.

t: Make an Offer They Can’t Refuse: Grounding Bayesian Persuasion in Real-World Dialogues without Pre-Commitment
a: Beijing Institute for General Artificial Intelligence
Beijing University of Posts and Telecommunications
Beijing University of Post and Telecommunication
Beijing Institute for General Artificial Intelligence
National Key Laboratory of General Artificial Intelligence
ab: Large language models (LLMs) still struggle with strategic persuasion, largely because existing approaches either neglect information asymmetry or rely on unrealistic pre-commitment assumptions. We introduce a type-induced commitment-communication mechanism that grounds Bayesian Persuasion (BP) in natural language dialogue without pre-commitment: the persuader narrates their potential types (e.g., honest vs. dishonest) to dynamically construct an information schema, enabling the persuadee to perform Bayesian belief updates within the conversation itself. We implement two variants: Semi-Formal-Natural-Language (SFNL) and Fully-Natural-Language (FNL), evaluating them against strong baselines across multiple LLMs and human judges. BP strategies consistently outperform baselines: SFNL excels in logical credibility, while FNL shows superior robustness and emotional resonance. We verify that gains stem from genuine Bayesian reasoning rather than superficial formatting, and we further show that supervised fine-tuning enables small models to match the persuasive performance of much larger ones.

t: MedFeat: Model-Aware and Explainability-Driven Feature Engineering with LLMs for Tabular Prediction
