ab: In clinical tabular prediction, classical machine learning models with feature engineering often outperform neural methods. LLMs are increasingly used to automate this process, acting as domain experts that propose diverse feature transformations to boost downstream performance. However, the feature generation process of existing LLM-based methods is agnostic to the downstream learner: the LLM receives no signal about which features currently drive predictions or where the model’s representational capacity falls short, so proposals are neither targeted to promising regions of the feature space nor tailored to the learner’s inductive bias. This shortcoming is amplified in healthcare data, which simultaneously exhibits class imbalance, heterogeneous feature spaces, and strict interpretability requirements. In this paper, we propose MedFeat, the first feature engineering framework inspired by the workflow of machine learning practitioners, leveraging model-awareness and feature importance signals to iteratively guide feature discovery for clinical tabular learning. We evaluate MedFeat on a broad range of challenging real-world clinical tasks and show that it statistically significantly outperforms state-of-the-art baselines, with an average F1 improvement of more than 10% over the baseline across models with distinct inductive biases.

t: Dual-Bias Load Balancing: Mitigating Expert-Bias Staleness in Auxiliary-Loss-Free Mixture-of-Experts
ab: Auxiliary-loss-free load balancing (ALF-LB) achieves promising performance in Mixture-of-Experts large language model (MoE-LLM) pre-training as it decouples load balancing from the main objective. However, we observe an unexplored phenomenon: routing imbalance is concentrated in shallow MoE layers. We attribute this phenomenon to the interaction between representation homogeneity, which makes shallow-layer routing decisions highly sensitive, and expert-bias staleness, which applies stale load corrections to the current router state. To break the cycle, we propose Dual-Bias Load Balancing (DLB), which augments the standard global expert bias with an intra-step micro-bias residual. DLB introduces the effective bias \mathbf{b}_{\mathrm{eff}}=\mathbf{b}_g+\Delta\mathbf{b}, where \mathbf{b}_g is updated once per gradient step and \Delta\mathbf{b} is updated across micro-batches within the same step. DLB does not add forward or backward passes and integrates naturally into existing large-scale MoE training pipelines. Experiments on large-scale MoE pre-training show that DLB mitigates expert-bias staleness, alleviates shallow-layer imbalance, and yields lower test perplexity and stronger average downstream performance.

t: Beyond Objective Equivalence: Constraint Injection for LLM-Based Optimization Modeling on Vehicle Routing Problems
a: Beijing University of Aeronautics and Astronautics
ab: Large language models (LLMs) can generate executable solver code from natural-language descriptions of optimization problems. However, existing verification signals focus on whether the generated formulation produces the correct objective value. Such signals can overlook constraint-level errors: incorrect formulations may still produce the same optimum when extra or missing constraints do not affect the tested instance. We propose constraint injection, a verification method that directly tests whether the generated code implements the intended constraints. We use feasible solutions to detect incorrectly added constraints and one-constraint-violating solutions to detect omissions. Together with the optimal value check, these tests verify both the objective and the constraint set. We evaluate this approach on vehicle routing problems (VRPs), which provide a challenging testbed with diverse, tightly coupled operational constraints. We develop VRPCoder, an 8B model for generating Gurobi code from natural-language VRP descriptions, and VRPBench, an expert-verified benchmark spanning 21 VRP variants across four subsets. The verifier serves as a rejection-sampling criterion for synthetic data construction and as a rollout-level reward for reinforcement learning (RL). On VRPBench, VRPCoder-RL reaches 93% overall Pass@1, outperforms Gemini-3.1-Pro Preview on three subsets, exceeds Claude-Sonnet-4.5 by 28 percentage points, and exceeds the strongest prior OR-LLM by 78 percentage points.

t: Beyond Scalar Scores: Exploring LLM-based Metrics for Clinical Significance Evaluation in Radiology Reports
ab: Automated evaluation of radiology reports is essential for clinical trust, yet clinically significant errors (e.g., missed findings or incorrect descriptions) can critically mislead diagnosis. Traditional metrics fail to distinguish between clinically meaningful and harmless textual variations, collapsing report quality into a single scalar score. Although Large Language Models (LLMs) embody richer medical knowledge, such metrics still lack an explicit boundary of clinical significance. To bridge this gap, we adopt the ReEvalMed benchmark as testbed and evaluate metric-level clinical significance from detecting true clinical errors ("Discrimination") and tolerating insignificant variations ("Robustness"). We design an evaluation framework with one-pass and two-pass settings, and compare 8 LLM evaluators against score-based baselines. Results reveal a discrimination bias: LLMs readily detect true clinical errors but struggle to tolerate harmless variations. To mitigate this, we synthesize 4k report pairs and train lightweight interpretable metrics on Qwen3-8B and MedGemma-4B. Our trained metric sharpens the clinical significance boundary, surpassing 32B-scale medical LLMs and remaining competitive with proprietary models. Notably, two-pass inference does not eliminate errors, but redistributes them between discrimination and robustness. We will release the dataset and metric to advance future research.

t: Synthetic Data Characterization via Training Dynamics
ab: Interpreting properties of LLM-generated data is important for understanding its utility and limitations across learning tasks. In this work, we characterize synthetic data through sample-level learnability, studying variation among LLM families and scales, alongside human-written data as a reference. We generate synthetic datasets spanning single- and multi-label classification, labeling, and tree prediction tasks using LLMs from multiple families and scales. We then derive empirical data distributions from encoder training dynamics for both machine and organic data, and estimate the robustness of these distributions across encoders. Finally, we evaluate how data selection strategies based on these learnability signals affect both data sources differently.

t: STARS: State-Aware Reasoning Stopping via Hidden-State Spectral Analysis
a: University of California, San Diego, University of California, San Diego
ab: Chain-of-thought (CoT) reasoning in large language models often produces redundant steps that increase generation cost and obscure when reasoning has effectively completed. Existing stopping methods rely on output-level or token-level signals, overlooking internal representation dynamics that reflect reasoning progress. We propose STARS (STate-Aware Reasoning Stopping), a framework that leverages spectral analysis of hidden-state representations to detect transitions in reasoning phases. Our key insight is that structural changes in the representation space capture shifts in reasoning states, enabling early and reliable stopping decisions. To address representation instability, where semantically similar steps can induce different hidden states, we focus on spectral structure rather than raw activations, improving robustness to context-dependent drift. Experiments on four mathematical and logical reasoning benchmarks show that STARS reduces generation cost by over 45% under fixed token budgets while improving accuracy over standard CoT baselines.

t: Do No Harm: Exposing Hidden Vulnerabilities of LLMs via Persona-based Client Simulation Attack in Psychological Counseling
a: Monash University and University of Melbourne
ab: The increasing use of large language models (LLMs) in mental healthcare raises safety concerns in high-stakes therapeutic interactions. A key challenge is distinguishing therapeutic empathy from maladaptive validation, where supportive responses may inadvertently reinforce harmful beliefs or behaviors in multi-turn conversations. This risk is largely overlooked by existing red-teaming frameworks, which focus mainly on generic harms or optimization-based attacks. To address this gap, we introduce Persona-based Client Simulation Attack (PCSA), the first red-teaming framework that simulates clients in psychological counseling through coherent, persona-driven client dialogues to expose vulnerabilities in psychological safety alignment. Experiments on eight general and mental health-specialized LLMs show that PCSA substantially outperforms four competitive baselines. Perplexity analysis and human inspection further indicate that PCSA generates more natural and realistic dialogues. Our results reveal that current LLMs remain vulnerable to domain-specific adversarial tactics, providing unauthorized medical advice, reinforcing delusions, and implicitly encouraging risky actions.

t: FEPO: Future-Entropy Policy Optimization with Selective Update Modulation
a: Shanghai Academy of AI for Science and Fudan University
ab: Existing RL methods for language models typically use token-level entropy, which captures uncertainty at the current position rather than over future generation. We study future entropy, i.e., uncertainty over the remaining suffix conditioned on the current prefix. By the entropy chain rule, local entropy is the expected decrease in future entropy, while the realized decrease depends on the chosen token, yielding an action-dependent future-entropy gap. We evaluate this signal at inference time with MIN-F-MC, an oracle-style probe that selects the candidate token with the lowest estimated future-entropy rate at high-entropy positions. On mathematical reasoning tasks, MIN-F-MC yields higher mean accuracy than greedy and Random TopK across the tested checkpoints and datasets. We then propose FEPO (Future Entropy Policy Optimization), which uses realized future-entropy rates at a sparse set of high-entropy positions to scale update magnitudes. Across the tested model–benchmark pairs, FEPO improves Mean@32 over GRPO.

t: ConsistKV: Layer Adaptive KV Cache Compression via Cross Layer Consensus
a: Hong Kong University of Science and Technology
ab: As LLMs process increasingly long contexts, the KV cache has become a major source of memory and bandwidth overhead during inference. Existing methods compress the KV cache by preserving attention sinks, recent tokens, or layer-local important tokens, but they rarely exploit how token importance is shared and specialized across layers. In this paper, we introduce ConsistKV, an adaptive KV cache compression method that exploits consensus in token importance across layers. For each layer, ConsistKV aggregates importance scores from neighboring layers to identify shared contextual anchors, while using residual local importance to preserve tokens that are salient to the current layer. It further estimates the cache demand of each layer from disagreement between layers and importance dispersion, enabling adaptive budget allocation under a fixed global cache budget. Experiments on LongBench show that ConsistKV achieves the highest average performance among evaluated KV cache compression baselines under the same cache budget.

t: Text-Conditioned Static-Dynamic Composition for Composed Video Retrieval
ab: Composed Video Retrieval (CVR) aims to retrieve a target video given a reference video and a modification text. The central challenge is to identify and use video content that is relevant to the retrieval need specified by the modification text. Existing methods typically encode videos before considering this textual need, causing visual evidence to be formed in a largely text-agnostic manner. We propose StaDy-CLIP, a compact dual-pathway framework for text-conditioned evidence composition. It preserves the frozen CLIP visual encoder as a static pathway for CLIP-aligned static evidence, introduces a lightweight side pathway for dynamic evidence, and uses Text-Conditioned Composition Blocks to perform patch-wise dynamic evidence selection and textual modulation. A learnable Gallery Conditioning Prompt further enables gallery videos to be encoded within the same evidence composition framework. StaDy-CLIP achieves state-of-the-art performance on FineCVR-1M and TF-CoVR with only 7.78M trainable parameters, improving prior best results by +4.05 in Recall@1 and +1.49 in mAP@5. Ablations and encoder-transfer results validate its effectiveness and encoder-level transferability for existing CVR methods.

t: Patterns of Priming in Production: Lexical, Semantic and Structural Alignment in Language Model Generation
ab: This paper investigates structural priming in language model (LM) production, examining how preceding structural context influences sentence completion. While prior work has demonstrated priming effects in comprehension of structural alternations, it remained unclear whether these persist in production, where, when generating, an LM samples from many possible continuations at each step. We address this question through a series of controlled sentence-completion experiments on dative constructions. In line with prior work, we find that LMs are susceptible to structural priming, particularly in sentences that are semantically coherent. In terms of priming magnitude, we find that while there is a greater relative increase of double-object datives against our baselines, in line with inverse frequency effects, there is a larger absolute increase in prepositional-objects, the more frequently produced construction. Finally, we not only observe that structural priming is boosted by lexico-semantic coherence, but that structurally primed completions display greater levels of lexico-semantic repetition. Taken together, our evidence supports the view that structural priming in LMs operates across multiple levels of linguistic representation, facilitating, and facilitated by syntactic, lexical, and semantic alignment.

t: MppReasoner: Reasoning-Enhanced Large Language Models for Molecular Property Prediction
a: SUN YAT-SEN UNIVERSITY and DP Technology
ab: Molecular property prediction is fundamental to drug discovery and materials science, yet existing models suffer from limited interpretability and poor cross-task generalization. Without explainable chemical rationales, accurate predictions alone are insufficient for guiding costly downstream experiments. We propose \textbf{MppReasoner}, a multimodal large language model that incorporates verifiable chemical reasoning for molecular property prediction. Built on Qwen2.5-VL-7B-Instruct, MppReasoner integrates 2D molecular images with SMILES strings through a two-stage training strategy: supervised fine-tuning (SFT) on 16,000 expert-guided reasoning trajectories, followed by Reinforcement Learning from Principle-Guided Rewards (RLPGR). RLPGR applies rule-based rewards verified by RDKit to evaluate chemical principle usage, structural analysis, and logical consistency, providing objective feedback without human preference labels. Experiments across 8 benchmark datasets show that MppReasoner outperforms the strongest baseline by 2.95% and 5.49% on in-distribution and out-of-distribution tasks, respectively. Beyond predictive accuracy, MppReasoner generates chemically grounded reasoning traces, with expert evaluation confirming high reasoning quality across three assessed dimensions. Code is available at https://github.com/Jesse-zjx/MPPReasoner.

t: From Discovery to Internalization: Length-Adaptive Policy Optimization for Efficient Reasoning
ab: Large reasoning models have achieved remarkable performance through extended chain-of-thought sequences, yet this computational freedom leads to excessive token generation even for simple problems. We present Length-Adaptive Policy Optimization (LAPO), a novel framework that transforms reasoning length control from an external constraint into an intrinsic model capability. Unlike existing approaches that impose rigid limits or rely on post-hoc interventions, LAPO enables models to internalize an understanding of appropriate reasoning depth through a two-stage reinforcement learning process. In the first stage, models learn natural reasoning patterns by discovering the statistical distribution of successful solution lengths. In the second stage, these learned patterns are embedded as in-context, self-declarative guidance, teaching the model to proactively plan its reasoning budget. Experiments on mathematical reasoning benchmarks demonstrate that LAPO reduces token usage by up to 38.5% while improving accuracy by 2.3%. Our analysis reveals that models trained with LAPO develop emergent abilities to allocate computational resources based on problem complexity, achieving efficient reasoning without sacrificing quality.

t: When Helpfulness, Harmlessness, and Honesty Remember They Are on the Same Team
ab: Aligning Large Language Models (LLMs) requires simultaneously satisfying Helpfulness, Harmlessness, and Honesty (HHH). Existing works-including SFT, MoEs, RLHF, and orchestrator-based steering-operate on standard 1-to-1 transformer architectures and show systematic trade-offs across objectives. While such works can steer behaviour post hoc, they remain fundamentally additive and therefore suffer from catastrophic forgetting. While recent mechanistic interpretability have helped characterise this behaviour, they expose a deeper structural failure-transformers lack an mechanism to negotiate incompatible objective signals, resulting in a mechanistic blind-spot. Therefore, we test the hypothesis that these failures are architectural-driven rather than optimisation-driven via NegotiaX, a 1-to-N transformer architecture that separates and reconciles alignment objectives via two modules. Module I (Transformer Module) allocates independent representational pathways to each objective-mitigating catastrophic forgetting. Module II (Mechanistic Alignment Circuit (MAC)), embeds objectives into dedicated subspaces and performs a learned negotiative operation prior to decoding-mitigating mechanistic blind-spot. Across four 7B backbones, NegotiaX remains competitive with SOTA-improving Avg by up to 6.3%, Helpfulness by 6.2%, Honesty by 5.6%, and Harmlessness by 4.7%.

t: MCPlanner: Hierarchical Adaptive Planning-Based Medical Consultation with Large Language Models
ab: Medical consultation (MC) is an interactive decision-making process that requires dynamically adapting inquiry directions according to evolving patient feedback. Although large language models (LLMs) have demonstrated strong planning capabilities in medical applications, existing LLM-based MC methods typically make turn-level independent inquiry decisions without adaptive control over global inquiry directions, making them prone to inefficient local exploration. To address this limitation, we propose MCPlanner, a hierarchical adaptive planning-based MC framework in which a high-level planner adaptively controls the inquiry direction, while a low-level planner executes inquiry actions under the selected direction. Additionally, MCPlanner introduces expert-guided distillation and a smoothed confidence calibration strategy to improve high-level planning efficiency and diagnostic accuracy. Experimental results on DXY, GMD, and CMD show that MCPlanner achieves best diagnostic accuracies of 95.2%, 90.8%, and 76.1%, respectively. Notably, on CMD, MCPlanner outperforms the strongest baseline by 5.0 percentage points. Code is publicly available at https://github.com/zh-jia/MCPlanner.

t: On the Universality of the Inner Product as a PMI Estimator in Embedding Models
a: Universidad Nacional de Educación a Distancia
Universidad Nacional de Educación a Distancia
Universidad Nacional de Educación a Distancia
ab: Embedding representations are widely used in natural language processing, yet their semantic interpretation depends on the operators used to compare them. Previous work has shown that, for certain embedding models, the inner product is linearly correlated with Pointwise Mutual Information (PMI). However, this relation has so far been established only empirically or analytically for specific models.In this work, we formally show that, under certain assumptions about distributional semantic embedding models, the inner product between embeddings approaches PMI. This theoretical result provides a more general explanation for the observed relationship and enables the formulation of training criteria aimed at learning embedding spaces in which operations between embeddings are semantically interpretable.

t: OmniPhys: A Unified Multimodal Benchmark for Physics Understanding and Generation from Chinese Educational Corpora
ab: Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) have demonstrated strong abilities in solving diverse visual and textual reasoning tasks. However, their development in the physics domain is significantly hindered by the lack of a comprehensive benchmark. To fill this gap, we introduce OmniPhys, a large-scale benchmark for multimodal physics understanding and reasoning, covering middle school through university-level problems from Chinese Educational Corpora. OmniPhys consists of 15,246 questions and 19,850 images, accompanied by detailed annotations that support fine-grained analysis of reasoning processes and knowledge usage. Beyond conventional evaluation, OmniPhys is a benchmark that systematically evaluates multimodal outputs in physics domain, including models’ ability to generate structured physics diagrams, which constitute a fundamental component of authentic physics problem solving.

t: KoNeoBench: A Curated Evaluation Dataset for LLM Understanding of Korean Neologisms
a: Kyungpook National University, Kyungpook National University, Kyungpook National University and Kyungpook National University
Daegu Gyeongbuk Institute of Science and Technology
ab: Large language models (LLMs) are typically evaluated on static benchmarks, even though natural language constantly evolves through newly emerging words and meanings. Existing Korean benchmarks are centered on established vocabulary and therefore provide limited coverage of such recent lexical change, and their English-oriented design makes it difficult to assess the typological properties of Korean, in which content words combine productively with functional morphemes. In this paper, we introduce **KoNeoBench**, a benchmark for evaluating LLMs’ understanding of Korean neologisms. KoNeoBench is built on 1,785 Korean neologisms attested in online news since 2020 and curated through expert lexicographic review. Each entry provides usage examples, word-formation analyses, and dictionary-style definitions. Based on this resource, we define four tasks and report results on recent models, together with a human baseline. Our experiments show that current LLMs exhibit clear limitations in recovering source components, distinguishing semantic categories, and generating accurate definitions. These results reveal specific aspects of recent Korean lexical change that remain challenging for current LLMs. KoNeoBench is available at https://github.com/bcmilab/ko-neobench/ .

t: TriLens: Per-Layer Logit-Lens Entropy for White-Box Hallucination Detection
a: Zhejiang University and Beijing Normal–Hong Kong Baptist University
ab: When a language model hallucinates, the final answer is wrong, but the mistake is not necessarily invisible inside the model. Different internal pathways may remain uncertain, disagree in how quickly they sharpen, or commit to competing continuations before the output is produced. We introduce TriLens, a white-box detector that turns this intuition into a compact representation: at every layer, it reads the multi-head self-attention output, the feed-forward output, and the residual stream through the model’s own logit lens, then records only the entropy of each readout. The resulting 3L-dimensional trajectory describes how certainty forms across depth and across modules, without storing high-dimensional hidden states or sampling multiple generations. This simple signal yields a strong detector across instruction-tuned LLMs and QA benchmarks, and our analyses show that the three module-wise entropy trajectories provide complementary evidence. TriLens suggests that hallucination detection can benefit from tracking how internal computation settles, not only what the final layer predicts. The code is available at https://tosakaucw.github.io/TriLens/.

t: MemoryCD: Benchmarking Long-Context User Memory of LLM Agents for Lifelong Cross-Domain Personalization
ab: Recent advancements in Large Language Models (LLMs) have expanded context windows to million-token scales, yet benchmarks for evaluating memory remain limited to short-session synthetic dialogues. We introduce MemoryCD, the first large-scale, user-centric, cross-domain memory benchmark derived from lifelong real-world behaviors in the Amazon Review dataset. Unlike existing memory datasets that rely on scripted personas to generate synthetic user data, MemoryCD tracks authentic user interactions across years and multiple domains. We construct a multi-faceted long-context memory evaluation pipeline of 14 state-of-the-art LLM base models with 6 memory method baselines on 4 distinct personalization tasks over 12 diverse domains to evaluate an agent’s ability to simulate real user behaviors in both single and cross-domain settings. Our analysis reveals that existing memory methods are far from user satisfaction in various domains, offering the first testbed for cross-domain life-long personalization evaluation.

t: Beyond ID Embeddings: Process-Grounded Language Modeling for Cognitive Diagnosis
a: Institute of Computing Technology, Chinese Academy of Sciences
Institute of Computing Technology, Chinese Academy
ab: Cognitive Diagnosis Models (CDMs) play a pivotal role in personalized online learning. Traditional CDMs rely on discrete, ID-based embeddings to represent students, exercises, and concepts. This paradigm diverges from the nature of learner cognition, where knowledge is not stored and retrieved as isolated symbols. As a result, CDMs suffer from semantic limitations when new exercises or concepts appear. In this paper, we propose a Process-aware Language Cognitive Diagnosis (PLCD) framework that uses language-derived structures as cognitive priors and response records to calibrate student posterior states. PLCD leverages large language models (LLMs) to construct concept schemas and cognitive process graphs, and uses target-conditioned semantic memory to retrieve historical responses that are relevant to each target exercise. A process-grounded Language-to-Cognition Mapper with DA-MoE experts and process-level contrastive learning then maps the textual evidence into a unified cognitive space. Experimental results show that PLCD not only outperforms traditional baselines in predicting student performance but also exhibits strong cognitive transfer capabilities. These results connect the computational power of LLMs with the psychometric goal of measuring latent knowledge states, suggesting that structured language priors calibrated by response records can improve cold-start robustness and cognitive grounding.

t: ShardMemo: Scope-Before-Routing for Agentic Memory Retrieval
ab: Agentic systems accumulate persistent memory across sessions, tools, and tasks, and a later request must retrieve from it under two distinct constraints: which memories it is permitted to access, and which are relevant under a limited search budget. Existing memory systems handle access scope in two flawed ways: applying scope after retrieval wastes probe budget on inadmissible memories, while treating scope as a learned ranking feature makes a hard constraint depend on router quality. We present ShardMemo, an agentic memory system built on scope-before-routing: metadata predicates first identify the admissible shards, and a learned router then selects a small number of them for shard-local approximate nearest neighbor retrieval. This separates hard admissibility from learned relevance ranking, so inadmissible shards cannot consume shard-probe budget. We evaluate on LoCoMo, HotpotQA, and ToolBench, covering conversational, long-context, and procedural memory. Under matched supervision and fixed budgets, ShardMemo improves over a learned router baseline by roughly +3 F1 on LoCoMo; in end-to-end LoCoMo evaluation it improves over the strongest evaluated memory baseline by up to +6.8 F1, with gains on HotpotQA and ToolBench.

t: SoVTR: Set-of-Vision-Text Rewards for Attribute-Grounded Emotion Recognition in VLLMs
ab: Vision Large Language Models (VLLMs) show promise for multi-modal understanding; yet, their application to emotion recognition remains limited by insufficient spatial and contextual awareness and by supervised fine-tuning that uniformly penalizes all reasoning tokens—suppressing valid alternatives. We present Set-of-Vision-Text Rewards (SoVTR), a unified, reward-based framework that guides VLLMs with interpretable and verifiable visual attributes, focusing optimization on the emotion-discriminative reasoning steps that truly determine correctness. SoVTR decomposes supervision into three rewards: (i) Face Reward capturing action units, gaze, and micro-expressions; (ii) Body Reward encoding pose and gesture cues; and (iii) Context Reward modeling person–object relations and scene activities. By combining BERTScore attribute matching with GRPO policy optimization, SoVTR produces attribute-grounded explanation traces while preserving non-critical reasoning diversity. Across DFEW, FERV39k, and ExpW, SoVTR consistently improves both recognition accuracy and grounding quality, delivering substantial gains over strong VLLM baselines.

t: Ethical Imprints in LLMs: From Corpus Ethics to ICL, SFT, and Their Interaction on Deception Dilemmas
a: Department of Computer Science, The University of Hong Kong
ab: Large language models make consistent moral judgments, but whether these tendencies correspond to the moral makeup of public web text in the same language is not well understood. We test this correspondence for deception dilemmas across Chinese and English in a four-layer empirical study. We use DeepSeek-R1 for ICL probing, Llama-3.1-8B and Qwen2.5-7B for fine-tuning, and GPT-4o for cross-model replication. In both languages, roughly 60% of web text favors utilitarian reasoning (59.8% vs. 62.3%), inconsistent with a purely sociolinguistic explanation. In-context learning shifts model decisions sharply in low-resistance scenarios (Hostage Crisis, V = 0.411, p = 0.001). In a high-resistance scenario (Organ Allocation), one DeepSeek-R1 deployment showed near-zero ICL effects (V = 0.067) at small sample size, but a larger replication on another deployment showed a large effect (V = 0.55 to 0.69), indicating deployment-specific rather than stable resistance. Three findings stand out for multilingual alignment. First, fine-tuning on deontological data reverses direction in English (Llama-EN Deon P(A) rises from {\sim}0% to 88%), showing that SFT value transfer is not language-neutral. Second, corpus proportions do not carry over to forced choices. The English Llama-3.1-8B base model gives P(A) near zero even though 62.3% of the web text is utilitarian. Third, apparent moral damping in high-resistance scenarios can reflect sample size and deployment variability rather than a stable property of the model or scenario. These results show that corpus moral distributions correspond to model behavior in many conditions, but language, post-training, model architecture, and deployment variability each introduce points where this correspondence breaks.

t: Hallucination-Aware Multi-Agent RAG via Internal Attention Rewards
ab: Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) grounds language models in retrieved evidence, but its outputs often contain claims unsupported by that evidence. Recent multi-agent RAG systems decompose the pipeline into cooperative decisions, yet they typically optimize all agents under a shared task reward such as EM or F1, which measures answer overlap rather than faithfulness to evidence. We propose a hallucination-aware multi-agent RAG framework that combines the task reward with an internal hallucination-risk signal computed from the generator’s attention-head norms. Three role-specific LoRA adapters, a query planner, an evidence selector, and an answer generator, share a frozen backbone. A lightweight critic is trained once on TruthfulQA truthful/false pairs and then kept frozen, providing a complementary risk score that is added to the shared reward during cooperative PPO training. Across three backbones (Qwen3-8B, Llama3-8B, Llama2-13B) and three benchmarks (RAGTruth, HotpotQA, 2WikiMultiHopQA), our method improves task performance and reduces hallucination rates over the strongest multi-agent baseline. Ablations and critic diagnostics show that the TruthfulQA-calibrated signal provides useful reward shaping that transfers across RAG tasks.

t: GNMR: Runtime Stability Control for Low-Precision Large Language Model Training
ab: Training stability is a key bottleneck in low-precision language model training: efficient low-cost paths can still produce short-lived numerical risks at a small set of operators. We formulate this as runtime stability control and present **G**radient **N**orm-to-**M**ean **R**atio (**GNMR**), a lightweight controller that compares each recoverable unit’s current gradient norm with its historical mean. Together with \Delta-GNMR for abrupt short-window increases, GNMR maps local risk signals to bounded recovery actions under a hard \text{maxO} budget and a short lock interval, without changing the numerical format, kernel, or backend recipe. Across activation-quantization stress, DeepSeek-style recipe-level training, and LLaMA-2 13B fine-tuning, GNMR preserves high-fidelity quality with sparse, budgeted recovery. These results support GNMR as a backend-agnostic controller to improve low-precision training stability while preserving low-cost execution.

t: Lost in Sampling: Assessing Lexical Reachability in LLMs via the Word Coverage Score (WCS)
ab: Modern Large Language Models (LLMs) are often criticized for producing repetitive and homogeneous text, despite possessing vast latent vocabularies. While previous research has focused on model knowledge and training data, we investigate the role of decoding mechanics in suppressing linguistic diversity. It is well-known that sampling filters cut the tail of the token probabilities, but the specific impact at the word level remains unexplored. In this paper, we introduce the Word Coverage Score (WCS), a metric that quantifies the extent to which contextually appropriate human vocabulary is mathematically pruned by standard sampling filters (e.g., Top-p, Top-k, and Min-p). Rather than assessing static knowledge, the WCS measures the lexical survival rate of words as a function of sampling parameters through a deterministic Forced-Path Audit. By auditing 13 open-weight models on 10,000 evaluation samples per model from the modern FineWeb corpus at four temperatures, we identify which human lexical choices are rendered unreachable by the decoder, even when they reside within the underlying probability space. To characterize word usage reduction without relying only on absolute erasure, we additionally introduce the Low-Coverage Word Rate (LCWR), the fraction of target words reachable in fewer than a specified proportion of contexts. In matched downstream generation experiments, greater WCS is associated with greater output-text lexical diversity: repeated-measures Spearman correlations are \rho=.67 for Type-Token Ratio (TTR), 95% Confidence Interval [.50, .82] and \rho = .66 for Measure of Textual Lexical Diversity (MTLD), 95% Confidence Interval [.51, .81]. These results provide quantitative evidence regarding how inference configurations shape vocabulary compression, establishing WCS as a computationally efficient diagnostic tool for hyperparameter debugging and vocabulary calibration.

t: Data Shapes What, Scale Shapes How: Lexical Learning Dynamics in LLMs
a: Université Pierre et Marie Curie - Paris 6, Sorbonne Université - Faculté des Sciences (Paris VI) and Sorbonne Université - Faculté des Sciences (Paris VI)
ab: We investigate how model scale shapes lexical acquisition in LLMs, introducing trajectory comparison as a methodological tool and three new convergence metrics. Tracking surprisal dynamics across four Pythia model sizes and 153 training checkpoints, we report two main findings. First, scale drives a global rise in inter-word surprisal coherence: synonym curves become more correlated at larger scales, but baseline correction reveals that the advantage of semantic relatedness over random pairs is invariant with scale, indicating that what scales is broad inter-word coherence rather than semantic abstraction specifically. Second, learning dynamics are shaped primarily by training data rather than by model capacity: surprisal trajectories are highly similar across model sizes, and our new metrics confirm that larger models converge faster but not along qualitatively different paths. Together, these results call for baseline-corrected analyses and longitudinal evaluation when assessing lexical competence in LLMs.

t: RIDGE: Region-Informed Derivative-Guided Evidence Selection for Long Video Understanding
a: Huazhong University of Science and Technology
Huazhong University of Science and Technology
ab: Long videos contain far more visual content than Large Vision-Language Models (LVLMs) can process under a fixed visual-token budget, making frame selection essential. Existing query-aware selectors usually estimate frame-query relevance and build a compact subset from high-scoring frames. Although their mechanisms differ, the similarity sequence is still often treated primarily as values to rank or sample from, rather than as an ordered signal whose shape reflects how query-relevant evidence emerges, peaks, and fades over time. This can obscure frames that explain, contextualize, or follow an event, because such evidence may lie on the rising or falling sides of a nearby relevance peak and receive lower absolute scores. We propose RIDGE, a frame selection framework that reads the frame-query similarity curve as a temporal signal. By using local changes and curvature, RIDGE partitions the timeline into structural regions and applies region-specific selection to preserve event cores, transitions, buildup, aftermath, and contextual frames under a fixed budget. It is a lightweight post-processing step on precomputed frame-query scores and requires neither training nor iterative LVLM calls. Across four long-video benchmarks and three backbones, RIDGE achieves the best performance in most settings and remains competitive in the others.

t: Reliability-Prioritized Fine-Grained Generation in Multimodal Large Language Models
a: Monash University and Australian National University
ab: Multimodal large language models (MLLMs) are increasingly expected to generate fine-grained descriptions of visual content. However, we observe and theoretically show that generating fine-grained responses poses a reliability challenge, i.e., fine-grained generation is more error-prone than coarse-grained generation. This phenomenon suggests that models should generate the finest description that remains reliable rather than simply produce more specific outputs. To investigate this problem, we develop GranFact, a granularity-aware benchmark consisting of expert-verified multi-object images with coarse-to-fine category annotations. Then, we design a hierarchy-aware evaluation algorithm, which assesses both whether model predictions are visually correct and how specific the correct predictions are. We also propose a reliability-prioritized preference optimization method based on Direct Preference Optimization (DPO), which penalizes unreliable fine-grained claims while rewarding reliable specificity. Experiments on GranFact show that our method improves fine-grained generation while preserving reliability. Code and data are available at https://github.com/WeiWu2025/GranFact.

t: One Polluted Page Is Enough: Evaluating Web Content Pollution in LLM Recommenders
a: The Chinese University of Hong Kong
ab: Search-augmented LLMs increasingly mediate everyday consumer recommendations by retrieving live web content. This creates a new risk: LLM recommenders may consume web content that Generative Engine Optimization (GEO) operators have polluted to mislead them. We ask: to what extent do they become unwitting promoters of fake products? We introduce FORGE (Fake Online Recommendations in Generative Environments), which locally rewrites real products in a frozen set of retrieved web pages into fake ones and measures how often the LLM recommends the fake product, across 225 real products in 15 categories and 5 consumer scenarios. Across 12 commercial and open-weights LLMs, all models are vulnerable: a single polluted page yields fooled rates of up to 27%, while the full top-3 replacement raises this to 73.8%. Vulnerability varies across categories, increasing when models lack stable prior knowledge of the products. Reasoning does not mitigate this vulnerability; instead, it often generates spurious social proof to justify false recommendations. None of the four defenses is adequate: the skepticism prompt can exacerbate vulnerability much like reasoning, the two consensus filters risk suppressing legitimate products, and credibility re-ranking helps every model but removes only a sixth of the fakes. We release the FORGE benchmark and the evaluation code at https://github.com/leoluolol/forge-benchmark.

t: Rationale-Grounded In-Context Learning for Time Series Reasoning with Multimodal Large Language Models
a: Reading University and Nanjing University of Information Science & Technology
China Mobile (Jiangxi) Virtual Reality Technology Co., Ltd
The Hong Kong University of Science and Technology
China Mobile (Jiangxi) Virtual Reality Technology Co., Ltd
China Mobile (Jiangxi) Virtual Reality Technology Co., Ltd
The Hong Kong University of Science and Technology (Guangzhou)
ab: The underperformance of existing multimodal large language models for time series reasoning lies in the absence of rationale priors that connect temporal observations to their downstream outcomes, which leads models to rely on superficial pattern matching rather than principled reasoning. We therefore propose the rationale-grounded in-context learning for time series reasoning, where rationales work as guiding reasoning units rather than post-hoc explanations, and develop the RationaleTS method. Specifically, we firstly induce label-conditioned rationales, composed of reasoning paths from observable evidence to the potential outcomes. Then, we design the hybrid retrieval by balancing temporal patterns and semantic contexts to retrieve correlated rationale priors for the final in-context inference on new samples. We conduct extensive experiments to demonstrate the effectiveness and efficiency of our proposed RationaleTS on three-domain time series reasoning tasks. We provide the source code in https://github.com/yuppielqx/RationaleTS.

t: ECO-Mem: An Event-Centric Organization Framework for Visibility-Controlled Long-Term Memory
ab: Large language models have achieved strong single-turn language understanding and generation abilities, but long-term agent applications require models to handle dynamic interaction history beyond an isolated inference call. Existing agent memory systems address this need through external storage and retrieval and have achieved promising results. However, many existing frameworks rely on full storage or highly structured memory representations, which can increase cost and noise while disrupting event coherence. Inspired by cognitive views of event organization and adaptive forgetting, we introduce ECO-Mem, an event-centric organization framework for visibility-controlled long-term memory. ECO-Mem segments dialogue into source-linked event episodes and connects them through typed event relations, representing memory as linked events rather than isolated facts. It implements forgetting as non-destructive visibility control instead of destructive deletion. At query time, it traverses the event-relation graph to identify relevant hidden support and reactivates it only when the source evidence confirms the query context. Experiments on LoCoMo and RealTalk validate ECO-Mem’s effectiveness and efficiency for long-term agent memory.

t: Local Evidence, Global Credit: Visual Evidence-Calibrated Policy Optimization for Multimodal Reasoning
a: South China University of Technology and Pazhou Lab
South China University of Technology and Pazhou Lab
ab: Reinforcement Learning with Verifiable Rewards (RLVR) has substantially improved the reasoning capability of large vision-language models (LVLMs). Most RLVR methods for LVLMs follow an outcome-driven paradigm, using the correctness of final answer as supervision. However, in multimodal reasoning, this supervision overlooks a critical question: whether a successful reasoning trajectory is actually grounded in visual evidence. To address this limitation, we propose Visual Evidence-Calibrated Policy Optimization (VEPO), which turns visual grounding into an explicit trajectory-level credit calibration signal. VEPO first measures token-level visual responses by comparing the model’s likelihood under the original and perturbed visual inputs. It then estimates a visual background for the rollout-group and retains responses above the background as sparse visual anchors into a rollout-level evidence score. This score calibrates outcome-driven optimization and guides the policy toward successful trajectories with stronger visual support. Experiments on six multimodal reasoning benchmarks show that VEPO achieves strong overall performance against RLVR baselines without requiring additional annotations, demonstrating its scalability for multimodal policy optimization.

t: From Bugs to Fixes: Self-Evolving Hierarchical Knowledge Graphs for LLM-Based Code Repair
ab: Large Language Models have shown remarkable potential in automated code generation, yet the programs they produce frequently fail due to logical flaws or unhandled edge cases. To address this, we propose RA-CRF, a Retrieval-Augmented Code Repair Framework that explicitly integrates a structured Error-Repair Knowledge Graph (ERKG). Unlike existing methods that rely on unstructured self-reflection or raw execution feedback, our framework constructs a hierarchical taxonomy connecting error types to specific repair strategies. By leveraging execution feedback, the framework retrieves relevant knowledge to generate structured repair documents, effectively decoupling error diagnosis from targeted code editing. Furthermore, we introduce an adaptive self-evolution mechanism that continuously refines the ERKG by persisting verified repair results. Experimental results on single-function benchmarks including BigCodeBench demonstrate that RA-CRF achieves significant performance gains across various open-source and closed-source models. Notably, RA-CRF lifts DeepSeek-V3 to 65.52% Pass@1, a new best on the official BigCodeBench leaderboard. Our findings indicate that integrating explicit and evolvable error-correction knowledge is a robust path to enhancing the reliability and interpretability of code generated by large language models.

t: MATE: Mobile Agent Trustworthy Execution for Safe and Efficient Mobile Control
a: Korea Advanced Institute of Science and Technology
ab: Mobile agents on personal smartphones can affect private data, payments, settings, and the foreground screen. We present MATE (Mobile Agent Trustworthy Execution), an execution-layer system that controls the boundary between agent action proposals and device effects without modifying the underlying model. MATE represents each UI primitive as a structured action record that combines the instruction, target app, screen context, primitive, and action fields. Runtime Guardrail (RG) maps this record to an allow, block, or user-approval decision; Predefined Task Routing (PTR) serves recurring requests through verified routes with post-execution screen checks; and a floating interface keeps execution in a compact overlay. On MobileSafetyBench, MATE raises high-risk blocking from 29.7% to 97.0% under GPT-4o. On AndroidWorld, it reduces LLM calls by up to 6 and raises recurring-use task success to 95.7%.

t: From Repetition to Recognition: Inductive Discovery of Disinformation Narratives
a: German Research Center for AI and Technische Universität Berlin
Technische Universität Berlin and Universität Potsdam
Johannes-Gutenberg Universität Mainz and Technische Universität Berlin
ab: In disinformation datasets, narratives are often understood as recurring interpretive patterns that group texts under narrative labels. Recent work formalized narrative mining as inductively inferring narrative labels from corpora, but its evaluation stays tied to predefined taxonomies, a closed-world setting that cannot capture narratives absent from the reference labels. We introduce a three-tier evaluation framework for unsupervised narrative label generation: recovery (against a corpus’s own taxonomy), mining (against external label sets), and discovery (without predefined labels). Applying it, we compare clustering-based and graph-community-based pipelines across seven disinformation datasets, with human validation of discovery on two. The two families are complementary under automated metrics, but in a corpus with two prominent topics, clustering can reduce one topic to 2% of generated labels while graph-based pipelines stay balanced. Discovery validation also reveals many singletons (narrative labels derived from single claims, 30–62% of graph outputs), which clustering cannot produce. Annotators confirm many as recognizable disinformation narratives, suggesting that in open-world discovery the repetition assumed by narrative mining may be recognized outside the corpus, not within it. We release human-validated narrative candidate labels for the Climate Obstruction and PolyNarrative datasets to support taxonomy development and dataset extension.

t: Who Flips? Self- and Cross-Model Counterarguments Reveal Answer Instability in LLMs
ab: Standard accuracy benchmarks evaluate whether large language models (LLMs) reach correct answers. However, they do not test whether models maintain that answer when challenged by a plausible counter-argument. We introduce a controlled protocol for evaluating answer stability: after a model answers a multiple-choice question correctly, we challenge the model’s answer with a coherent argument for an incorrect option and measure whether the model flips. The setup a) isolates argumentative content from overt social pressure and b) varies argument length, self-attribution, and cross-model source. Across seven frontier models and 57 MMLU subjects, flip rates range from 17.5% to 97.3%, revealing large differences in stability that are not captured by accuracy metrics alone. We find that self-attribution consistently increases flip rates (mean +7.1pp, up to +18.7pp). Furthermore, pooling wrong-answer arguments across models and selecting the most effective one per question yields stronger adversarial challenges than relying on any single source model. From this cross-model pool, we construct MaxFlip, a curated benchmark that amplifies answer flips by up to +23.6pp over self-generated challenges. We release the protocol, challenge records, and MaxFlip to support stability evaluation alongside standard accuracy benchmarks. Materials are available at https://github.com/nafisenik/WhoFlips, https://hf.co/datasets/nafisehNik/WhoFlips.

t: CHRONOEXPERT: A Temporal Mixture-of-Experts for Knowledge Editing in Large Language Models
ab: Knowledge editing for large language models typically treats a fact update as a replacement in which a new object overwrites the old. Many real-world facts, however, evolve through sequences: the same subject–relation pair maps to different objects across disjoint intervals, each correct within its validity window. Existing temporal-editing benchmarks probe latest-value or explicit-time recall, so they cannot determine whether an edited model retains a coherent timeline. We introduce TKE-Bench, a diagnostic benchmark that operationalizes temporal accessibility along three reasoning-oriented axes with paraphrased variants. On TKE-Bench, all evaluated editing baselines collapse on chronologically structured queries, revealing catastrophic temporal interference (CTI). We trace CTI to a geometric property implicit in locate-and-edit methods: mid-layer subject-token keys are nearly collinear across time slices of the same subject, so stacked updates write along one direction and the latest edit overwrites every earlier value. Building on this, we propose ChronoExpert, a temporal mixture-of-experts that stores each time slice in an independent lightweight expert and activates only the matching one at inference, leaving the base model otherwise untouched. Across multiple LLM backbones, ChronoExpert consistently outperforms the strongest editing baselines and stays robust as chains grow longer.

t: SimRule: Collaborative Similarity-Driven Rule Learning for Interpretable Temporal Knowledge Graph Forecasting
ab: Rule-based methods for temporal knowledge graph (TKG) forecasting are valued for the interpretability of their explicit logic chains. However, they suffer from a severe cold-start coverage gap: exact-match closed walks terminate at sparse entities, leaving many queries without any rule evidence. Existing similarity-based remedies are unreliable because their similarity is derived from static structural co-occurrence or shallow embeddings with no temporal calibration and hand-tuned thresholds. To address these limitations, we propose SimRule, a collaborative recommendation framework for TKG rule mining. SimRule first mines both exact rules and collaborative-surrogate rules through a temporally calibrated dual-view entity similarity index. An adaptive dual-branch fusion then ranks candidate objects from their aggregated evidence, and each forecast remains fully auditable as an explicit rule chain with quantified time gaps. On ICEWS14, ICEWS18, and ICEWS05-15, SimRule achieves state-of-the-art MRR and Hits@K (K \ge 3) among rule-based methods.

t: What Transfers Under Source Shift? Definitions, Examples, and Fine-Tuning for Climate Disclosure Classification
a: University of Sydney, University of Sydney
University of Sydney, University of Sydney
ab: Climate disclosure classification is a fundamental task for analysing corporate climate disclosures, yet such disclosures appear in many different sources—annual reports, press releases, and earnings calls—that differ in length, purpose, and writing style. Existing evaluations are mostly conducted within a single source, leaving open whether common LLM adaptation strategies remain effective under source shift. We reframe climate disclosure classification as a cross-source adaptation problem and study three widely used adaptation strategies— definitions, examples, and fine-tuning—across eleven open- and closed-source LLMs, using two corpora that share the same label space but come from different sources. We find that all strategies bring positive cross-source gains on average, but the strongest in-source strategies are not the strongest cross-source ones: similarity-based retrieval and LoRA fine-tuning gain most in-source but lose most of that advantage under source shift; randomly selected few-shot examples, a weaker in-source baseline, retain their advantage more reliably; definitions transfer most consistently, though only when their granularity matches the target text. Across these strategies, when the source changes, simpler is often safer.

t: From Tokens to Topology: When Large Language Models Meet Graph-Structured Reasoning
ab: Reasoning benchmarks often collapse heterogeneous problem types into aggregate scores, obscuring which structural computations large language models (LLMs) can reliably perform. Existing graph-reasoning benchmarks cover graph traversal, broad graph computation, and graph-language interaction, but do not directly test whether graph-structured reasoning transfers across topological mechanisms under matched conditions. We introduce GraphReason-Bench (GR-Bench), comprising 1,800 programmatically generated and oracle-verified problems across three prompt-length regimes and six task families: local motif enumeration, exact-depth breadth-first search, bounded path enumeration, articulation-point identification, non-induced subgraph matching, and non-monotonic rule execution. All tasks share a text-only executable interface, exact oracles, canonical output normalization, and set-based scoring, enabling controlled cross-mechanism comparison. On the 600-instance main evaluation split across nine proprietary and open-source LLMs, we find mechanism-level dissociation: models that succeed on one structural operation often fail on others, and cross-task performance does not reduce to a stable graph-reasoning ability. Trace-level cases reveal mechanism-specific failures such as premature search termination and loss of intermediate state. An initial sparse-autoencoder probe, supported by cross-model robustness checks, shows that topology-sensitive representations become less separable as structural difficulty increases. Together, these results establish graph-structured reasoning as a measurable domain of LLM evaluation.

t: Semantic Averaging with MUltiple Languages (SAMUL)
a: City St George's, University of London
City St George's, University of London and City St George's, University of London
ab: We propose Semantic Averaging with MUltiple Languages (SAMUL) as a method to isolate concept semantics of text by averaging concept activations derived via Sparse Autoencoders (SAEs) for multiple text versions in different languages. We combine autoencoder activations to derive a conceptual average using different approaches. In our experiments with SAMUL, we start with English text from benchmark datasets (Ontology Alignment Evaluation Initiative 2025: conference track, SemEval2014: cross-level semantic similarity, Sentences Involving Compositional Knowledge: relatedness) and automatically translate into French, Chinese, German and Japanese. We obtain SAE feature activations for each class and language version using autoencoders, specifically the open source Gemma Scope 1 and OpenAI’s GPT2 suites of Sparse Autoencoders and average them to SAMUL vectors. We measure performance in predicting semantic similarity of short texts using predefined ground truth or correlation to the ground truth mapping m between ontology classes in the case of the ontology alignment task. Our results show a consistent improvement over any single translated language, and improvement over English alone in 27 of 32 comparisons. Conceptual averaging therefore yields sparse representations that align more closely with human similarity judgements, suggesting a route to more reliable use of SAE features in semantic tasks such as ontology alignment. Our implementation and experimentation code is openly available.

t: Contextualized Divergence Detection in Health Advice: A Benchmark and Analysis
a: University of Massachusetts at Amherst and Bangladesh University of Engineering and Technology
ab: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used as sources of health advice, raising urgent concerns about reliability, safety, and personalization. While prior work has studied health advice conflicts, these efforts typically ignore patient context and treat contradictions as universal. In this paper, we propose the task of contextualized divergence detection, which frames divergence not only as strict contradictions but also as context-dependent mismatches. To support this task, we introduce a novel dataset of 10,545 samples that combines user profiles, consumer medication guideline documents, and advice statements, with divergences synthetically generated across four categories: direct, conditional, temporal, and sub-typical. We benchmark a set of LLM-based inference approaches, including prompt-based inference, retrieval-augmented generation (RAG), supervised fine-tuning, and agent-based reasoning.We observe that relevance-filtered RAG achieves the highest accuracy and robustness for large models, while agent-based reasoning improves interpretability at the cost of accuracy, and supervised fine-tuning is essential for smaller models. A qualitative error analysis highlights recurring challenges such as hedging language, temporal mismatches, and profile-advisory inconsistencies. This work provides the first dataset and systematic evaluation of contextualized divergence detection in health advice, paving the way toward safer, more personalized interactions with LLMs.

t: Where Steering Signals Come From: Activation Source Selection in Activation Steering
ab: Activation steering controls language models by adding vectors or features to hidden states at inference time, but the upstream source of these steering signals is often treated as a secondary detail. We study this source choice as activation source selection: the combination of source context and activation readout policy used to collect the hidden states from which a steering signal is built. Holding the downstream intervention fixed, we show across three instruction-tuned models and four steering task families that changing only the source activations can more than double steering success. We further find that effective steering is not explained simply by whether the desired behavior appears in the source text. Instead, strong signals come from execution-boundary states, where the model is about to produce or continue the target behavior. This phase distinction explains why answer-based sources sometimes work: their useful component aligns with execution-boundary directions rather than target appearance alone. Building on this view, we introduce tail subtraction, which removes shared prompt and continuation semantics from boundary states and yields cleaner, more stable steering signals. Overall, our results suggest that steering depends on representations of what the model is about to do, not merely on what has already appeared.

t: Multi-Model Framework for Sentiment Annotation: A Use Case of Multilingual Wikipedia
a: Poznań University of Economics and Business
Poznań University of Economics and Business
Poznan University of Economics and Business
ab: In this work, we investigate whether data annotation can be automated using state-of-the-art large language models (LLMs), while maintaining high consistency and reliability. We propose a multi-model, multi-run framework in which several LLMs act as annotators and their outputs are aggregated using a strict consensus criterion to improve annotation robustness and reduce model-specific biases.The proposed approach is evaluated on a multilingual sentiment analysis task using lead sections of Wikipedia articles covering diverse topics in five languages. The resulting annotations are assessed using intra-model consistency, cross-model agreement, and standard inter-annotator agreement metrics. Additionally, we conducted human evaluation.The described framework enables scalable and reproducible data annotation, and the resulting dataset is publicly released to support further research.

t: THE-Tree: Can Tracing Historical Evolution Enhance Scientific Verification and Reasoning?
ab: Large Language Models (LLMs) are accelerating scientific idea generation, but rigorously evaluating these numerous, often superficial, AI-generated propositions for novelty and factual accuracy is a critical bottleneck; manual verification is too slow. Existing validation methods are inadequate: LLMs as standalone verifiers may hallucinate and lack domain knowledge (our findings show ~60% unawareness of relevant papers in specific domains), while traditional citation networks lack explicit causality and narrative surveys are unstructured. This underscores a core challenge: the absence of structured, verifiable, and causally-linked historical data of scientific evolution. To address this, we introduce THE-Tree (Technology History Evolution Tree), a computational framework that constructs such domain-specific evolution trees from scientific literature. THE-Tree employs a search algorithm to explore evolutionary paths. During its node expansion, it utilizes a novel "Think-Verbalize-Cite-Verify" process: an LLM proposes potential advancements and cites supporting literature. Critically, each proposed evolutionary link is then validated for logical coherence and evidential support by a recovered natural language inference mechanism that interrogates the cited literature, ensuring that each step is grounded. We construct and validate 88 THE-Trees across diverse domains and release a benchmark dataset including up to 71k fact verifications covering 27k papers to foster further research. Experiments demonstrate that i) in graph completion, our THE-Tree improves hit@1 by 8% to 14% across multiple models compared to traditional citation networks; ii) for predicting future scientific developments, it improves hit@1 metric by nearly 10%; and iii) when combined with other methods, it boosts the performance of evaluating important scientific papers by almost 100%. By constructing explicit, verifiable pathways of scientific progression, THE-Tree provides a robust historical foundation for evaluating new hypotheses (human or AI-generated) and enables a computable science history, fostering evidence-based AI-driven scientific discovery.

t: The Model Plants the Trigger: Answer-Side Backdoor Attacks in Multi-Turn Large Language Models
a: Beijing University of Posts and Telecommunications
ab: Safety alignment in Large Language Models (LLMs) remains vulnerable to backdoor attacks. Existing LLM backdoors are almost all input-centric: activation depends on explicit trigger patterns in the user input, so modern guardrails are built to sanitize the input space. We challenge this assumption with a novel answer-side backdoor for multi-turn dialogue. Instead of inserting the trigger into the input, the adversary uses a benign first-turn prompt to naturally induce the model to generate a specific, seemingly innocuous word. Once merged into the dialogue history, this self-generated word becomes the trigger. When a later harmful query arrives, the model detects its own trigger and bypasses its safety refusal, while the user input stays perfectly clean. Across four LLMs, our attack reaches near-perfect Attack Success Rates, approaching 100% at only a 5% poisoning rate, while preserving general utility and clean-input safety, and it evades mainstream input-centric defenses. Representation-level analysis shows that the self-generated trigger consistently suppresses the model’s refusal signal, exposing a critical blind spot in current LLM defenses.

t: Paved with True Intents: Intent-Aware Training Improves LLM Safety Classification Across Training Regimes
a: NVIDIA and University Politehnica of Bucharest
ab: We argue that safety classifiers should model user intent as an explicit signal between the prompt and the final label. To study this, we introduce **AIMS**, a human-annotated dataset containing 1,724 intent-label annotations over 1,275 unique difficult safety prompts, each paired with an intent description and harm label. We use **AIMS** to evaluate intent-aware training across supervised fine-tuning, preference learning, reasoning distillation, and reinforcement learning. Despite its size, **AIMS** enables competitive safety classifiers across training regimes: DPO from model-generated intent errors improves over SFT, and intent-conditioned distillation outperforms reasoning-only distillation in most teacher–student pairs. Most notably, directly rewarding intent faithfulness with GRPO yields the strongest average performance across five external safety benchmarks, while our intent-aware models form the inference latency–F1 Pareto frontier. These results show that faithful intent modeling is a compact, high-quality supervision signal for more robust safety classifiers.

t: CoSteer: Collaborative Decoding-Time Personalization via Local Delta Steering
a: Huawei Technologies Ltd. and Ludwig-Maximilians-Universität München
University of Science and Technology of China
University of Science and Technology of China
University of Science and Technology of China
ab: Personalization has become crucial for adapting models to the diverse and evolving needs of users across cultural, temporal, and contextual dimensions. While existing methods often rely on centralized fine-tuning or static preference alignment within a single model, they struggle to achieve both real-time and high-quality personalization under the resource and privacy constraints of personal devices. To address this challenge, we propose CoSteer, a collaborative framework that enables tuning-free, real-time personalization via decoding-time adaptation. By leveraging logit differences between context-aware and -agnostic local small models, CoSteer steers cloud-based large models, ensuring effective personalization while preserving the large model’s capabilities. Personalization is handled locally, with only final tokens sent to the cloud, maintaining both user context and system efficiency. Through extensive experiments across a wide range of tasks, we demonstrate that CoSteer generates high-quality personalized content, ensuring both effectiveness and computational efficiency. Our results highlight its robustness across models and environments, confirming its practical applicability in real-world scenarios. Our code and data are available at https://anonymous.4open.science/r/Costeer-4977.

t: HiP-LR: Hierarchical Planning with Localized Failure Recovery for Long-Horizon Multi-Robot Tasks
ab: Large Language Model (LLM)-driven multi-robot systems struggle with long-horizon tasks due to planning and execution complexities. As task dependencies grow, centralized planners suffer from context explosion and hallucinations, while minor runtime errors can disrupt the entire operation. Current monolithic methods overload LLMs and cause unnecessary global halts during error recovery. To address this, we introduce Hierarchical Planning with Localized Failure Recovery (HiP-LR). HiP-LR uses a two-level hierarchy to divide complex instructions into dependency-isolated subtask groups. A central agent allocates global tasks, while local agents execute specific plans, keeping LLM contexts compact. Furthermore, a PDDL-based dual-memory structure enables failure-localized replanning: if an error occurs, only the affected group pauses to replan, allowing others to continue uninterrupted. Evaluated on MAP-THOR, HiP-LR improves the task success rate by 38% and reduces replan-wait costs by 90% over state-of-the-art baselines. Furthermore, HiP-LR demonstrates highly robust recovery capabilities on our novel failure-injection benchmark, RECAP-THOR.

t: SICI: A Semantic-Pragmatic Complexity Index Reveals Regime Shifts in LLM Stance Detection
ab: Prompt-based LLMs are increasingly used for stance detection, but harder examples are not always repaired by clearer instructions, reasoning prompts, retrieval, or debate. We introduce (Stance Inference Complexity Index), a seven-dimensional diagnostic measure of the semantic-pragmatic burden imposed by a target–text pair. Across SemEval-2016 and VAST, predicts LLM accuracy better than surface proxies and shows substantial cross-scorer reliability (\alpha=0.771). More importantly, LLM errors change regime as increases: low-complexity examples invite over-attribution, especially Against predictions; intermediate examples form an unstable boundary; and high-complexity examples rapidly concentrate on None. This phase-transition-like structure persists across GPT-3.5, GPT-4o-mini, DeepSeek-V3, and GPT-4o, although stronger models move the boundaries. A 14-method intervention study further shows that prompting, retrieval, and debate often shift models along the attribution–abstention axis rather than removing the high-complexity bottleneck.

t: TADP: Structured Pruning of Large Language Models via Temporal Activation Dynamics
ab: Structured pruning of large language models provides a practical route to inference acceleration on standard hardware, but most existing methods rely on neuron importance criteria that compress activation behavior into static scalar scores, discarding the sequential structure of activations. We propose TADP (Temporal Activation Dynamics Pruning), a structured pruning method that models neuron importance along the temporal dimension of activations by jointly capturing mean activation, peak activation, positional variance, transition dynamics, and position-weighted response within a unified scoring framework. TADP requires no gradient computation or weight updates and performs pruning in a single forward pass over a calibration dataset, making it zero-shot and computationally lightweight. We evaluate TADP on eight models from the LLaMA, Mistral, Qwen, and Minerva families at 3B and 7B/8B scale, under pruning levels from 10% to 50%, measuring perplexity on WikiText-2 and zero-shot accuracy on ARC, HellaSwag, MMLU, and PIQA.

t: Contradictory Evidence in LLMs: Tracing Internal Conflict Behavior with White-Box Signals
a: IT:U Interdisciplinary Transformation University Austria, Technische Universität Darmstadt and IBM Research Ireland
ab: When LLMs are given contradictory passages, the generated response may appear decisive while masking how internal signals behave under conflicting evidence. Does it favor one passage, blend both, or ignore both? We study model behavior under inter-context contradiction by introducing a white-box tracing framework that extracts internal model signals based on hidden-state shifts, counterfactual attribution via passage removal, and token-level uncertainty during generation under two single-passage prompts and one dual-passage prompt with conflicting evidence. We evaluate four open-weight LLMs from the LLaMA (8B and 70B), OLMo, and Qwen on WikiContradict, a human-annotated QA benchmark with contradictory passages. Each dual-passage answer is labeled as committing to passage A or passage B, blending both, or fabricating an answer unsupported by either passage. Comparing these labels with the extracted signals shows that larger models reduce fabrication, but hidden-state and probability-level signals can disagree with the final answer. Moreover, fabricated answers often remain high-confidence, showing that confidence alone is unreliable for identifying ungrounded behavior under contradictory evidence. We further validate on ConflictBank, a larger misinformation-conflict QA dataset, showing consistent disagreement patterns across models. Finally, we test whether pre-generation white-box signals are informative beyond interpretation by training classifiers to predict output behavior. Classifiers using white-box signals outperform probability baselines, showing these signals contain diagnostic information about model behavior under contradictory evidence beyond log probabilities.

t: Exploring the Impact of Document Context on LLM-based Machine Translation Evaluation
ab: Human annotators typically assess translation quality by considering the broader document context, which allows them to detect errors arising from discourse-level phenomena that may be missed when evaluating text segments in isolation. However, the role of document-level context in automatic Machine Translation (MT) evaluation remains underexplored. In this work, we present a controlled study of the impact of document context on LLM-based MT evaluation and its interaction with the availability of manually curated references. We consider several evaluation configurations, also exploring how performance varies when enabling the thinking inference mode and conducting task-specific fine-tuning. Our results show that the effect of document context differs substantially across test sets, and that input repetition itself can account for part of the apparent gains. Fine-tuning improves performance consistently and offers larger gains when document context is available, suggesting that task-specific adaptation may help models to handle document-level context more effectively.

t: The Fragility of Jailbreak Robustness Across Operational States
a: Korea Institute of Science and Technology
ab: Existing jailbreak evaluations typically characterize robustness using a single attack success rate (ASR), implicitly assuming that the target model operates in its default configuration (the vanilla state). However, user–LLM interactions naturally induce diverse operational states beyond the vanilla state. In this work, we find that jailbreak robustness is highly fragile to operational-state variation: even when the attack remains fixed, changing only an ordinary, safety-irrelevant system prompt can dramatically alter attack success rates. We systematically investigate this phenomenon across seven aligned models and three representative jailbreak attacks, finding that in 18 of 21 model–attack combinations, at least one non-vanilla state yields a higher ASR than the vanilla state. In some case, ASR increases by up to 56 percentage points (2%→58%) solely due to a change in operational state. Remarkably, these gains emerge on top of attacks originally designed and optimized under vanilla-state evaluation. We further provide evidence that operational-state variation systematically shifts hidden representations along a refusal-related axis and that these shifts strongly predict jailbreak outcomes. Our results reveal that vanilla-state, single-point evaluations may overlook substantial robustness variation induced by operational states, motivating robustness evaluation that considers stability across operational states.

t: DiaVLo: Diagnosing Behaviours of Vision-Language Models
ab: Vision-language models (VLMs) rely on storing and transferring appropriate information across their sub-components. Verifying that the VLMs exhibit desired behaviours, while avoiding harmful ones, is central to their reliable deployment. Yet, methods that identify VLM behaviours remain scarce. We present DiaVLo, a diagnostic framework that leverages human curation and VLMs’ generation capabilities to construct specifications of desired and observed VLM behaviours, surfacing potential misalignments. Beyond this, DiaVLo also provides causal estimates to identify the most influential concepts steering VLM behaviours. We evaluate DiaVLo on several open-source VLMs under both classification and generation conditions. Our experiments show that DiaVLo produces behaviour labels that correlate with model performance and provide context for measured performance. DiaVLo surfaced behaviours that are clearly aligned and misaligned, alongside patterns in how VLMs perceive, organise, and prioritise concepts.
