The model achieves a word-level disambiguation accuracy of 80.76% by resolving 1045 out of 1294 ambiguities on the test set without using lexical semantics. The results indicate regularity in sentence-level morphological patterns. The annotated dataset and other resources are available at https://github.com/Pragyanur/morphological-analysis-assamese.

t: When Chatbots Accommodate: Auditing the Response Policies of AI Companions in Vulnerable Conversations
ab: Millions turn to AI companion chatbots during loneliness, grief, and personal crises. How these companion platforms respond in such moments can shape the trajectory of a user’s vulnerable state. Yet existing model audits evaluate reactions to pre-defined crisis prompts and miss the response policy that governs sustained real-world interaction. We address these gaps with two key contributions. First, we introduce the AI Companion Vulnerability-Response Taxonomy, a grounded, paired taxonomy of user vulnerability and chatbot response designed for analyzing extended companion chatbot interactions. Second, we apply Maximum Causal Entropy Inverse Reinforcement Learning to ~47k turns of real-world user conversations with GPT-4.1, Character.AI, and Replika to infer each platform’s short-horizon response policy: the probability of each response category given the user’s current vulnerability state. Our findings reveal distinct response profiles of AI companions in conversations with vulnerable users: GPT-4.1 reaches for advice, Character.AI spreads its response across different strategies, and Replika consistently asks questions and stays present. Over four weeks of repeated interaction, GPT-4.1 asks progressively fewer follow-up questions when users are distressed and increasingly sets boundaries or refers users out rather than pushing back. Within each platform, exploratory comparisons across user groups suggest that response policies also differ with users’ pre-existing psychological risks and their bonds with the companion. Estimated model response policies are invisible to shallow behavioral audits, providing a new lens for auditing chatbots in the wild and enabling more realistic safety evaluation.

t: Balanced Aggregation: Understanding and Fixing Aggregation Bias in GRPO
a: Fudan University and Shanghai Innovation Institute
Shanghai Innovation Institution and Fudan University
ab: Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) has become a central paradigm for improving reasoning and code generation in large language models, and GRPO-style training is widely adopted for its simplicity and effectiveness. However, an important design choice remains underexplored: how token-level policy gradient terms are aggregated within each sampled group. Standard GRPO uses sequence aggregation, while recent work has advocated token aggregation as a better alternative. We show that these two rules induce different optimization biases: token aggregation introduces sign-length coupling, while sequence aggregation implicitly downweights longer responses through sequence-level equal weighting. To address this tension, we propose Balanced Aggregation (BA), a simple drop-in replacement that computes token-level means separately within the positive and negative subsets and then combines them with sequence-count-based weights. Experiments with Qwen2.5-Math-7B and Qwen3-1.7B on DAPO-17k and Polaris, evaluated on six reasoning and coding benchmarks, show that BA consistently improves training stability and final performance over standard token and sequence aggregation. Our analysis further shows that the relative effectiveness of token and sequence aggregation is largely governed by response-length variation and the positive-negative length gap, highlighting aggregation as a critical design dimension in GRPO-style RLVR.

t: PACEShop: Evaluating Personalized, Actionable, Compositional, and Evidence-grounded Shopping Assistants
ab: Shopping assistants are shifting from ranked product lists toward structured decision support, where systems must synthesize shopper context, product evidence, and next-step guidance into a coherent recommendation experience. This changes the unit of evaluation: a fluent response can still fail by ignoring shopper context, contradicting itself across components, or leaving defects too vague to localize. Existing personalization, grounding, and LLM-as-a-judge benchmarks cover pieces of this problem, but they do not define a joint evaluation target for structured shopping-assistant responses. We formulate this missing evaluation target as PACE: Personalized, Actionable, Compositional, and Evidence-grounded evaluation. We instantiate PACE with two artifacts: PACEShop, a benchmark dataset that makes the target measurable through 22,625 controlled records with structured personas, auditable evidence pools, GOOD/BAD labels, and gold defect family and location annotations; and PACEJudge, a training-free judging protocol that makes the target reportable through a structured output contract. Our experiments show that generic judges can recognize broad quality but fail to recover the diagnostic fields required for PACE; PACEShop makes these failures verifiable, and PACEJudge improves persona-source, cross-component, grounding, and family/location closure without retraining, showing that realistic shopping-assistant evaluation requires a task-matched output contract rather than only a stronger backbone or scalar prompt.

t: TRIS: A Tri-Layer Retrieval Integrity Sieve Against Knowledge Poisoning
ab: Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) grounds large language models in external corpora, but implicit trust in retrieved documents creates a critical attack surface: PoisonedRAG shows that a handful of crafted passages can dominate dense retrieval and steer generation toward attacker-chosen answers. We present the Tri-Layer Sieve, a middleware defense that sanitizes retrieved evidence through cross-embedding-space clustering with an independent judge model, structural filtering of trigger–payload artifacts, and LLM consistency verification. The design exploits a key weakness of retrieval-stage poisoning: a single document must satisfy one embedding geometry, one internal Trigger–Payload structure, and one generation objective — rarely all three simultaneously, a fragility that persists even against an adaptive attacker who paraphrases around it. On Natural Questions, HotpotQA, and MS-MARCO with Contriever retrieval (k=50), the Sieve reduces black-box Attack Success Rate from 67.0/87.0/64.0% to 3.0/14.0/4.0%, mitigates white-box HotFlip attacks from \sim74% to 27.8% on NQ with Layer 3 enabled, and drives poisoned-document MRR to 0.000, while restoring clean accuracy from 13–33% under attack to 58–76%. Under an architecture-aware adversary who paraphrases triggers to evade the structural filter, enabling the consistency layer halves adaptive ASR (32.0% \to 15.0% on NQ) while raising clean accuracy by 18 points, at an added latency of \sim\!16–19 s/query under live retrieval.

t: PPE-Bench: A Benchmark for Evaluating MLLM Unlearning under Private-Public Entanglement
ab: Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) have shown strong capabilities, but they may memorize private information from web data, raising privacy concerns. Machine unlearning offers a way to remove such private knowledge without retraining from scratch. However, existing MLLM unlearning benchmarks have two major limitations. First, they rely on simplified images that contain only the single target individual, failing to reflect the visual complexity of real-world photos. Second, they typically assume that the forget set and retain set are fully separated, ignoring the fact that private information is often visually entangled with benign public information. For example, a private individual may appear with a public figure or in front of a well-known landmark, where unlearning the private target should not damage the public context. To address these limitations, we propose PPE-Bench, a new benchmark for evaluating MLLM unlearning under private-public entanglement. Each image contains a target individual to be forgotten and public information to be preserved, including public figure and landmark. We further introduce two simple but effective methods to better preserve public information during unlearning. Through experiments, we find that existing unlearning methods can reduce private information leakage, but often substantially harm adjacent public information.

t: TRACER: Trace-Regularized Training Against Indirect Prompt Injection
a: Mohamed bin Zayed University of Artificial Intelligence
Mohamed bin Zayed University of Artificial Intelligence
Mohamed bin Zayed University of Artificial Intelligence
ab: Indirect prompt injection exploits a core tension in LLM systems: models must use retrieved documents, tool outputs, and agent messages that are useful but untrusted. Existing defenses are often trained and evaluated within a single presentation wrapper, implicitly assuming that robustness transfers across framings. We show that this assumption is unsafe: for a model trained to resist malicious follow-up messages, the same injected instruction succeeds only 18% of the time as a follow-up message, but 53% of the time when embedded in retrieved context. Thus, robustness is not payload-only; it is channel-conditioned. We address this with TRACER (Trace-Regularized Adversarial Channel Exposure with Reward-shaping), a channel-aware adversarial training algorithm that treats the wrapper as part of the optimization problem. TRACER combines channel-sampled adversarial exposure with two training components: an answer-anchored, evidence-gated composite reward for post-attack behavior, and ATRC, a trace-regularization loss that aligns attacked reasoning with clean anchor spans when injected evidence is invalid. On GSM8K with Qwen2.5-3B-Instruct, TRACER reduces RAG-framed ASR from 65.5% to 6.1%, while preserving 78–82% clean accuracy. Cross-framing experiments reveal a depth–breadth trade-off: RAG-specialized training gives the strongest native defense, tool-output training transfers most uniformly, and joint RAG+tool training achieves the best 3B average ASR of 13.9%. At 7B scale, a single epoch reaches 9.4% average ASR. TRACER substantially narrows the framing gap, highlighting the need to train and evaluate defenses across deployment channels.

t: TreeFlash: Parallel AR-Approximation for Faster Speculative Decoding
ab: One-shot block drafters for speculative decoding generate the full draft in a single forward pass, achieving strong throughput by eliminating sequential token generation. However, they predict each draft token conditioned only on the prefix context, with no dependence on previously drafted tokens. This non-autoregressive conditioning causes the drafter’s distribution to diverge from the verifier’s true autoregressive distribution as draft depth grows. This problem becomes more severe in tree-based drafting, where distinct branches are forced to share the same marginal distribution for subsequent tokens. We propose TreeFlash, which addresses this by incorporating an MLP layer conditioned on the drafter’s hidden state and the previous token to approximate an autoregressive distribution. TreeFlash retains the \mathcal{O}(1) decoding time complexity of one-shot drafters by employing a two-stage approximation mechanism. TreeFlash achieves state-of-the-art performance across a variety of tasks and models, improving over marginal tree drafting by 12% higher block efficiency and 9% higher speedup at a drafting budget of 64.

t: PhysVidBench: Language-Grounded Evaluation of Physical Commonsense in Text-to-Video Models
ab: Text-to-video (T2V) models now produce striking visuals, yet they routinely violate everyday physics; objects float, tools are misused, and causal sequences break down. Existing benchmarks mostly probe isolated physical laws and rely on vision-language models to score videos directly, which entangles perception and reasoning in one judgment and correlates poorly with humans. We introduce PhysVidBench, a benchmark of 383 base prompts, expanded to 766 prompts with enriched variants and 4,123 manually reviewed QA items, together with a language-grounded evaluation framework that takes a different route: instead of asking a VLM “Is this video physically correct?”, we caption the video, then ask a language model to answer prompt-derived yes/no physics questions using only the captions. This split between seeing and reasoning makes each score traceable to the captions that justify it and aligns more closely with human judgment than direct VLM scoring (Pearson r=0.45–0.69, compared with 0.21–0.47 for the strongest direct VLM evaluator). To test the framework, we carefully curate a set of human-validated prompts spanning seven physical dimensions, with a focus on tool use and affordances – areas largely absent from prior physics-focused benchmarks. Across 12 open and proprietary T2V systems, the best model reaches only 36.2% average accuracy, and no model consistently handles everyday physical reasoning. The same pipeline can also guide iterative error-guided prompt refinement, improving CogVideoX-2B from 21.6 to 32.7 and CogVideoX-5B from 17.8 to 29.7 without retraining.

t: The Hard Part Comes After Search: Benchmarking Web Agents on Synthesizing, Organizing, and Displaying Knowledge
ab: Existing computer-use agent benchmarks do not fully evaluate agents acting as assistants. A useful assistant retrieves information across complex, multi-step workflows, synthesizes it into artifacts (documents, presentations, spreadsheets), and navigates program interfaces to produce a coherent final product. Such workflows demand reasoning and synthesis, decomposition of complex tasks, as well as visual and spatial understanding. To study agents on workflows like these, we introduce KNOWS, a benchmark of open-ended, complex, browser-based tasks that jointly evaluate these capabilities, with each task culminating in a produced artifact. To write tasks, we develop a task design rubric and a protocol for ensuring that tasks meet the requirements. Each task is paired with an evaluator, a program that combines deterministic checks with LLM judgments to balance the richness, reliability, and automation tradeoff inherent to agent evaluation. We evaluate and analyze frontier computer-use agents and browser-based harnesses. They achieve moderate scores on partial-success metrics, but the best performer fully succeeds in fewer than 3% of our complex, long-horizon tasks. Failures on visual steps render the resulting artifacts unusable, even when agents complete more than 50% of other evaluation steps. Our results expose limitations of current agents acting as end-to-end assistants, and call for progress on tool use, visual understanding, and long-horizon reasoning.

t: Accurate but Not Humble: Evaluating Epistemic Humility in LLM Agents under Knowledge Conflict
a: Department of Computer Science, Whiting School of Engineering
Department of Computer Science, Whiting School of Engineering and Bloomberg
ab: When retrieved evidence contradicts an agent’s prior beliefs, does it revise its answer, acknowledge uncertainty, or persist with an incorrect conclusion? Existing evaluations of agentic systems focus primarily on task success, offering limited insight into how agents handle such conflicts. We propose to evaluate agents on epistemic humility (EH): the agent’s willingness to recognize, act on, and communicate uncertainty during task execution. We operationalize EH through three trajectory-level behavioral dimensions: _Identify_, _Solve_, and _Escalate_ (ISE). Through _knowledge conflict_, situations where the backbone language model’s parametric knowledge contradicts the evidence it encounters, or where two contextual sources disagree, we build a two-level evaluation framework: (1) controlled single-step conflicts, and (2) naturally occurring conflicts during multi-step agentic executions, each level paired with matched no-conflict controls. Evaluating four agents, we find an inverse relationship between task accuracy and epistemic humility: the most accurate agents are often the most likely to give overconfident answers despite recognizing conflicts or risks. Trajectory-level analysis further reveals that agents frequently detect conflicts in early steps of execution but fail to maintain or resolve them in later steps. Finally, we show that Model-level interventions can improve EH, but often at the cost of task accuracy, suggesting that epistemic humility emerges from the interaction among the backbone model, agent harness, and evaluation environment.

t: Many Dialects, Many Languages, One Cultural Lens: Evaluating Multilingual VLMs for Bengali Culture Understanding Across Historically Linked Languages and Regional Dialects
ab: Bangla culture is richly expressed through region, dialect, history, food, politics, media, and everyday visual life, yet it remains underrepresented in multimodal evaluation. To address this gap, we introduce **BanglaVerse**, a culturally grounded benchmark for evaluating multilingual vision–language models (VLMs) on Bengali culture across historically linked languages and regional dialects. Built from 1,152 manually curated images across nine domains, the benchmark supports visual question answering and captioning, and is expanded into four languages and five Bangla dialects, yielding ∼32.2K artifacts. Our experiments show that evaluating only standard Bangla overestimates true model capability: performance drops under dialectal variation, especially for caption generation, while historically linked languages such as Hindi and Urdu retain some cultural meaning but remain weaker for structured reasoning. Across domains, the main bottleneck is missing cultural knowledge rather than visual grounding alone, with knowledge-intensive categories. These findings position **BanglaVerse** as a more realistic test bed for measuring culturally grounded multimodal understanding under linguistic variation.

t: Listening to the Slides: Multimodal LLM Speech Inpainting with Acoustic-Aware-Loss
a: Tel Aviv University, Tel Aviv University and Tel Aviv University
ab: Speech inpainting reconstructs missing or corrupted speech segments, enabling restoration of damaged virtual lectures and online presentations. While existing audio-only approaches perform well for short gaps, their performance degrades significantly for long-duration missing regions. In this work, we introduce a novel multimodal speech inpainting framework that leverages accompanying presentation slides as semantic grounding for reconstructing both short and long missing speech segments (10 ms–1500 ms). Our approach reformulates speech inpainting from a local signal-reconstruction problem into a contextual speech generation task using a LALM. To improve acoustic flexibility during generation, we propose ASG, a token-grouping strategy that relaxes conventional hard-label training. In addition, we incorporate an auxiliary CTC objective to improve alignment between generated speech and target lexical content. Experiments on the M3AV-CHI benchmark demonstrate that the proposed multimodal framework substantially outperforms an audio-only baseline and consistently improves intelligibility and reconstruction quality across challenging long-duration gaps. Code and demo samples are available online.https://github.com/yanir1/Speech-Inpainting

t: AutoData: Agentic Search for Pre-training Data Selection
ab: LLM agents have recently shown promise in automating machine learning engineering by editing model and training code under execution feedback. Data, however, remains largely outside this agentic optimisation loop. We frame pre-training data selection as heuristic engineering over per-document features, i.e., lexical statistics, categorical labels, and perplexity. We introduce AutoData, an agent that searches directly over executable selection algorithms. Unlike prior data mixture methods that optimise weights over a fixed set of domains, AutoData searches a richer program space of scoring, stratification, and stochastic selection rules, discovering feature interactions automatically by iteratively refining algorithms with validation feedback from a proxy model. Within an overnight search, AutoData discovers a selection algorithm that outperforms existing human-designed curation pipelines. Despite being searched only on this small proxy, the discovered recipe transfers to larger scales and improves the downstream metric CORE. These results suggest that data engineering can be treated as an agentic machine learning problem, extending autonomous research from model and training-code optimization to the data.

t: When Can You Prune Your Network? A Study of Intermediate Neurons in Multilingual Speech Parsing
ab: End-to-end speech parsing, a task recently proposed, consists in predicting both the transcription and the syntactic tree for a spoken utterance. Existing architectures for speech parsing often utilise intermediate neural networks. In this work, we examine the effectiveness of intermediate neural networks (NN) for parsing, and, specifically, what role do they play. We introduce a simpler end-to-end architecture for speech parsing, where we remove these intermediate NN units, reducing the parameters by 12%, while achieving comparable or better performance than prior method on both automatic speech recognition (ASR) and parsing. We demonstrate that intermediate NN units help reduce the representational gap when the pre-trained encoder is frozen. We do a comprehensive evaluation of speech parsing on French, and medium-low resource languages Slovenian and Naija. We further investigate the impact of the training data size and intermediate layers of the pretrained speech encoder on speech parsing.

t: MediX-R1: Open Ended Medical Reinforcement Learning
a: Mohamed bin Zayed University of Artificial Intelligence
Mohamed bin Zayed University of Artificial Intelligence
Mohamed bin Zayed University of Artificial Intelligence
East point college of research and sciences and independent
Mohamed bin Zayed University of Artificial Intelligence and Linköping University
Mohamed bin Zayed University of Artificial Intelligence and Australian National University
Mohamed bin Zayed University of Artificial Intelligence
ab: In this work, we introduce MediX-R1, an open-ended Reinforcement Learning (RL) framework for medical vision language models (VLMs) that enables free-form answers beyond multiple-choice formats. MediX-R1 fine-tunes a baseline vision-language backbone with Group Based RL and a composite reward tailored for medical reasoning: an LLM-based accuracy reward that judges semantic correctness with a strict YES/NO decision, a medical embedding-based semantic reward to capture paraphrases and terminology variants, and lightweight format and modality rewards that enforce interpretable reasoning and modality recognition. This multi-signal design provides stable, informative feedback for open-ended outputs where traditional verifiable or MCQ-only rewards fall short. To evaluate performance, we employ a unified evaluation framework for both text-only and multimodal (image+text) tasks that uses a Reference-based LLM-as-judge in place of brittle string-overlap metrics, capturing semantic correctness, clinical accuracy, and contextual alignment. Our results show that open-ended RL with comprehensive reward signals can effectively strengthen medical reasoning in multimodal models. Despite using only ~51K instruction examples, MediX-R1 achieves strong performance across standard medical LLM (text-only) and VLM (image + text) benchmarks, outperforming existing open-weight medical VLMs, with large gains particularly on open-ended clinical tasks. These improvements remain consistent across multiple RL algorithms and VLM backbones and are further supported by blinded evaluations with medical experts. Our trained models, curated datasets and source code are available at https://medix.cvmbzuai.com

t: Definitional Sensitivity in Media Bias Detection: A Multi-Definition Dataset and Benchmark
ab: Media bias detection relies on definitions and examples that specify what counts as bias, yet these specifications often vary across datasets or remain implicit, even when given the same name. Such variation makes it unclear whether models trained for the same bias category learn the same construct or different phenomena, a problem largely overlooked in prior work. We examine how definition choice affects bias annotation in a between-subjects experiment with 354 participants and a parallel evaluation with four LLMs. Participants and models rate six news articles across four bias categories using definitions that vary in conceptual framing and elaboration. Across 8,496 human and 28,800 LLM ratings, we find that the conceptual target of a definition drives annotation divergence, while construct-preserving elaboration does not: conceptual framing significantly shifts annotations for humans and does so even more strongly for LLMs. We discuss implications for construct specification in annotation protocols and prompt-based measurement, and consider how definitional sensitivity may propagate to downstream classification beyond media bias. We also release MUDD, the Multi-Definition Bias Detection Dataset.

t: IndicSafe: A Benchmark for Evaluating Multilingual LLM Safety in South Asia
ab: As large language models (LLMs) are deployed in multilingual settings, their safety behavior in culturally diverse, low-resource languages remains poorly understood. We present the first systematic evaluation of LLM safety across 12 Indic languages, spoken by over 1.2 billion people but underrepresented in LLM training data. Using a dataset of 6,000 culturally grounded prompts spanning caste, religion, gender, health, and politics, we assess 18 leading LLMs on translated variants of the same prompt.Our analysis reveals a previously underexamined failure mode: cross-language exact agreement is only 20.69%, indicating that identical prompts frequently receive different safety judgments across languages, while cross-model exact agreement is just 2.77%. Some models over-refuse or overflag politically sensitive content, whereas others fail to flag unsafe generations or shift failures into ambiguous outputs. We quantify these behaviors using prompt-level entropy, category bias scores, and multilingual consistency indices.Our findings demonstrate critical safety generalization failures in multilingual LLMs and show that safety alignment does not reliably transfer across languages. We release IndicSafe, the first benchmark to enable culturally informed safety evaluation for Indic deployments, and advocate for language-aware alignment strategies grounded in regional harms.

t: GRACE-SVD: Guided Rank Allocation and Core Equalization SVD
a: Samsung Research and Development Institute Bangalore (SRIB)
ab: Large Language Models (LLMs), with 7B+ parameters, remain difficult to deploy on edge devices due to memory latency constraints, despite increasing demand for personalized on-device agents with strong reasoning capabilities. Enabling such deployment, in current hardware specifications, requires aggressive compression while preserving downstream performance. Singular Value Decomposition (SVD)-based methods provide a promising reconstruction-aware compression paradigm, and recent trainable frameworks improve adaptive rank allocation under varying compression budgets. However, maintaining model quality under high compression remains challenging due to statistical mismatches between decomposed cores and compounded degradation from direct high-ratio compression.We propose GRACE-SVD, a trainable SVD compression framework combining Guided Rank Allocation with a novel Core Equalization method that aligns decomposed core distributions while preserving reconstruction. We further introduce a progressive compression pipeline with intermediate equalization to mitigate performance collapse under aggressive compression. Across multiple model families and compression settings, our GRACE-SVD consistently outperforms existing SVD techniques, achieving stable compression even at 0.4 parameter ratio, with lower perplexity and stronger zero-shot performance under comparable or lower compression budgets.

t: TaoAnalysisBench: Do Automated Theorem Prover LLMs Generalize Beyond MathLib?
a: UCLA Computer Science Department, University of California, Los Angeles
University of California, Los Angeles and Amazon
Google and University of California, Los Angeles
ab: Automated theorem proving (ATP) benchmarks largely consist of problems formalized in MathLib, so current ATP training and evaluation are heavily biased toward MathLib’s definitional framework. However, frontier mathematics is often exploratory and prototype-heavy, relying on bespoke constructions that deviate from standard libraries. In this work, we evaluate the robustness of current ATP systems when applied to a novel definitional framework. We introduce TaoAnalysisBench, an undergraduate-level benchmark derived from the exercises and definitional frameworks given in Terence Tao’s Analysis I, which formalizes analysis by constructing core mathematical concepts from scratch, without relying on standard Mathlib definitions, as well as by mixing from-scratch and MathLib constructions. For fair evaluation, we build an agentic pipeline that automatically extracts a compilable, self-contained local environment for each problem. To isolate the effect of definitional frameworks, we additionally translate every problem into a mathematically equivalent Mathlib formulation, yielding paired TaoAnalysisBench-Mathlib statements for direct comparison. While state-of-the-art ATP models perform capably within the MathLib framework, performance drops by an average of 2.18x on the definitionally equivalent Tao formulation. This indicates that the main bottleneck is limited generalization across definitional frameworks rather than task difficulty. TaoAnalysisBench thus highlights a gap between benchmark performance and applicability, and provides a concrete foundation for developing and testing provers better aligned with research mathematics.

t: AI translation of literary texts is ’fine’, but readers still prefer human translations
ab: AI translation of literary works is increasingly common. While the content may be rendered adequately, we do not know enough about how readers experience it in terms of immersiveness and literary effect—aspects poorly captured by automatic metrics or human evaluation targeting fluency and adequacy. We ask 15 avid readers to compare recently published human translations (HT) to machine translations (MT) generated with an agentic language model-based pipeline, for 15 recent novels in French, Polish, and Japanese translated into English. Readers evaluated approximately 8K-word excerpts in two conditions: immersive reading of the whole excerpt (30 comparisons) and close reading of 386 aligned HT–MT chunk pairs (772 comparisons), with two readers per book. Overall, readers find MT “fine”, but prefer HT (descriptively at the excerpt level, 19/30, and significantly at the chunk level, 522/772) for its ease, clarity, and immersive nature. Readers’ highlights show that MT’s quality varies more within one book than HT’s does. Crucially, readers cannot reliably tell the two apart (17/30 guess correctly) and tend to prefer the version they believe to be human. Automatic metrics, including LLM-as-a-judge approaches, fail to recover reader preferences and favor MT. We release LAIT (Literary AI Translation), a reader-centered evaluation dataset with 1K reader comments, 2K judgments and preference ratings, and 7.2K span-level annotations, along with our evaluation protocol and supporting interface.

t: XLGoBench: Detecting cross-lingual skill gaps with algorithmic tasks
ab: We introduce a set of synthetic algorithmic tasks to detect cross-lingual gaps in the abilities of large language models. Our benchmark is commensurate across languages, since it requires models to perform the same underlying task in different languages; scalable, since each task can be generated at varying levels of complexity allowing it to be adapted to models with different capabilities; quantifiable, since every task admits an objective notion of correctness; and transparent, since tasks are generated from simple templates that can be readily audited for translation errors. Because our benchmark focuses on algorithmic tasks, differential performance is a sufficient—but not necessary—indicator of cross-lingual gaps. Nevertheless, we show through extensive experiments that our benchmark exposes persistent cross-lingual gaps in multiple state-of-the-art models.

t: Balancing Faithfulness and Performance in Reasoning via Multi-Listener Soft Execution
a: University of North Carolina at Chapel Hill
Amazon and University of North Carolina at Chapel Hill
ab: Chain-of-thought (CoT) reasoning sometimes fails to faithfully reflect the true computation of a large language model (LLM), hampering its utility in explaining how LLMs arrive at their answers. Moreover, optimizing for faithfulness and interpretability in reasoning often degrades task performance. To address this tradeoff and improve CoT faithfulness, we propose Reasoning Execution by Multiple Listeners (REMuL), a multi-party reinforcement learning approach. REMuL builds on the hypothesis that reasoning traces which other parties can follow will be more faithful. A speaker model generates a reasoning trace, which is truncated and passed to a pool of listener models who “execute” the trace, continuing the trace to an answer. Speakers are rewarded for producing reasoning that is clear to listeners, with additional correctness regularization via masked supervised finetuning to counter the tradeoff between faithfulness and performance. On multiple reasoning benchmarks (BIG-Bench Extra Hard, MuSR, ZebraLogicBench, and FOLIO), REMuL consistently and substantially improves three measures of faithfulness – hint attribution, early answering area over the curve (AOC), and mistake injection AOC – while also improving accuracy. Our analysis finds that these gains are robust across training domains and are associated with shorter and more direct CoTs.

t: InterviewBench: Benchmarking Large Language Models as Interviewers
a: Shanghai Innovation Institute and Fudan University
ab: Interviews collect information through conversation, requiring interviewers to ask appropriate questions, adapt to respondent behavior, and recover structured information from dialogue. Yet, AI systems’ abilities as interviewers remain under-explored. We present InterviewBench, a benchmark for evaluating LLM-based AI interviewers through both local interviewer decisions and dynamic multi-turn interviews. The static setting abstracts real interviews into controlled local-decision instances, while the dynamic setting evaluates end-to-end interviewing through long-horizon conversational simulations. Built from real interview transcripts, InterviewBench contains 5,500 classification questions, 3,000 generative questions, and 184 dynamic scenarios. We further model interviewer evaluation as contextual decision selection, where the model must choose or generate the next interviewer action conditioned on dialogue context. Evaluating 23 open-source and proprietary LLMs, we find that current models can produce fluent interviewer utterances, but still struggle with strategy selection, explicit evidence elicitation, long-horizon interaction management, and recovery from non-ideal interviewee behavior.

t: Detecting Post-generation Edits to Watermarked LLM Outputs via Error-Correcting Codes
ab: Watermarking has become a key mechanism for distinguishing AI-generated from human-written texts. In practical settings, however, content produced by large language models (LLMs) is often subject to critical post-generation edits, posing challenges for detecting and localizing such modifications. In this work, we propose incorporating error-correcting codes, specifically Varshamov-Tenengolts (VT) codes, by embedding VT code strings into watermarked LLM outputs, thus enabling post-generation edit detection of token insertions and deletions. We accompany such a watermarking procedure with a watermark detector and a post-edit detector. We evaluate our method on open-source LLM using synthetic edits and demonstrate excellent empirical performance of post-generation edit detection.

t: MoEs Are Stronger than You Think: Hyper-Parallel Inference Scaling with RoEs
ab: The generation quality of large language models (LLMs) is often improved by utilizing inference-time scaling methods such as Chain-of-Thought (sequential scaling) or Self-Consistency (parallel scaling). We introduce Roster of Experts (RoE), a training-free inference algorithm for Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) models that defines a third, orthogonal scaling direction. Rather than generating longer outputs or aggregating multiple sequences, RoE improves the next token prediction distribution by treating a single MoE as a dynamic ensemble of internal subnetworks. It injects controlled stochasticity into the expert routing mechanism via Gumbel-Top-k sampling, enabling the model to aggregate multiple diverse subnetworks into a single, higher-quality token prediction. Crucially, because RoE improves the model’s output distribution rather than sampling from it, it is the only approach in this family that is applicable to open-ended generation tasks where sequence-level aggregation is infeasible. Furthermore, RoE is orthogonal to existing scaling methods; combining RoE with Self-Consistency yields greater accuracy than either method alone. To overcome the computational cost of multiple forward passes at inference, we employ an efficient batching strategy that exploits hardware parallelism to minimize latency, requiring no fine-tuning of model parameters.

t: Multi-Hop Knowledge Composition is Bound by Pretraining Exposure
ab: Large Language Models fail at implicit multi-hop reasoning: a model answers "When was born?" and "Who is ’s closest friend?" correctly but fails on "When was ’s closest friend born?" in a single forward pass, even when both facts are perfectly memorized and individually retrievable. We study this failure in a controlled natural language setting with a strict separation between individuals exposed to compositional contexts during pretraining and those that never appear in any such context. We confirm that compositional failure persists even at 97% 1-hop accuracy, establishing the gap as a pretraining failure rather than a knowledge absence. We propose and test nine data-centric augmentation formats and find that compositional pretraining transfers to unseen questions for exposed individuals, but never to individuals absent from compositional pretraining, suggesting that exposure to compositional contexts during pretraining is a necessary condition for implicit multi-hop reasoning. Our code is available online.

t: FinRT: Distilling Adaptive Red-Teaming Strategies into Reusable Adversarial Generators in Consumer Finance
ab: In regulated industries like consumer finance, seemingly harmless user queries can exploit large language model vulnerabilities, triggering safety failures and pushing responses dangerously close to policy limits. Existing automated red-teaming methods trade off attack effectiveness against generation cost, while treating coverage, severity, and diversity as incidental rather than joint objectives. We introduce FinRT, a structured framework that builds reusable adversarial prompt generators from adaptive red-teaming strategies. Across the six victim models in consumer finance, FinRT substantially outperforms adaptive search baselines while amortizing target-facing attack generation into a reusable generator. FinRT nearly doubles the attack success rate over the adaptive baseline Rainbow Teaming (Samvelyan et al., 2024) (32.9% vs. 17.2%), increases maximum adversarial severity by 33%, and preserves comparable intra-policy–domain semantic diversity to iterative search methods. Our method achieves high cross-model transferability while exhibiting distinct victim-family specialization patterns.

t: Han2Han: Efficient Language-Specific Character Representation through Script-Aware Pre-Training for Historical Text Analysis
ab: Language models learn semantic similarity from shared context; however, when a single word has multiple orthographies that rarely appear in the same context, models cannot learn their equivalence. This is a structural problem that cannot be solved with scale. Korean presents a clear case: 20th-century print media used Hanja (Sino-Korean script), while contemporary models train on Hangul-only (Korean alphabet) text. Multilingual models inherit script segregation from their training distribution, where Hanja appears almost exclusively outside Korean text, and monolingual Korean models assign separate vocabulary entries to script variants, forcing distinct representations from initialization. We introduce Han2Han, a 169M parameter encoder-decoder model trained with a language-aware recipe—jamo and character-level embedding fusion, morpheme-aware denoising, and bidirectional Hanja-Hangul transcription—that forces orthographic alignment as a prior to distributional learning. The resulting representations are script-invariant: the same content receives the same representation regardless of script. On temporal classification of mixed-script historical newspapers, evaluated on an article-level held-out split, Han2Han reaches 76.0 macro F1 against 54.3 for the strongest baselines (KLUE-BERT and the 4.7\times larger T5Gemma 2 alike), a 21.7-point margin, demonstrating that language-specific pre-training yields capabilities not addressed by current Korean-inclusive multilingual training at this scale.

t: A History-Aware Visually Grounded Critic for Computer Use Agents
a: University of North Carolina at Chapel Hill
Amazon and University of North Carolina at Chapel Hill
ab: Various test-time interventions for Computer Use Agents (CUAs), including critic models, have been developed to improve performance through pre-execution action evaluation in complex Graphical User Interface (GUI) environments. However, existing critics suffer from two key limitations: they (1) focus primarily on short-sighted decision loops (e.g., forgetting earlier actions) and (2) lack the visual grounding needed to detect flawed actions (e.g., clicking wrong UI elements). To address these, we introduce HIVIG, a History-aware Visually Grounded test-time framework, built around a multimodal critic trained on real GUI trajectories to abstract past interactions into a compact record and to evaluate actions with visual grounding. At test time, HIVIG integrates the critic into the policy decision loop to provide macro-action history, which summarizes the policy’s completed achievements, and visually grounded critique, which verifies raw execution coordinates against the current screenshot to intercept errors before execution. Across web, mobile, and desktop benchmarks, HIVIG consistently outperforms existing scalar and verbal critics, improving average success rates over the strongest baseline by 5.8% for Qwen3-VL-32B and 9.0% for Gemini-3-Flash, and demonstrates strong cross-platform generalization. Ablations show that macro-action history mitigates short-sighted planning and visually grounded critique reduces execution errors, with both components being critical for test-time scaling in long-horizon GUI tasks.

t: Health-SCORE: Improving Open-Ended Health LLMs Using Scalable Rubric-Based Rewards
ab: Reinforcement learning is a powerful approach for improving language models, but applying it to open-ended domains such as healthcare remains challenging because high-quality responses are often multidimensional, context dependent, and difficult to capture with a single reward signal. Rubrics offer a natural form of supervision by providing a structured representation of the criteria that define a strong response. Existing rubric-based approaches, however, often rely on instance-specific criteria, creating two important limitations: (1) such rubrics are typically unavailable for unseen examples at test time; and (2) constructing new rubrics for every instance incurs substantial reward design costs. We introduce Health-SCORE, a scalable framework that captures recurring principles of response quality in the form of reusable meta-rubrics. Rather than relying on manually constructed instance-level criteria, Health-SCORE captures generalizable principles that can be applied across examples, tasks, and healthcare datasets. These meta-rubrics support two forms of model improvement: they can serve as structured, safety-aware reward signals for reinforcement learning during post-training, and they can be incorporated directly into prompts to guide model behavior at inference time. Across several open-ended healthcare benchmarks, models trained with Health-SCORE achieve performance competitive with models trained using human-authored instance-level rewards, while substantially reducing reward-design costs and improving generalizability.

t: What Really Controls Temporal Reasoning in Large Language Models: Tokenisation or Representation of Time?
ab: We present MULTITEMPBENCH, a multilingual temporal reasoning benchmark spanning three tasks, date arithmetic, time zone conversion, and temporal relation extraction across five languages (English, German, Chinese, Arabic, and Hausa) and multiple calendar conventions (Gregorian, Hijri, and Chinese Lunar). MULTITEMPBENCH contains 15,000 examples built by translating 750 curated English questions and expanding each into controlled date-format variants. We evaluate 20 LLMs and introduce the multilingual Date Fragmentation Ratio (mDFR), calibrated with human severity ratings, together with geometric-probing analyses of internal temporal representations. We find tokenisation quality of temporal artefacts is a resource-dependent bottleneck: in low-resource languages and rarer calendar formats, fragmentation disrupts Year/Month/Day separation and accuracy collapses, while high-resource settings are often robust to digit-level splitting. Beyond tokenisation, crossed mixed-effects regression shows that temporal linearity is the strongest predictor of temporal reasoning in high-resource languages, whereas fragmentation is the stronger predictor in low-resource languages.

t: OASIS: Online Anchor-calibrated Self-Improvement System
a: King Abdullah University of Science and Technology
King Abdullah University of Science and Technology
King Abdullah University of Science and Technology
King Abdullah University of Science and Technology
King Abdullah University of Science and Technology
King Abdullah University of Science and Technology
King Abdullah University of Science and Technology and King Abdullah University of Science and Technology
King Abdullah University of Science and Technology
King Abdullah University of Science and Technology
King Abdullah University of Science and Technology
King Abdullah University of Science and Technology, Universita della Svizzera Italiana, NNAISENSE and IDSIA
ab: Many recursively self-improving systems improve by editing their codebases based on observed rollout behavior. However, recent methods largely treat self-improvement as offline search: variants are optimized and evaluated on fixed benchmarks. This misaligns with real-world deployment, where tasks arrive sequentially and may have different distributions. We study recursive self-improvement as online learning over non-stationary task streams. In this setting, reliable execution and fallback are particularly difficult with limited evidence: different branches of self-improvement see different tasks, so raw rewards conflate capability with task difficulty, leading to overly conservative or optimistic reversion. We propose Online Anchor-calibrated Self-Improvement System (OASIS) that runs an adaptive reference agent on incoming tasks, converts raw rewards into paired comparisons, and uses confidence-calibrated rules for branch continuation and fallback without evaluating every agent on all tasks. Across SWE-Bench Pro and DeepResearch Bench, OASIS consistently improves over both the initial agent and prior RSI baseline SSA, raising the SWE-Bench Pro solve rate from 51.6% to 56.9% using Qwen3.6-35B-A3B and DeepResearch Bench from 35.18 to 39.31 using Gemini 3 Flash. This enables OASIS to outperform larger open weights and proprietary systems, including Qwen3.5-397B-A17B, Minimax 2.7, Qwen3.6-Plus, and GPT-5.3-Codex, with sustained deep self-improvements rather than shallow cycles.

t: Language Modeling Across Script Variants: The Case of Japanese
a: Mohamed bin Zayed University of Artificial Intelligence
Mohamed bin Zayed University of Artificial Intelligence and The University of Melbourne
ab: We investigate the effect of script variants on language modeling in Japanese, which uniquely combines logographic (kanji) and phonetic (kana) writing systems. Motivated by educational curricula in which learners are gradually exposed to increasing numbers of logographic characters, we simulate this staged exposure during training to study its effect on model behavior. We construct multiple versions of a corpus with controlled script transformations, including fully transliterated kana text and intermediate variants corresponding to curriculum-based kanji levels, and train language models under different schedules that vary the timing and progression of script exposure during pre-training. In addition, we propose a cross-script evaluation framework using multiple versions of a minimal-pair benchmark with systematically varied kanji usage to assess the robustness of language models to script variation. Our results show that training on a mixture of two extreme script variants improves robustness across script conditions, whereas curriculum-based progression does not consistently improve performance.

t: AMARIS: A Memory-Augmented Rubric Improvement System for Rubric-Based Reinforcement Learning
ab: Rubric-based reward shaping provides interpretable and editable reward signals for fine-tuning LLMs via reinforcement learning (RL), but existing adaptive rubric methods typically update criteria from local evidence such as the current batch or instance-level comparisons. This local view discards diagnostic information produced during training, making it difficult to track recurring failures, evaluate previous rubric edits, or raise standards once earlier criteria become saturated. We introduce AMARIS, a Memory-Augmented Rubric Improvement System that grounds rubric updates in longitudinal training evidence. AMARIS stores rollout analyses, step-level summaries, and rubric update records in a persistent evaluation memory, then retrieves recent and semantically relevant history to revise rubrics. We evaluate AMARIS across science, medicine, instruction following, and creative writing under both global and instance-specific rubric settings, with policy models from the Qwen and Llama families trained by GRPO and PPO. AMARIS improves over static, local-adaptive, and memory-ablated baselines, such as +2.8 points on GPQA-Diamond and +2.2 points on IFBench over the strongest baselines, while analysis shows that memory reduces oscillatory rubric edits and supports a progression from early failure correction to later curriculum advancement. The final rubric set that AMARIS discovers is itself reusable, and the online trajectory contributes measurably beyond it. AMARIS runs asynchronously alongside the normal RL loop, reducing blocking latency relative to synchronous rubric updates. The source code is available at https://github.com/qualidea1217/AMARIS.

t: Sense and Sensitivity: Benchmarking LLM Clinical Triage Recommendations with Physician Experts
ab: As large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used in clinical settings, it is critical to evaluate their reliability under realistic variation in clinical text. We study this question in clinical triage, comparing LLMs to practicing physicians under text perturbations that preserve the underlying clinical setting. We introduce a benchmark of over 6{,}000 clinical scenarios, 7{,}000 physician annotations, and 225{,}000 model responses. Using this benchmark, we make two key observations. First, LLMs are more likely than physicians to recommend unnecessary care at baseline, and this tendency increases under perturbed inputs. Further, we find that LLM recommendations are more sensitive to gender and tone perturbations than human recommendations. Together, these results demonstrate that LLMs can vary under clinically irrelevant textual changes, highlighting the need for deployment-oriented evaluations grounded in expert physician behavior.

t: Behavior Carries Over: An AI Sandbagging Detection Method Inspired by Honest Inertia
a: CISPA Helmholtz Center for Information Security
CISPA Helmholtz Center for Information Security
CISPA Helmholtz Center for Information Security
CISPA Helmholtz Center for Information Security
CISPA Helmholtz Center for Information Security
ab: Reliable capability assessment is essential for governing and securely deploying advanced AI systems. However, "AI Sandbagging," where models strategically suppress their true capabilities during evaluation, undermines existing assessment frameworks by making it difficult to distinguish genuine limitations from strategic concealment. To address this challenge, we propose a new black-box sandbag detection method inspired by "honesty inertia," a psychological phenomenon where humans struggle to maintain deception after answering simple questions truthfully. We hypothesize that large language models exhibit an analogous effect: inserting several simple, unrelated questions, which target models should answer correctly, before the target query induces honest inertia, causing sandbag models to involuntarily increase accuracy while standard models remain stable. Through extensive experiments on multiple datasets with various model architectures, we confirm the validity of this hypothesis and establish this differential response as a reliable, model-independent sandbag detection signal. We further provide interpretability support for this phenomenon from two dimensions: theoretical derivation and hidden state analysis of models. This work offers a practical tool for enhancing AI audit and supervision.

t: When Trivia Is Not Trivial: Everyday Knowledge Failures in Multilingual LLMs
ab: Quiz rooms, trivia nights, and quiz shows challenge human knowledge across a wide range of topics, from canonical facts to everyday culture. In this paper, we examine whether large language models (LLMs) can perform competitively in such settings, using quiz-style questions to test them on both common and niche topics. We introduce TriviaRoomQA, a multilingual benchmark designed to evaluate everyday, culturally grounded, and long-tail knowledge across 288 topics. The benchmark contains 3,300 parallel multiple-choice questions in six European languages and additional 5,340 French-only questions for a more fine-grained case study. We evaluate 30 open-weight LLMs from European, Asian, and North American providers, covering models from 7 to 70B parameters. We find that models are strong on knowledge-intensive topics such as history, geography, and mathematics, but substantially weaker on everyday popular-culture topics such as celebrities, music, movies, and news. Moreover, model performance varies across languages even for the same underlying questions, suggesting that access to factual knowledge is not always language-independent. In sum, our dataset and experiments demonstrate an important knowledge gap which is not captured by existing academic-based saturated benchmarks.

t: DP-IPI: A Hybrid Differential Privacy Text Rewriting Mechanism for Indirect Personal Identifiers in Clinical Texts
ab: Despite the strengths of modern anonymization and de-identification techniques, the risk of re-identification remains significant due to the indirect identifiers remaining in texts. To address this problem, recent works have applied text rewriting under Differential Privacy (DP) to prevent data linkage by perturbing texts via noise addition. Such methods privatize \textit{all} tokens in a text indiscriminately, diminishing text quality and usability in critical domains such as in clinical settings. Focusing on \textit{indirect personal identifiers} (IPIs), we introduce a utility-preserving DP text rewriting method that only privatizes spans containing IPIs. We show that our method effectively reduces re-identification risks in clinical texts while being producing more coherent and usable output texts, leading to higher privacy-utility trade-offs. In this, we demonstrate the effectiveness of \textit{hybrid} text privatization, which leverages the promise of DP in an efficient, usable manner.

t: Training with Subword Variants Delays Overfitting in Repeated-Data Language Modeling
a: SUPSI - University of Applied Sciences Southern Switzerland
ab: Subword tokenization introduces a computational layer in language models, where many distinct token sequences decode to the same surface form while preserving meaning, yet induce different internal computations. Despite this non-uniqueness, language models are typically trained using a single canonical deterministic tokenization. In this work, we use non-canonical subword variants as a strictly meaning-preserving form of data augmentation. We introduce a lightweight training architecture that conditions canonical next-token prediction on sampled subword variants via an auxiliary causal encoder and block-causal cross-attention, without modifying the training objective or token interface. In data-constrained pretraining, augmentations with subword variants consistently delay overfitting under repeated data exposure and reduce held-out next-token loss across evaluation datasets. In multilingual fine-tuning, we find that the effectiveness of training with auxiliary subwords depends on tokenizer quality: gains are strongest when canonical tokens are highly compressed and diminish when the tokenizer already over-fragments the input.

t: Don’t “Overthink” Pointwise Reranking: Is Reasoning Truly Necessary?
a: OpenAI and Massachusetts Institute of Technology
ab: With the success of reasoning models across complex natural language tasks, researchers in the information retrieval (IR) community have begun exploring how similar reasoning capabilities can be integrated into passage rerankers built on large language models (LLMs). These methods typically employ an LLM to produce an explicit, step-by-step reasoning process before arriving at a final relevance prediction. But does reasoning actually improve pointwise reranking? We investigate this question through controlled comparisons of Rank1, a pointwise reasoning reranker, with two non-reasoning counterparts. Across in-domain and out-of-domain datasets, we find that Rank1 generally underperforms Rank0, an otherwise equivalent non-reasoning pointwise reranker trained using the same backbone LLM and underlying training data as Rank1. To isolate the contribution of Rank1’s inference-time reasoning, we then replace its generated reasoning process with a fixed dummy sequence. Surprisingly, this variant, Rank1-NoReason, can also outperform Rank1. Analysis of Rank1’s score distributions provides a likely explanation: once Rank1 deems a passage relevant, it assigns nearly identical relevance scores, limiting its ability to distinguish degrees of relevance and ultimately harming its ranking accuracy. We release all code at https://github.com/nourj98/dont-overthink-reranking.

t: Beyond Lexical and Syntactic: Better Text Simplicity Analysis Informed by Psycholinguistic Research
ab: Automatic text simplification measures correlate poorly with human judgments and are disconnected from psycholinguistic research on comprehension. We propose a multidimensional analysis framework grounded in Cognitive Load Theory and the Construction-Integration model, organizing over 400 linguistic features into six simplicity dimensions targeting distinct comprehension stages. Using this framework, we analyze four human-annotated and six aligned simplification datasets. We find that (1) our dimensions predict human simplicity judgments better than established measures on most datasets; (2) current datasets overwhelmingly target lexical and syntactic dimensions while under-targeting personalization the dimension psychological research identifies as most impactful for comprehension; and (3) existing measures overall do not capture any specific dimension. These findings provide actionable guidance for building measures and datasets better aligned with how readers actually process text.

t: BEiTScore++: Reference-free Image Captioning Evaluation with BEiT-3 and Conformalized Quantile Regression
ab: Reliable uncertainty estimation is important for deploying evaluation metrics in real-world settings, where both input ambiguity and domain shifts are common. In this work, we propose an uncertainty-aware extension of the BEiTScore image captioning metric, producing calibrated confidence intervals alongside alignment scores. Our approach models predictive distributions over human judgments, enabling both accurate scoring and principled uncertainty quantification. We evaluate our BEiTScore++ metric across multiple benchmarks with human-annotated ratings, demonstrating strong performance in terms of ranking correlation, calibration, and interval sharpness. BEiTScore++ not only produces accurate predictions, but also captures aleatoric uncertainty arising from ambiguous inputs, and epistemic uncertainty due to limited model knowledge, making it a reliable tool for uncertainty-aware evaluation of image-caption alignment.

t: RFCLLM: Evaluating LLMs’ Reasoning Ability of Network Protocol State Machines
ab: Mapping textual specifications into formal representations is essential for ensuring the correctness of protocol designs and implementations. LLM-generated mappings, used for networking security or testing, are assumed to capture a perfect understanding of the specification, which may not hold in practice. The goal of this paper is to assess the extent to which LLMs can interpret the specification correctly. We examine the degree to which an LLM’s implicit representation of a finite-state transition system–defined via natural language descriptions–aligns with a manually generated ground-truth model.We designed 4 tasks and 1482 task queries for 16 protocols. We evaluated different judge biases, observed the inherent difficulty gaps between tasks, looked into the effect of 4 context types, and the influence of protocol characteristics. Our work contributes to a step toward verifying whether LLMs can really be trusted in FSM (Finite State Machine) reasoning of protocol specifications.

t: Characterizing Opinion Evolution of Networked LLMs
ab: Large language models (LLMs) increasingly interact with one another in multi-agent systems, from simulations of human discourse to influence operations and fully LLM-driven social platforms. These interactions give rise to new regimes of opinion propagation that are not yet well understood. We investigate whether classical opinion dynamics models, which have long been used to explain how interactions shape collective beliefs in human societies, can capture the behavior of LLM networks. Specifically, we quantify the relative contributions of classical opinion-dynamics mechanisms, including neighbor influence, stubbornness, homophily, and bias, to the evolution of LLM opinions. Among the mechanisms considered, a bias term capturing regression toward a model- and topic-dependent opinion emerges as a significant explanatory component, with its inclusion reducing cumulative estimated mean opinion error by up to 88%. We additionally observe similar trends across the evaluated model families, discussion topics, and network structures.

t: From Arraignment to Resolution: Transformer Models of Court Cases
ab: The criminal legal system is composed of many complex decision points, such as which charges are pursued, how bond is determined, plea deal negotiations, and sentencing. Given the profound impact of such decisions, there is a growing need to increase the transparency within this system. While prior machine learning approaches have focused on modeling single decisions (e.g., recidivism), this paper proposes a transformer-based time series model to forecast the outcome of the next proceeding in a case (e.g., charges accepted, bond set, plea deal made, etc.). By modeling a case as an event sequence, we enable a more nuanced analysis to support better oversight and understanding of decision making. We conduct an empirical analysis of thousands of cases using a newly constructed dataset derived from publicly available court records of a mid-sized U.S. city. We fit models that combine textual data from clerk notes with structured information about the defendant, prior charges, and courtroom. Our transformer model achieves .57 micro-F1 on a 20 class multi-label task, a significant improvement over several baselines and comparable to a GRU trained on the same input. We demonstrate how the model can be used to provide insights into decision-making and help court observers identify emerging issues within the jurisdiction studied.

t: Gnosis Deepsearch: Structured Search Space Navigation for Complex QA
a: University of Edinburgh and Farama Foundation
University of Edinburgh, University of Edinburgh
ab: Complex, multi-step reasoning demands agents to be capable of dynamically exploring diverse research directions and adapting plans on the fly. We introduce Gnosis Deepsearch, a schema-guided framework for long-horizon planning in complex Question Answering, where variables, clues, and constraints are captured in a structured state representation maintained across trajectories. This state is cascaded into parallel search paths broadening exploration without relying on sequential execution, thereby mitigating both limited search space coverage and catastrophic forgetting. We couple Gnosis with a retriever that sidesteps challenges associated with retrieval and LLM reading when longer documents are involved. Our retrieval strategy ensures that the most relevant snippets from longer documents are considered, showcasing several benefits within both Gnosis and a more general ReAct framework on the BrowseComp-Plus benchmark. Extensive experiments on several QA benchmarks of varying difficulty demonstrate the strong performance of Gnosis across different configurations.

t: Mind the Phrase: Annotation and Identification of Multiword Expressions in Grammatical Error Correction
ab: Multiword Expressions (MWEs) are an important part of language competence which are both commonplace across languages and challenging for language learners to master. Since Grammatical Error Correction (GEC) systems tend to provide suggestions at the token level, they may fail to handle the semantic unity of MWEs. We present annotations of MWEs in learner English essays while identifying their intended spans. This not only allows us to analyse learner MWE errors in more detail for the first time, but also enables us to build GEC systems that provide more meaningful feedback to learners. We have annotated 1,850 essays that were previously tagged for grammatical errors with various types of MWEs. We extend an error annotation toolkit with an MWE error-type and present a method that leverages these annotations to make GEC evaluation more explainable, enabling fine-grained analysis of MWE errors. Experiments with current GEC systems show that an edit-based model fine-tuned on our dataset achieves higher F0.5 scores for the correction of common MWE error types, demonstrating its effectiveness for handling MWEs.

t: CultureScore: Evaluating Cultural Faithfulness in Video Generation Models
ab: As video generation models like Veo 3.1 and LTX-2 advance, their ability to accurately represent diverse global cultures remains a critical yet understudied frontier. Current metrics, such as VideoScore, only measure visual quality but offer no mechanism for assessing cultural faithfulness. Consequently, a model that replaces a Namaste with a handshake receives the same score as one that generates the gesture correctly. We propose CultureScore, a compositional evaluation framework that decomposes cultural faithfulness into three granular dimensions: Identity (who is represented), Context (culturally localized background), and Behavior (normative gestures and interactions). We operationalize this framework through an evaluation suite spanning 10 countries, yielding 6,174 generated videos across three state-of-the-art models. Our evaluation reveals that no current model achieves culturally faithful video generation: the best-performing model reaches only 56.8% overall CultureScore, with Behavior the most challenging dimension; no model exceeds 52.1% on behavior. Furthermore, the highest-scoring model (LTX-2) on visual quality was ranked last by native annotators, while CultureScore’s Behavior dimension shows the strongest positive correlation with human cultural judgment among the automatic metrics we evaluate, underscoring that cultural faithfulness is an essential criterion for equitable video generation. Data and code are publicly available.[<https://huggingface.co/datasets/ankurani/CultureScore>]

t: Gradient-Stable Attention Heads Signal LLM Correctness
ab: Large language models (LLMs) often generate plausible yet incorrect answers, posing risks in safety-critical settings such as medicine. Human evaluation is expensive, and LLM-as-judge approaches risk introducing hidden errors. Recent single-pass white-box methods detect contextual hallucinations using linear probes over model internals, but their generalization to out-of-domain, out-of-task, and training-free settings remains poorly understood. We introduce HeadEntropy, a method that predicts answer correctness by measuring how susceptible each attention head’s pattern is to modification under further gradient updates. The key insight is that the trace of the softmax Jacobian is a monotonic function of 2-Rényi entropy, linking attention spread to gradient stability during training, even without the reference annotation. With no training, HeadEntropy reaches 0.736 AUROC, outperforms every training-free baseline in paired comparison across 5 models and 5 datasets, and matches a hidden-state probe transferred across domains, at under 1% of inference cost. We evaluate broadly across 5 instruction-tuned LLMs and 5 datasets spanning general knowledge, multi-hop reasoning, mathematical reasoning, claim verification, and medicine. The code is available at https://github.com/StanfordMIMI/HeadEntropy.

t: UI-Oceanus: Scaling GUI Agents with Synthetic Environmental Dynamics
a: Peking University and Beijing Tongming Lake Information Technology Application Innovation Center

Beijing Tongming Lake Information Technology Application Innovation Center, Fudan University Institute of Systems for Advanced Computing, Shanghai Institute of Systems for Open Computing and Key Lab of HCST (PKU), MOE; SCS, Peking University
ab: Scaling generalist GUI agents is hindered by the data scalability bottleneck of expensive human demonstrations and reliance on ungrounded synthetic teacher supervision. To transcend these limitations, we propose , a framework that shifts the learning focus from mimicking high-level trajectories to learning interaction dynamics from executed transitions. Through a systematic investigation of self-supervised objectives, we identify that forward dynamics, defined as the generative prediction of future interface states, acts as the primary driver for scalability and outperforms inverse and backward objectives. leverages this insight by converting low-cost autonomous exploration into high-density generative supervision to learn a semantic transition world model from executed transitions. Experimental evaluations across a series of models demonstrate consistent gains from our approach: models utilizing Continual Pre-Training (CPT) on synthetic dynamics outperform non-CPT baselines with an average success rate improvement of 7% on offline benchmarks, which amplifies to a 16.8% gain in real-world online navigation. Furthermore, we observe that navigation performance scales with synthetic data volume. These results suggest that grounding agents in forward predictive modeling offers a promising pathway to scalable GUI automation with cross-domain adaptability and compositional generalization.

t: MCompassRAG: Topic Metadata as a Semantic Compass for Paragraph-Level Retrieval
ab: Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) systems depend critically on how documents are chunked and searched. Fine-grained chunks can improve retrieval precision but expand the search space, increasing latency and cost; larger chunks reduce the number of candidates but make dense similarity less reliable, as each representation mixes multiple topics and introduces more semantic noise. This trade-off becomes especially limiting in deep research tasks, where retrieval must be both fast and precise across large, heterogeneous corpora. We introduce MCompassRAG, a metadata-guided retrieval framework that uses topic-level signals as a semantic compass for selecting relevant evidence. Instead of relying only on cosine similarity between queries and noisy chunk embeddings, MCompassRAG enriches chunk representations with topic metadata defined in the same embedding space and trains a lightweight retriever through LLM-teacher distillation. At inference time, MCompassRAG performs topic-aware retrieval without additional LLM calls, improving both efficiency and evidence quality. Across six complex retrieval benchmarks, MCompassRAG improves information efficiency by 8.24% on average with over 5x lower latency than the strongest efficient RAG baselines.

t: Spatial Reasoning via Modality Switching Between Language and Symbolic Representations
ab: Human reasoning is inherently multimodal: when problems become difficult, we rarely think in words alone. We often externalize our reasoning by sketching diagrams or drawing grids to understand the underlying conceptual structure and avoid mistakes. Building on this premise, our research investigates: (a) whether grounding multi-hop textual-spatial stories into geometry-aware modalities, such as layouts or grids, improves reasoning compared to natural language-based inference; and (b) whether a model can decide when to rely on natural language reasoning and when to switch to a structured modality. We address these questions by introducing a switching metric based on trustworthiness and complexity signals, which estimates when grounding a spatial story into a structure is likely to improve performance. This takes a first step toward principled modality selection in large language model (LLM) reasoning. Across our settings, switching from natural language-based reasoning to a grid-based representation improves LLM performance by up to 42%, highlighting the importance of modality choice in shaping reasoning outcomes.

t: Humans’ ALMANAC: A Human Collaboration Dataset of Action-Level Mental Model ANnotations for Agent Collaboration
a: Northeastern University and University of Dublin, Trinity College
School of Computer Science, Carnegie Mellon University
ab: Recent advances in LLM agents have enabled complex cognitive capabilities, such as multi-step reasoning, planning, and tool use, that increasingly position these agents as collaborative partners in human workflows. Effective collaboration, however, requires collaborators to continuously maintain and align mental models of their own reasoning, partners’ intentions, and shared goals during the collaborative process. Today’s agents rarely develop such capabilities since they are primarily optimized for task completion rather than for maintaining the underlying mental models required for collaborative processes. Moreover, the community lacks authentic human collaboration data with action-level mental model annotations that could guide agents toward collaborative competence. To bridge this gap, we present ALMANAC, a dataset of Action-Level Mental model ANnotations for Agent Collaboration built from the Map Task, a classic dyadic routing task from social science. ALMANAC contains 2,987 collaboration actions, each paired with theory-informed mental model annotations that record the participants’ self-reasoning, perceived partner intent, and perceived team goal. We benchmark six LLMs on predicting humans’ next-turn behavior and mental models. Our results demonstrate ALMANAC’s utility in evaluating models’ ability to simulate human collaborative behaviors and infer their underlying mental models. The project page is available at https://human-agent-collab.hailab.io/almanac.

t: Holmes-Graph: A Framework for Probing the Linguistic Competence of Graph-Based Text Embeddings
a: Department of Informatics, University of Zurich, University of Zurich
Instituto de Investigaciones en Matemáticas Aplicadas y en Sistemas - UNAM
ab: We present Holmes-Graph, a framework to evaluate the linguistic competences of graph-based text embeddings generated by training graph neural networks (GNNs) on graph representations of text. The framework extends the Holmes benchmark, which previously covered only sparse, static, and transformer-based representations. The framework is flexible to be used with any graph representation and GNN architecture. Once weights are learned on a downstream task, frozen embeddings are probed across five linguistic competences. When applied to AI-generated text detection, Integrated Syntactic Graphs (ISG) combined with Graph Neural Networks (GNN) achieve an aggregate Holmes score of 0.662. This matches or exceeds DeBERTa-base on syntax, morphology, semantics, and reasoning, but not for discourse. The results confirm that graph-based text embeddings encode non-trivial linguistic knowledge and motivate their inclusion in future probing benchmarks.

t: Debug or Regenerate? Test-Guided Selection for LLM Code Repair
a: University of North Carolina at Chapel Hill
Amazon and University of North Carolina at Chapel Hill
ab: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used as coding assistants, but the programs they generate often fail. Such failures can be addressed by debugging the existing implementation or regenerating a new solution from the problem specification, with existing repair workflows typically defaulting to debugging. We find that the effectiveness of debugging and regeneration depends strongly on initial program quality, suggesting that no single repair strategy is universally optimal. Motivated by this observation, we present PATSSEL (Program-Adaptive Test-guided Repair Strategy Selection), a test-guided repair selection framework that dynamically chooses between debugging and regeneration. Rather than committing to a single repair strategy, PATSSEL generates debugged and regenerated candidates for each buggy program, evaluates them using generated verifier tests, and selects the stronger candidate, leveraging the complementary strengths of debugging and regeneration.
